title: Poland  May  Intervene  Again to Curb Zloty Volatility - Central Bank  Governor
text:
WARSAW--Poland's central bank may again intervene in the local currency market to limit the Polish zloty's volatility, central bank governor Marek Belka told state news agency PAP late Friday, hours after the bank intervened in the market for the first time since December 2011.

The central bank's intervention Friday took the market by surprise as it came only two days after the governor said the recent weakening of the zloty was a welcome trend as it helped the slowing economy regain competitiveness.

"We never pre-announce these things, and if someone thought that we will not do it then I am sorry, but we do not act in the interest of FX market speculators," Mr. Belka said. "Somebody thought he will make money on the zloty weakening and got burned."

As a result of the bank's actions the zloty strengthened to around 4.23 against the euro from above 4.30 before the intervention.

Poland's finance ministry and the central bank have a history of intervening in the local currency market. When both institutions acted to strengthen the zloty in 2011 the currency was not only weaker against the euro than it is now, but the country's public debt was closer to an automatic austerity threshold of 55% of GDP.

However, recent fiscal tightening has pushed the debt level to 52.7% of GDP in 2012 while the government changed the way it values its foreign debt pile, limiting the forex market's impact on debt size.

"The timing is quite strange given Governor Belka tried to talk the zloty down during the press conference on Wednesday. He said the PLN weakening was very welcome and hasn't influenced the recent rate cut at all," ING economist Rafal Benecki wrote Friday.

Mr. Belka explained that the central bank's goal was not to defend some specific zloty level but rather curb recent volatility in the currency, which pushed it to the weakest level in a year against the euro on Thursday.

"This absolutely isn't an attempt to fight a trend or anything, things just got a little wild recently and we had to give [the market] a kick," Mr. Belka said.

The zloty, Polish bonds and other emerging market assets have been under immense pressure since the Federal Reserve indicated late last month that it may consider unwinding its bond-buying stimulus program if the U.S. economy continues to improve.

The prospect of tighter policy in the U.S. has prompted investors to exit riskier assets and rush to safe-haven currencies and bonds.

The Polish central bank's signal that it was close to ending its rate-cutting cycle also prompted global investors to sell the country's treasury bonds.

title: UPDATE 3- Poland intervenes  to bolster zloty
text:
* Several interventions after zloty hit one-year low

* Central bank had earlier said weak zloty not a concern

* Zloty gains as much as two percent versus euro

* Intervention aimed at trimming excessive volatility, c.bank head says

By Dagmara Leszkowicz

WARSAW, June 7 (Reuters) - Poland's central bankintervened on the currency market on Friday to prop up the zloty for the first time in 18 months after the currency hit a one-year low the previous session.

Over the past month, the zloty has fallen because of lower Polish interest rates and fears that the U.S. Federal Reserve could wind down its quantitative easing campaign, something which has hit emerging market currencies around the world.

Some analysts thought Polish officials were moved to act by concerns that a falling zloty could boost the value of the country's debts, which could trigger painful spending cuts.

The central bank confirmed it sold some foreign currencies on the spot market. Dealers said it had entered the market several times and that state-owned BGK bank also stepped into the market in the late afternoon trade, helping the zloty to extend its sharp gains.

Poland's central bank governor, Marek Belka, told the state news agency PAP that the bank's move was aimed at trimming excessive fluctuation on the foreign exchange market.

"It is absolutely not a test of betting against the trend. We just had a couple of crazy days recently (on the FX market) and we had to stop it," Belka said, adding that further interventions are not ruled out.

The currency jumped by around 2 percent versus the euro after the central bank's move. By 1615 GMT it had given up some gains to trade at 4.2325 per euro.

Traders said the bank intervened for the first time at the zloty level of 4.30 to the euro. They did not give details on the total amount of intervention or the amount of zlotys.

The bank last stepped into the market to lift the zloty in December 2011, when officials were seeking to keep the value of the government's foreign-denominated debt below a constitutionally set level of 55 percent of gross domestic product.

Breaching the level would have forced the government to reduce spending substantially.

On Thursday, the zloty fell to its lowest levels since June 2012 after Belka said currency weakness was not a concern.

Rafal Benecki, chief economist at ING Bank Slaski, said the intervention was a surprise that contradicted the governor's statement.

"It's strange, because Belka seemed as if he had wanted to weaken the zloty on Wednesday and now they are strengthening it," Benecki said.

"The bank most likely wants to reduce the volatility of the currency, because there is a large risk of debt breaching the 55 percent of GDP threshold."

The ratio stood at 52.7 percent of GDP at the end of last year, according to Polish accounting rules.

The central bank brought its main rate to a new low of 2.75 percent earlier this week, 200 basis points lower than in November, when it launched an easing campaign to help boost the flagging economy.

title: CEE MARKETS 2-Leu hits two-month low, Polish PMI data supports zloty
text:
* Romania sells bonds as planned, yields edge up


    * Retreat from Romanian debt hits leu
    * PMIs help zloty, forint, but rate outlooks hurt
    By Jason Hovet
    PRAGUE, June 3 (Reuters) - The leu hit a two-month low on
Monday, dropping for a second day as investors started to
retreat from Romanian bonds and as concerns over how long global
stimulus programmes would last rattled central European markets.
    The Polish zloty - hard hit in the past week - steadied off
recent lows after a purchasing managers' survey showed a slight
pickup in manufacturing activity in Poland although the prospect
of lower interest rates still weighed on the currency.
    Central European markets have become more volatile in the


past month with investors rattled by uncertainty over when the U.S. Federal Reserve might slow its stimulus programme - part of the "wall of money" that has fuelled investor appetite for emerging market assets. Any cutback would hit the region. Romania sold a planned 500 million lei ($147.5 million) in five-year treasury bonds on Monday, with the average accepted yield up 13 basis points from two weeks ago. Analysts said investors were starting to back off Romanian debt, reversing a rally seen earlier in the year that had sent yields in Romania and around central Europe to record lows. Czech 10-year yields hit a two-month high on Monday. Moves in Romania's smaller debt markets can have a bigger impact on the leu than elsewhere in the region and the retreat has caused the leu to lose 1.1 percent since Thursday's close. It bid down 0.3 percent on the day at 4.402 to the euro and had weakened as far as 4.42 before the auction. "The weakening appears to be a short squeeze ... and now some profit taking after yields at the bond tender were somewhat higher," one trader in Bucharest said. 


    
    RATE CUTS WATCHED
    The zloty was up less than 0.1 percent to bid at
4.266 to the euro - after touching a session low of 4.28. The
forint also inched up 0.1 percent to 295.4. Both were
just off 11-month and one-month lows, respectively.
    A Polish manufacturing purchasing managers' index (PMI)


edged up slightly in May but business activity still shrank for the 14th month running. Hungarian manufacturing also contracted, according to a PMI survey, but Czech manufacturing grew last month for the first time in more than a year. The zloty has weakened on expectations the Polish central bank will cut borrowing costs by a quarter percentage point to a new low of 2.75 percent at a meeting on Wednesday.


    "EUR/HUF and EUR/PLN continue to be weak given the prospect
of further monetary policy easing ... and a global environment
characterised by increasing uncertainty with regards to central
bank policy," Raiffeisen analysts said in a note.
    "In Poland, we would also not exclude verbal intervention in
favour of the zloty in the days ahead."
    Some analysts said the recent weakness in the zloty might
prompt the central bank to hold fire on rates for now. A Reuters
poll last week, though, showed 17 of 19 analysts expected a cut
on Wednesday. 
    In May, the bank defied analysts' forecasts and cut rates in
response to data that showed the economy was hovering on the
brink of recession. 
    Elsewhere, the Czech crown was a touch weaker
after benefitting last week from the unwinding of short
positions versus the zloty and forint, helping it recover from a
three-year low. 
    Analysts see further downside for the crown given a still


weak Czech economy, stuck in its longest recession in two decades, and persistent threats from the central bank that it could intervene to weaken the currency if it needs to ease monetary policy now that interest rates are near zero. Stock markets in central Europe fell by up to 1 percent because of concerns over the U.S. Fed's bond-buying programme.

title: WSJ BLOG: Polish  Central Bank  Chief Wants Criterion Waived Ahead of Euro Entry
text:
(This story has been posted on The Wall Street Journal Online's Emerging Europe blog at http://blogs.wsj.com/emergingeurope.)

By Patryk Wasilewski

WARSAW--Poland's central bank governor said the country should be allowed to join the euro without first putting its currency through the usual two-year transition in the European Union's exchange rate mechanism known as ERM2, which he claimed could be an open invitation to currency speculators.

Marek Belka's comments mark the strongest call yet from a Polish official for the euro entry rules to be relaxed. Poland has the biggest economy among the ex-communist euro candidates.

Countries adopting the euro are obliged to keep their currencies in the ERM2 grid where they must trade within a relatively narrow band for two years. Poland must also meet other fiscal and monetary criteria.

"I dislike ERM2 very much," Mr. Belka told a meeting of economists alongside President Bronislaw Komorowski on Thursday. "We should openly say that ERM2 is bad for Poland, bad for a country like Poland. The spot market in the zloty is bigger than in the Brazilian real."

Brazil's population and its economy are about five times the size of Poland's in nominal terms.

"If the Swedes wanted to join the euro for political reasons, a red carpet would be rolled out and they'd say: forget about that ERM2. I'm waiting for a moment like this for Poland," Mr. Belka said, adding the currency grid is "very dangerous" for the Polish economy because it would "invite massive speculation" in the zloty.

The central bank chief is an influential voice in Poland's euro debate. On his watch the National Bank of Poland has intervened several times to support the zloty during the euro's debt crisis.

Poland doesn't have a target date for adopting the euro but government officials have said they would like the country to meet all the criteria by 2015 with the exception of the two-year ERM2 stint. A political decision would follow parliamentary elections set for that year.

Dropping the ERM2 condition would require a treaty change accepted by the EU's soon-to-be 28 nations. Mr. Belka said that he was aware of the obstacle but that "the EU has shown a flexible approach" to its treaties.

It doesn't look very realistic in the short term "but it doesn't mean we shouldn't talk about it," he said.

The central bank believes it will be able to keep its inflation in check to meet the price stability criterion without changing its consumer price index targeting, where it aims for annual inflation of 2.5%.

title: CEE MARKETS 1-Hungary's forint extends gains, crown firmer before cbank
text:
PRAGUE, March 27 (Reuters) - The forint climbed more against a weak euro on Wednesday after Hungary cut interest rates again but refrained from any radical easing measures, while the crown edged up on bets that the threat of Czech intervention has eased.

Poland's zloty also edged up against the euro after Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk dropped his objections to a referendum on joining the shared currency on Tuesday.

The Hungarian central bank, which is trying to jumpstart a recession-hit economy, cut interest rates to a record low on Tuesday but avoided any policy surprises under its new governor, helping the forint jump almost 1 percent.

By 1004 GMT on Wednesday, the forint had risen another 0.2 percent and was bid at 303.74 to the euro.

The currency is now 1.5 percent off a 14-month low hit last week, and some say that if Hungary's central bank is cautious in its policy moves it could avoid a long-term slide that would hurt the many Hungarian households and companies with loans in euros or Swiss francs.

"The press release (after the rate decision) was rather cautious and in line with expectations, which we see as a tactical way for it to gain the markets' confidence back and take some pressure off the weak currency," SEB said in a morning trading note.

"(The forint) can potentially reach the (record low) at 324 but our forecast is 310 in one month and end of Q2, 305 at the end of Q3, and thereafter stabilising at the 300 level."

Still, the central bank indicated on Wednesday it was exploring "tools" other than interest rates to aid economic growth, while underlining that any steps it takes cannot jeopardise its primary goal of keeping inflation under control.

Prime Minister Viktor Orban has picked close ally and former economy minister Gyorgy Matolcsy to head the bank with a mandate to help the economy, sparking fears it may implement unconventional measures that would weaken the forint.

All three of central Europe's bigger former communist economies have been cutting rates steadily in a bid to bolster growth as most of the euro zone falters.

Only Romania, which meets on Thursday, has stayed on hold due to inflation pressures. Analysts do not expect loosening there until later in 2013.

The Romanian leu, the Polish zloty and the crown all gained around 1 percent, with the latter bid at 25.714 to the euro.

With Czech interest rates already at "technical zero", the central bank has said interventions could be its next easing tool to help the contracting economy. But the weakening of the crown to a nine-month low in the past month has reduced those chances, analyst have said.

The Czech central bank meets on Thursday and investors will look for clues of whether more easing is ahead. Six of 21 economists said they now expected the bank to intervene, versus 12 who said so in February. Those who foresaw intervention generally predicted it would happen some time in the second half of this year.

"We have been testing 25.800/850 area without breaking higher, so now a bit of a correction," a Prague dealer said.

"I don't think that people expect anything exciting from tomorrow's (central bank) meeting with EUR/CZK at these levels."

title: Polish Central Bankers to Reassess Policy
text:
WARSAW--Poland's rate setters are in the process of reassessing their monetary policy options for the medium term, Marek Belka, the central bank governor, told The Wall Street Journal.

At its March sitting, the 10-member rate panel will likely choose between a cut or a pause in the easing cycle that has so far taken the benchmark rate down one percentage point to 3.75%. But the four monthly cuts made to date mean the central bank is close to the end of the current policy phase.

"What we need, we think, is to look at the next projections--inflation and gross domestic product projections that will be issued in a matter of weeks. Secondly, we have to look at the things we usually haven't looked at, like the situation on the treasury-bond market," Mr. Belka said. "It's not really about making a pause or not. It's about realizing that we're at a certain moment in the Polish economy, when we need to ask: what do we need now? This is something we're discussing at the moment."

Following the February rate cut, the central bank said that a similar move in March was less of a done deal, although it kept its informal easing bias.

The Polish economy is going through a rough patch. Growth slowed to 2% last year from 4.3% in 2011, and the government has put part of the blame on the central bank, calling cuts to borrowing costs too little too late. The central bank currently expects average inflation to ease to 2.5% with growth slowing further to 1.5% in 2013.

The economy is, however, expected to bottom out this year, with contraction unlikely in any quarter and growth accelerating in the second half of the year.

The central bank also has an additional factor to consider--a rally last year pushed yields on 10-year Polish government bonds sharply lower, from more than 5.6% in early 2012 to around 4% at present, with foreign investors increasing their holdings. With that comes additional risks, Mr. Belka said.

"Growing demand for Polish bonds could be interpreted as fantastic, but we're not extremely happy about the increasing share of non-residents in this market," Mr. Belka said.

Foreign investors have flocked to Poland in search of higher yields, which despite all the buying remain significantly above those of many euro-zone sovereigns. The rally has pushed yields down more quickly than the Polish central bank has cut its benchmark rate, which has made the paper less attractive for Polish financial institutions.

The central bank said capital flight from Poland could destabilize the bond market as well as the Polish currency, which would weaken rapidly. The National Bank of Polandintervened several times in 2011 to stop investors from betting against the zloty, which was depreciating at the time. The zloty was around PLN4.19 ($1.33) to the euro on Monday afternoon, some 3% weaker than at the beginning of the year, with recent poor macroeconomic readings boosting expectations of more rate cuts.

title: WSJ BLOG: CEE Morning Briefing: Poland Seen Cutting Rates, Czechs to Focus on  FX
text:
(This story has been posted on The Wall Street Journal Online's Emerging Europe blog at http://blogs.wsj.com/emergingeurope .)

By Sean Carney

TODAY'S CALENDAR


   -- Local/GMT 
 
   -- N/A - Poland central bank monetary policy decision 
 
   -- 1300/1200 Czech central bank monetary policy decision 

Monetary policy in the cooling Polish economy and the recession-struck Czech Republic will be in focus Wednesday, with the entrenched bias toward easing likely to result in lower rates in Warsaw and talk of intervention in Prague.

Poland's central bank is expected to cut interest rates for the fourth time in a row, bringing the benchmark rate to 3.75% from 4%. The Polish economy sharply decelerated last year with growth slowing to 2% annually from 4.3% the previous year.

With investors and analysts already counting on an interest rate cut, the market will be looking for hints in the post-decision commentary that the rate-setting panel is ready to pause in its easing campaign.

In Prague, the Czech central bank has nowhere to go with interest rates, having cut the benchmark rate to 0.05% late last year.

But as inflation is tame and the economy has been contracting steadily since late 2011, policy makers may focus on ways to counteract slowing price growth while giving exports a boost.

Continued talk of foreign-exchange market intervention is also in the offing.

Last autumn, the Czech central bank issued a series of verbal warnings that resulted in the koruna losing roughly 5% to the euro. For the central bankers, that easing in conditions may be sufficient, as no intervention has yet taken place and the warnings have become less frequent.

The central bank is also due to issue its latest macroeconomic forecasts, which analysts say will likely include downward revisions to gross domestic product expectations, meaning the economy is expected to remain weaker for longer than previously expected.

OTHER NEWS

POLAND: Poland's biggest gas consuming companies will derive the first benefits from market determined gas prices starting July this year, with all other businesses following a year later, the energy regulator URE said Tuesday.

From July 2014, gas trading on the recently launched commodity exchange is expected to cover about 70% of the market.

POLAND: Poland's government drew a line in the sand ahead of the upcoming European Union's summit, saying proposed 30 billion euros ($39.9 billion) of additional budget cuts were "inconceivable."

EU leaders will Feb. 7-8 meet to try to agree on the size and structure of the bloc's budget for 2014-2020 after the failure of their previous attempt in November over the EUR30 billion of more cuts proposed by Germany.

HUNGARY: Hungary plans to double the volume of its trade with Turkey by 2015 to goods and services worth 5 billion euros ($6.79 billion), Prime Minister Viktor Orban said after talks with his Turkish counterpart Recep Tayyip Erdogan Tuesday.

Mr. Orban echoed Czech Prime Minister Petr Necas's comment Monday, saying his government also fully backs Turkey's European Union bid for membership.

HUNGARY: Hungary's governing Fidesz party Tuesday night denied a local press report that the decision has been made to name Economy Minister Gyorgy Matolcsy as the successor to departing central bank Governor Andras Simor.

Business daily Vilaggazdasag's report in its online edition earlier in the evening, which cited "a trusted source" about the matter, is unfounded and a hoax, Fidesz communication director Mate Kocsis told state news agency MTI.

ROMANIA: Romania's central bank kept its key interest rate unchanged at 5.25% for the seventh consecutive meeting Tuesday, in line with expectations, despite a weakening economy, news agency Mediafax reported.

The central bank also maintained the minimum reserve requirements unchanged at 15% for Romanian leu-denominated liabilities and at 20% for foreign currency liabilities.

BULGARIA: Bulgarian investigators on Tuesday for the first time linked Shiite group Hezbollah to a deadly July bomb attack on Israeli tourists in the country and identified two of the perpetrators as residents of Lebanon traveling on Australian and Canadian passports.

text:
TODAY'S CALENDAR 
Local/GMT 
N/A - Poland central bank monetary policy decision 
1300/1200 Czech central bank monetary policy decision 
 

Monetary policy in the cooling Polish economy and the recession-struck Czech Republic will be in focus Wednesday, with the entrenched bias toward easing likely to result in lower rates in Warsaw and talk of intervention in Prague.

Poland's central bank is expected to cut interest rates for the fourth time in a row, bringing the benchmark rate to 3.75% from 4%. The Polish economy sharply decelerated last year with growth slowing to 2% annually from 4.3% the previous year.

With investors and analysts already counting on an interest rate cut, the market will be looking for hints in the post-decision commentary that the rate-setting panel is ready to pause in its easing campaign.

In Prague, the Czech central bank has nowhere to go with interest rates, having cut the benchmark rate to 0.05% late last year.

But as inflation is tame and the economy has been contracting steadily since late 2011, policy makers may focus on ways to counteract slowing price growth while giving exports a boost.

Continued talk of foreign-exchange market intervention is also in the offing.

Last autumn, the Czech central bank issued a series of verbal warnings that resulted in the koruna losing roughly 5% to the euro. For the central bankers, that easing in conditions may be sufficient, as no intervention has yet taken place and the warnings have become less frequent.

The central bank is also due to issue its latest macroeconomic forecasts, which analysts say will likely include downward revisions to gross domestic product expectations, meaning the economy is expected to remain weaker for longer than previously expected.

title: POLL-Poland to cut rates for 4th straight month in Feb
text:
* All 27 analysts polled see 25 bp rate cut on Feb.6

* Rates seen down to 3.50 pct by end-March-median

* Easing seen coming earlier as economic data disappoint

By Marcin Goettig

WARSAW, Feb 1 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank will cut interest rates by 25 basis points for the fourth successive month in February as a sharp economic slowdown and a drop in inflation open the way for more easing, a Reuters poll showed on Friday.

All 27 analysts polled by Reuters from Jan. 29 to Feb. 1 expect the central bank's 10-strong Monetary Policy Council (MPC) to cut the key rate to 3.75 percent at the Feb. 5-6 meeting.

With inflation back below the central bank's 2.5 percent target for the first time in more than two years and retail sales in December recording their sharpest drop in eight years, analysts brought forward the expected timing of gradual rate cuts.

Now they expect the Council to cut rates again by 25 basis points in March, which would bring the key rate to 3.50 percent. Last month analysts predicted that rates would not fall to this level earlier than the end of June.

Rates in Poland have never been below 3.50 percent and the last time they were at that level was more than two years ago.

"The combination of weak growth and low inflation mean there is no reason to stick to a policy that is too restrictive," said Piotr Bielski, senior economist at Bank Zachodni WBK.

Polish rates are still the third-highest in the European Union after Hungary and Romania, but as price growth has exceeded the central bank's target for most of the past five years, many council members have favoured cautious reductions.

Economic growth fell to its weakest in three years in 2012, data showed earlier this week, signalling that one of Europe's most resilient economies risks dipping into recession.

This prompted one of the rate-setters, Anna Zielinska-Glebocka, to say a 25 basis point cut in February is a "pretty much done deal."

"The Council is following a strategy of small steps. It decided to start cutting too late and too slowly, (so) it should make two more steps," BZ WBK's Bielski added.

One of the most fervent supporters of lower rates on the MPC, Elzbieta Chojna-Duch, said this week that it was already too late for a larger cut and that the policy of gradual easing should be continued.

Following the string of disappointing data central bank governor Marek Belka abandoned his earlier talk of a possible pause in cuts, saying instead that Poland is "in the midst of a monetary easing cycle".

On top of that, voting records have shown that even the most resolute hawks have finally backed a 25 basis point cut in December.

Poland launched a cycle of monetary easing in November, having last raised its benchmark interest rate in May.

The central bank sees growth slowing to 1.5 percent this year, the lowest rate in eleven years. The bank will publish its new inflation and GDP projections in March.

Poland is lagging other countries in the region in relaxing monetary policy. Hungary cut rates for the sixth month running in January, while the Czech central bank has reduced its key rate to near zero and signals possible intervention to weaken the crown currency.

(Reporting by Marcin Goettig)

title: Polish  Central Bank  May React to Zloty Rise If It's Too Rapid - Deputy Head Kozinski
text:
The National Bank of Poland may intervene in the foreign-exchange market to quell zloty instability or an excessive rise in the currency, state-owned newswire PAP quotes Deputy Governor Witold Kozinski as saying Tuesday.

The bank intervened several times in 2011 to stop the zloty from depreciating sharply amid the euro zone's crisis.

Since the beginning of 2012, however, the zloty has strengthened about 8% against the euro, leading to concerns among some economists that it has made Poland's exports less competitive and may additionally weigh on the country's economy, that is slowing sharply amid a government fiscal-tightening regime.

title: CEE MARKETS 2-Hungarian, Polish  currencies  firmer
text:
(Adds Hungary bond, bill auction, updates markets)

* Hungary's CPI slows in Nov, c.bank seen cutting rates

* Forint, zloty firmer, Czech crown, leu shade weaker

* Hungary flags possible FX debt issue in Q1

* Romania's CPI slows, markets focus on politics

By Krisztina Than

BUDAPEST, Dec 11 (Reuters) - The Polish zloty and the forint led Eastern European currencies higher on Tuesday and Hungarian bond yields dropped on expectations of further interest rates cuts this month.

A 3-month treasury bill auction attracted strong demand with the average yield falling to 5.77 percent from 5.96 percent at the previous auction a week ago.

Hungary, which has not tapped international markets since 2011, also flagged a possible foreign currency bond issue in the first quarter of 2013 after talks with the IMF on a financing backstop have stalled.

Hungary's headline inflation rate slowed to an annual 5.2 percent in November from 6 percent in October, which may allow dovish rate setters to vote for a fresh rate cut at the bank's meeting next week, analysts said.

The forint rose, tracking the euro/dollar which also pushed the Polish zloty higher, dealers said. Hungarian bond yields dropped 10-20 basis points from Monday's fixing , with the 3-year bond trading at 5.70 percent.

"Inflation was expected to slow due to base effects, so this had been priced in and... the market is now expecting the next rate cut," a fixed income trader in Budapest said.

Another trader said the market was fairly illiquid.

With a majority of rate setters viewing inflation risks as manageable, the Hungarian bank has cut rates by 100 basis points since August to help the recession-hit economy.

Its peer, the Czech central bank, has cut its main rate to 0.05 percent and has signalled the next tool available is intervening against the crown, possibly next year.

Poland's central bank has also cut its key rate twice, by 25 basis points each time, pushing borrowing costs down to 4.25 percent, their lowest since May 2011.

Its Governor Marek Belka said on Tuesday the bank was "very likely" to cut rates further and he also expected inflation to return to the bank's target within months.

The zloty added half a percent on Tuesday while the forint was up 0.4 percent at 1110 GMT.

The Czech crown was 0.1 percent lower and the Romanian leu also eased a shade after a weekend election gave a clear victory to Romanian Prime Minister Victor Ponta.

title: UPDATE 2-Poland cuts rates again, flags more easing in January
text:
* Polish central bank cuts rates by 25 bps, as expected

* Governor signals another cut in January

* Bank to stick to policy of gradual policy easing

(Adds quotes, details)

By Karolina Slowikowska

WARSAW, Dec 5 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank cut interest rates for the second consecutive month on Wednesday and signalled more cuts in January and beyond to help an economy that has slowed to its lowest pace in three years.

The bank's 10-strong Monetary Policy Council (MPC) cut rates by 25 basis points as widely expected, bringing the key rate in the largest central European economy to 4.25 percent, its lowest since May 2011.

Poland, the sole European Union member to avoid a recession since 2008, joined other regional central banks only last month in starting to easing monetary policy, and some analysts say it has acted too late to tackle the deepening slump.

But central bank governor Marek Belka said on Wednesday the situation was not "dramatic" and recession highly unlikely in an economy that has seen uninterrupted expansion for two decades.

"Changes in rates should be gradual unless some dramatic events take place," Belka told a news conference after the decision, adding the MPC did not want to surprise the markets with a larger cut.

Asked about the possibility of another cut in January, Belka said: "The Council is working hard and can't afford a pause in easing."

The "amazing" stability of the zloty currency, which benefits the economy, may reflect Poland's shrinking current account deficit, Belka said, also hinting it could be a result of past currency interventions.

SLOWDOWN

Poland's economic growth slowed to a much lower-than-expected 1.4 percent year-on-year in the third quarter, prompting the government to acknowledge expansion this year would come in below its 2.5 percent forecast.

The central bank expects the economy to slow to 1.5 percent next year, which would be its lowest growth rate since 2002, while the MPC said in its statement that growth in the European Union's largest eastern economy was likely to be "moderate" over the next few years.

But when pressed on the possible scale of the monetary easing cycle ahead, Belka reiterated that the majority of the Council preferred to keep interest rates above inflation, unless there was an acute crisis in the economy.

Price growth eased to an annual 3.4 percent in October and for the first time in nearly two years fell below the upper limit of the bank's 1.5-3.5 percent permitted fluctuation band.

"A larger cut was probably also justified but nobody really expected the Monetary Policy Council to have enough courage to make a bolder move," said Piotr Bielski, a senior economist at Bank Zachodni WBK.

The zloty inched up after the decision, while bond yields fell, reflecting expectations of further policy easing.

"As the economy is weakening and monetary easing is very likely to continue, we expect the EUR/PLN to slightly drop to 4.15 at the end of the year," Erstegroup said in a note.

The zloty traded at 4.1217 to the euro by 1709 GMT.

The market expects a further 75 basis points to be chopped off the main rate in the next nine months, although pressure has been mounting for more decisive action to help ease credit for households and companies.

Elsewhere in the region, recession-stricken Hungary has cut rates four times by a total of 100 basis points, while the Czech Republic has hinted at currency market interventions since the country's interest rates are already near zero.

title: WRAPUP 1-Czech, Polish manufacturing falls, outlook weak
text:
* Polish, Czech PMIs rise to 48.2, still show business shrinking

* Analysts say data point to further contraction in forth quarter

* Data suggests more central bank easing, Poland to cut on Wednesday

By Michael Winfrey

PRAGUE, Dec 3 (Reuters) - Manufacturing in the EU's two biggest eastern economies shrank for the eighth straight month in November, pointing to a further slowdown in Poland and a fifth month of recession for the export-dependent Czechs.

With the euro zone debt crisis hitting consumers in their main export markets, the countries of central and Eastern Europe have cut output of the cars, electronics and other manufactured goods that are their main source of national income.

Combined with government austerity measures at home that have deterred consumers and companies from spending, that has extended a Czech recession that started at the end of 2011. In Poland, a once robust expansion is slowing to its weakest rate since the height of the economic crisis in 2009.

A slower decline in euro zone manufacturing, especially in the bloc's biggest economy Germany, has raised some hopes that manufacturing orders can arrest their slide some time next year, but analysts said Monday's data indicated recovery was still far away.

The Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) in both Poland and the Czech Republic rose to 48.2 points in November, showing a slower decline than in the previous month but still below the 50 level that divides contraction from growth.

The figures were less weak than Poland's 47.3 in October and 47.2 for the Czechs, and well above the 47.5 predicted by analysts for both countries in Reuters polls. They showed a similar picture to the euro zone, where the manufacturing PMI in the currency bloc firmed to 46.2, from 45.4 in October. Even so, that marked a 16th month of shrinking euro zone activity.

In Hungary, where the PMI is calculated under different methodology and is often very volatile, the numbers rose to 52.3 in November, showing significant growth, from 49.9 in October. But analysts said the picture remained grim.

"The situation will not improve dramatically but rather only gradually," said Piotr Bujak, chief economist at Nordea Poland.

"This turnaround in the euro area will not be strong enough to avoid further slowdown in the Polish economy in the final months of this year and will not be strong enough to help the Czech and Hungarian economies to get out of a recession."

Economists largely consider PMI one of the best forward looking indicators for economic performance, although in Poland analysts often look more to local consumer and business surveys.

The region's currencies were virtually flat after the data.

DECLINE

In Poland, the region's largest economy, output, new export orders and employment all declined at a slower pace.

Buoyed by its 38-million-strong consumer market, Poland is the only European Union state to have avoided recession since 2008. While growth has slowed dramatically, it has suffered less than its regional peers from the fall in euro zone demand.

But plummeting euro zone demand for consumer goods such as cars has spelled trouble for the Czechs, whose exports account for 85 percent of economic output.

Data showed on Monday new car registrations in France fell 19.2 percent in November, meshing with last month's announcement by a Czech car factory run by Toyota and Peugeot Citroen that it would cut production this year by 20 percent.

Czech new export orders fell for the 13th straight month, and on a quarterly basis, data for the fourth quarter signalled the sharpest contraction since third quarter 2009.

The Czech economy shrank 1.5 percent year-on-year from July to September, extending a recession dating from the end of 2011, and analysts said they expected no recovery before the year end.

"The Czech economy has contracted in the last four quarters to third quarter 2012, and the PMI does not point to a turn to positive growth in the last quarter of this year either," said HSBC economist Agata Urbanska

The Czech central bank has slashed interest rates to 0.05 percent, leaving it armed with only unconventional tools such as currency intervention if it needs to take further action.

Poland's central bank has been more hesitant to cut quickly. But following data on Friday showing growth at 1.4 percent in the third quarter - its slowest since 2009 - analysts said they expected at least another quarter point cut to 4.25 percent on Wednesday.

"The MPC could seriously consider an interest rate cut of 50 basis points, but we believe that it will feel satisfied with a cut of 25 bps, although it may be open to more monetary easing down the road," ING wrote in a note to clients.

title: DJ Polish Government Takes Step Toward Easing Public Debt Cap
text:
WARSAW--Poland's government Tuesday took another step towards relaxing its regulations over the ceiling on public debt by approving the finance ministry's proposals aimed at better protecting it against volatility of the Polish zloty, the government said.

The main regulation forcing Poland's government to start painful austerity measures, including spending cuts and tax increases, once public debt exceeds 55% of gross domestic product will remain in place. In 2012 public debt, calculated under Polish standards, is expected to reach 52.4% of GDP.

However, the government will now use an average annual foreign exchange rate to value the country's sizeable debt pile, which will reduce the threat of breaking the key threshold due to the weakening of the zloty.

The government will be also be allowed to take from debt funds used to earlier fund next year's borrowing needs.

Existing regulations, under which the zloty rate from last day of December was used to value the foreign debt, made the currency prone to high volatility late in the year and last year forced the country's finance ministry and central bank to intervene on the local foreign exchange market.

Poland already financed more than 29 billion zlotys ($9.15 billion) of next year's borrowing needs.

The government's decision still has to be approved by the parliament, in which the governing coalition of Civic Platform and Poland's Peasants Party has a narrow majority.

title: Poland  Keeps Inflation Target at 2.5%, Allows  FX Interventions
text:
WARSAW--Poland's monetary policy council kept its direct inflation target at 2.5% with a tolerance range of 1.5%-3.5% in its updated monetary strategy for 2013, the council said Friday.

In recent months, some MPC members argued the target should be revised as it seems to be too low given the inflationary nature of external factors, like global food and fuel prices, that are beyond the Polish central bank's control.

However, the council decided to keep most of the policy assumptions unchanged from prior years, keeping a door open to local FX market interventions as well as other open market transactions in case of significant market turmoil and a deepening global crisis.

The central bank intervened on the FX market several times in 2011 to prop up the Polish zloty and limit its volatility.

title: INTERVIEW-Polish c.bank deputy downplays need for  FX interventions
text:
* Deputy cbank head Kozinski sees relatively stable zloty

* Cites solid Polish economy, euro zone summit deal

* Does not expect major capital outflows in banking sector

* Doesn't expect near-term mergers in sector either

By Karolina Slowikowska and Pawel Florkiewicz

WARSAW, July 9 (Reuters) - Poland does not expect the zloty to exhibit high volatility, a deputy governor of the central bank said, playing down chances of a repeat of last year's heavy interventions that ate into the bank's hard currency reserves.

In an interview with Reuters, Witold Kozinski said western Europe looked to be moving closer to solving its debt problems, welcoming a deal at last month's EU summit to leverage the region's rescue funds to better support struggling states' finances..

He said the agreement meant less market turmoil for Poland, whose assets were additionally underpinned by the government's efforts to cut the public deficit and healthy, albeit slowing growth rates.

"Poland's economic outlook is very positive in my opinion. It is no wonder then that the zloty is faring well," Kozinski, responsible for market interventions at the central bank, said.

The bank, which acts to reduce zloty volatility rather than target a specific exchange level, last intervened on the currency market in December, but dealers remain on alert for further interventions.

Poland's economy was the only one in the European Union not to tip into recession since 2008, but weakness in the euro zone - to which Poland is heavily exposed - drove strong volatility in the zloty last year, when it fluctuated between 3.9 and 4.6 against the euro.

Since the start of 2012, the Polish currency has gained 5.5 percent and held in a much more stable trading pattern.

"I believe (volatility) .. will not be a big (this year)," Kozinski, who does not sit on the central bank's ratesetting panel, Kozinski added in comments cleared for publication on Monday.

"Since the zloty is the most liquid currency in the region, it is more prone to volatility. But it is not the kind of volatility that would worry us, at least for now."

"...The euro zone did not fall apart. Greece is rebuilding itself after its election...the euro zone is consolidating... All this together has, of course, an impact on the zloty's stability."

BANKING BUFFER?

Kozinski, who also oversees the banking sector as a member of Poland's banking supervisory body, downplayed the risk of banking troubles in the euro zone leading to significant capital outflows from Poland.

Some two-thirds of the Polish banking sector is in foreign hands and many of the parent banks have been squeezed for cash, raising fears that their Polish affiliates may have to reduce their lending capacity, undermining the country's growth.

The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), set up in 1991 to manage the transition of former communist countries to market economies, recently warned that a new banking crunch in the euro zone risks prompting sharp a retreat by western parent banks.

"We do not see capital outflows from Polish banks that are foreign-owned. There is no so-called deleveraging, no loan withdrawals or sucking deposits out of the sector," Kozinski said.

The central bank was also ready to respond with funding in case a troubled parent bank was forced to sell its local business.

"The central bank would be willing to participate in such an undertaking," which would not mean taking the lender over, he said.

"(But) I do not expect any mergers in the commercial banking sector any time soon."

Kozinski cast doubt on Poland's approval of a European Union's drive to create a regionwide banking union.

"We've always had the view that national banking supervisory bodies should not be stripped of any of their current competencies."

(Editing by John Stonestreet)

title: *DJ Weak Zloty Won't Push Poland's Debt Above Limit - BGK
text:
31 May 2012 08:43 EDT *DJ  BGK Deputy Chief Kowalczyk: Ready To Take Unorthodox PLN Measures

31 May 2012 08:43 EDT *DJ  BGK Kowalczyk: EUR/PLN Fair Value Is Around 4.0

31 May 2012 08:43 EDT DJ  INTERVIEW: Weak Zloty Won't Push Poland's Debt Above Limit - BGK

By Patryk Wasilewski

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

WARSAW (Dow Jones)--Poland's public debt won't breach the country's self-imposed safety thresholds this year despite the zloty's recent and potential future weakening because of government steps to reduce the public debt and deficit, the deputy head of state-owned BGK bank Wojciech Kowalczyk told Dow Jones Newswires.

The bank acts as the Polish finance ministry's agent in the zloty market, where it has been present since last year selling foreign currencies for the zloty. It was particularly active at the end of last year to prop up the Polish currency.

A weak zloty inflates the value of Polish public debt that's denominated in foreign currencies, boosting overall public debt, which was near 55% of economic output at the end of last year. Foreign debt makes up some 30% of Poland's total.

The breach of the 55% threshold would trigger austerity measures aimed at balancing the budget.

Calculated in line with local methodology, which excludes some debt categories from the tally, Poland's public debt was at 53.5% of gross domestic product last year. Poland expects debt to fall to 50.5% of GDP in 2012.

BGK's Kowalczyk said the bank and the finance ministry are closely watching the market and are ready to step in to "take unorthodox measures" if the ministry deems it necessary.

"This year Poland is reducing its debt. Deficit will fall below 3% and debt to 50.5%, and thus the zloty is not a threat to debt," Kowalczyk said.

"Moreover, the zloty's weakening is not justified by [Poland's] fundamentals. Investors are taking into account both of these facts in their strategies for the zloty," he added.

Poland's currency rallied in first four months of this year against the euro, temporarily going below PLN4.1 to the euro, but rising worries about the euro zone's future and risk aversion sent the zloty back to around PLN4.4 to the euro as of Thursday afternoon.

Verbal interventions from both the ministry and Poland's central bank officials, as well as BGK's currency selling reported by traders, have helped moderate losses in the zloty amid the euro's fall against the U.S. dollar.

The BGK deputy chief also said Poland's economic fundamentals are strong and the zloty is undervalued as a result of negative global sentiment because of the situation in Greece. The zloty's fair value is around PLN4.0 against the euro, he said.

"Our strong fundamentals can be seen in prices of [Poland's] 10-year paper... If Poland was weak fundamentally, we would be seeing outflows, not inflows by international investors," Kowalczyk said.

The yield on Polish 10-year government bonds was at 5.46% Thursday, below 5.82% for Italian paper and 6.51% for Spanish paper.

After the verbal interventions, which signaled the readiness of the government and central bank to act, the zloty's stabilized temporarily but some market participants questioned whether the ministry and the central bank have enough firepower to support it in the longer term.

The BGK deputy chief noted Poland has $30 billion available in a flexible credit line from the International Monetary Fund, and that central bank reserves of $88 billion provide an additional safety cushion.

title: DJ UPDATE:  Poland 's  Central Bank  Says Ready For Zloty  Intervention
text:
-- Polish central bank official reiterates intervention warning if zloty weakens further

-- Finance minister "not surprised" by zloty's recent weakening

-- Market thinks central bank will stay out unless the zloty weakens much more

(Adds detail, comment.)

By Marcin Sobczyk and Patryk Wasilewski

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

RADOM, Poland (Dow Jones)--The National Bank of Poland is able to step into the zloty market at any time, a central bank official said Thursday, but market participants doubt the Polish currency is weak enough for the bank to intervene.

"We have high foreign currency reserves and we're always able to counteract any significant weakening and volatility in the zloty," Witold Kozinski, a member of the bank's executive board, told reporters Thursday.

The zloty has been under pressure since Greek political leaders failed to form a coalition government in the wake of inconclusive elections earlier this month. The Polish currency was trading at around EUR4.37 Thursday, nearly 4% lower than in early May.

The Polish central bank intervened several times in the second half of last year, with the first intervention in September when the zloty was above EUR4.50 and weakening rapidly. Within minutes, the central bank pushed the exchange rate well below EUR4.40, with its governor saying the bank saw the intervention as a warning to market participants not to bet against the Polish currency.

Polish monetary authorities have in recent days repeatedly warned that they could re-enter the market at any time. But the finance ministry, which Wednesday returned to selling its euros in the spot market, said the zloty is stronger and less volatile now than when the ministry and the bank intervened last year.

"I'm not surprised that the zloty is reacting this way," Finance Minister Jan Vincent-Rostowski said Thursday. "It always does when the euro weakens," he said, adding that the Polish currency is stronger than at the end of 2011, even though the euro is at a roughly similar level to the U.S. dollar.

title: Emerging Market  Currencies , Debt Slip In Anxious Markets
text:
--Emerging market currencies see more modest losses

--Emerging market debt weakens slightly

--Central-bank intervention to shore up currencies becoming more frequent


 
   By Erin McCarthy 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--The downward slide in emerging market currencies and debt seen this week slowed slightly Thursday, though these assets were still under pressure in anxious markets.

Ongoing concerns about Europe's sovereign-debt crisis and political uncertainty in debt-laden Greece put broader markets on edge this week, hitting higher-yielding assets, like emerging market currencies and bonds, especially hard. Fears that Greece could exit the euro zone have escalated, with Fitch Ratings downgrading its ratings on Greece two notches further into junk territory and pointing to increased risk that Greece may exit the monetary union.

Meanwhile, disappointing U.S. economic data Thursday reminded investors of the potential for a sluggish U.S. and global recovery. The Philadelphia Fed said its index of general business activity within the factory sector fell to -5.8 in May from 8.5 in April, marking the first negative reading in eight months.

"Everyday it seems like it's either [the] U.S. slowdown, euro-zone debt crisis or China" worrying markets, said Win Thin, Brown Brothers Harriman's global head of emerging market strategy. "I don't think anyone's going to go long risk right now, given the uncertainty."

The risk premium on emerging market sovereign debt, as seen on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global, or Embig, widened by four basis points to 399 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms, the index fell 0.3%.

Among currencies, the Mexican peso underperformed, falling 0.3% against the dollar, which bought MXN13.8142, according to CQG. The Mexican peso often tracks broader markets, as it is one of the more easily and widely traded emerging market currencies. In addition, it typically underperforms when U.S. data disappoints, given the close economic ties between Mexico and its northern neighbor.

Elsewhere in the region, the Chilean peso fell heavily, on the back of deteriorating international copper prices. As Chile is the world's largest producer of the metal, the peso often tracks copper prices. The Chilean peso dived to its weakest level against the dollar in four months. The dollar traded above the key CLP505 level, to buy CLP505.50 late Thursday, according to CQG.

Emerging European currencies saw more modest losses than in previous sessions. The Hungarian forint slipped 0.4% against the euro, which changed hands at HUF297.88 from HUF296.63 late Wednesday.

The Polish zloty traded flat on the day against the euro, which changed hands at PLN4.3570. Investors are on guard for further intervention to shore up the currency from Polish authorities. Poland's Finance Ministry has already sold foreign currencies to support the zloty this week, while Poland's central bank said Thursday it is ready to step into the currency market if necessary.

Intervention to protect flagging emerging market currencies has become a recurring theme. India's central bank has been noted to be frequently intervening in the currency markets lately, and was suspected of intervening Thursday. Still, the Indian rupee slid to an all-time low against the dollar Thursday. Later in the session, the dollar was up 0.2% at INR54.41, according to CQG.

title: INTERVIEW-Poland may issue Swiss-franc debt in April, eurobonds by summer
text:
* Poland has met 56 pct of 2012 borrowing needs - deputy finmin Radziwill

* Most EU funds will be swapped at central bank in coming months

* Poland's economy may expand 4 pct in Q1, around 3 pct in 2012

By Dagmara Leszkowicz and Pawel Sobczak

WARSAW, April 10 (Reuters) - Poland may issue a small amount of Swiss franc-denominated bonds as early as this month, and it is mulling a benchmark bond issue either in dollars or euros before the summer, deputy finance minister Dominik Radziwill told Reuters in an interview.

Poland, the largest economy in Europe's eastern wing, has already met 56 percent its 2012 borrowing needs and plans to reach two-thirds by the end of the first half, Radziwill said in comments authorised for release on Tuesday.

"If market conditions are favourable, we will hold a Swiss franc issue worth several hundred million (francs)," Radziwill said, adding that Warsaw may also get a headstart on its 2013 borrowing requirement.

"I assume that we will do some 2013 prefinancing, but the level will be lower compared to the previous year."

Radziwill kept up the threat of market intervention to support the zloty, saying Poland could exchange EU funds for the local currency in the spot market if necessary.

A flood of cheap money from major central banks, most recently the European Central Bank, has fuelled demand for Polish bonds and other emerging market debt since the start of the year, and Polish yields hit multi-year lows in mid-March.

But hawkish rhetoric from the national bank and the prospect of cheap money supply from the Fed and other major central banks drying up as their economies improve have led Polish yields to rise some 20 basis points since.

That rhetoric has not helped the Polish zloty, however, and the currency - along with regional peers - has been under pressure as concern over the euro zone's debt problems kept investors away from riskier assets.

In 2011, the finance ministry together with the central bank helped the Polish currency by the joint action of exchanging EU funds through state-owned bank BGK for zloty.

This year, both institutions have announced plans to reduce their activity on the spot market in the second and third quarter, although Radziwill kept open the option of direct intervention.

"When it comes to exchanging EU funds, we make current decisions whether they should be exchanged at the central bank or in the market," Radziwill said.

"I assume most funds will be exchanged at the central bank in coming months. But we always have a possibility of exchanging funds on the spot market if we see such a need."

UPGRADE?

The minister was optimistic about the growth prospects and ratings outlook for the biggest of the European Union's ex-communist economies.

"(Poland's) economy will probably expand by more than 3 percent in the whole of 2012, while in the first quarter it should be around 4 percent," Radziwill said.

The full-year forecast is in line with analysts estimates, but they expect less growth in the first three months of 2012 - around 3.5 percent.

These prospects and Warsaw's fiscal steps aimed at reducing the general government deficit to below 3 percent this year should help improve Poland's outlook at credit rating agencies, the minister said.

"I don't rule out that ratings' improvement may take place as early as in the fourth quarter (of 2012)," Radziwill said.

Standard & Poor's and Fitch currently rate Poland at A- with stable outlooks, while Moody's A2, also with stable outlook.

29 Feb 2012 12:19 EDT DJ  IMF Paper Builds Case For Temporary Emerging-Market FX Intervention

--IMF: Currency intervention can be helpful tool against volatility

--IMF paper counters conventional view of FX intervention

--IMF study includes Korea, Turkey, Poland, Brazil, other emerging markets

By Ian Talley

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--Turning decades of conventional wisdom on its head, a new research paper published Wednesday by International Monetary Fund economists builds a case for emerging markets to intervene in their exchange rates.

The IMF research paper advocates central banks in emerging markets smoothing out strong movements in their exchange rates, particularly when caused by external economic shocks that fuel hefty cash flows into or out of their economies.

The paper reflects a broader shift in IMF economic policy thinking that has given credence to some emerging market actions that have come under advanced-country censure, including a new backing of the use of capital controls.

"If two policy instruments are available (the policy interest rate and foreign exchange market intervention), then they should be used in tandem to achieve both price-stability and exchange-rate objectives," the economists wrote.

In the paper, "Two Targets, Two Instruments: Monetary and Exchange Rate Policies in Emerging Market Economies," the economists argue that instead of undermining central bank credibility for inflation targeting--long a conventional view--currency intervention can actually support central bank credibility. Such trust built by central banks makes their policies more effective.

"The idea of using more tools to address economic problems is one that has been gaining traction in the wake of the financial crisis," said Jonathan Ostry, deputy head of the research department and one of the three IMF economists who authored the paper.

"A narrow view in which all will be well as long as central banks deliver stable consumer prices simply doesn't hold water," he said.

The paper studied 14 countries and the currency policies, including Brazil, South Korea, Turkey, Poland, Hungary and Thailand. Many of the countries have come under criticism for their currency intervention.

In fact, the authors say that foreswearing intervention in the face of wild swings in currencies "might actually serve to undercut rather than boost credibility."

title: UPDATE:IMF Paper Advocates Temporary Emerging-Market  FX Intervention
text:
--IMF: Currency intervention can be helpful tool against volatility

--IMF paper counters conventional view of FX intervention

--IMF study includes Korea, Turkey, Poland, Brazil, other emerging markets

(Adds IMF economists' comments, background and details throughout, starting in the third paragraph)

By Ian Talley

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--Turning decades of conventional wisdom on its head, a new research paper published Wednesday by International Monetary Fund economists builds a case for emerging markets to intervene in their currencies.

The IMF research paper advocates central banks in emerging markets smoothing out strong movements in their exchange rates, particularly when caused by external economic shocks that fuel hefty cash flows into or out of their economies.

Far from being reluctant to use exchange rate intervention, "central banks should embrace its use as being fully consistent" with inflation-targeting, the economists said.

The paper reflects a broader shift in IMF economic policy thinking, giving credence to some emerging-market actions that have come under advanced-country censure, including a new backing of the use of capital controls.

"If two policy instruments are available (the policy interest rate and foreign exchange market intervention), then they should be used in tandem to achieve both price-stability and exchange-rate objectives," the economists wrote.

In the paper, "Two Targets, Two Instruments: Monetary and Exchange Rate Policies in Emerging Market Economies," the economists argue that instead of undermining central bank credibility for inflation targeting--long a conventional view--currency intervention can actually support central bank credibility. Such trust built by central banks makes their policies more effective.

"The idea of using more tools to address economic problems is one that has been gaining traction in the wake of the financial crisis," said Jonathan Ostry, deputy head of the research department and one of the three IMF economists who wrote the paper.

"A narrow view in which all will be well as long as central banks deliver stable consumer prices simply doesn't hold water," he said.

The paper studied 14 countries and their currency policies, including Brazil, South Korea, Turkey, Poland, Hungary and Thailand. Many of the countries have come under criticism for their currency intervention.

In fact, the authors say that forswearing intervention in the face of wild swings in currencies "might actually serve to undercut rather than boost credibility."

The authors argued against sustained exchange rate intervention, saying it would prove too costly to an economy. Rather, under permanent market pressures, policy makers should allow the currency to adjust. Unlike Brazil or South Korea, which are largely recognized as floating economies despite some currency intervention, China's yuan has long been seen as persistently undervalued as the central bank buys foreign currency and sells yuan to give it a competitive advantage.

"You should not be intervening to sustain a misaligned exchange rate, you should be intervening to mitigate misalignment," Ostry said.

Emerging markets are particularly exposed to large international capital flows because government balance sheets don't have the depth to offset such investments and their economies aren't as flexible as industrialized countries. Like reeds in the wind, emerging markets have had to weather massive capital movements in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis and euro debt woes.

The Institute of International Finance, an industry group representing more than 400 of the world's largest financial firms, expects capital flows to emerging markets to fall this year by an estimated $164 billion, contributing to a near-30% plummet in cash flows to those regions since 2010. That's likely to mean continuing pressure on their exchange rates. Earlier this month, Brazil's finance minister revived fears of an international currency war.

But the IMF staff said that as long as countries are simply seeking to return their currencies back into equilibrium with underlying economic fundamentals, intervention can play a stabilizing role in regional and global economies. By combining forex intervention with policy-rate decisions, central banks can afford to weaken their rate actions to achieve the same objective. That prevents a competition of too-low interest rates across emerging markets and avoid the resulting competitive interventions, the authors say.

The shift in perspective also highlights the growing say of emerging markets within the fund and the academic fallout from the financial crisis that eroded many long-held economist assumptions. The condoning of currency intervention--on a limited basis--addresses complaints from many developing countries that advanced nations should take into account the international impacts of monetary and economic policy. Brazil, for example, repeatedly cited the U.S. Federal Reserve's easing as helping to drive capital flows damaging to its economy. Brazil has intervened to prevent the real from further harm, drawing criticism from abroad.

title: CEE MONEY-Polish govt, c.bank fall out over  intervention
text:
WARSAW, Jan 26 (Reuters) - The honeymoon is over in the unusual marriage between Poland's government and central bank in supporting the zloty, with barbs flying over the bank's independence.

If the two sides don't patch things up, the most liquid currency and bond market in the European Union's eastern wing may suffer as policy transparency suffers and foreign investors eye the exits in markets exposed to the euro zone crisis or debt-laden Hungary.

After nearly a year of cooperating to support the currency, Finance Minister Jacek Rostowski appeared to overstep the mark in early January, calling on the central bank to be ready to intervene in the bond market in the event of panic selling or a "foreign virus".

The comments from the British-born former academic raised hackles at the independent central bank, though they were still a far cry from Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban's open moves to tighten his grip on the central bank in Budapest.

"It looks like something has cracked between the central bank and the Finance Ministry," said Piotr Kalisz, chief economist at Citibank Handlowy in Warsaw.

"So far we've had smooth cooperation, and this could be the first sign of a small conflict. The central bank simply wants to show its independence. They don't want to be seen as the arm of the Finance Ministry."

But Rostowski, who in the past spoke with reverence of the central bank's independence, then raised even more eyebrows by saying that the dogma of an independent central bank is out of whack with its original purpose as a state lender.

The central bank's response was swift and unequivocal.

It shot back within hours that it "may not substitute the government in its functions, especially with respect to public debt management" - a ringing slap compared with the usually dull rhetoric of economic policy.

Rate-setters made their point again after their monthly meeting two weeks later, saying the bank's guidelines "do not allow for the possibility of the NBP (National Bank of Poland) purchasing Treasury securities as a monetary policy instrument".

Thu Lan Nguyen, an economist at Commerzbank in Frankfurt, praised the bank for defending its independence.

"The central bank has to make its stance clear, so the government doesn't rely on them and people do indeed expect them to take actions if we would see such a scenario of rising bond yields," he said.

"It is the purpose of a central bank to be independent, and the NBP has made that clear."

In any case, the institutional tag-team was a rare departure from the typical model in emerging Europe, where burgeoning economies have fought to shrug off their centrally planned communist past to build the type of credibility seen elsewhere in the EU, where rules shield central banks from government meddling.

Still, that model has suffered erosion over the past year.

Hungary has drawn fire - and the threat of court action - from the European Commission, which has accused Orban's government of undermining the central bank's independence with a series of new laws.

And even as many politicians criticise Budapest, some of the same officials are encouraging the European Central Bank to buy up bonds of troubled euro zone economies, a move that does not sit well with more conservative policy chiefs.

TRANSPARENCY

In Poland, the government and the central bank have a vested interest in protecting the zloty, which shed as much as 17 percent from peak to trough last year.

The central bank had intervened in the currency market several times since September to help prevent inflation from seeping in from abroad via imported energy and commodity prices.

The Finance Ministry, which agreed with the central bank to convert EU funds on the open market through state-owned BGK bank in April, wants a stronger zloty to keep down the value of the one-third of Poland's borrowings denominated in foreign currency, keeping state debt below a key constitutional level.

BGK's role as the ministry's market arm has been growing, assuming a function similar to what Rostowski had suggested for the central bank by defending the zloty and bonds.

Market players widely expect BGK to cast a constant shadow in the spot market and keep potential sellers guessing, diving in even more at the end of the year, as it did in the last two, to protect the government's year-end debt calculations.

But BGK has less than a tenth of the central bank's reserves, making it more vulnerable to a sustained attack.

"We expect BGK to be some kind of a moderator on the spot market throughout the year. The question is: to what extent can it play that role?" one Warsaw-based dealer said.

BGK's interventions pose other problems, too.

It is normally the central bank's duty to protect the zloty with its 76 billion euros of reserves and its mandate to keep prices stable, so an interventionist finance ministry clouds the policy environment.

"The issue with involving a more directly politically controlled institution and an institution with a leveraged balance sheet is that this transparency, accountability and predictability are muddied," said Peter Attard Montalto, economist at Nomura.

"The central bank backstop is more transparent and more accountable."

title: CORRECTED-POLL-Polish rate cut seen delayed to Q3 on zloty risks
text:
(Corrects in 2nd paragraph to median expectation instead of all analysts)

* All 24 analysts polled see unchanged rates at Jan 10-11 meeting

* Median shows first cut postponed until Q3 2012, from Q2 last month

* Analysts say risk of weaker zloty feeding into CPI will prevent cuts

By Marcin Goettig

WARSAW, Jan 3 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank will probably cut interest rates in the third quarter, later than previously expected due to concerns that a weaker zloty might further fuel inflation, a Reuters poll showed on Tuesday.

The median expectation of 24 analysts polled by Reuters between December 23 and January 3 sees the central bank's Monetary Policy Council cutting the key interest rate by 25 basis points in the third quarter and by another 25 basis points in the fourth.

Last month analysts also expected a total of 50 basis points in rates cuts this year but saw the first cut coming in the second quarter.

All of the 24 analysts polled predict the MPC will hold fire at its January 10-11 rate meeting.

"With the persisting depreciation pressure on the zloty, elevated level of current CPI and still strong economic activity indicators, the MPC will keep rates on hold and maintain the hawkish rhetoric in order to safeguard the local currency," said Piotr Bujak of Nordea Bank Polska.

Poland's central bank raised the main interest rate

by a total of 100 basis points in the first half of last year, bringing it to 4.50 percent by June. It has adopted a wait-and-see approach since then.

The bank last cut interest rates in June 2009 to help the economy fight the spreading global economic crisis.

The zloty has lost around 11 percent against the euro since August 2011 on fears that the euro zone debt crisis might spiral out of control, causing a retreat of investors from emerging markets.

The weakening domestic currency pushed inflation higher through higher prices of imported goods, exacerbating a global rise in energy and food prices.

Price growth is expected to stand at an annual 4.6 percent year-on-year in December, remaining significantly above the central bank's 2.5 percent target.

But the slide of the zloty also helped the economy to beat forecasts in the third quarter of 2011 and post growth of more than 4 percent year-on-year.

Zloty depreciation, coupled with a large internal market of 38 million consumers, helped Poland avoid recession after the collapse of Lehman Brothers.

Poland's growth is now set to slow again to around 3 percent in 2012, with the government's fiscal consolidation plan additionally weighing on economic activity.

"I do not think the central bank may afford to cut rates soon as it will weaken the zloty that will feed into higher inflation," said Guillaume Tresca, emerging market strategist at Credit Agricole, adding the situation in the euro zone should stabilise by summer.

Forward rate agreements currently price in the first 25 basis point rate cut in July.

Poland's central bank has already intervened six times on the foreign exchange market since the start of September to defend the weakening zloty and any cut in interest rates could hurt the currency more due to a lower risk premium of investing in Polish bonds.

"Inflation will decelerate rather slowly, remaining above 4 percent in the first quarter due to the earlier zloty depreciation and, among others, a rise of the diesel excise tax," said Dariusz Winek, chief economist at Bank BGZ.

"In the coming weeks one should expect more zloty weakness so it is hard to speak of a fast start of rate cuts," Winek added.

Polish state bank BGK intensified its euro sales from European Union structural funds ahead of the year-end currency fixing that is used to calculate Polish state debt.

Some analysts expect that its reduced presence on the market at the beginning of the year might leave the zloty more exposed to global risk aversion and a possible further deterioration of the situation in Hungary.

(Reporting by Marcin Goettig; editing by Anna Willard)

title: UPDATE 1-Polish c.bank may buy bonds only if deep crisis
text:
(Recasts with c.bank comments, analyst)

WARSAW, Jan 2 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank would only buy the country's debt on the secondary market if the domestic financial sector were at risk, it said on Monday, clarifying its stance after the finance minister suggested the central bank could buy bonds if Polish yields rose sharply.

Earlier on Monday Finance Minister Jacek Rostowski, in an interview with the Polish edition of Newsweek magazine, said it might be adviseable for the central bank (NBP) to intervene in the secondary debt market if Poland's debt yields rose sharply on the back of market panic or a crisis.

"The main goal of the NBP is to keep prices stable," the central bank said in a statement. "The independent central bank supports the government's economic policy, but cannot fill in for it, especially as regards public debt management."

The central bank said Poland's constitution bans direct financing of the country's budget deficit by the central bank, but said the bank was also obliged to support the stability of the financial sector.

"That means NBP purchases of debt on the secondary market could only take place under extraordinary circumstances if the financial sector's stability was endangered," it read.

"The current macroeconomic conditions and Poland's financial situation (...) show the financial sector's stability is not threatened by the state of public finances."

So far, the Polish central bank has not bought bonds on the secondary market.

However, Warsaw used state-owned bank BGK to intervene in the debt market last September, buying bonds in a move that soothed market nervousness and sent yields on longer-dated papers several basis points lower.

"NBP debt purchases is in fact printing money and that would spark a huge depreciation pressure on the zloty and cause serious troubles for the monetary policy. So one should be wary of that," said a Warsaw-based dealer.

"At this point there is no market need for such an operation, there is no reason for any large-scale unloading of the Polish debt," the dealer added. "Yields on Polish debt are still relatively low compared to what is going on elsewhere."

The yield on Polish 10-year paper is hovering around 5.88 percent, well below that of countries' on the euro zone periphery, which have seen borrowing costs soar in the past year as the currency bloc's sovereign debt crisis deepened.

But analysts say foreign investors, who now hold some 31 percent of Poland's total outstanding domestic bonds, could shift away from central and east European assets, which as emerging market assets are riskier than core European ones, should the economic crisis in Europe deepen significantly.

(Reporting by Dagmara Leszkowicz and Gabriela Baczynska; Editing by Susan Fenton)
