title: Polish  Central Bank : No Legal Objections To Buying Bonds
text:
WARSAW (Dow Jones)--Poland's central bank could intervene in the bond market only if a "deep" crisis threatened the stability of the country's financial system, the bank said Monday, admitting the constitution doesn't forbid such a move.

However, the bank added, Poland's bond prices and financial system remain stable and its banks don't require a significant increase in capital, suggesting there are no grounds for such an intervention at the moment.

"This means purchase of bonds on the secondary market by the [National Bank of Poland] could take place only in situations of deep crisis, when stability of the financial system is threatened," the bank wrote, adding the Polish banking and financial system remains sound at the moment.

The central bank added that its monetary policy council didn't include bond market intervention as one of potential policy instruments in monetary policy guidelines for 2012.

Poland's finance ministry and central bank were active on the currency market last year to defend the zloty from excessive weakening and earlier on Monday, Finance Minister Jan Vincent Rostowski said the bank could step into the bond market in case of panic or contagion from abroad.

The bank warned speculation about a significant drop in bond prices or a need for its intervention in the market "could lead to unwanted perception of such information by financial markets," and could prove a self-fulfilling prophecy by affecting bond and zloty prices.

title: DJ 2nd UPDATE: Poland Defends Zloty To Keep Public Debt At Bay
text:
-- Polish state-owned bank bought large amounts of zloty ahead of 1000 GMT fixing

-- Zloty strengthens to PLN4.41 to euro on intervention, weakens again after 1000 GMT

-- Central bank steps in late in session with low volumes

(adds details on debt, quotes) 


 
   By Patryk Wasilewski 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

WARSAW (Dow Jones)--Poland's finance ministry intervened on the currency market for a second day in a row in order to keep its foreign debt at bay and avoid the necessity of introducing painful austerity measures.

The foreign debt, making up for around one-third of Poland's total public debt, is priced based on the zloty's last fixing each year, and in order to strengthen the currency just ahead of that time the ministry's agent, BGK bank, was heavily buying zlotys.

"We saw significant supply of the zloty from London, but then BGK started buying heavily," a dealer said.

As a result, the zloty was on a rollercoaster ride Friday as state-owned bank BGK soaked up zloty supply from foreign investors. But once the bank's support ceased, the zloty quickly weakened even further, hitting the session's high of PLN4.47.

The ministry later Friday announced that public debt for 2011 will be slightly below 54% of gross domestic product, not far off its 53.7% forecast, and reiterated its targets for the next year.

The ministry added it has some PLN30 billion in cash, mostly foreign currencies at its disposal.

Poland's government wants to keep total debt under 55% of gross domestic product, a level that would trigger painful austerity measures, including tax increases and quickly limiting government spending to tighten public finance.

Economists earlier estimated that the zloty would have to weaken to around PLN4.7 against the single currency in order to threaten the 55%-of-GDP debt threshold.

The finance ministry, wary that using the fixing makes it prone to market participants' speculation as they position themselves to profit from expected intervention, wants to change the way public debt is valued in the future by using an average euro/zloty rate instead.

Late in the session, the central bank was also spotted on the market, dealers said, sending a signal that even in the new year it will be ready to step in to defend the zloty from too rapid moves.

BGK's and the central bank's intervention Friday followed coordinated action with the central bank Thursday, when both institutions also stepped into the market to defend the currency from weakening.

By Dagmara Leszkowicz

WARSAW, Dec 29 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank and state-owned BGK bank stepped into the foreign exchange market on Thursday to support the zloty a day ahead of a final fixing for the year that will be key in determining the level of the national debt.

The multiple intervention was the central bank's fifth in around three months as it seeks to limit falls in the local currency, which has lost around a 10th of its value against the euro since June as investors fled riskier assets.

Poland is keen to keep a floor under the zloty to prevent its state debt, largely denominated in foreign currency, from exceeding 55 percent of gross domestic product, a level that would trigger constitutionally mandated spending cuts.

"The bank just wanted to remind market participants about its presence and discourage those who wanted to speculate on the unit."

The public debt is expected to stand at 53.7 pct of GDP, and analysts said the 55 percent threshold would only be breached if the zloty weakened past 4.7-4.8 to the euro.

text:
--The central bank said it bought zlotys Thursday

--Dealers said the finance ministry also intervened in the market

--The intervention pushed EUR/PLN to around 4.41 from 4.46


 
   By Patryk Wasilewski 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

(Adds central bank confirmation, details on BGK)

WARSAW (Dow Jones)--Poland's central bank and finance ministry intervened in the foreign-exchange market Thursday to shore up the zloty, just ahead of the last trading day of the year when the local currency's fixing is traditionally used to value the country's foreign-currency debt pile.

The central bank, NBP, stepped in to buy the zloty after the Polish currency weakened significantly Thursday to 4.462 against the euro. The move quickly pushed it to around 4.41.

"Today in the afternoon NBP sold some foreign currencies in exchange for the zloty," the bank said in a statement.

Dealers said state-owned bank BGK, which acts as the finance ministry's agent in the market, was also selling euros Thursday, supporting the zloty's strengthening.

The finance ministry uses the zloty's last fixing of the year to determine the size of the country's foreign-currency debt; a stronger zloty reduces the country's debt ratios. Around a third of Poland's debt is foreign currency-denominated.

Deputy Finance Minister Dominik Radziwill said earlier this month that the ministry would be selling on the market "significant amounts" of euros it has available from the European Union's funds.

title: CHARTING MARKETS: Polish  Central Bank  Weakens Support
text:
--The Polish Central Bank bought the zloty earlier Thursday

--Now a euro move below PLZ4.3791 would point to PLZ4.2477


 
   By Stephen Cox, CMT 
   A DOW JONES NEWSWIRES COLUMN 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--The intervention by Poland's central bank and finance ministry to strengthen the zloty Thursday appears to have been well timed.

It very well may have weakened the EUR/PLZ pair by pulling technical support out from the euro.

The operation pushed EUR/PLZ to around 4.41 from 4.46 earlier Thursday, observers noted. The Polish central bank dipped into its stock of euros to buy zlotys after its currency weakened significantly against the European currency on Thursday, when the euro reached PLZ4.462.

But well before Thursday's intervention it was clear on the daily chart that a technical breakdown of the euro might be complete.

In fact the euro broke down on the daily chart on Dec. 16 when it took out trend channel support at PLZ4.5037. That move by itself pointed the euro to the PLZ4.3881-PLZ4.3633 support band. Sure enough, the euro's lowest reading since the technical breakdown is Wednesday's low, PLZ4.3791.

Now PLZ4.3791 may be the last euro support in the way of an eventual test of PLZ4.2477.

It's apparent in any case that the euro has been compromised for now. Earlier the euro recorded a strong intraday high, PLZ4.4660. Current trading is PLZ4.4119. The current intraday low is now PLZ4.3861.

WARSAW (Dow Jones)--The Polish central bank's interventions in the zloty market have limited the currency's short-term volatility, said Marek Belka, governor of the National Bank of Poland.

The central bank has intervened several times since September to prop up the zloty, weakened by the euro-zone's debt crisis. At 1110 GMT Wednesday, the zloty was around PLN4.43 to the euro, some 11% weaker than in August.

Poland's central bank has spent "a much smaller amount" then EUR5 billion on interventions, Belka told a parliamentary committee Wednesday, acknowledging local reports of EUR1 billion spent on interventions in September and October. With reserve assets above EUR70 billion, Poland can afford to intervene in the foreign exchange market, he said.

Belka reiterated the Polish central bank has no exchange rate target for the zloty and intervenes to counter speculative moves. The currency is more exposed to speculation than regional peers, like the Czech koruna or the Hungarian forint, because of the much larger depth of the Polish financial market. The value of Polish assets are similar to Brazil's, while the Polish economy is several times smaller, Belka said.

"When people want to speculate, they will speculate with the zloty. With the Czech koruna, there's no money to be made because there are no Czech assets," Belka said.

In the longer term, the zloty is very stable, Belka added, noting the currency was around PLN4 to the euro in 2001 and again ten years later in early 2011. Short-term volatility helps stabilize the Polish economy, with consumers switching to domestic production when the zloty weakens which makes imported products more expensive, he said.

title: UPDATE 1-Polish cbank head: zloty has potential to appreciate
text:

WARSAW, Dec 21 (Reuters) - The Polish zloty has stabilised due to the possibility of central bank interventions on the foreign exchange market and the currency has potential to appreciate in value, the head of the central bank said on Wednesday.

The zloty has lost as much as 12 percent versus the euro since August as investors fled riskier assets due to the euro zone crisis but has regained some ground since last week on expectations of ramped up euro sales by Poland's state bank BGK.

"If we observe the situation in the last few months when the zloty depreciated from fundamental levels then there exists the potential for appreciation," Marek Belka told a parliamentary hearing.

The zloty traded up 0.3 percent to the euro from Tuesday's close at 4.437 at 1022 GMT, rising for the sixth consecutive session.

Polish authorities have intervened to prop up the zloty four times since September and many observers assume the central bank and the finance ministry -- through BGK -- will remain active to prevent the breaching of a key debt ceiling at the end of the year.

A third of Polish state debt is denominated in foreign currencies and so it is vulnerable to currency swings.

Belka said the central bank had spent "several times less than 5 billion euros" in its recent market interventions to support the zloty.

The governor also told lawmakers Poland would lend 6.26 to 6.27 billion euros in additional funds to the International Monetary Fund under a plan to raise the fund's crisis-fighting capability so it can help indebted euro zone states.

His comments echoed an earlier statement by Finance Minister Jacek Rostowski.

Poland, the largest eastern European Union economy, is not a member of the euro.

title: REFILE-CEE MONEY-PLN  intervention  made less likely by market moves
text:
(Removes extra headline at top of text)

* Polish authorities may not need to step into FX market

* Fear of interventions prompts investors to close long EURPLN

* Warsaw improves its debt through bills buyback, selling debt to local govt

By Dagmara Leszkowicz

WARSAW, Dec 20 (Reuters) - The fear among traders of being on the wrong side of possible interventions by Poland in the thinning pre-holiday market means authorities may achieve their goal of keeping the zloty relatively strong this month without having to act.

Poland has already intervened to prop up the zloty four times since September and many observers had assumed the central bank and the finance ministry -- through a state-owned BGK bank -- would remain active to prevent breaching a key debt ceiling at the end of the year.

A third of the state debt is denominated in foreign currencies and so it is susceptible to currency swings.

But the jumpy foreign players, which helped chop a tenth off the zlotys' value since August, have instead given the currency a short term boost in recent days.

"Those big names who have recently bet on the zloty fall, apparently started to buy the currency," said Karol Zaluski, chief FX dealer at ING Bank Slaski. "It looks like either the central bank or the BGK intervention won't be necessary, at least for now."

Another trader said, "Investors probably felt that there is no use to collide with BGK and to post losses."

Yet, there are other reasons why the zloty has come off its recent lows of 4.6 to the euro set earlier this month and now trades closer to 4.46.

Under Polish law, if public debt breaches 55 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), the government is required to make painful spending cuts.

The public debt is expected to stand at 53.8 pct of GDP and analysts see the 55 percent threshold being breached only if the zloty weakens past 4.7-4.8 to the euro.

OTHER WAYS

Concerned that the gathering clouds of the euro zone could cast a shadow over the zloty, the finance ministry has moved to reduce the debt on its own books by shifting a part of it to local governments.

"Buying of the treasury papers by local governments will lower public debt by their nominal value," said Piotr Marczak, the head of the Finance Ministry's debt department.

So far only Warsaw confirmed it could buy the government's papers for up to 550 million zloty. But the proposal has been put forward also to other local governments.

"Information about a possibility of putting money in treasury's papers was sent to those local governments that reported a solid amount of free cash at the end of the second quarter," said a deputy head of the ministry's debt department, Bogdan Klimaszewski.

To trim state debt, the ministry also bought back a total of 4.2 billion zlotys in treasury bills this year, with the last buy-back tender held on Monday. The recent tender lowered this year's ratio of debt to Gross Domestic Product by around 0.15 percent.

"After the Monday buyback, we estimate that the debt/GDP ratio stands at 54.1 percent," said Marcin Mazurek, senior analyst at BRE bank in Warsaw.

Some economists say that Finance Minister Jacek Rostowski is determined to improve the country's indicators in terms of debt and deficit as he sees a real chance of a ratings upgrade.

Two rating agencies -- Moody's and Standard & Poor's -- have recently pointed to Poland's fiscal situation as key to the country's rating.

Moody's confirmed the country's rating on Tuesday and said the outlook was stable due to Warsaw's fiscal strategy and a strong track in the face of significant external shocks.

S&P also said that deep, long-term structural reforms would put Poland in a good position to unlock its growth potential.

Moody's rates Poland at A2, while S&P and Fitch rates it at A-, all with a stable outlook.

(Reporting by Dagmara Leszkowicz; editing by Ron Askew)

Consumer price pressures are rising throughout the region while economic activity and currency values fall, raising concerns over a possible bout of stagflation on the European Union's eastern flank.

In Poland, November inflation is expected to spike to 4.5% from 4.3% in October, while in Hungary inflation is seen rising to 4.3% on the year in November from 3.9% the month before.

The upcoming readings are set to follow a spike in inflation announced late last week, in which the consumer price index accelerated to 2.5% on the year in November, above market expectations of 2.4% and above a 2.3% rate in October.

Piotr Bujak, an economist at Nordea Bank in Warsaw, said one of the culprits behind the spike in consumer prices is weakness among regional currencies over the last few months due to risk aversion amid the euro-zone crisis.

"This will fuel inflation, especially of food and fuels, as well as other imported products," Bujak said.

Unlike in neighboring countries, Polish consumer demand remained resilient in November, as Poles continued shopping.

In Hungary, analysts are attributing the spike to a recent excise tax hike, but the heavy forint depreciation may also become more visible in the figures, they said.

Erste Bank expects to see a jump again in January, when the value-added tax will rise to 27% from 25%.

This will likely push the annual figure well above 5% in the first few months of next year and then inflation should slow to 4% by year-end as consumer demand is weak.

Erste said it expects the Hungarian central bank to lift interest rates by 50 basis points to 7% this month, and that this tightening will allow rates to be stable next year.

title: DJ UPDATE:  Poland 's  Central Bank  To Continue Zloty  Interventions
text:
-- The National Bank of Poland ready to step in if zloty weakens dramatically again

-- Interventions have proven effective, NBP chief Belka says

-- No change of monetary policy view, Polish rates may go either way

(Adds comments on the zloty versus regional peers from the fifth paragraph, background on rates in the seventh.)

By Marcin Sobczyk

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

WARSAW (Dow Jones)--Poland's central bank plans to continue buying zloty to help the Polish currency weather the euro-zone crisis, its chief said Wednesday.

Marek Belka reiterated that the central bank has no particular exchange rate target, describing its interventions as designed to create a risk for currency speculators.

"We intend to continue interventions in line with rules so far," the governor of the National Bank of Poland told a news conference. "We intervene when we recognize signs of destabilization in the foreign currency market."

The bank has intervened several times since September to shore up the zloty, weakened by the euro-zone crisis. The zloty was around PLN4.47 to the euro Wednesday afternoon local time, some 12% weaker than in August.

He said the forays have been effective in stabilizing the zloty against other currencies in the region.

"Over the past two months that we've been present in the market, the zloty hasn't weakened anymore and its volatility is lower than of the currencies we usually compare ourselves with--for example the Hungarian forint and the Czech koruna," he said. "Before our interventions, the koruna was much more stable than the zloty. Now it's quite the opposite."

Earlier, the bank's rate-setting council left its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 4.5%. The Monetary Policy Council acknowledged in a statement that the weak zloty could stoke inflation, which was running at 4.3% on the year in October, above the central bank's target of 2.5%.

So far this year, the bank has raised rates by one percentage point. The council believes this should bring Poland's inflation back towards target in the mid-term, and slower economic growth and fiscal tightening should also have a moderating effect.

-By Marcin Sobczyk, Dow Jones Newswires, +48 22 447 2432;

marcin.sobczyk@dowjones.com

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

December 07, 2011 12:11 ET (17:11 GMT)

title: UPDATE 2- Poland  keeps rates on hold, warns of more  intervention
text:
* Poland leaves key rate flat, as expected, at 4.5 pct

* Bank sees CPI back in target in mid-term, elevated for now

* C.bank to intervene again if zloty "unstable"

By Marcin Goettig and Maciej Onoszko

WARSAW, Dec 7 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank left interest rates on hold again on Wednesday and said it sees inflation returning to target in the medium term, but it warned of more currency intervention if the zloty continues to be volatile.

Rates have now been on hold since June as a weak zloty, which has fallen 12 percent against the euro since June and fuelled inflation, has prevented the central bank from cutting interest rates to shore up a slowing economy.

In the first half of this year the central bank raised its key interest rate by a total of 100 basis points to 4.5 percent.

"The significant monetary policy tightening implemented in the first half of 2011 should enable inflation to return to the target in the medium term," the bank said in a statement after the monthly meeting of the rate-setting Monetary Policy Council.

"The impact of the situation in the global financial markets on the zloty exchange rate continues to be an upside risk to domestic price developments," it said.

FX INTERVENTIONS

The central bank has intervened four times this year to defend the zloty, most recently in November. The zlotyposting a similar performance to the currency of Hungary that saw its credit rating downgraded to "junk".

"We plan to continue our interventions (...) This means we are intervening when we believe that there is some destabilisation in the market," central bank Governor Marek Belka told a conference after the bank's decision.

The zloty has been hit by weaker demand for emerging market assets in recent months as the deepening euro zone debt crisis has hurt risk appetite. It has performed as badly as the Hungarian forint, which has been hit by a downgrade of Hungary's credit rating to junk status and concern about Budapest's unorthodox policies.

On Wednesday, the zloty gained around 0.2 percent to the euro after Belka's comments and traded at 4.4710 by 1631 GMT.

"We do not intend to have any exchange rate target," Belka said.

"We are intervening so that the risk of hitting a central bank intervention was also present in market participants' balance of risks."

He said the bank's interventions curbed volatility in the zloty, which is now weaker than the Czech crown, whereas it was stronger that the crown before the Polish central bank stepped into the market for the first time in September.

Analysts say further interventions will depend on developments in the euro zone.

"There are no grounds now to intervene on the FX market, neither the volatility nor the exchange rate level justify this," said Mateusz Szczurek, chief CEE economist at ING.

"The economic data is still too good to make the MPC cut rates. The probability of a zloty weakening is also too high, so it is hard to consider rate cuts, as long as inflation does not return to levels around 3.5 percent," Szczurek added.

Inflation stood at 4.3 percent in October.

A Reuters poll on Monday forecast Poland's central bank would keep interest rates on hold in the first quarter of 2012 and will then cut rates by a total of 50 basis points next year to support the slowing economy.

Poland's economy grew by 4.2 percent year-on-year in the third quarter of 2011, statistics office data showed on Wednesday, just down from 4.3 percent in the second quarter but above a forecast of 4.0 percent.

Analysts polled by Reuters expect growth to slow to 3.0 percent in 2012.

(Additional reporting by Filip Kochan; Writing by Marcin Goettig and Dagmara Leszkowicz; Editing by Susan Fenton)

Central European markets will watch the euro zone and United States Thursday, gauging whether regional currencies and bonds will be able to build on gains made Wednesday after six major central banks took coordinated action to boost liquidity.

The Czech koruna firmed 1.5% to the euro on the news as risk appetite grew, which in turn pushed Prague stocks 4.2% higher on the day.

The volatility shows that it hardly needs much to push the koruna to higher levels, said Michal Brozka, economist at Raiffeisenbank, adding that it also indicates how much the Czech currency is fundamentally undervalued.

Other assets also rose, namely prices on government bonds throughout the region as yields retreated sharply across the board after spiking in some cases as much as 100 basis points in November.

Yet developments today are a tough call.

"Hopes for a strong rally are rather weak and the positive effect on risky assets is mild," as can be seen from the less dramatic gains made by the zloty and forint on Wednesday, Brozka said.

Quoted bond yields sharply retreated from recent highs, but overall trade volumes remain tame as most hot money is instead moving into commodities rather than bonds, said Filip Lesch, a fixed income-trader at CSOB in Prague.

In Budapest, Hungary's treasury auctions of bonds maturing in 2014, 2016 and 2020 follow the central bank's raising its base rate 50 basis points Tuesday to 6.50%, in line with market expectations.

The rate hike, however, was below what some on the markets had already priced into Hungarian assets, leading to some disappointment and casting a shadow over Thursday's auction.

title: UPDATE: Polish State-Owned BGK Props Up Zloty
text:
--Polish state-owned bank BGK seen propping up zloty Wednesday

--The action comes a week after Poland's central bank intervened to defend the currency


 
   By Clare Connaghan 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

LONDON (Dow Jones)--Polish state-owned Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego was seen buying zloty in "significant amounts" Wednesday, in a move interpreted by traders as an intervention.

The Polish currency rose sharply in response, pushing the euro down to PLN4.4944 from around PLN4.5370. The dollar fell to a low of PLN3.3344 from PLN3.36. The bank had dipped into the market to sell foreign currencies earlier in the session, but this latest round was much more aggressive.

"(BGK) took an opportunity when the market was in risk-on mood because of the announcement of the swap agreements," said emerging market strategist Thu Lan Nguyen at Commerzbank.

Sentiment across emerging markets improved markedly after the world's largest central banks took coordinated action to shore up the global financial system, under threat from Europe's rolling debt crisis.

The Hungarian forint and Czech koruna immediately climbed. But the zloty lagged until BGK jumped into the market for at least the second time Wednesday.

All emerging market currencies have come under heavy selling pressure since the summer when a toxic combination of global economic fears and escalating euro-zone debt worries set off a huge exodus from emerging markets. But Poland's close ties with the troubled euro zone mean the zloty has suffered more than most.

As result, Polish authorities have taken action to stem currency weakness, which can pose inflationary problems by lifting the cost of imported goods. For countries burdened with large amounts of debt denominated in foreign currencies, a weak currency is particularly harmful because these debts become much more expensive to pay back.

For Poland, that is a particularly sticky issue, as the country has a self-imposed limit on the ratio between debt and gross domestic product. Crossing its 55% limit would trigger an automatic tightening of fiscal policy. The weaker the zloty gets, the closer Poland gets to that limit.

Last week, Poland's central bank was seen intervening in the currency markets to defend the zloty. BGK, which acts on behalf of Poland's finance ministry, is often active in the foreign exchange market. It regularly sells euros it receives as European Union subsidies directly on the market instead of converting them at the central bank.

At 1708 GMT the euro was trading at PLN4.5032 against the Polish zloty, compared with a session high of PLN4.5575.

WARSAW, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Polish bond yields fell as much as 13 basis points in late Friday trade on talk that the finance ministry was buying Polish debt on the secondary market, dealers said.

Polish debt took a hit earlier in the day after Moody's cut Hungary's credit rating to "junk", casting a shadow over central and eastern European markets.

"There's a rumour that the finance ministry is buying bonds," one Warsaw dealer said.

There was also talk in the market that the finance ministry had asked various banks about a potential intervention on the secondary market.

"The Finance Ministry asked us today how to positively impact the market. The state-owned bank (that is used by the ministry to conduct purchases of bonds) did not buy bonds today," said one Warsaw-based dealer.

title: CEE MARKETS 3-Hungary debt yields jump,  Poland  talks of new  interventions
text:
(Adds Polish cbanker, updates levels)

* FX markets fragile, Polish cbank warns may intervene again

* Czech, Polish debt stable after selloff; Hungary down

* Spreading euro zone crisis weighs

By Sandor Peto

BUDAPEST/WARSAW, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Hungarian bond yields soared to 2-1/2 year highs on Thursday and Poland's central bank warned of further interventions as emerging European currencies remained under pressure on concerns the euro zone debt crisis is threatening even Germany.

The yield at an auction of 12-month Hungarian Treasury bills rose to its highest since September 2009, at 7.07 percent, although the debt agency managed to sell all 30 billion forints of paper on offer.

On secondary bond markets, Hungarian yields rose up to 20 basis points to highs last seen in the summer of 2009 following a similar rise in the previous session, when a German bond auction described as "disastrous" hit central European debt.

"We saw an almost continuous rise in yields," one Budapest-based fixed income trader said. "I hope this will not continue next week as that would already be real big trouble... European markets are in a panic which has spilled over into our market."

"I hope things will improve next week when U.S. investors return from their holidays," he added.

Hungary has been the central European market most vulnerable to investors cutting back their exposure to risk, and the forint, which lost more than 1 percent on Wednesday, stayed near record lows, slipping 0.3 percent to 310.99 per euro.

In Poland, where the zloty hovered close to multi-month lows, the central bank's deputy governor in charge of interventions told Reuters it was likely to intervene again after stepping into the market on Wednesday for the fourth time in less than three months.

The Polish currency was nearly flat at 4.49, a nudge below the key psychological level of 4.50 and year-lows just beyond.

"The comments by the deputy governor temporarily supported the zloty," one Warsaw trader said. "I think a further retreat of the zloty towards this year's minimum of 4.42-4.53 to the euro is still possible."

"The question is whether the central bank will defend these levels," he added.

Both the zloty and forint have lost more than 10 percent in 2011, mostly in the latter half of the year.

The Czech crown slipped 0.4 percent against the euro to 25.76, and a Prague-based dealer said it could be heading towards 26.300-500 if it stays weaker than 25.300-400, an area that has offered support.

A Hungarian dealer said the forint had no room to firm in the short term as concerns remain that Standard & Poor's may cut Hungary's debt rating to junk even though the government has applied to the IMF for a precautionary credit line.

"The forint has almost lost all its gains posted since the news about the (planned) IMF deal, but can firm in the longer term on the news flow about the talks and the deal," another dealer said.

Romania's leu, which has seen support from prospects of intervention there, firmed 0.1 percent.

Fears that the worsening euro zone sovereign debt crisis will cripple economic activity, leaving central Europe's export-reliant economies vulnerable, have hammered the region's markets.

The Czech 10-year yield was quoted up 6 bps at 4.489 pct

after a jump of 40 basis points on Wednesday in a usually stable market.

The region's main equity indices were little changed.

title: UPDATE 1-Polish  central bank  warns of further  interventions
text:
* Fewer funds used in last move

* More interventions likely

(Adds quote, trader, background)

By Pawel Sobczak

WARSAW, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank may intervene in the foreign exchange market to support the weak zloty, and on a larger scale than during its latest move on Wednesday, its deputy governor said on Thursday.

The central bank stepped into the market for the fourth time in less than three months on Wednesday as the Polish currency neared the psychologically key 4.50 line versus the euro, but the move failed to have a sustained effect.

"The funds that were used in the last intervention were much smaller than in September and October," Witold Kozinski told Reuters. "The goal of the last intervention was not to bring the zloty to a specific level, but to stabilise the market."

Kozinski, who is responsible for the central bank's interventions, said Wednesday move was "cautionary".

"Further interventions are likely. This will depend on our view of the market. New interventions may be conducted on a large scale," he added.

The zloty picked up after the comments, dealers said. It was up 0.1 percent against the euro as of 1500 GMT.

"The comments by the deputy governor temporarily supported the zloty," one Warsaw trader said. "I think a further retreat of the zloty towards this year's minimum of 4.42-4.53 to the euro is still possible."

"The question is whether the central bank will defend these levels," he added.

The zloty has lost about 11 percent of its value to the euro since June.

title: WSJ/Emerging Europe:  Poland 's Zloty  Interventions  Turn Predictable
text:
(Emerging Europe Real Time is The Wall Street Journal Online's site for news and analysis on Central and Eastern Europe http://blogs.wsj.com/emergingeurope)


 
   Posted by Marcin Sobczyk 
 

Poland's central bank contradicted some of its earlier public declarations when it unsuccessfully intervened to prop up the depreciating zloty on Wednesday.

The central bank insists it isn't defending any particular exchange rate, yet the four interventions so far have always occurred when the zloty was in the range of 4.42-4.52 to the euro.

Poland's rate-setters also pledged to introduce an element of uncertainty for speculators, yet the timing of its intervention on Wednesday was painfully predictable.

Soon after it intervened for the first time on Sept. 23, central bank governor Marek Belka said the only goal of the move was "to make life more difficult for those who speculate against the zloty."

"We're not defending any particular level in the exchange rate. We want to add a risk factor to the game for those who bet the zloty will weaken," he said a day after the first intervention to boost the zloty.

The currency had been in free fall despite Poland's comparably healthy growth prospects and resilience to crises as investors fled emerging markets amid the euro-zone debt crisis. As in the post-Lehman crisis of 2008-2009, speculators placed bets the zloty would continue to depreciate.

When the central bank sold about EUR1 billion on Sept. 23, it quickly moved the Polish currency from 4.52 zlotys to the euro to about 4.38 zlotys, burning those speculators' fingers. Still, despite the central bank's efforts, the zloty has fallen about 13% since early August, rendering it one of the worst-performing emerging market currencies in the current crisis. Only the Hungarian forint and the South African rand have done worse.

The central bank's first intervention took the market by surprise. But all of the National Bank of Poland's interventions that followed--on Sept. 30, Oct. 3 and Nov. 23--have so far taken place in the range of 4.42-4.52 zlotys to the euro.

Market participants go on alert, therefore, when the currency is in what's now routinely referred to as "intervention territory," while the central bank's repeated warnings of its readiness to strike has made it quite easy for the markets to guess when the hit is coming.

"Usually when the NBP speaks of intervention, it comes soon after," Citigroup said at 0808 GMT on Wednesday. The intervention came less than 30 minutes later.

title: WSJ/Emerging Europe:  Poland 's Latest  Intervention  To Boost Zloty Deemed 'Failure'
text:
(Emerging Europe Real Time is The Wall Street Journal Online's site for news and analysis on Central and Eastern Europe http://blogs.wsj.com/emergingeurope)


 
   Posted by Clare Connaghan 
 

Blink and you might have missed Poland's central bank intervention on Wednesday. The initial leg higher in the zloty has been all but erased now, leaving little trace of the central bank's action.

Peter Attard Montalto, an emerging-market economist at Nomura in London, calls the National Bank of Poland's intervention a "failure" and it certainly looks that way judging by the price action.

The zloty was around 4.47 to the euro on Thursday morning, exactly where it was when the central bank sold an undisclosed amount of euros in the market Wednesday.

Up until yesterday, the bank's previous attempts at intervening had been successful in bringing the zloty down for at least a few days. But Wednesday was no normal day--the tide the Polish currency was up against was simply too strong.

Germany--long thought of as the safest of euro-zone havens--failed to sell all the bonds it wanted too, cranking up concern about the euro-zone crisis to a new level. The auction result sent shockwaves to investors and emerging-market currencies sold off aggressively as a result.

No one was immune from the selloff, but currencies in central Europe--such as the zloty--with close banking and trade ties with the troubled euro zone, suffered more than most.

The question now is what will Polish authorities do. It is clear that Wednesday's intervention has been ineffective, but that doesn't mean the bank won't intervene again.

Currency weakness can pose inflationary problems and in countries burdened with debt denominated in foreign currencies, the situation is particularly harmful because these debts become much more expensive to pay back as the foreign currencies strengthen.

For Poland, that is a particularly thorny issue, as it has a self-imposed limit on the ratio between debt and gross domestic product. Crossing its 55% limit would trigger an automatic tightening of fiscal policy. The weaker the zloty gets, the closer Poland gets to that limit, setting the scene for further interventions.

"We will see the NBP back in the market and state-owned Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego or BGK with more aggression too," says Nomura's Montalto.

title: WSJ/Emerging Europe:  Poland Intervenes  Again To Boost Zloty, More Action Likely
text:
(Emerging Europe Real Time is The Wall Street Journal Online's site for news and analysis on Central and Eastern Europe http://blogs.wsj.com/emergingeurope ) 


 
   Posted by Marcin Sobczyk 
 

Poland's central bank was seen intervening in the currency markets Wednesday to support the zloty, currency traders said. More interventions are likely before the year is out.

The Polish currency rose sharply against the euro and U.S. dollar in response to the suspected intervention, which pushed the euro down to 4.4423 zlotys from around 4.4792 zlotys. The dollar fell to a low of 3.3995 zlotys from 3.3271 zlotys.

Last week, Polish state-owned Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego--the finance ministry's agent--was seen intervening in the market to support the zloty.

Wednesday's intervention won't have a lasting effect, said BGZ, a local bank, as investors move to safer assets ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday in the U.S.

According to economists, more interventions are likely before the end of the year. The National Bank of Poland and the finance ministry are determined to keep the zloty from spinning out of control, each for different reasons.

One of the main reasons behind the central bank's efforts to boost the zloty is concern that a weak currency would stoke inflation, central bank governor, Marek Belka, said in an interview published Wednesday on the central bank's website. The bank started intervening in September, when mounting concern over Europe's unresolved sovereign debt problem prompted investors to dump emerging market currencies wholesale. Despite Poland's comparatively sound finances and growth prospects, the zloty failed to escape this trend. Wednesday's intervention--if confirmed by the central bank--marks the fourth time that Poland's central bank stepped in to shore up the embattled zloty.

In comments for The Wall Street Journal earlier this month, Mr. Belka reiterated the central bank's readiness to intervene at any time "to fight disorderly behavior." He said the central bank was "encouraged" by the result of the interventions.

The government, on the other hand, is determined to prevent the currency's weakness from inflating the Poland's foreign debt, which could push it above Poland's self-imposed level of 55% of economic output, triggering austerity. The state-owned BGK bank has about 7 billion euros-8 billion euros it can sell to boost the zloty, said Rafal Benecki, senior economist at ING.

The country's debt pile is measured against the 55% limit at the end of the year, which is why interventions may intensify in December. The zloty will likely strengthen toward the end of the year, BGZ said.

* Poland, India, Singapore c.banks step in to support currencies

* Turkey lira, bonds weaken ahead of c.bank meeting

* Egypt, Bahrain CDS surge to freshj 2-1/2 year highs

By Sujata Rao

LONDON - Emerging stocks fell 1.8 percent to six-week lows on Wednesday, battered by fresh signs of weakening growth in China, while several central banks across Asia and central Europe stepped in to support their currencies versus the dollar and euro.

A slump in China's factory sector reinforced fears of a hard landing for the world's second largest economy. The data came a day after the United States cut its third quarter growth estimate, while Markit flash PMIs showed the euro zone private sector remains deep in contractionary territory, including in powerhouse Germany.

"We are still in risk aversion mode and local currencies are teetering. It's less about specific country fundamentals, it's a corrosion of fast-moving events encouraging deep deleveraging," said RBS strategist Imran Ahmad, referring to European banks' efforts to unwind overseas positions amid dollar funding stress and higher capital requirements.

The latest Chinese PMI was especially dismaying for markets, he said, adding: "We thought China was going to save the world (but) there are lots of cracks emerging."

The data flow fuelled a flight to safe-haven assets, weighing on emerging stocks, bonds and currencies almost across the board, with benchmark emerging equities falling 1.8 percent

by 1040 GMT, its seventh straight session in the red. The index has shed more than 10 percent so far in November.

All major equity indices lost ground, with India leading falls in Asia, a day after its rupee currency fell to record lows against the dollar. Export-reliant Korean markets fell 2.3 percent after the Chinese and U.S. numbers, while the won slipped to one-month lows.

Central banks in India, Singapore and Indonesia were spotted selling dollars to buoy their currencies. That helped the rupee rebound 0.7 percent, with some traders estimating recent Reserve Bank intervention at around $4 billion.

In emerging Europe, Poland's central bank stepped in to selll euros for the fourth time in less than three months, briefly helping the zloty 0.5 percent higher.

The move comes a day after the central bank's deputy governor said the market situation had raised the possibility of intervention. Stubbornly high inflation is seen forcing the central bank to continue combating zloty weakness.

"Concerns over further interventions should curb speculation on short euro/zloty positions," a dealer in Warsaw said.

The Hungarian forint fell 0.6 percent against the euro while the Czech crown fell 0.35 percent, Both countries are seen as particularly vulnerable to deleveraging by euro zone banks.

Hungary has appealed to the International Monetary Fund for assistance but analysts are sceptical Budapest can get the kind of aid package it seeks. Failure to secure a deal could see the country lose its investment grade credit rating, fear of which pushed credit default swaps to their highest levels since 2008.

"The main risk comes from very high refinancing needs of Hungarian hard currency redemptions in 2012 and 2013 in an environment where bond issuance has become more and more difficult, even for core EU17 countries," ING analysts said, noting external needs of 5.3 billion euros in 2012.

A 'disastrous' German 10-year bond auction on Wednesday raised concerns the euro zone debt crisis is even beginning to threaten Berlin.

Turkish markets were rangebound ahead of a central bank meeting that is unlikely to take any concrete steps following the bank's move towards a strategy that effectively sets policy every day via overnight rates and liquidity tightening.

The lira fell a quarter point to a new one-month low against the dollar while the stock market slipped to fresh three-month lows. The benchmark yield rose 7 basis points to 10.59 percent.

The South African rand fell almost 1 percent to a two-month low against the dollar. The currency has lost 20 percent this year and is one of the world's worst performing emerging currencies.

The rand's weakness has intensified price pressures and data on Wednesday showed annual consumer inflation quickening to 6 percent last month, at the top end of the central bank's target. While the central bank is unlikely to raise rates in the current environment, the data would appear to rule out rate cuts in the near term as well.

"... Six percent has sufficient shock value to finally erase any remnants of rate cut expectations -- we would have to see a considerable deterioration in global and South African growth to justify new easing," Standard Chartered analyst Razia Khan said.

In the Middle East, Egyptian protests entered a sixth day pushing the pound to fresh seven year highs to the dollar while stocks extended losses to a new 2-1/2 year low. The index has fallen 12 percent since protests began on Friday.

Egypt's five-year credit default swaps rose 18 bps to a fresh March 2009 high of 560, Markit said.

Unrest was also sweeping Bahrain, raising the cost of insuring debt exposure by 14 bps to 410 bps for a five-year period, the highest since May 2009, Markit data shows.

However the turmoil has failed to deter bond issuance from the Gulf with Qatar planning a bond in coming weeks. It will follow on the heels of successful issues from Abu Dhabi Islamic Bank while energy company Taqa and United Arab Shipping Company have mandated banks to manage upcoming bonds.

title: Poland's Belka Doesn't Rule Out Euro Breakup
text:
DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

WARSAW -- For all their determination to save the euro zone, European leaders must allow for the possibility of a breakup of the currency union, Poland's central bank chief said Wednesday.

Marek Belka, governor of the National Bank of Poland, said that in the crisis roiling Europe, no scenario can be ruled out. "For this reason, the euro zone must move forward," he said in an interview on the central bank's news website Obserwator Finansowy.

"Many fear a two-speed Europe. I prefer a two-speed Europe than an entire Europe in stagnation," he said, referring to the idea of moving ahead with integration in the 17-nation euro zone, leaving a looser outer band of the 10 EU countries that don't use the euro.

Poland should eventually join the euro zone, but "we don't want the euro that it is today," Belka said.

As for entering the European Union's currency grid, he said that would also be unwise right now. The EU's Exchange Rate Mechanism is designed to limit volatility of national currencies ahead of euro-zone membership.

"Introducing the zloty to the currency grid today is a recipe for confusion in the foreign exchange market. Speculation couldn't be stopped in such a situation. Investors would wish to check if we're able to keep the zloty within a range [to the euro]," he said.

Poland's central bank has intervened since September to boost the zloty, weakened by the exit of investors from emerging markets amid the euro-zone debt crisis.

title: Emerging Europe Central Banks Vulnerable To Mounting Attacks
text:
--Emerging European currencies fall victim to euro-zone debt crisis concerns

--Central banks in this region seen with less firepower than other emerging markets to fight currency weakness

--Currency market interventions, however, may continue as these currencies underperform

By Erin McCarthy


   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Having spent much of the past two years trying to weaken their currencies, emerging-market central banks are now trying to do the opposite, for which they are increasingly tapping the foreign currency reserves they accumulated through those previous actions.

Some of them, especially those in Eastern and Central Europe, may find that the war chests they built up aren't deep enough to fight off an intensifying attack by speculators as fears of another global crisis grow.

Poland and Romania's central banks have been seen intervening in the foreign exchange market to prop up their currencies recently, while Turkey's central bank holds daily foreign exchange-selling auctions to help its currency. Despite these efforts, the attacks on their currencies keep growing.

The selloff is global, with nervous investors shifting en masse into dollars and safe havens such as the yen. But the problems that poses aren't felt universally.

Latin American countries such as Brazil and Chile and Asian nations such as South Korea and Taiwan all went on aggressive dollar-buying campaigns when the dollar was in constant decline against their currencies. That has left them in better shape now to address the problem of an ascending dollar, less vulnerable to speculators' attacks, and thus less of a natural target. Even Mexico, which has largely kept out of markets, has about $76 billion of reserves combined with a $72 billion flexible credit line arrangement with the International Monetary Fund.

But emerging European currencies are under much more pressure, mostly because of their ongoing exposure to the euro zone debt crisis, which crimped their capacity to amass the reserves needed to arrest the mounting attacks on their currencies.

In any intervention, these countries' central banks will have to pit themselves against global investors who likely won't find their reserve levels or other policy tools all that impressive. This will especially be a problem for economies whose reserve levels are marred by large economic imbalances, like Turkey's massive current account deficit and Hungary's high levels of foreign currency debt.

"There aren't too many economies out there that we should be able to expect good things from a currency intervention," said Michael Lee, senior portfolio manager of the Wells Fargo Advantage International Bond Fund.

Hungary holds about $53 billion in reserves, tiny compared to Brazil's $352.9 billion. That weakness, combined with high levels of foreign currency debt--which means a weak forint puts households and banks holding such debt under pressure--has seen investors running for the door from the forint.

With such meager reserves, the Hungarian forint's only defense may be a substantial one-time rate increase, which could hamper already bleak growth. And if it cannot get financial assistance from the International Monetary Fund, as it requested earlier this month, the forint could head for another freefall.

Turkey is in a similar boat. After holding foreign-exchange selling auctions and directly intervening in the market in October, its central bank ultimately tightened monetary policy with a back-door rate hike, whose effect has since seemingly waned. With about $95 billion in reserves, Turkey must still tread very cautiously, since reserve depletion can unnerve foreign creditors, whose financing helps fund its massive current account deficit.

And even Poland, which has better economic fundamentals and sturdier reserve levels at about $110 billion, is struggling to fight the market. Its bank stepped into the market Wednesday to fight off speculative flows hurting the zloty, bringing the euro down as low as PLN4.4423. But the intense selloff across risk assets ultimately erased the effect of the intervention within hours, leading some to bill it as a failure.

Still, some market watchers say emerging Europe's central banks could catch a break, since dangerously illiquid markets and high trading costs may keep speculators out of the market altogether. Instead, investors may chase currencies whose central banks are standing back. These include the South Africa rand, which has dropped nearly 22% against the dollar since September.

title: South African Rand Hits Fresh Two-Month Low Against Dollar
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging-market currencies tumbled sharply Wednesday as euro-zone debt crisis worries sent investors fleeing out of riskier currencies.

The South African rand hit a series of fresh lows, ultimately reaching its weakest level against the dollar since May 2009. The dollar rose more than 1.5% to ZAR8.5436, from ZAR8.3885 late Tuesday, according to CQG.

The Polish zloty also fell sharply, hitting a two-month low against the euro, despite an intervention earlier Wednesday by Poland's central bank to prop up the currency. The euro rose to PLN4.50 against the zloty, from PLN4.4597 late Tuesday.

Rising European government bond yields and a failed German bond auction Wednesday helped trigger the risk-off move, as investors remain concerned about the region's debt crisis spreading to its larger economies.

title: WSJ/Emerging Europe: Polish Prime Minister To Address Markets In Parliament Speech
text:
(This article has been posted on Emerging Europe Real Time, The Wall Street Journal Online's site for news and analysis on Central and Eastern Europe http://blogs.wsj.com/emergingeurope)


 
   Posted by Marcin Sobczyk 
 

Faced with the euro-zone crisis and nudged by his central bank chief, Poland's prime minister will talk to the financial markets rather than his voters and lawmakers when he asks parliament on Friday for a vote of confidence. He has little choice but to promise an ambitious fiscal overhaul program designed to slow the growth of public debt, lead to a higher credit rating for Poland, and help it graduate from the emerging markets camp.

Poland went bankrupt in the 1980s after several decades of severe mismanagement by communists. Poles may not remember that, the central bank governor, Marek Belka, told The Wall Street Journal in an interview published this week. But the financial market has a long memory.

Since a shock transition to a free market that began in 1989 with the collapse of communism, Poland has been growing rapidly, but has so far failed to restore full trust of the markets. Despite a sound economy and remarkable resilience to crises, the zloty has been strongly volatile since the global crisis that began in 2008. Economists tend to focus more on risks the country faces and less on its proven strengths.

Belka has repeatedly urged the cabinet of Donald Tusk to take more action to reduce public deficit. He said in an interview with The Wall Street Journal that a rating upgrade from A-/A2 is within reach if the government presents a credible plan. The central bank governor holds a position independent from the government. Since Belka's appointment by the ruling camp in 2010, cabinet officials and the prime minister have lauded cooperation with the central bank.

Through a combination of higher taxes, lower spending and a cut of cash transfers to private pension funds, the government will likely manage to trim the country's deficit from 7.8% of economic output at the end of last year to likely below 5.6% at the end of December.

But that level is high, above the 3% all European Union member states agreed not to exceed. The government has said it's determined to bring the gap below that level by the end of 2012, a goal that will likely be reiterated on Friday. It will be an ambitious one, and exactly what the markets want to hear.

According to local press reports here, the prime minister, at the onset of his new term, will promise a set of measures cutting public spending, reducing tax breaks and overhauling the pension system. The government will eradicate childbirth benefits and tax breaks for families with children, daily Rzeczpospolita said this week without citing sources.

Social security contributions paid by the self-employed may go up and people in creative professions--like artists and journalists--may have to start paying taxes on all of their income instead of on 50%. The government has said earlier that it would raise value-added taxes further if deficits remain stubbornly high.

Polish officials have earlier repeatedly said they would like to be part of the EU core, and in their view this would require a signal that Poland remains committed to joining the euro zone, albeit when the crisis there ends--a distant prospect. According to daily Gazeta Wyborcza, Mr. Tusk wants his country to join the currency grid that keeps currencies floating within a limited range.

All countries seeking to adopt the euro are expected to participate in this grid, the European Exchange Rate Mechanism, for at least two years. In the ERMII system, currencies are allowed to float within a range of plus or minus 15% to the euro.

Participation doesn't automatically lead to euro-zone membership, however. Denmark has been part of the ERMII since 1999, despite having decided to stick with the krone. The Lithuanian litas has been in the mechanism since 2004 and the Latvian lats since 2005.

Poland agreed to join the euro zone before it entered the European Union in May 2004. But the euro-zone debt crisis has complicated the plan, possibly delaying the currency switch until 2019, the country's finance minister said earlier this year.

Tusk's speech on Friday is unlikely to signal any significant steps toward abandoning the zloty. But Poland's entry into the ERMII exchange rate mechanism could stabilize its currency that now requires regular government and central bank interventions to limit volatility. It could also give Poland--the largest economy in the EU's eastern flank and the second-largest EU member outside the single-currency union--a stronger voice on EU and euro-zone matters.

During Tusk's first term in power, Poland's per-capita wealth versus the EU average has likely jumped 10 percentage points to about 64%. The prime minister now needs to make sure the country grows at least as fast in his second term, in an increasingly unstable external environment.

title: UPDATE 1-Polish zloty within acceptable range-deputy cbank head
text:
(Adds quotes, details)

* Zloty should be stronger

* Central bank could finance domestic purchases of Polish lenders

WARSAW, Nov 16 (Reuters) - The Polish zloty

is trading within an acceptable rang but should be stronger based on its fundamentals, the deputy head of the central bank was quoted as saying on Wednesday.

The unit has lost more than 10 percent of its value since the start of June as the euro zone debt crisis fueled investors flight from riskier assets.

"When it comes to fundamentals, it (the zloty) should be stronger," Witold Kozinski said in an interview published by Warsaw daily Rzeczpospolita. "But considering what is happening currently on the markets, I expect the zloty to remain around the current level."

Poland's central bank has intervened three times this year -- twice in September and once in October -- to prop up the zloty and, according to the central bank's governor, it would not hesitate to step into the spot market further to limit speculation.

Polish authorities are anxious to prevent the currency from a sharp weakening at the end of the year as almost one-third of Poland's debt is in foreign currencies and a sharp fall of the unit would mean breaching the key debt level of 55 percent of GDP.

Kozinski also said that the central bank could help finance the purchase of Polish units put up for sale by troubled foreign parents in order to increase local participation in the financial sector.

Central bank governor Marek Belka and other Polish officials have said they hope the sales would allow domestic players to reduce foreign ownership of the local banking sector from the current 70 percent.

title: *DJ NBP Won't Shy Away From More Zloty  Intervention  - Belka
text:
14 Nov 2011 00:00 EDT *DJ  NBP Determined To Fight Disorderly Market Behavior In Zloty - Belka

14 Nov 2011 00:00 EDT DJ  INTERVIEW: NBP Encouraged By Result Of Zloty Interventions-Belka

-- Polish central bank chief reiterates NBP won't shy away from more zloty intervention

-- NBP determined to fight disorderly zloty market behavior, Belka says 


 
   By Marcin Sobczyk and Gordon Fairclough 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

WARSAW (Dow Jones)--The National Bank of Poland's interventions to prevent the zloty from weakening rapidly have produced an encouraging result and the central bank is ready to step in again if investors exit the Polish currency in a disorderly fashion, said Marek Belka, the central bank's governor.

"We've shown that we wouldn't shy away from emerging in the market and the markets know that they should in their behavior take into account the risk of an NBP intervention. At the same time, we've also stressed that we're not trying to defend any specific exchange rate level," he said in an exclusive interview.

"What we're determined to fight is disorderly behavior. If we see something not substantiated by global tendencies--something that is Poland-specific and unfounded, and not based on our fundamentals--then we'll step in. We've chosen a moment like this a few weeks ago and the result is encouraging for the moment," he added.

The NBP intervened in September to boost the zloty, weakened by the fallout of euro-zone sovereign debt concerns, when it was around PLN4.50 to the euro, bringing it to PLN4.38 within 15 minutes. It has intervened twice since the original move and said its intention was to limit zloty volatility. On Friday afternoon, the zloty traded around PLN4.42 to the euro.

A catastrophic event in the euro zone, which Poland doesn't wish for, would likely weaken the zloty at first, but Poland's sound economy and proven resistance to crises could eventually prompt investors to buy the currency, Belka added.

"The immediate effect would probably be the usual one, which is the weakening of the zloty as the markets react in an instinctive way, escaping to safe havens and most liquid markets, which is the U.S. market," he said. "I wouldn't, however, assume away a reversal and an opposite movement, strengthening the zloty, because the Polish economy seems to be relatively crisis-resistant and then it will be reflected in the zloty."

"But of course we'd rather not take the risk of this tsunami. Surfing a tsunami is always a very risky business," Belka said.

A catastrophic event in the euro zone, which Poland doesn't wish for, would likely weaken the zloty at first, but Poland's sound economy and proven resistance to crises could eventually prompt investors to buy the currency, Belka added.

"The immediate effect would probably be the usual one, which is the weakening of the zloty as the markets react in an instinctive way, escaping to safe havens and most liquid markets, which is the U.S. market," he said. * Polish central bank will step into FX market if necessary

* FX interventions are norm, not extravagance

* Needs to coordinate actions with finance ministry

(Adds background)

WARSAW, Nov 14 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank will not hesitate to intervene further in foreign exchange markets to limit speculation, its head was quoted on Monday as saying.

The Polish central bank stepped into the spot market three times this year -- twice in September and once in October -- to prop up the zloty, which has lost almost 10 percent of its value since the start of June on a global flight from risk.

"Interventions are the absolute norm, a lack of interventions -- an extravagance," Marek Belka said in an interview with daily Gazeta Wyborcza. "If we decide that further actions are necessary, we won't hesitate."

Belka added the central bank needed to keep the finance ministry in the loop about any potential move because the ministry could also boost the zloty by selling EU funds on the foreign exchange market.

State-owned BGK is mandated by the government to regularly convert part of the funds Poland receives from the European Union into zlotys, but it is never clear whether the bank is acting on its own account or for the finance ministry.

Polish authorities used BGK in late December to sell euros on the market, buoying the zloty ahead of the year-end fixing that determines the level of the country's public debt, almost one quarter of which is kept in foreign currencies.

title: WSJ: Polish Bank Chief Builds Defenses
text:
WARSAW (Dow Jones)--Poland should strengthen its defenses against financial contagion from the euro zone by tightening public spending and making plans to intervene if Western European banks with operations here start to falter, the country's central bank chief said.

"We're bracing ourselves for a slowdown," said Marek Belka, governor of the National Bank of Poland. Still, he said, he is confident the country "will be crisis-proof in its ability to avoid a recession," even if conditions in the neighboring euro area deteriorate further.

So far, the Polish economy has proved remarkably resilient. Poland was the only European Union nation that didn't slip into recession after the start of the 2008 global financial crisis. This year, gross domestic product is on track to expand around 4%, but the pace of growth is likely to slow in 2012.

Even so, Mr. Belka called on the government to push ahead with a "more transparent and ambitious fiscal policy" to shore up state finances and win investor approval.

"A rating upgrade is clearly within reach, so why not grab it," Mr. Belka said in an interview. "There's a chance for Poland to be clearly on the right side of the bond market" and to avoid the mistakes of Italy, whose borrowing costs have soared recently because of investors' doubts about the country's commitment to austerity.

"Two months earlier, even two weeks earlier, a clear program of reforms would have changed the game" in Italy, Mr. Belka said. These days, Mr. Belka said, "you have to be ahead of the curve, pre-empt the markets."

Poland is in far stronger financial shape than Italy, whose public debt is equivalent to about 120% of annual economic output. At the end of 2010, Poland's public debt stood at about 55% of GDP.

This year, the general government deficit is set to shrink to 5.6%. The government says it is aiming for a budget gap of less than 3% next year, but the European Commission has said Poland is unlikely to hit that target without deeper cuts in spending, revenue increases or both.

Mr. Belka, who has previously served as finance minister and prime minister of Poland, said pushing through wide-ranging structural change is never easy. But he said now there "is an ideal environment for sending a clear signal to the markets."

Prime Minister Donald Tusk, whose coalition government was re-elected with a solid parliamentary majority last month, has political capital and a respite from elections. He has pledged strong measures to close the budget deficit.

One way the euro crisis could affect Poland, is through its banks, Mr. Belka said. Roughly 70% of Poland's banking assets are controlled by Western European banks. "We're looking at this with some concern," Mr. Belka said. He said that overall, banks in Poland are well-capitalized, liquid and relatively free of bad loans. But he said the central bank was worried about "those banks that may become orphans because their parent banks are in trouble."

Mr. Belka said Polish government institutions and local investors should be prepared to step in if that happens. "We should use the resilience of Polish capital to inject funds," he said, adding that the central bank would stand ready to provide liquidity if necessary.

"I'm not looking for the state to become a shareholder-that's absolutely a last-resort option," Mr. Belka said. But he said Poland has private capital that could be used to put a larger share of the country's banking sector into Polish hands. "There's nothing unusual for a country Poland's size to think about such an evolution," he said.

Belgium's KBC Group NV and Portugal's Banco Comercial Portugues have said they are considering sales of their Polish holdings. Others are also considering selling Polish operations, Polish bankers say. Poland's largest lender, PKO Bank Polski SA, and insurer PZU SA, are potential buyers.

On interest rates, Mr. Belka said the central bank, which last Wednesday held the benchmark rate steady at 4.5%, has leeway to raise or cut as conditions warrant.

"We'd like to keep the economy afloat, with a decent growth rate, but at the same time keep inflation firmly in grip," he said. "If we manage it, we will emerge from the crisis much stronger."

Mr. Belka said the bank resisted rate-cut calls earlier this year from observers worried about the impact of the euro-zone slowdown. After the European Central Bank cut rates, Mr. Belka said: "We sent a signal. Just hold on a minute. We are fighting inflation. Don't forget inflation. We want to keep growing in a healthy way."

-By Gordon Fairclough And  Marcin Sobczyk, The Wall Street Journal; Gordon.Fairclough@wsj.com, Marcin.Sobczyk@wsj.com [ 14-11-11 0501GMT ]

(Emerging Europe Real Time, The Wall Street Journal Online's site for news and analysis on Central and Eastern Europe, can be found at http://blogs.wsj.com/emergingeurope)


 
   Posted by Marcin Sobczyk 
 

WARSAW--The National Bank of Poland's interventions to prevent the zloty from weakening rapidly have produced an encouraging result and the central bank is ready to step in again if investors exit the Polish currency in a disorderly fashion, Marek Belka, the central bank's governor, said in an interview with The Wall Street Journal.

Here is the transcript of his comments:

ZLOTY INTERVENTIONS

"We've shown that we wouldn't shy away from emerging in the market and the markets know that they should in their behavior take into account the risk of an NBP intervention. At the same time, we've also stressed that we're not trying to defend any specific exchange rate level.

"What we're determined to fight is disorderly behavior. If we see something not substantiated by global tendencies--something that is Poland-specific and unfounded, and not based on our fundamentals--then we'll step in. We've chosen a moment like this a few weeks ago and the result is encouraging for the moment."

A catastrophic event in the euro zone, which Poland doesn't wish for, would likely weaken the zloty at first, but Poland's sound economy and proven resistance to crises could eventually prompt investors to buy the currency, he said.

"The immediate effect would probably be the usual one, which is the weakening of the zloty as the markets react in an instinctive way, escaping to safe havens and most liquid markets, which is the U.S. market. I wouldn't, however, assume away a reversal and an opposite movement, strengthening the zloty, because the Polish economy seems to be relatively crisis-resistant and then it will be reflected in the zloty.

"But of course we'd rather not take the risk of this tsunami. Surfing a tsunami is always a very risky business."

POLISH ECONOMIC PROSPECTS:

"My perception of the prospects of the economy isn't bleak at all. Even with a very bad scenario in the euro zone, the Polish economy will be crisis-proof in its ability to avoid a recession. Of course, we're bracing ourselves for a slowdown, but I think it won't be as bad as the pessimists expect.

"If you stay in Brussels too long, you come back with gloom. There's more sunshine in Poland now than in other places. It doesn't mean we are entirely unaffected by what is happening."

POLAND'S CREDIT RATINGS

"We deserve a higher credit rating. For that, we need a more transparent and ambitious fiscal policy. This is something we all expect from the new government. It's not just about playing with the numbers, but also about structural reforms. Poland isn't the most unreformed country in the European Economic Area. We have many strengths, but we also have weaknesses.

"The Prime Minister has recently confirmed in private what he says in public: that he's determined to present a plan of far-reaching reforms, which may be difficult. It's very difficult to propose far-reaching reforms in Poland because we're saying we're not in a crisis---and we're not, but people will then ask what the reform is for.

"But here you have to be ahead of the curve, pre-empt the markets. You have to be on the right side of the bond markets. What we see now in Italy is the exact opposite to what should have been done. Two months earlier, even two weeks earlier, a clear program of reforms would change the game. Now, it will cost them much more, and us too, of course.

"I hope the government understands this. We hope for an ambitious reform plan. You don't have to do everything all at once. But this is optimal timing. The government has three years with no elections, they have a clear parliamentary majority, the opposition in disarray, and the economy is doing much better than all expected. This is an ideal environment for sending a clear signal to the markets that this is a country fit for an upgrade.

"There's a chance for Poland to be clearly on the right side of the bond market. I don't think we'll waste this opportunity. It won't be easy but the alternative is very costly. A rating upgrade is clearly within reach, so why not grab it.

"The zloty could revert to where it belongs---clearly it is undervalued now, which helps exports. But if the zloty weakened, then it should come back by something close to that."

POLAND'S MONETARY POLICY

"As far as monetary policy is concerned, Poland is in a pretty comfortable position. With our interest rates, we can go both ways, depending of what's necessary. We haven't put ourselves in the corner of ultra-low rates.

"We're one of the few countries in the advanced world that is serious about fighting inflation. We're betting for the whole stake. We'd like to keep the economy afloat, with a decent growth rate, but at the same time keep inflation firmly in grip. If we manage it, we'll emerge from the crisis much stronger. We'll keep growing, in a healthy way. When inflation gets out of control, the cost of reducing it to sustainable levels is immense.

"A few weeks ago, the markets were pleading for a rate reduction, because of the tsunami from Western Europe. The ECB cut rates. But we sent a signal. Just hold on a minute. We are fighting inflation. Don't forget inflation. We want to keep growing in a healthy way. Low inflation is one thing, moderate dependence on foreign capital is another. It's a vulnerable spot in the Polish economy. If you compare averages, we look very good. But the fact is that most of the increase in public debt last year and this year was financed with foreign capital. This is obviously vulnerability and we have to do something about it."

POLAND SHOULD PREPARE FOR BANKING SECTOR ORPHANS

"There are many channels through which the crisis may propagate itself. I'm less worried about the trade channel. The real unknown is how the European banking sector will survive this. We cannot forget that most of our banks in Poland are subsidiaries of European banking groups. We're looking at this with some concern.

"Our banks very well capitalized and free of toxic assets. Non-performing loans are moderate, at worst. The banks are well provisioned and liquid. However, in these days you don't look at averages. You look at the weakest links in the chain, at those banks that may become orphans because their parent banks are in trouble. And we look at those banks that are excessively engaged in foreign-currency lending.

"The flow is very moderate now. But there is the stock, which clearly has the potential to destabilize those banks. Even a minor problem is something you have to worry about these days.

"Poles have forgotten that 20 years ago we were a bankrupt. We weren't in the situation of Greece---everything was different---but we benefited from debt reduction. Without a very smart licensing policy and opening the banking sector to foreign investors, we would have had a banking crisis.

"Those banks have been, by and large, very good corporate citizens of this country. They've behaved in an exemplary way. But some of those banks could be orphaned.

"We're not talking about nationalizing them, but we should look at domestic capital. We should use the resilience of Polish capital to inject funds. There's nothing unusual for a country Poland's size to think about such an evolution. The country should be prepared for it.

"We should look at private equity, there's enough money now of various origins that can be mobilized by private equity funds. Don't forget PZU, which almost publicly admitted that if there is an opportunity, they'll look at it. If the price is right, the insurer wouldn't be loath to participate. Of course there are some banks with Polish identity, but I wouldn't treat this as the first option.

"I don't have a plan in the sense that there is a ready buyer looking to grab low hanging fruit.

"In this country, we've been educated in the transition to the market. In many respects, we've learned the lessons too eagerly. We have believed all the fairy tales about the free-market economy, so now anything that smells of economic nationalism looks dirty---but just look around. It's like Keynes said: When the facts change, I change my mind.

"We're not talking about grabbing the whole sector. But if there is a situation where a foreign-owned bank becomes an orphan, we should be ready to take action. What's more important here is support for such solutions. Our bank can play a role if necessary. We can provide necessary liquidity, which is by definition short-term. I'm not looking for the state to become a shareholder - that's absolutely a last resort option."
