title: UPDATE 3-Poland presses banks to aid borrowers, orders probe of franc lending
text:
* Over half a million Poles hold mortgages in Swiss francs

* Bankers say won't rush to act, but politicians face election

* Government wants banks to apply Swiss negative interest rates (Updates with central bank governor, paragraph six)

By Marcin Goclowski and Adrian Krajewski

WARSAW, Jan 20 (Reuters) - Poland pressed its banks on Tuesday to provide relief for half a million homeowners faced with soaring repayments on mortgage loans denominated in Swiss francs and ordered an investigation into the lending practice.

A surge in the value of the franc since the Swiss National Bank scrapped its cap against the euro last week has seen mortgage instalments jump on Poland's stock of franc-denominated home-loans - $36 billion-worth as of November, or almost 8 percent of output in central Europe's biggest economy.

Stressing he saw no threat to the banking system as a whole, Finance Minister Mateusz Szczurek said local banks should apply the below-zero interest rates of Switzerland on franc-denominated mortgage loans in Poland.

Szczurek spoke after several hours of talks with the governor of the central bank and heads of commercial banks. He told private broadcaster TVN24 BiS there had been no discussion of freezing the exchange rate of the Swiss franc against the national currency, a move Croatia is pursuing, or additional loan collateral on the part of banks.

"The client accepts the foreign exchange risk, while the bank accepts the interest rate risk. That's a fair deal," he said, adding the finance ministry did not plan to intervene in support of the zloty against the franc.

Poland's central bank governor Marek Belka said the franc was unlikely to reach the psychologically important level of 5 zlotys from its present 4.27 level. "What was to happen, has already happened," he told TVN24.

Many home buyers in central and eastern Europe took out Swiss franc-denominated mortgages in the 2000s. Despite warnings about the risks from some economists at the time, they opted for the loans which carried interest rates in the low single digits over paying double-digit rates on zloty mortgages.

With the franc up about 20 percent against the zloty since last week, these borrowers now face a huge jump in their mortgage repayments, piling pressure on the Polish government to act with parliamentary elections due in October.

"When I heard the news about the franc my first reaction was disbelief. Then came slight horror - what would happen next," said 40-year-old lawyer Jacek Sledzinski, whose monthly mortgage instalment on a two-bedroom flat in Warsaw has shot up more than 900 zlotys ($241) since Wednesday last week.

"SITUATION VOLATILE, EMOTIONAL"

Prime Minister Ewa Kopacz ordered an investigation on Tuesday into the lending practice.

The government issued a statement that the regulatory inquiry should verify that the banks' activities "do not affect the legally protected interests of borrowers-consumers".

Poland's anti-monopoly watchdog also said it would investigate whether such mortgage deals took into account the Swiss central bank's imposition of negative interest rates, and whether Polish banks were seeking to impose additional insurance costs on borrowers.

Croatia said on Monday it would fix the franc exchange rate against the local kuna currency for one year, and Hungary said both Zagreb and Warsaw had shown interest in Budapest's move late last year to convert foreign currency mortgages into forints.

Serbia's government also said banks were looking at possible steps to extend the term of franc loan repayments, partial conversions of the loans or possibly lowering interest rates.

But Serbian Finance Minister Dusan Vujovic appeared to rule out fixing the franc rate against the dinar. "They cannot do anything about the exchange rate," he said in Vienna.

Poland's plight dwarfs that of Serbia or Croatia, but Zagreb, like Warsaw, faces an election later this year and is under pressure to act.

The Croatian rate-fixing plan is expected to come before parliament this week, and the country's banking association urged lawmakers to reject it, saying the freeze should last only three months pending a longer-term solution.

"The situation is volatile and emotional; it's not the time to take violent decisions," one Polish banker, who asked not to be named, told Reuters. "We will analyse the situation to assess how the franc influences our asset quality, and will take the decision no earlier than in three months."

Banks, however, may not have that long, given the pressure on the ruling Civic Platform party to act before the election in which it is running neck-and-neck with the Law and Justice party, according to an opinion poll published by the Rzeczpospolita daily on Tuesday.

"I know that some banks are working (on this) and in the next few weeks they will suggest, most likely, keeping the December exchange rates (for some time)," Krzysztof Pietraszkiewicz, the head of the Banks Association, told private radio TOK FM. ($1 = 3.7365 zlotys) (Additional reporting by Pawel Sobczak, Pawel Florkiewicz, Wiktor Szary and Jakub Iglewski; Writing by Matt Robinson; Editing by David Stamp and Pravin Char)

title: Swiss Move Shows  Central Bank  Can't Operate in Isolation
text:
By Michael J. Casey

Swiss National Bank's game-altering move to end the Swiss franc's ceiling against the euro creates challenges for its European counterparts, while traders are given a new safe haven option.

The lesson: No central bank is an island.

Three years ago, when the SNB capped the Swiss franc's value against the euro, it diminished the currency's traditional role as a parking space when other currencies were in trouble. That limited the options for a stampede of investors leaving the euro and later became an issue for those fleeing the Russian ruble.

Switzerland's historical reputation for financial stability -- and the fact that it was an advanced European economy outside the European Union -- kept a modest money flow going there. But without the prospect of exchange gains, many money managers went elsewhere. Some went to traditional havens such as the dollar or the yen, others chased European alternatives like the Polish zloty, Swedish krona or Czech koruna. Those smaller central banks found themselves in the middle of a battle between two bigger players, the SNB and the European Central Bank. The latest development once again puts them in the crossfire.

In ending the 1.20 Swiss-franc floor at which it vowed to buy euros, the SNB blasted a dam and unleashed a monetary flood. Most eyes are watching where that flow is going: into the Swiss franc, which has soared versus the euro. But it's also worth thinking about where it's coming from. The euro is the obvious loser, but consider the zloty: Poland's currency immediately dropped 21% against the franc in the aftermath, but also 2.2% against the dollar and 1.45% against the euro.

In truth, both Poland's and Sweden's currencies had been weakening against the euro well before the SNB's latest move, which is saying something, given that the euro is down around 15% versus the dollar over the past 12 months. But their declines were an indirect result of the SNB's interventions, which forced euro sellers into their currencies. That initially led to overvaluations, and prompted those countries' central banks to tamp them down. The Swedish Riksbank slashed rates to zero and revisited the idea of negative rates it had first used during the global financial crisis. The National Bank of Poland employed a periodic intervention policy to push the zloty lower. Markets eventually got the message, but not before inflation in both countries, as well as the Czech Republic, was headed inexorably toward zero.

Now, these central banks must suddenly return to the drawing board. On Wednesday, Poland's central bank announced it was considering cutting rates, a suggestion that it still thought the zloty was too strong. A day later it's worried about a plummeting zloty. Polish rate cuts are likely off the table for now.

The fallout from this is a reminder that central banks never operate in a bubble -- not the National Bank of Poland, not the Swiss National Bank, not even the European Central Bank or the U.S. Federal Reserve, though it's always true that the actions of the bigger bank impact the smaller one more than the other way around.

In fact, the SNB policies over the past three years are direct responses to those of a bigger bank. The ECB's struggle to, first, resolve the eurozone debt crisis and, then, to contain the regional economic deterioration, drove a steady flow of euros into francs. If that flow had been allowed to boost the franc's valuation, it would have hurt Swiss exporters -- hence the SNB's imposition of a euro price floor. Ultimately, though, it was again the ECB that foiled the Swiss central bank's policy. In hinting at a big new bond-buying, or quantitative easing, program, the ECB drove a new, large influx of euros into francs, so many that its Swiss counterpart could no longer keep buying them to maintain the CHF1.20 rate.

Today's move "reflects the absence of central bank coordination" and the need for it, says Larry Goodman, President of the Center for Financial Stability in New York. "It shows how central bank policies radiate from the Fed to the ECB to the Swiss National Bank."

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Emerging-market assets get respite as dollar pulls back
text:
LONDON, Oct 9 (Reuters) - A decline by the dollar boosted most emerging-market assets on Thursday, with the main equity index up 1 percent and bond yields at multi-week or even record lows. The rouble steadied after hefty central bank interventions.

Bond yields in Poland hit record lows across the curve after a larger-than-expected rate cut, dragging down yields in central Europe. South African yields tumbled to one-month lows, tracking U.S. Treasury moves.

The dollar and U.S. bond yields fell after minutes of the Federal Reserve's last meeting suggested the Fed would maintain its accommodative monetary policy. Traders said some expectations for the Fed's first rate rise have shifted to September 2015 from June.

"Dollar weakness, EM happy!" said Ilan Solot, a strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman. "I personally think this is an opportunity to go long dollar again. It's obvious this is a temporary pullback for the dollar."

MSCI's emerging equity index rose 1.2 percent . Russian stocks jumped almost 2 percent, getting help from slightly higher oil prices . Bourses in central Europe rose 1 to 2 percent .

Currencies from the Malaysian ringgit to the South African rand rose from multi-week lows against the dollar. The rand gained 0.3 percent, rising for the fourth straight day. South African bond yields meanwhile fell to one-month lows, having declined more than 30 basis points this week.

But the mood towards Russia remained bearish. Western sanctions and corporate demand for dollars to repay external debt have pushed the rouble to record lows and kept foreigners out of local stock and bond markets.

Ten-year rouble bond yields were at three-week highs and the rouble held near the psychologically key level of 40 per dollar , even though by some estimates the central bank sold around $3.5 billion from Friday to Wednesday.

The bank moved the rouble trading band against a euro-dollar basket by 20 kopecks on Wednesday, implying heavy dollar sales.

Benoit Anne, head of emerging markets strategy at Societe Generale said Russia needed to change its tactics on the rouble.

"This piecemeal, soft intervention is simply a waste of reserves. The intervention is too gentle to influence the market ... which means that the central bank is set to burn $1 billion a day or so in official reserves for the foreseeable future," Anne said in a note.

"I would rather see a central bank that would engage in much more powerful action ... In fact, I would prefer to see an interest-rate defense of the currency," he added.

The central bank kept rates on hold last month but hinted it might raise them if its inflation target was in danger.

Central European bonds extended gains after Poland cut rates by a 50 bps, more than expected. Polish yields tumbled to record lows across the curve, with 10-year yields now at 2.75 percent , down 20 bps from their Monday close.

Hungarian yields also fell to record lows, with the 10-year down 25 bps to 4.15 percent.

Citi analysts advised buying 10-year Polish and Hungarian bonds, noting the trade also benefits from euro zone stimulus.

"We are getting back to central European bonds, we are buying (zloty and forint) unhedged," they told clients.

The Turkish lira rose to two-week highs after the Fed message. Ten-year bond yields fell around 15 bps. Stocks rose 2.5 percent to one-week highs

Analysts advise caution on Turkish assets because of fighting in Syria. At least 21 people were killed on Wednesday after Turkish Kurds protested against the government for doing nothing to protect Kurds in Syria.

"Given the confluence of negative political and economic developments, Turkish assets should underperform," Solot of BBH said.

text:
WARSAW, June 3 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank governor Marek Belka said on Tuesday the bank has the option of intervening in the foreign currency market if it believes the zloty is too volatile.

The Polish zloty gained more than one percent versus euro in the last two weeks on speculation that the European Central Bank may cut rates, increasing the credit cost disparity between Poland and euro zone.

"We are here adhering to a policy of a free-float for the zloty, supplemented with the possibility of an intervention when we recognize that market dynamics are extensive," Belka told a news conference when asked if he was worried about the strength of the zloty. title: *Poland Reserved About Euro Adoption -- Finance Minister
text:
27 May 2014 10:30 ET *Poland Needs More Time to Get Ready for Euro -- Finance Minister

27 May 2014 10:30 ET *Poland Needs Lower Public Debt to Join Euro Area -- Finance Minister

27 May 2014 10:30 ET *Poland's Finance Minister Szczurek Comments from WSJ Interview

27 May 2014 10:30 ET  Poland Remains Reserved on Euro Adoption, Says Finance Minister


By Patryk Wasilewski 

WARSAW--Poland remains reserved about adopting the euro, its finance minister said in an interview Tuesday, despite suggestions that euro-zone membership could offer added security amid concerns about potential Russian aggression.

Mateusz Szczurek said Tuesday that Poland would consider joining the European single-currency area when the country thinks the move will benefit the economy and won't threaten its financial stability.

"Indeed in relation to the Ukrainian crisis there are voices in Poland and in the [Central European] region that for security and political reasons a quicker euro entry is needed," Mr. Szczurek said. "Our view is unchanged. Euro entry can improve our security and guarantee us a bigger impact on the European Union's policies only in tandem with our growing economic strength."

The conflict between Russia and Ukraine has made Poland and others in the European Union's east nervous that they could potentially become targets of Russian aggression in the future.

Amid those concerns, Poland's central bank Gov. Marek Belka said in March that the conflict adds another element to the discussion about adopting the euro.

Romania recently set its euro-entry target for 2019.

Poland originally planned to replace the zloty with the euro in 2012 but abandoned the target when it failed to meet criteria for candidates during the global financial crisis.

Mr. Szczurek said Poland needs to bridge the wealth divide that separates it from the more affluent EU nations before setting a new target date for adopting the euro.

The euro-zone debt crisis demonstrated that membership of the bloc alone doesn't strengthen the economy, Mr. Szczurek said.

With the bloc struggling to grow and some of the euro zone's members suffering financial problems, support for the euro in Poland has waned, with recent TNS OBOP opinion poll showing only a small minority now supporting accession over the next 10 years.

Opponents argue that Poland is already taking full advantage of being part of the EU and that retaining its own currency allows the economy to absorb shocks and increase competitiveness.

Without a floating currency, one of the few tools at Poland's disposal to intervene in the economy, the country would need to increase public spending and deficits at times of downturn. To create room for such actions after joining the euro, Poland will have to cut its public debt to around 40% of gross domestic product, Mr. Szczurek said.

Public debt is around 50% of GDP and the country continues to run fiscal deficits.

Increased government spending at the height of the global financial crisis in 2009, as well as a steady stream of EU funds into the country, made Poland the only EU member to avoid a recession that year.

After a period of slow economic growth, Poland's economy is now recovering.

Mr. Szczurek said growth this year could top the ministry's forecast of 3.3% GDP growth, with the public finance deficit "very likely" narrowing to 3.5% of GDP from 4.3% in 2013.

Another obstacle Poland faces on its path toward euro-area membership is the requirement for candidates to keep their currencies in a relatively narrow corridor to the euro for two years.

Poland's central bank governor previously said this would lead to interventions and pressure on the zloty to strengthen, which would reduce Poland's competitiveness.

Mr. Szczurek echoed those concerns in the interview, saying that some of the requirements to join the euro area, such as keeping a lid on public spending, "are worth pursuing even without the plan to join the euro zone" but that keeping the zloty in the pre-euro currency grid isn't a good idea.

Poland will also likely wait before joining a proposed banking union for the EU, Mr. Szczurek said.

Poland's policy makers have said the European banking regulator may prove to be less prudent than its domestic counterpart, whose conservative approach is seen as one of the reasons why Poland's banking sector weathered the global financial crisis well.

Poland also has its own bank-deposit guarantee program financed by the banks themselves.

"Our domestic banking sector, regulator and guarantee systems are too good to risk changing them without making sure how the European mechanisms work in practice," Mr. Szczurek said. "However, we are interested in the success of the banking union because a strong and stable banking system in the European Union is beneficial to Poland."

title: Polish  Central Bank  Keeps Benchmark Rate Unchanged--Update
text:
WARSAW-Poland's central bank on Wednesday extended its informal neutral bias faced with subdued price growth, a moderate economic recovery and the Russian-Ukrainian conflict, the bank's governor said.

The bank left the benchmark rate unchanged at 2.5%, the lowest on record, and said borrowing costs would remain unchanged until at least the end of the third quarter of this year and possibly even longer. Poland's central bank previously said rates would remain on hold until at least the end of the second quarter.

Poland should have very low consumer price inflation for longer than previously expected, said Marek Belka, head of Poland's central bank. The bank said CPI would likely be near the 2.5% target some time in 2016.

The Russian-Ukrainian conflict and what Poland sees as an armed intervention in Crimea accelerated the extension of the Polish central bank's neutral stance on rates.

"The situation in Ukraine sped up our decision to show that we don't see any threats for the economy, at least as to monetary policy," Mr. Belka said. "We wanted to show our confidence in the strength of the economy's fundamentals and the zloty."

Following Russia's actions in Ukraine, Mr. Belka said this week Poland could reconsider its stalled euro-zone membership bid to integrate even more closely with the rest of Europe.

By joining the euro area, the core of the European Union, Poland would be able to shield itself better from any turmoil from outside the bloc, Mr. Belka said Wednesday.

"When you're a euro zone member, the situation in the country more directly impacts other euro-zone countries. Imagine Italy's economic problems 30 years ago-would Germany or France lament over them?" he said.

"Today what's going on in one large euro-zone country directly impacts the economic stability of other countries. That is the point of entering the single-currency area," he added.

In economic terms, risks are huge and benefits more modest than they appeared previously, Mr. Belka also said. Poland's current government originally planned for the country to join the euro zone in 2012 but abandoned the plan amid the global financial crisis. In recent months, officials have been reserved about the membership prospect.

The Polish currency briefly reacted to heightened tensions between Russia and Ukraine this week, moving near 4.22 zlotys to the euro on Monday. On Wednesday afternoon, it was back near 4.18, stable on the day.

Sharing land borders with Russia and Ukraine, Poland has encouraged its European Union and North Atlantic Treaty Organization allies to stand up to the Kremlin. One of the main reasons behind its push in the 1990s to join Western European economic and political organizations was hope that even a resurgent Russia would be less likely to challenge Poland as part of a larger alliance.

title: Polish PM Says No Need to  Intervene  to Prop Up Zloty - Report
text:
WARSAW--Poland has no need to intervene to prop up the zloty hit by a broader emerging-markets selloff, the country's prime minister said over the weekend.

The Polish currency has weakened some 2.5% to the euro since mid-January, trading near 4.25 on Monday morning.

"When we compare the situation of the zloty with [the currencies of] other emerging markets, the weakening is luckily incomparably smaller than is the case with other currencies, whether it's the forint, the Turkish currency, the Indian rupee, or currencies of Argentina or Brazil," Donald Tusk said, according to state newswire PAP.

"We have institutions that have various tools and instruments to act in situations that require such action. At this point, fortunately there's no such need, but we're watching this very closely," he said.

Poland's central bank, independent from the government, intervened in 2011 and again in June 2013 to prop up the zloty when it was weakening rapidly. In 2013, the intervention occurred with the zloty above 4.30 to the euro. In 2011, they intervened with the zloty around 4.50 to the euro.

The government has the ability to buy zlotys in the market with the euros and other currencies at its disposal. At the end of December, the Polish finance ministry held an equivalent of 3.16 billion euro ($4.26 billion). It can also buy currencies through the state-owned bank BGK.

Mr. Tusk said intervention at this time may not be effective because the zloty is weakening due to global factors.

"If we recognized the zloty was a victim of speculation, of any action focused on our currency, we intervened more than once in a rapid and effective way," he said. "If the Polish currency is exposed to global events, interventions bear risk and may not be effective. In any case, there's no reason for any non-standard reaction for now."

text:
(Adds new comments, prices)
    * Forint hovers near 2-year lows, rate outlook uncertain
    * Leu bucks trend after Romanian central bankintervenes
    * Poland says would worry more about zloty gains than falls

    By Sandor Peto
    BUDAPEST, Jan 30 (Reuters) - The forint fell to two-year
lows against the euro on Thursday, extending losses after the
central bank suggested it could cut interest rates again and as
a further sell-off in emerging markets hit Central Europe's most
liquid assets.
    The leu bucked the regional trend after the Romanian central
bankintervened in the market to provide support in its first
such move this year, dealers said. 
    A rout in emerging market currencies has started to spread
to Central Europe, which had previously held up relatively well
compared to currencies such as the Turkish lira or the South
African rand, because the region was supported by better
economic fundamentals.
    The forint has seen the biggest hit, which
accelerated on Wednesday after central bank Governor Gyorgy
Matolcsy said low inflation left some room for the bank to cut
its base rate further from a record low 2.85 percent.
    That prospect made investors nervous, contrasting with
rising Hungarian bond yields and rate hikes in several other
emerging markets.
    The forint fell against the euro on Thursday to levels
unseen since early 2012. It rebounded from technical support
levels at 312.50 three times during the session, and at 1526 GMT
it was bid at 310.41, still down 0.6 percent from Wednesday.
    The forint is by far central Europe's worst-performing
currency this year, with losses of more than 4 percent.
    Government bond prices recovered from sharp early falls.
    The yield at a 12-month Treasury bill auction jumped to 3.51
percent from 2.84 percent two weeks ago. Forward rate agreements
also signalled uncertainty over interest rates, pricing in 55
basis points worth of rate hikes for the next 3 months.
    Market participants said further fast falls in the forint
could make the Hungarian central bankintervene or halt its rate
cuts, but any bets that it could be forced into reversing
monetary easing stood little chance of materialising.
    "They (investors) single out the forint instinctively but
they forget that this market is not what it used to be a few
years back," one Budapest-based dealer said.  
    "They cannot force the central bank into rate hikes," the
dealer added. "The current account is massively in surplus,
there is a huge inflow of euros from EU funds, so even if they
try they will get nowhere."
    Societe Generale analyst Benoit Anne said in a note that
hedge funds which pushed the Turkish and South African central
banks into interest rate hikes could do the same in other
emerging markets including Hungary. 
    "I have quite a bit more faith in the NBP (central bank) in
Poland, but I would also like to point out that the PLN (zloty)
is quite expensive relative to its peers and therefore
constitutes a prime target," he added.
   
    POLAND PLAYS DOWN CONTAGION
    Hungarian markets have been worst hit in the region because
the central bank headed by Matolcsy, a key ally of Prime
Minister Viktor Orban who is seeking re-election in April, has
been aggressively cutting rates from 7 percent in 2012.   
    The Polish central bank has already finished its own rate
cuts and Poland has better debt ratings than junk-rated Hungary.
But the zloty is still vulnerable to emerging market contagion
as the region's most liquid unit, making it easy to sell.
    The zloty also rebounded against the euro in the
afternoon. It was weaker by 0.4 percent from Wednesday, but at
4.232 it is still far from 4.35, the level where the Polish
central bank last intervened to defend the currency last year.
    "The current EM currency weakening is chiefly of a
speculative character," one Warsaw-based dealer said. "So a time
will come when the speculators will be booking profits and then
the zloty should rebound thanks to its strong fundamentals."
    Polish Finance Minister Mateusz Szczurek said the zloty's 2
percent weakening since last Thursday was no concern and it was
more worrying that strong economic fundamentals could lead to a
strengthening of the currency.     
    The leu firmed 0.6 percent to 4.508 per euro after
Romania's central bank bought it in the market through
commercial banks to defend it, dealers said. ING said in a note
that "4.50/EUR looks like a close target on the near-run radar."
    One dealer in Bucharest said: "It was a good moment to step
in indirectly. The amount sold is pretty large."

title: Poland's c.bank not concerned about zloty - official
text:
WARSAW, Jan 29 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank is not worried about the zloty currency, because the fundamentals of the economy are strong and the currency weakened due to external factors, a member of the bank's board said.

Eugeniusz Gatnar also told state news agency PAP that a rise in the currency's volatility would be a negative development, but there was no reason for concern for now.

The zloty has fallen 1.3 percent to 4.2150 to the euro since last Thursday, hit by turmoil in other emerging markets that led the Turkish central bank to an emergency rate hike to defend the tumbling lira currency.

"Markets are nervous, investors act under the influence of emotions and there is herding among investors," Gatnar said. "Our fundamentals are strong though, so there are no reasons for zloty weakening."

Poland's central bankintervened to support the zloty in June last year when it traded at around 4.3 zlotys to the euro. Poland's central bank has repeatedly said that it is ready to intervene to curb excessive volatility.

"We monitor the situation closely, as always. It would be a negative phenomenon if volatility increased. But for now we don't see a reason for concern, " Gatnar said. ($1 = 3.0910 Polish zlotys) (Reporting by Marcin Goclowski; Editing by Elaine Hardcastle)

title: Polish Rate Setter Zielinska: Zloty Secure, Economy Safe and Sound
text:
WARSAW--Poland's currency is safeguarded from market turbulence despite its current weakness because the country's economy is viewed as stable and it will grow robustly again this year, while monetary policy is conservative, a central banker said in an interview.

Some emerging currencies depreciated this week as investors sold riskier assets and sought the safety of U.S. papers amid fears about the robustness of the global economy's recovery.

Tracking the euro's decline against the U.S. dollar, the Polish zloty Friday hit a four-month low against the euro and traded at 4.22 at around noon local time. The Hungarian forint traded at its weakest level since March 2013, around 306 forints to the euro after Hungry's central bank this week cut its benchmark rate to 2.85%, a level many economists consider excessively low for the economy.

The Czech koruna was broadly stable Friday at its weakest level since 2009, where it has been since early November when the country's central bank intervened to weaken the currency and spur inflation and growth.

The Polish currency continues to be supported by Poland's relatively resilient economy and the central bank's conservative policy, Anna Zielinska-Glebocka told The Wall Street Journal. The benchmark rate in the European Union's largest emerging economy is 2.5%, despite a series of cuts in 2012-2013 it remains significantly above the euro zone's 0.25% or neighboring Czech Republic's 0.05%.

"For the time being, no risks for the zloty are in sight and let it remain so," Mrs. Zielinksa-Glebocka.

The Polish central bank has intervened into the local market several times since 2011 to prop up the currency at times when it said volatility and the pace of weakening was excessive.

"[We] won't start engaging in currency wars [now]," Mrs. Zielinska-Glebocka said. "Although of course we monitor the spread between interest rates in Poland and for example the euro zone."

The central bank's governor, Marek Belka, has repeatedly said the National Bank of Poland is at all times ready to intervene again to prevent any rapid changes to the zloty exchange rate.

The 10-strong rate panel in January reiterated interest rates will remain unchanged at least until June.

"Certainly our next move will be to increase interest rates, but when that happens will depend on the forecasts due in March," Mrs. Zielinska-Glebocka said. "At the moment it is really difficult to say when monetary policy tightening will begin."

Poland's central bank releases its official inflation and growth projections every four months. In its latest projections in November, it forecast growth at 2.9% and inflation at 1.7% this year. However, Mrs. Zielinska-Glebocka said growth will likely be higher than 3%.

At this rate, Poland's growth would be faster than the respective central bank forecasts of 1.5% for the Czech economy and 2.1% for Hungary.

"It is possible that annual growth will be at 3.5%-3.8% in particular quarters," Mrs. Zielinska-Glebocka said.

Poland's economy will in turn once again grow relatively fast after a slump last year, when it grew only 1.3%, according to the central bank, one of the worst figures for the past two decades.

Polish CPI could reach the bank's 2.5% target but only in 2015 and will likely be lower than projected in November, she said.

This may mean the Polish central bank will keep rates on hold beyond the first half of this year and it's not certain borrowing costs will go up in 2014, Mrs. Zielinska-Glebocka said.

been boosted by expectations the U.S. Federal Reserve will keep

government shutdown.

percent.

forecast that we will see the first interest rate hikes in Q3 of
2014," Millennium Bank analyst Mateusz Sutowicz said.
    "Moreover, due to the government shutdown in the U.S., the
Fed should be less likely to taper its QE3 programme this year."
    The Fed's stimulus has sent cheap money into emerging
markets, buoying currencies in the region at a time when central
bank have been cutting rates to boost slumping economies.
    Serbia's central bank cut its main interest rate by 50 basis
points to 10.5 percent on Friday, its first cut since June. 
   The bank said it had been able to cut its benchmark rate,
which is still the highest in the region, because its policies,
combined with low agricultural prices and weak demand had helped
bring down inflation.

title: DJ South African Rand Leads Gains Among Emerging  Currencies
text:
The South African rand recovered and led a strengthening of most emerging-market currencies against the dollar Wednesday.

The dollar fell 0.87% against the rand, according to CQG data.

As the U.S. government shutdown heads into its second day, market participants are uncertain as to how long the impasse in congressional negotiations would last. Some investors have scaled back from long dollar positions, and added exposure, at least temporarily to emerging-market currencies.

"Our view is that this is a dollar negative," said Lauren van Biljon, strategist at First Advantage Wells Fargo International bond fund.

In her firm, they have added exposure to the Polish zloty but scaled back some of the exposure to the Mexican peso last week. But, for the most part, she said they were waiting for more clarity before stepping back into the market.

"It's just stunned silence now," she said. "Nothing is happening, so we can't trade on it."

The Mexican peso has lagged other emerging-market currencies over the past two days as investors take into account Mexico's close ties to the U.S. and on worries that if the U.S. economy were to slow down once again, Mexico would be affected too.

The short-term outlook on Mexico also has weakened as the country's growth rate is expected slow down below 1.5% this year under the double whammy of hurricanes Ingrid and Manuel.

The dollar fetched MXN13.1478 on the day, a tad better than the MXN13.1543 close the previous day.

The rand benefited from the improved sentiment among investors.

The currency, which had trailed in recent sessions on global factors and concerns about local mining strikes, was once again edging closer to ZAR10 to the dollar, a critical level. Earlier in the day, the dollar-rand pair had soared to ZAR10.1526 for the first time in a week.

Similarly, the Brazilian real has come back on the expectations of more rate increases, a policy with a focus on bringing more investment dollars into the country and a central bank that has been intervening to support the currency.

In Poland, the central bank at its meeting left its key policy rates unchanged and said it didn't expect to be affected by the U.S. government shutdown or debt-ceiling negotiations.

The euro traded at PLN4.2142, a slightly weaker on the day, according to CQG data.

title: DJ Monetary Easing to Continue in Central Europe Next Week
text:
PRAGUE--Further monetary easing is likely in Central Europe next week with an expected lowering of interest rates in Poland, following a cut in Hungary and dovish talk of foreign exchange interventions in the Czech Republic.

In Warsaw, Poland's central bank is expected to cut its benchmark interest rates 0.25 percentage point to a new all-time low of 2.5%, all 18 analysts polled by Dow Jones Newswires said.

The aim is to help the slowing economy regain momentum and to bring slowing inflation closer to the central bank's target of 2.5%, which is the midpoint in the wider 1.5% to 3.5% tolerance range.

The rate council has lowered borrowing costs by two percentage points since November 2012 as the economy nearly stagnated in the first quarter with annual growth of 0.5%, while inflation eased to 0.5% in May.

Originally some market participants saw a risk of a deeper interest rate cut but the recently weakening zloty has shifted expectations.

Since the rate council's early June meeting the zloty has weakened from 4.25 against the euro to 4.32 midday Friday.

"If you asked me a few weeks ago I would have said there is a risk of a 0.5 percentage point rate cut," Raiffeisen Bank economist Marta Petka-Zagajewska said. "However, with the zloty where it is I see a risk there will be no cut at all."

The cut in Poland would follow a similar move in Hungary, where the central bank cut the policy rate 25 basis points to 4.25% on June 25 amid an easing cycle that began in August 2012 in a bid to liven up its lackluster economy.

And would come as the Czech central bank, which has its benchmark rate at the historic low of 0.05%, on Thursday said the likelihood of launching an intervention to weaken the koruna is increasing as it foresees "no tangible inflationary risks."

As it has no more room to lower interest rates, the next available tool is the exchange rate.

"Risks to [the economy] are generally disinflationary; they are pointing towards the need for looser monetary conditions than is expected in [the bank's] forecasts," the central bank said without adding when a move may come.

In Prague, households are slowing returning to shops and spending, but the annual increase in retail sales posted in April is likely to be offset by a minor decrease in May.

The data will follow the early-Friday release of revised Czech gross domestic product data that showed household consumption contracted by a mild 0.5% annually in the first quarter and it actually increased by 1.7% on a quarterly basis in the period.

Households are spending more in step with the government increasing its spending by 1.2% on year and 1% on a quarterly basis in the first three months of this year.

title: CEE MARKETS 2- Currencies  gain, central banks in focus
text:
* Zloty leads Central European currencies stronger


    * Central bank seen intervening to prop up weak zloty
    * Czech, Hungarian central banks meet this week
 (Updates markets, adds stocks, bonds)
    WARSAW/BUDAPEST, June 24 (Reuters) - Central European


currencies traded stronger on Monday led by the previously battered Polish zloty, with investors anticipating further intervention from Poland's central bank if the currency slides again. The zloty, the region's most liquid currency, was up half a percent against the euro by 1437 GMT, the Hungarian forint gained 0.4 percent, the Romanian leu a third of a percent and the Czech crown 0.1 percent. "We are at such weak (zloty) levels and depreciation has been so fast that there could be more and more comments from the central bank about a possible intervention to scare the market," said one Warsaw-based dealer. The Polish currency has shed around 5.3 percent in two months to hover around one-year lows. In response, the central bank stepped to buy the currency on June 7 for the first time in 18 months, and dealers think it may do so again. The Hungarian and the Czech central banks hold policy meetings this week against a backdrop of generally poor sentiment toward emerging market assets. Hungary's central bank is expected to cut rates again on Tuesday but may express concerns that the emerging markets sell-off has hit forint assets and signal that the bank's easing cycle could end soon, a Reuters poll showed. "They are expected by the market to cut this one time by another 25 basis points, then take a breather," a currency dealer said in Budapest. The forint, which is usually among the more volatile currencies in the region, could recoup some of its recent losses once the rate cut is executed, he said. The currency gains happened despite a still-nervous investor mood highlighted by bond yields rising by about 40 basis points in Hungary and a mixed performance on stock markets. Prague stocks fell 2.5 percent to an 18-month low, dragged down by Erste Bank shares, while indexes in Budapest and Warsaw were little changed. title: INSTANT VIEW 2-Polish C/A swings to highest surplus in at least 13 years
text:
WARSAW, June 17 (Reuters) - Poland's current account swung in April to its highest surplus on the record spanning back 13 years, central bank data showed on Monday. The surplus of 468 million euro ($624.31 million), boosted by a rise in exports, contrasted with analysts' expectations of a 185 million deficit. Poland's exports rose by 12.3 percent year-on-year, data show, pointing to an improvement in the country's main export market, Germany. 


    
    FORECAST:
    Analysts polled by Reuters expected a current account
deficit of 185 million euro. 
    
    MARKET REACTION
    The Polish zloty was little changed immediately
after the data.
         
    ANALYSTS' COMMENTS:
    PETER ATTARD MONTALTO, ECONOMIST AT NOMURA: 
    "This record bumping monthly C/A number was partly due to


transfer timing issues but underneath there is strenght in services, which is an ongoing trend, but the weakness in domestic demand versus an export sector that continues to do O.K. is the key story looking through the monthly volatility. "It shows however that PLN is a 'safe' currency given its smaller currency account deficit than some other EM peers."


    
    JAROSLAW JANECKI, ECONOMIST AT SOCIETE GENERALE IN WARSAW:
    "The data proves that trade is strong and has significantly
contributed to economic growth. The highest ever surplus is 
mainly a result of a higher export growth. 
    "In the short term the data may support the Polish currency.
It is rather neutral for the Monetary Policy Council." 
    
    PIOTR BIELSKI, SENIOR ECONOMIST AT BZ WBK:
    "The figures are double positive. First, they indicate a
surplus and second is the source. We saw a great reading in
exports, they rose by 12 percent.
    "It's too early to say whther this reverses the trend.
Perhaps there were some one-off factors.
    "These figures improve our view of the economic outlook. We
now expect that the rise in GDP in the second quarter will be
higher than we earlier thought.
    "These numbers should have a positive impact on the zloty. I
don't think they will be a deciding factor for the MPC. The
Council keeps an eye on inflation which will be near zero in the
coming months."

title: CEE MORNING BRIEFING: Hungary Debt Sale Eyed as Yields Rising
text:
TODAY'S CALENDAR 
Local/GMT 
1130/0930 Hungary government bond auction 
1400/1200 Polish May inflation 
 

Rising bond yields on markets across Europe are making Thursday's debt sale in Budapest an event to watch, while in Poland fresh inflation data may put the country's central bank in a pickle.

Hungary's Government Debt Management Agency plans to sell a total of 38 billion forints ($169.5 million) worth of bonds at auction, which comes as the country's sovereign yields have risen around 150 basis points over the past two weeks.

Amid global concerns that the U.S. Federal Reserve and other central banks may wind down their easy money policies, investors have reduced exposure to regional bond markets, pushing yields higher and making currencies volatile.

Dalimil Vyskovsky, a fixed-income trader at Komercni Banka in Prague, said that rising yields create a good buying opportunity.

On Wednesday, the Czech Finance Ministry auctioned two bond issues. Demand for a 15-year paper was subdued, but the six-year paper was nearly twice oversubscribed, indicating that cash-rich local banks are eager to invest in higher yielding assets, Mr. Vyskovsky said.

In Warsaw, Poland's consumer inflation is expected to edge down further, putting the country's Monetary Policy Council in a bind about whether to further cut interest rates in July to stimulate economic growth, but risking additional zloty sell-offs.

Poland's central bankintervened last Friday, pushing the zloty to about 4.22 against the euro from 4.30 earlier that week. Central bank officials have said their intention is not to fight a trend, but to curtail speculator-driven volatility.

title: Poland May Struggle to Support the Zloty
text:
WARSAW--The Polish central bank is expected to further intervene in markets to strengthen the zloty following its surprise move to bolster the currency Friday, but it could find itself swimming against a very powerful tide of emerging-market currency weakness, analysts said Monday.

Market watchers believe the bank sold some 200 million euros ($264 million) Friday, pushing the zloty to about PLN4.22 from above PLN4.30, after it weakened sharply earlier in the week.

Many saw it as a pre-emptive move to support the currency against the likely negative impact of the U.S. Federal Reserve phasing out its quantitative easing plan.

Poland has a history of using currency intervention to help achieve its economic goals. In 2011, the central bank and the finance ministry repeatedly sold foreign currencies in exchange for the zloty. The central bank wanted to clamp down on unruly market behavior while the finance ministry aimed to keep Poland's foreign debt below levels that would trigger austerity measures under the country's self-imposed system of debt thresholds.

It may not be so straightforward this time. Some analysts warn that Poland's central bank doesn't have enough foreign currency firepower to prop up the zloty if there is a strong a downward trend across the emerging market currencies.

"The big difference is that in 2011 we had local factors at play and local goals," said BZ WBK economist Piotr Bielski.

This time the zloty is coming under pressure alongside all emerging market currencies and bonds following the U.S. Federal Reserve's recent comment that it could soon start winding down its bond-buying program.

The prospect of tighter U.S. monetary policy has prompted many investors to sell riskier assets in favor of safe-haven currencies and bonds.

A Warsaw-based currency dealer said that if the U.S. were to unwind QE quickly, the Polish central bank could be left struggling if it tries to bet against the market. "It could be able to smooth the ride or slow it down at most," the dealer said.

In 2011 the Polish central bank sold foreign currencies worth much less than EUR5 billion, governor Marek Belka said at the time. In May the bank's foreign currency reserves stood at EUR84.7 billion.

The central bank seems aware it is unlikely to buck the global trend and wants instead to show that investors who speculate against the zloty will be punished.

"Somebody thought he will make money on the zloty's weakening and got burned," Mr. Belka said after Friday's intervention.

ING BSK's chief Warsaw economist, Rafal Benecki, suggested investors should heed the governor's words if they are looking for clues about future intervention. Instead of looking at how close the zloty is to PLN4.3 against the euro they should monitor the speed of any changes and the broader regional currency trend.

"The zloty was weakening faster than other currencies in the region and this is what most likely worried the NBP," said ING's Mr. Benecki.

The zloty fell 0.75% against the euro on Monday, slightly less than the Hungarian forint and slightly more than the Czech koruna.

Still, the Polish central bank's intervention didn't scare everyone.

"The intervention really doesn't change my view. The Polish zloty remains a sell," said Benoit Anne, head of emerging market strategy at Societe Generale in London. "The market forces are going to prevail. I've yet to see a central bank that will be credible enough to generate fear on the part of emerging market investors betting for weaker currencies."

Romania is another candidate for intervention, although it hasn't done so yet despite the leu falling to its weakest level against the euro since late October. It is down 3% from the beginning of June.

"Emerging markets enter this week vulnerable, with the potential for markets to test policy makers further in terms of their willingness to act," said Gillian Edgeworth, chief emerging Europe, Middle East and Africa economist at UniCredit in London. "In Romania we have been surprised by the absence of the National Bank of Romania from the market, particularly given such a large move in the Romania leu against the euro."

title: DJ Poland May Take Further Zloty Action
text:
(FROM THE WALL STREET JOURNAL 6/10/13) 
   By Patryk Wasilewski 

WARSAW -- Poland's central bank may again intervene on the local currency market in order to limit the Polish zloty's volatility, central bank Governor Marek Belka told state news agency PAP late Friday, hours after the bank stepped into the market for the first time since December 2011.

The intervention Friday took the market by surprise as it came only two days after the governor said the recent zloty weakening is a welcome trend as it helps the slowing economy regain competitiveness.

"We never preannounce these things, and if someone thought that we will not do it, then I am sorry, but we do not act in the interest of FX market speculators," Mr. Belka said. "Somebody thought he will make money on the zloty weakening and got burned."

As a result, the zloty strengthened against the euro to about 4.23 from above 4.30 before the intervention.

Mr. Belka explained Friday the central bank's goal wasn't to defend some specific zloty level, but rather curb recent zloty volatility that pushed the currency to a weakest level in a year against the euro on Thursday.

title: 2nd UPDATE: Polish  Central Bank Intervenes  To Weaken Zloty
text:
(Adds comment, detail.) 
 
   By Malgorzata Halaba and Marynia Kruk 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

WARSAW (Dow Jones)--The National Bank of Poland intervened Friday afternoon to weaken the rapidly strengthening zloty, for the first time since its floatation in April 2000.

And while the intervention will probably only weaken the currency temporarily, economists agree it has shown that the central bank is going to be an active player and may come back to the market when needed.

"The move is of a signaling nature," Mateusz Szczurek, chief economist at ING Bank Slaski, said in a note. "But it does signal the readiness and capability to act, not something obvious after years of idleness."

Still, the central bank's move will "ease" the scope of the strengthening, added Maciej Reluga, chief economist at Bank Zachodni WBK in Warsaw.

"The intervention will not change the trend," he said. "But the average zloty rate will be slightly higher."

Also, because of the intervention, the zloty rate "will not be a one-way bet any longer," Reluga added.

"We maintain an overall positive view on the PLN in a longer term perspective," Nordea said in a research note.

Among positive drivers Nordea listed the relatively healthy economic outlook, potential privatization revenue and polls favoring a ruling Civic Platform president in the presidential elections in the autumn.

"Today's intervention is likely to be followed by more verbal and actual interventions and rate hikes might be postponed if the PLN remains strong," Nordea said.

On Friday, the central bank bought an undisclosed amount of euros at PLN3.8450-PLN3.8500, according to a dealer at ING Bank Slaski.

Thus the bank implemented its earlier warning that it's "technologically and psychologically" prepared to intervene in the currency market to prevent the excessive strengthening of the zloty, which could hamper economic growth.

The zloty has been highly volatile over the past two years, reaching its strongest level ever at PLN3.20 against the euro in July 2008 and weakening dramatically during the global financial crisis to near its all-time weakest level of PLN4.92 against the euro in February 2009.

Over the past 14 months, the Polish currency has regained much of its pre-crisis strength. At 0539 GMT Friday, it stood at PLN3.8468 to the euro. At 1149 GMT, the zloty was at PLN3.8826 to the euro from PLN3.8454 early Friday.

title: CEE MARKETS 4- Poland intervention , Bulgaria ERM-2 delay hit  FX
text:
* Zloty knocked down by central bank intervention

* Bulgaria drops ERM-2 entry plans, mkt spooked

* Investors in wait-and-see mode ahead of Hungary election

(Updates throughout)

By Marius Zaharia and Dagmara Leszkowicz

BUCHAREST/WARSAW, April 9 (Reuters) - The zloty fell on Friday after the Polish central bank's first intervention in 10 years, while other central European currencies were pressured by Bulgaria's decision to delay its euro plans after revealing a hidden budget deficit.

Poland's central bank said in a statement it bought foreign currencies in the market, following a string of comments from officials this week trying to talk the zloty down. [ID:nWSF008905] [ID:nLDE63806P]

The central bank's deputy governor Witold Kozinski said later in the day the bank could not rule out further interventions in the currency market. [ID:nWSF008910]

The intervention raised concerns that policymakers in other central European countries might favour undervalued currencies to help economies recover from their worst recession in decades.

"There is a sentiment others will do the same as Poland. Romania has already done it and now investors are encouraged to think more ... is to come," a dealer in Bucharest said.

Another case of regional contagion occurred after Bulgaria announced it was delaying plans to enter the ERM-2 euro entry waiting zone because of unaccounted procurement deals that have widened the deficit to 3.7 percent of GDP last year from an initial 1.9 percent gap. [ID:nLDE63813A] [ID:nLDE63813L]

Dealers in Romania said investors became concerned that other countries in central Europe could have hidden deficits like Greece, and the leu was worst hit by the Bulgarian news. [ID:nBUC003670]

"Obviously, we may see a deterioration of investor sentiment. We've already seen an impact on the leu," said Melania Hancila, chief economist at Volksbank in Bucharest.

"I do believe that investors will be very carefully assessing data coming from Romania and other countries in the region. CDS quotations may rise because of this situation in Bulgaria."

At 1413 GMT, the zloty <EURPLN=> was down 0.6 percent at 3.871 per euro, off almost two-week lows hit earlier in the session.

The leu <EURRON=> was down 0.5 percent, while the Czech crown <EURCZK=> was almost flat and Hungary's forint <EURHUF=> gained 0.3 percent from Thursday's close.

HUNGARY'S ELECTION

Hungarians will vote on Sunday in the first round of an election that looks set to bring a landslide victory for the opposition centre-right Fidesz party, giving it a strong mandate for reforms. [ID:nLDE6351AW]

Fidesz, which campaigned on tax cuts and job creation, could even secure a two-thirds majority, which would empower the party to pass broader structural reforms.

"The market is in a wait-and-see mode," one trader in Budapest said. "Indications for a chance of a two-thirds majority (for opposition party Fidesz) on Sunday could reassure markets and be mildly forint positive."

Hungarian bonds were steady, and analysts say their bull run may continue after the election as an expected strong majority government, a supply squeeze and hopes for more rate cuts bode well [ID:nLDE62U1OZ].

The forint, however, is set to give up some ground in the next few months after the elections, a monthly Reuters poll showed on Friday, but is poised for a modest gain of less than 1 percent over a 12-month horizon.[ID:nLDE6380S7]

title: SNAP ANALYSIS-Polish  central bank  may slow, not stop zloty gains
text:
* Analysts see zloty up mid term on strong fundamentals

* Demand for Polish debt, state assets to underpin zloty

By Kuba Jaworowski

WARSAW, Apr 9 (Reuters) - Intervention by Poland's central bank on the currency market will probably only slow, not stop, the zloty's gains given that Poland's economic fundamentals are relatively strong and investors are keen to buy into Polish assets.

Around midday on Friday the central bank intervened for the first time since Poland let the zloty float freely ten years ago. The move prompted a 1 percent fall in the zloty which has recently hovered around 16-month highs against the euro, raising concerns that further appreciation could hurt the economy.

But analysts said Poland's status as the only economy in the 27-strong EU to avoid recession last year provided a solid base for zloty gains in the medium term.

"Today's move of the central bank does not... change Poland's image as an economy with strong fundamentals," Raiffeisen Bank Polska analysts wrote in a note to clients.

"...that's why we expect the zloty to stay strong and the intervention only to weaken the appreciating move."

The zloty was trading around 3.876 per euro in late trade on Friday, after falling to an almost two-week low of 3.8907 earlier in the session. <EURPLN=>

BONDS, PRIVATISATION

Poland's economic growth is expected to accelerate to about 3 percent in 2010 from 1.7 percent a year earlier.

Analysts say foreign investors are still lining up to buy zloty-denominated assets ranging from government debt to state assets. To do this they need to exchange their euros and dollars into zlotys.

"Factors supporting the zloty include demand for Polish bonds and the privatisation plans," Raiffeisen analysts wrote.

The total value of state assets on sale this year in the government's ambitious privatisation plan is seen at 25 billion zlotys. Poland's borrowing needs this year total 197 billion zlotys and the lion's share will be covered by local currency bonds.

"We expect more noise on spot (...) but we remain confident in the medium-term uptrend in the zloty," Koon Chow, FX strategist at Barclays Capital wrote in a note to clients.

"We think the central bank wants to slow the pace of zloty appreciation so as not to imperil the cautious cyclical recovery."

title: UPDATE 2- Poland intervenes  to curb zloty, sets precedent
text:
* Central bank in first zloty intervention since 2000 float

* Govt says it fully supports move, shares c.bank concern

* Zloty falls 0.5 pct, but analysts say uptrend could resume

(Recasts, adds analysts, MPC member, detail)

By Marcin Goettig and Dagmara Leszkowicz

WARSAW, April 9 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank sold zlotys on Friday, surprising markets with its first intervention since introducing a free float in 2000 as it sought to temper the surging currency's impact on exports and the wider economy.

The central bank said in a statement it had bought "some currencies" on the market around Friday. It gave no other details, but a Warsaw-based dealer said he believed the central bank bought about 40-50 million euros for zlotys.

The action, which the government said it backed fully, drove the zloty down 0.5 percent against the euro, though economists said the currency might strengthen again.

The European Union's biggest ex-communist member, Poland is the only country in the bloc to have avoided recession last year and currency investors have taken note.

Before Friday's move, the zloty had gained 6 percent against the euro in the year so far and was near a 16-month high.

"This is a battle with our own success because the zloty's rise in the last three months is a result of the large demand for Polish bonds from abroad, as well as privatisation inflows," said Rafal Benecki, senior economist at ING Bank.

The country's robust growth prospects stand in stark contrast to a number of European countries, notably peripherals such as Greece or Spain.

Poland's debt levels are also well below the EU average, making Polish debt attractive to investors.

FINMIN STAMP OF APPROVAL

"This is definitely a beneficial move. It's a factor that the market needs to take into account in its analysis. We fully agree with the central bank's policy on that matter," Deputy Finance Minister Dominik Radziwill told Reuters by telephone.

He said the ministry shared the central bank's concern over the zloty's strength.

At 1305 GMT, the zloty was at 3.8720/50 per euro, sharply weaker than 3.8340 earlier on Friday.

The currency's strength has prompted concern that Poland could pay an economic price as zloty gains have made exports less competitive.

But some analysts doubt the central bank will be able to halt the zloty's rise.

"We remain confident in the medium-term uptrend in the zloty," said Koon Chow, FX strategist at Barclays Capital. "We think the central bank wants to slow the pace of zloty appreciation so as not to imperil the cautious cyclical recovery."

Chow said this kind of strategy was employed in other emerging market economies and there were good reasons for authorities not to try to weaken the currency too much either.

A bout of currency weakness could stoke inflation and affect Poland's external debt position.

title: =DJ UPDATE: Polish  Central Bank  Prepared For  Currency Intervention
text:
(Adds analyst comment, wraps in other zloty stories.) 


 
   By Marcin Sobczyk and Malgorzata Halaba 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

WARSAW (Dow Jones)--The National Bank of Poland is prepared for an intervention in the currency market to prevent excessive strengthening of the zloty that could hamper economic growth, a management board member of the central bank said Thursday.

"We're prepared technologically and psychologically for a currency intervention," Witold Kozinski told a conference.

The zloty has been highly volatile over the past two years, reaching its strongest level ever at PLN3.20 against the euro in July 2008 and weakening dramatically during the global financial crisis to near its all-time weakest level of PLN4.92 against the euro in February 2009.

Over the past 14 months, the Polish currency has regained much of its pre-crisis strength. At 1321 GMT Thursday, it stood at PLN3.8519 to the euro.

Kozinski added that the zloty appears to be in a long-term upward trend, and warned that its rapid appreciation against major currencies has a negative impact on the economy and may impair the ability of Polish exporters to compete.

Polish government officials have also expressed concern that the strengthening of the zloty may have a negative impact on the country's economic recovery. Polish Economy Minister Waldemar Pawlak said Thursday that excessive zloty appreciation would "complicate the economic situation."

Pawlak also said the Polish Monetary Policy Council should keep key interest rates flat to curtail excessive growth of the zloty against core currencies.

"The growth forecast for this year is 3%, which is possible to achieve in a favorable environment," Pawlak said. "Because inflation is going down, there's no pressure to hike rates."

Poland's annual inflation rate fell to 2.6% in March from 2.9% in February, according to estimates released by the finance ministry.

Poland's key reference rate is at the historic low of 3.5%. Analysts expect that monetary tightening may take place later this year or be delayed until 2011.

MPC member Elzbieta Chojna-Duch said separately Thursday that the council will take the strength of the zloty compared with other currencies into consideration when making interest rate decisions.

The MPC is watching the situation on the currency market and the stability of the Polish currency is one of its policy goals, she added.

Poland's annual inflation rate fell to 2.6% in March from 2.9% in February, according to estimates released by the finance ministry.

Poland's key reference rate is at the historic low of 3.5%. Analysts expect that monetary tightening may take place later this year or be delayed until 2011.

Citi economist Piotr Kalisz said Thursday that the central bank may intervene on the currency market on a much higher scale than the markets are anticipating, while the government is not expected to intervene, but will no longer buy more euros on the market.

title: UPDATE 1-Polish  FX interventions  possible - cbanker
text:
(Combines with POLAND-ZLOTY/, adds more detail)

WARSAW, April 8 (Reuters) - Poland may decide to intervene on the foreign exchange market if the zloty's appreciating trend proves to be long-term, a member of the central bank's Monetary Policy Council (MPC) said on Thursday.

The zloty currency is near 16-month highs against the euro, though it was down some 0.5 percent on Thursday amid concerns over Greece's debt crisis. The 10-strong MPC can take a decision to intervene on the FX market.

"If this trend proves long-term than we may start considering interventions. The government and the central bank have a plan prepared for such a scenario," Anna Zielinska-Glebocka told TVN CNBC in an interview.

She also reiterated comments made on Wednesday that the zloty gains could prove temporary.

At 1557 GMT the euro traded at 3.8480 zlotys and despite Thursday's decline the Polish currency was still 6.5 percent up from the beginning of 2010.

The deputy governor of the Polish central bank, Witold Kozinski, said on Thursday he believed the zloty was in a long-term appreciating trend. [nnWSF008896]

The zloty has become a hot topic in Poland, with some analysts saying further rises could jeopardise the country's still-fragile economic recovery.

Some government officials have already expressed concerns that zloty gains are harming exports and fuelling imports.

Since the zloty became a free-floating currency in 2000 no interventions on the FX market have been conducted, but during a broad sell-off of emerging markets at the start of 2009 Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggested this could happen.

Analysts expect Poland's economic growth to accelerate to 2.8 percent in 2010 from 1.7 percent in 2009.

The Paris-based Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) said on Thursday it would probably revise upwards its 2010 growth forecast for Poland of 2.5 percent.

In a report, the OECD also said Poland's good economic fundamentals could trigger further zloty gains over the medium term as the country prepares for euro membership, noting that this could harm the competitiveness of Polish exports. (Reporting by Gabriela Baczynska and Kuba Jaworowski)

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Shares hit new year high,  currencies  off peaks
text:
* Emerging shares hit new 2009 high

* Russian rouble advances to new 2009 high

* Hungary's forint backs off after hitting nine-month highs

By Sebastian Tong

LONDON, Oct 20 (Reuters) - Emerging shares rose on Tuesday in tandem with their global peers to hit new 2009 highs boosted by robust corporate earnings and resurgent commodity prices, while Russia's rouble scaled fresh peaks against its currency basket even as the dollar slid to a 14-month low.

Several emerging currencies backed off from recent multi-month gains, including Hungary's forint, which eased after rising to nine-month highs versus the euro <EURHUF=>.

Helping to set the buoyant market mood were forecast-busting quarterly earnings from computing giant Apple Inc whose record sales numbers for its iPhones and iMacs suggested the return of U.S. consumption. [ID:nN19395089]

The dollar's weakness <.DXY> is also driving investors to higher-yielding emerging markets, where the pace of economic recovery is quickening.

The magnitude of investment flows into Brazil prompted the country to unveil on Monday plans for a capital inflows tax. [ID:nN19264977]

Fellow emerging giant Russia said an exit from the recession was in sight while a Chinese vice-premier said China's economy was growing faster with every month. [ID:nPEK195317] [ID:nLK281969]

The benchmark emerging equities index <.MSCIEF> firmed 0.3 percent to 980.16 by 1045 GMT, its highest level since August 2008, while emerging sovereign debt spreads <11EMJ> were flat to trade 302 bps over U.S. Treasuries.

"Emerging markets have been very strong for the last few days, it would take quite a bit of a negative event to break or reverse that trend," said Beat Siegenthaler, chief strategist emerging markets at TD Securities.

"The news from Brazil...implies the government is becoming increasingly nervous about currency strength," TD Securities' Siegenthaler said.

CURRENCIES OFF PEAKS

Polish shares <.WIG20> advanced to a new 12-month high while Israeli equities <.TA25> continued to hover at their highest levels in 15 months.

Russian <.IRTS> and South Africa <.JTOPI> shares stayed aloft at 13-month peaks, buoyed by a commodities rally which saw oil <CLc1> peeking above $80 a barrel and gold rising close to last week's record highs <XAU=>.

Russia's central bank allowed the rouble <RUS=MCX> to climb to a new 2009 high against its dollar-euro basket, a move that analysts said confirmed Moscow's intention to move towards a free floating currency. [ID:nLK333254]

Most emerging currencies, however, were off recent highs.

The Israeli shekel <ILS=> backed off from 10-month peaks versus the dollar it reached on Monday, when its strength was said to have sparked intervention by the country's central bank. [ID:nLJ81201]

Poland's zloty softened a touch to the euro <EURPLN=> after an over one-percent gain in the previous day. A Polish monetary policymaker was quoted in a newspaper on Tuesday arguing that the country's interest rate should not be raised for the next six to seven months.

The policymaker is one of the nine of the ten members in the Polish central bank's Monetary Policy Council to be replaced early next year. [ID:nLK292958]

Hungary's forint <EURHUF=> also eased after touching a nine-month high against the euro earlier in the day on its central bank head's comments that the scope for further rate cuts was limited. [ID:nLJ68323]

Meanwhile, Iceland's parliament is mulling an amended bill to repay Britain and the Netherlands more than $5 billion in deposits lost in the island state's financial meltdown. [ID:nLJ220595]

The passing of the bill would pave the way for a release of a $10 billion aid package led by the IMF. (Additional reporting by Carolyn Cohn; Editing by Andy Bruce)

1400/1300  Polish February CPI

BUDAPEST (Dow Jones)--Poland is releasing a flurry of economic indicators Friday, of which February consumer prices and revised January inflation figures will likely be the most important.

The finance ministry has already predicted an uptick in annual inflation to 3.4% in February, mostly due to the depreciating zloty and regulated price hikes for residential utilities. But analysts' forecasts are all over the map, ranging from 2.9% to 3.6%.

A high-end figure would likely give an extra nudge to the rallying zloty but not necessarily keep the central bank from easing interest rates later this month, as the rate-setting Monetary Policy Council has already flagged its readiness to ignore any inflation uptick as a strictly short-term blip.

Poland's January current account data will also be watched, especially for how well foreign direct investment is holding up as both exports and imports hit the skids due to the euro zone's deepening recession.

title: FOREX -Dollar, euro soar vs Swiss franc as SNB  intervenes
text:
* Dollar, euro jump vs Swiss franc after SNB intervention

* SNB to buy foreign currencies to avert deflation risk

* SNB move to benefit other European emerging markets (Updates prices, adds comment, changes byline)

By Nick Olivari

NEW YORK, March 12 (Reuters) - The U.S. dollar and euro jumped against the Swiss franc on Thursday after the Swiss National Bank said it was intervening in the foreign exchange market as it faced the growing risk of deflation.

The Swiss central bank said it was implementing its decision to buy foreign currencies. The SNB also cut interest rates on Thursday by a quarter percentage point to a historic low, offering three-, six- and 12-month funds at 0.05 percent.

The SNB, which last intervened in August 1995, further said it will buy not only foreign currencies but bonds as well. Switzerland is facing its worst recession in over three decades. For the SNB statement, click on [ID:nSNBTEXT]. Past interventions [ID:nLC337364].

A "very, very strong statement from the Swiss National Bank about what they are doing and about to do," said Karthik Sankaran, Portfolio Manager and Principal at Covepoint Capital Advisors LLC In New York. "They are the first central bank that is actually using the purchase of foreign currency as a means of quantitative easing."

In late afternoon New York trading, the dollar rose 2.96 percent to 1.1876 francs <CHF=>, on track for its biggest one-day gain since August 1995, at current prices. It rose as high as 1.1965 francs, a three-month high, according to Reuters data.

The Swiss franc is one of the world's most traded currencies, at times prized as a safe haven for investors.

The euro climbed to 1.5302 Swiss francs, the highest since December. It last traded at 1.5234 <EURCHF=>, up 2.9 percent, the euro's best day ever against the Swiss currency.

SNB's move to zero rates and quantitative easing was expected, traders said, but the immediate move to intervene was a surprise.

Bank of New York-Mellon senior currency strategist Michael Woolfolk said "the way this was communicated was intended at maximizing its shock value." He said there were no hints from SNB officials ahead of time that intervention would be immediate.

"They changed their economic outlook, they not only lowered interest rates to effectively zero but also announced quantitative easing and currency intervention. This was the full monty," Woolfolk said.

POLAND, HUNGARY BENEFIT FROM SNB ACTION

Quantitative easing has been deployed by central banks in countries including Britain, where the central bank is buying assets with newly created money.

Marc Chandler, global head of FX strategy at Brown Brothers Harriman in New York, said the SNB intervention should ease pressure on Poland and Hungary, two European emerging market countries seriously hit by the global credit crisis.

These two countries had taken advantage of ultra-low Swiss interest rates, borrowing heavily in Swiss francs and investing in riskier assets.

"The strength of the Swiss franc compounded their woes. Today's dramatic weakening of the Swiss franc may ease this pressure," said Chandler.

Gains in the dollar versus the Swiss franc boosted the greenback against other major currencies such as the euro and sterling.

The euro fell 0.1 percent to $1.2871 <EUR=>. The euro zone single currency was also pressured by comments from European Central Bank President Jean-Claude Trichet that euro zone interest rates could be cut further. [ID:nLC956324]

The ECB cut its benchmark rate to a record low 1.5 percent last week and economists expect it to cut to 1.0 percent, most likely in April.

Sterling rose 0.1 percent to $1.3867 <GBP=>.

The SNB news overshadowed all other events and data in the market including U.S. retail sales numbers that were better than expected and weekly jobless claims data that were not far from analysts' forecasts. [ID:nN12352975]

Against the yen, the dollar erased early losses, partly because of firmer U.S. stocks, still one of the key drivers in the currency market. Stocks were lifted by energy shares and the U.S. retail sales report. The dollar rose 0.6 percent to 97.81 <JPY=>. (Additional reporting by Steven C.
