title: CEE MARKETS 4- FX  rally on forint rise; leu up after aid talks
text:
* Forint, stocks rally lead FX higher, aid bonds

* Hungary c.bank talks up forint, may have intervened

* Leu edges up as Romania closer to IMF deal

(Recasts with forint, adds bonds, updates prices)

By Marius Zaharia and Jason Hovet

BUCHAREST/PRAGUE, March 10 (Reuters) - The forint led gains in central Europe on Tuesday after Hungary's central bank said it was actively supporting the forint and Romania sought aid to ride out the global crisis.

The forint jumped more than 2 percent over Monday levels in the late afternoon, pushing the Polish zloty higher and the Czech crown -- the region's best performer this year -- to a two-month high as a rally in stocks added to gains.

Hungarian central bank Governor Andras Simor signalled in a TV interview that the bank was actively supporting the forint currency, though he would not say how and in what amounts the bank had bought forints.[ID:nLA544310]

The pledge followed a weekend statement saying the bank would channel European Union funds into the market and pump euro liquidity into the banking system to prop up the forint, which sank to a record low of 317.45 to the euro last week.

The Hungarian forint <EURHUF=> firmed 1.9 percent to 304.3 to the euro by 1602 GMT, but has lost 13.9 percent this year, outpacing up to 12 percent losses for the region.

"It's hard to say anything, I can only make guesses," a local dealer said, giving a 70 percent probability the central bank had bought forints. "We haven't seen the (central bank) and we saw interest from hedge funds to buy the forint."

In Poland, the zloty <EURPLN=> gained 1.4 percent and the Czech crown <EURCZK=> rose 1.7 percent, helping lift bond prices, dealers said. The leu <EURRON=> gained just 0.3 percent to 4.287 to the euro, with dealers saying only the size of any IMF-led aid deal was likely to benefit the Romanian unit.

Central European stocks jumped, riding a boost in global sentiment after news banking giant Citigroup was profitable to start 2009. [ID:nLA118651]

Policymakers have become more vocal in support of currencies that have dropped sharply in 2009 as the global economic slowdown punishes central Europe's export-heavy economies.

On Monday, Poland's central bank said it was ready to intervene if needed to prop up the zloty. Last month it sold EU funds on the market when the zloty neared a record low.

ON THE GROUND

Capital flows to emerging Europe that once fuelled booming growth have reversed, putting strain on many countries. In Tuesday note, Merrill Lynch analysts estimated the region would need combined gross external financing of $460 billion in 2009.

Romania said on Tuesday it had started talks with the European Commission, the International Monetary Fund and other institutions to seek "medium-term foreign financial assistance", a bailout which economists said could reach 20 billion euros.

"The leu would have firmed on the IMF news, had it depreciated in line with the region in the past," one dealer said, adding news on the size of the deal could be a mover.

"The market is pricing in 5-10 billion euros, but if (Romania) gets 20 billion euros, the leu should rally."

Dealers have said the central bank has sold euros in the market in this year, helping the unit fare better than peers.

An IMF team was due to start a two-week visit to Bucharest on Wednesday to discuss a potential loan programme. President Traian Basescu told Parliament on Monday a foreign loan was the only solution to aid the troubled economy. [ID:nL9487165]

"The package should ease fears of a complete financial meltdown in Romania," Neil Shearing, emerging European economist at Capital Economics, said in a note.

"More generally, an IMF rescue package does not alter the fact that the leu remains fundamentally overvalued."

Hungary secured a $25 billion IMF-EU package in October, becoming the first EU member to get aid. Analysts have speculated for weeks that Romania would become the third bloc member -- after Hungary and Latvia -- to get help.

Unlike Latvia, Romania has not experienced large street protests but analysts believe social pressures will continue to mount, threatening the new government coalition's stability.

Policymakers have repeatedly stated over the past weeks that currencies were undervalued, and stronger countries like the Czech Republic and Poland have tried distancing themselves from neighbours' problems. But analysts predict further FX weakening.

"The previous flow of capital is turning into an ebb which is fundamentally what will maintain pressure on currencies," Swedish bank SEB's chief emerging markets strategist Mats Olausson said.

text:
(Adds earlier comments by a member of the central bank's Monetary Policy Council on possibility of intervention.) 


   WARSAW (Dow Jones)--Poland's central bank is considering entering the foreign exchange market with very small transactions to develop a better understanding of the market's dynamics and participants, Central Bank President Slawomir Skrzypek said Thursday. 

"These transactions would be much too small to have an effect on the zloty exchange rate," Skrzypek said.

Skrzypek's comments coincide with remarks by a member of the central bank's Monetary Policy Council, or the RPP, Dariusz Filar, earlier in the day.

In an interview with the daily Rzeczpospolita released Thursday, Filar reiterated that a significant rebound in inflation, partly resulting from the weak zloty, would make the central bank's intervention in the foreign exchange market "justified."

"And that's what we said in the statement after the RPP's latest meeting," Filar said, adding that the central bank has all the necessary tools to intervene and that "right now it's up to the central bank's dealers to decide when to enter the market."

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Stocks lower, zloty weakens further
text:
* Emerging equities broadly weaker led by Asia

* Regional currencies are mixed, zloty lower

* Latvian lat remains above intervention level

* Ukraine assets little hit by ratings downgrade

By Martina Fuchs

LONDON, Feb 26 (Reuters) - Emerging equities were broadly lower on Thursday, led down by Asian stocks and underperforming global markets, with Poland raising the spectre of intervention as the zloty currency weakened again after Wednesday's rate cut.

Benchmark emerging equities <.MSCIEF> fell 0.27 percent by 1145 GMT, after a 1 percent rise the previous day, but remain down 11.11 percent on the year -- still above multi-year lows set late last year.

In contrast, the benchmark global equity markets index <.MIWD00000PUS> was up 0.15 percent supported by fresh steps from the British government to shore up its banking sector.

Much of the emerging fall was down to Asian stocks, with Chinese equities <.SSEC> down 3.87 percent. Israeli stocks <.TA25> lost 0.32 percent, but some of the other exchanges in the region were up.

Hungarian equities <.BUX> were amongst the largest gainers, up 0.76 percent but still down 18.62 percent on the year, while Czech stocks <.PX> were up 0.55 percent.

"We've had a slight rebound in the last couple of days, but now we are back and worries have not gone away," said Danske Bank chief emerging markets analyst Lars Christensen. "There is a little weakness in the currencies but it's relatively neutral."

Benchmark emerging sovereign debt spreads <11EMJ> were five basis points narrower at 648 over US Treasuries, implying a slight rise in appetite for emerging debt compared to US government paper.

Two of the region's worst performing currencies -- Hungary's forint <EURHUF=> and Russia's rouble <RUS=MCX=> -- were slightly stronger, up 0.51 and 0.17 percent respectively but both remain down around 13 percent this year.

POLISH INTERVENTION?

The Czech crown <EURCZK=> was up 0.49 percent, but the Polish zloty <EURPLN=> lost 0.1 percent to deepen its recent losses, but remained above all time lows set earlier this month.

Poland's central bank cut interest rates by 25 basis points on Wednesday, saying a sharp slowdown in the economy justified the cut. Poland has now cut rates by 200 basis points in recent months to 4.0 percent, although Wednesday's cut was not as sharp as previous ones.

Polish central bank governor Slawomir Skrzypek said on Thursday that the bank might intervene in the currency markets to support the zloty. [ID:nWAR007969]

The Latvian lat <EURLVL=> was slightly weaker within its trading band but remained short of Wednesday's intraday lows, when it fell sharply to the level where the central bank intervenes to support it.

A government collapse, ratings downgrade and accelerating economic crisis have increased pressure on the currency, but it could get short-term support in the coming days as Latvia receives the first part of a 7.5 billion euro International Monetary Fund and the European Union-led package.

The cost of protecting Ukranian sovereign debt in the credit default swaps market fell 124.5 basis points to 4162.5, meaning it would cost $4.16 million a year to cover $10 million of five-year debt -- amongst the highest in emerging markets.

Standard & Poor's slashed Ukraine to a CCC+ "junk" rating on worries about destabilised banks, falling industrial output and political disunity that puts at risk a $16.4 billion International Monetary Fund loan programme. [ID:nLP372975]

"The two-notch ratings downgrade appears premature in terms of timing and too aggressive in terms of magnitude," said Sergei Voloboev, emerging markets analyst at Credit Suisse. "There was no significant market reaction. It seems that the market has not paid too much attention to the arguments that the rating agency made yesterday. But of course, Ukraine continues to trade extremely wide." (editing by Peter Apps ad Toby Chopra)

title: UPDATE: Poland's  Central Bank  Says May Act To Support Zloty
text:
(Adds further comment, background.)


 
   By David McQuaid 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

WARSAW (Dow Jones)--The Polish central bank's Monetary Policy Council Wednesday supported government efforts to defend the zloty, explicitly reminding markets that direct intervention on currency markets remains an option for the bank.

"The Monetary Policy Council is following a direct inflation-targeting strategy under a floating exchange-rate regime. Within this strategy, the central bank may deploy instruments directly influencing the zloty exchange rate," the rate-setting panel said in a statement after Wednesday's monthly rate meeting.

Earlier Wednesday, the 10-member MPC - presided over by central bank President Slawomir Skrzypek but fully independent of the central bank's top management - decided to ease key interest rates 25 basis points, despite a 14.9% annual fall in January industrial output the council said confirms "a significant slowdown" is underway.

The cautious easing - less than the 50 basis points expected by economists only a week ago - followed sharp depreciation of the Polish zloty and other regional currencies this month, which prompted a coordinated verbal intervention Monday from the Czech, Hungarian, Polish, and Romanian central banks.

The zloty's plunge led Prime Minister Donald Tusk last week to warn his government would start selling euros to support the currency. That verbal intervention, backed by the finance ministry's sale of euros Feb. 18, produced a 5% rebound in the zloty.

The MPC's reminder of intervention also served to correct an impression made by Poland's dovish central bank president Slawomir Skrzypek, who several times in recent weeks has explicitly ruled out currency interventions as costly and ineffective.

Analysts said such comments were a signal to investors betting against the zloty.

title: =DJ UPDATE: Poland's  Central Bank  Says May Act To Support Zloty
text:
(Adds further comment, background.) 


 
   By David McQuaid 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

WARSAW (Dow Jones)--The Polish central bank's Monetary Policy Council Wednesday supported government efforts to defend the zloty, explicitly reminding markets that direct intervention on currency markets remains an option for the bank.

"The Monetary Policy Council is following a direct inflation-targeting strategy under a floating exchange-rate regime. Within this strategy, the central bank may deploy instruments directly influencing the zloty exchange rate," the rate-setting panel said in a statement after Wednesday's monthly rate meeting.

Earlier Wednesday, the 10-member MPC - presided over by central bank President Slawomir Skrzypek but fully independent of the central bank's top management - decided to ease key interest rates 25 basis points, despite a 14.9% annual fall in January industrial output the council said confirms "a significant slowdown" is underway.

The cautious easing - less than the 50 basis points expected by economists only a week ago - followed sharp depreciation of the Polish zloty and other regional currencies this month, which prompted a coordinated verbal intervention Monday from the Czech, Hungarian, Polish, and Romanian central banks.

The zloty's plunge led Prime Minister Donald Tusk last week to warn his government would start selling euros to support the currency. That verbal intervention, backed by the finance ministry's sale of euros Feb. 18, produced a 5% rebound in the zloty.

The MPC's reminder of intervention also served to correct an impression made by Poland's dovish central bank president Slawomir Skrzypek, who several times in recent weeks has explicitly ruled out currency interventions as costly and ineffective.

Analysts said such comments were a signal to investors betting against the zloty.

In its statement, the MPC retained language that it wants Poland to enter the European Union's ERM2 Exchange Rate Mechanism - a two-year currency grid required of euro-zone applicants - "as soon as possible, after securing the necessary political backing for changes in the constitution and other laws needed for Poland to adopt the euro."

That at least partially meshes with government's fast-track plans to enter the euro zone by Jan. 1, 2012 - a timetable central bank President Skrzypek has said is too ambitious.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-E.Europe wins respite, rouble sinks
text:
* Central, Eastern European FX stabilise after falls

* Falling oil pressure as Russia's rouble, stocks fall

* Emerging stock markets lower on global worries

* Worries persist over Dubai state firm refinancing

By Peter Apps and Martina Fuchs

LONDON, Feb 18 (Reuters) - Central and Eastern European currencies saw some respite on Wednesday after hitting multi-year lows the previous day, but weaker oil put Russia's rouble under renewed pressure and global emerging stocks sank.

Ongoing concern over contagion from emerging Europe into Western banks continued to undermine the euro, while in the Middle East concerns remained high Dubai might struggle to refinance loans for state companies.

Having dropped across the board on Tuesday undermined by worries from rating agencies and worsening economic outlooks, emerging European currencies were mixed in morning trade.

The Polish zloty was up 1.39 percent by 1230 GMT, now down 15 percent since the start of the year and bouncing off record lows against the euro, and the Czech crown also rose 1.63 percent supported by rate hike expectations.

The Hungarian forint was up 0.97 percent off its own all-time lows, but still down 13.65 percent on the year and with the central bank warning it might take unspecified "unconventional means" to support the currency.

"The general picture is that there is some consolidation from yesterday," said Royal Bank of Scotland analyst Tim Ash.

But he said he he saw potential drastic policy responses across the region, which was until recently seen as one of the most attractive emerging markets but is now regarded amongst the most exposed to the global financial crisis.

"There is now talk of intervention in Czech Republic (and) of rate hikes, and intervention in Poland on the back of dismal economic growth," he said.

Worries over growing defaults on foreign currency loans in central and eastern Europe and the knock-on effect on local and Western parent banks helped push the euro to a 10 month low, a sign emerging Europe's woes might affect the whole continent.

Benchmark emerging sovereign debt spreads narrowed by one basis point to 692 oh the US Treasuries, a sign of slightly heightened appetite for emerging debt.

FALLING OIL HITS RUSSIA

But benchmark emerging equities lost 0.75 percent, now down 8.83 percent on the year with investors worried by global bank problems, plunging economic output and little sign of recovery despite the signing of a $787 billion US stimulus package into law.

Stocks in the Czech Republic and Russia were among the biggest losers, down 5.85 percent and 6.51 percent.

Falling oil prices renewed pressure on the Russian rouble, which fell 0.21 percent to reach 40.63 against its euro-dollar basket, again nearing the bottom of the basket at 41.

Having called a halt to a series of many devaluations last month by widening the basket sharply, Russia has vowed to defend the lower level but the market has repeatedly tried to test it.

"The support has been knocked out from under the market," said Andrei Kukk, dealer at Uralsib.

The cost of insuring Russia's debt against default in the credit default swaps market also increased slightly to 772 basis points from 769 on Tuesday, meaning it would cost $772,000 a year to cover $10 million of five-year debt.

The cost of insuring Dubai's debt against default was slightly lower at 940 basis points from Tuesday's 977 having topped 1000 late last week.

Magazine MEED reported on Tuesday state-owned Bourse Dubai would get a $1 billion bailout from the United Arab Emirates federal government to avoid default on a $3.4 billion loan.

While United Arab Emirates has benefited from colossal oil revenues in recent years, only 3-4 percent of Dubai's GDP comes from oil and it has racked up debt to fund expansion.

Some analysts believe Dubai might be forced to turn to oil-rich Abu Dhabi for support.

Deutche Bank estimates state owned companies in Dubai will need to refinance some $18 billion in obligations this year including the Bourse Dubai loan. (Editing by Andy Bruce)

title: INTERVIEW-Polish cbanker does not rule out  FX intervention
text:
WARSAW, Feb 17 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank may decide to intervene on the currency market to ensure steep zloty losses do not threaten the bank's inflation target, Monetary Policy Council (MPC) member Dariusz Filar said on Tuesday.

Speaking to Reuters in an interview, Filar also said he supported the government's plan to use European Union funds to intervene on the foreign exchanges but without setting a target rate at which intervention would start.

"One cannot rule out there would be scope for interventions by the central bank but they would not be aimed at defending a certain level but at preventing the exchange rate from endangering the inflation target," Filar said.

"I'm a strong supporter of...selling a part of EU funds on the FX market rather than at the central bank," he added.

He was speaking before Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Tuesday the government would use EU funds to support the zloty if the currency hits 5 zlotys to the euro.

The MPC targets inflation at 2.5 percent, plus or minus one percentage point. In January, the inflation rate was 3.1 percent.

The zloty has weakened in recent weeks and at 1542 GMT, it was trading at 4.9075 against the euro, only slightly above a record low. (Reporting by Kuba Jaworowski and Pawel Florkiewicz, editing by Stephen Nisbet)

title: Polish Ctrl Bk's Kozinski: Against  Intervention  Unless CPI Risk
text:
WARSAW (Dow Jones)--Poland's central bank shouldn't intervene to prop up the zloty until its depreciation begins to pose an inflation risk, central bank Deputy President Witold Kozinski said Monday.

Kozinski, who supervised the central bank's "managed float" currency regime in the mid-1990s, stirred controversy in early 2008 when he said the central bank should intervene to curb the strengthening of the now free-floating zloty.

"Just as I favored intervention when we had an appreciating currency, I now oppose intervention when the zloty is depreciating - at least until that depreciation starts to pose an inflationary threat," Kozinski told journalists at a news briefing.

Kozinski's comments came amid a renewed bout of global risk aversion that sent the zloty plunging 4% against the euro Monday, to a new five-year low of PLN4.8270.

title: UPDATE 3-Polish cbanker-may discuss  FX intervention  in Feb
text:
(Adds prime minister's comments on the zloty in paras 5-6)

WARSAW, Feb 6 (Reuters) - Poland's Monetary Policy Council (MPC) may discuss currency market intervention at its meeting in February and decide whether such a move is warranted by the market situation, MPC member Dariusz Filar said on Friday.

The zloty has shed 30 percent against the euro since touching an all-time high last July. It is down about 16 percent since just before the first interest rate cut of the current monetary easing cycle was made last November.

"The situation is such that the MPC must consider whether the current weakening of the zloty may be impacting inflation," Filar told Reuters. <EURPLN=> <PLN=>

"This does not mean that an (FX) intervention will be carried out. It is too early to formulate an opinion that a currency market intervention is needed or that it is not. We will be able to better answer this question at our February meeting."

Poland's Prime Minister, who recently said he did not see a need to intervene on the FX market, said on Friday the zloty weakening would not be long-lived as the currency should get support from the inflow of European Union (EU) funds.

EU's largest ex-communist member is entitled to 67 billion euros ($85.82 billion) from the bloc's 2007-2013 budget perspective.

Poland's central bank has not intervened in the foreign exchange market in support of the zloty since the introduction of the free float regime nearly a decade ago, Filar noted. Poland's foreign currency reserves <PLCBFX=ECI> rose to 46.13 billion euros in January from 44.14 billion euros in December, the central bank said on Friday.

The central bank holds reserves in U.S. dollars, euros and British pounds, but does not publish allocation details.

The MPC is set to hold its monthly meeting on Feb. 24-25.

Filar said monetary policy guidelines for 2009 allow for possible currency market intervention to help stabilise prices.

Central bank governor Slawomir Skrzypek, who this week ruled out interventions, said on Friday the weakening of the zloty was not caused by recent interest rate cuts.

When asked if the zloty had tumbled because of the monetary easing policy, Skrzypek told reporters: "There are completely different factors behind the currency's weakening."

The governor also said he saw no impact of the zloty exchange rate on this year's inflation figure.

Analysts have said recently that the sharp zloty falls, mirroring other currency losses across the region as investors flee riskier emerging markets assets due to the global crisis, may spark inflationary risks and threaten the economy.

Some have signalled they are scaling back their interest rate cut expectations because of the zloty's depreciation.

"At a time of significant zloty weakening there is of course the question of whether it will affect inflation. If we decide that the exchange rate may be impacting future inflation, then this will limit scope for interest rate cuts in a decisive way," Filar said.

Concerns over sharp economic slowdown prompted the MPC to slash rates by a total of 175 basis points since November to 4.25 percent as the euro zone, Poland's main trade partner, headed into deep recession.

Underlining the deterioration in Poland's economy, a Labour Ministry source told Reuters on Friday unemployment likely rose to 10 percent last month from 9.5 percent in December. (Additional reporting by Maciej Onoszko, writing by Karolina Slowikowska and Dagmara Leszkowicz, Editing by Andy Bruce)

BUDAPEST/WARSAW, Feb 6 (Reuters) - Central European currencies were mixed on Friday, with the forint and the zloty firming due to planned central bank measures, even though Hungary published dismal industrial output data.

The Czech crown <EURCZK=> and the Romanian leu <EURRON=> stayed near Thursday's levels after central bank interest rate cuts in both countries earlier this week, just like Croatia's kuna <EURHRK=>, while the Serbian dinar <EURRSD=> eased.

Analyst forecasts in a Reuters poll showed that the region's main currencies were expected to weaken in the next months and not expected to recover from the steep falls of the past months until the second half of the year. [ID:nL5740488]

The currencies have been hit by figures showing a drastic economic slowdown in the export-heavy region or recession in the case of Hungary, and because central banks have delivered rate cuts to help their economy weather the global crisis.

The latest in a string of bad economic figures was a 19.6 percent annual plunge in Hungary's industrial output in December according to figures published early on Friday. [ID:nL6235673]

Despite the figures, the forint extended gains posted on Thursday after the central bank announced that it would launch a five billion euro facility of six-month swaps to help domestic banks maintain last year's levels in lending to companies.

Dealers said the news also helped the Polish zloty and later both currencies, which have been tightly correlated in the past days, received additional support from comments about possible currency market intervention by Poland's central bank. [ID:nL662315]

The forint <EURHUF=> traded at 289.76 against the euro at 1542 GMT, firmer by 1.2 percent, while the zloty gained 1.23 percent to 4.556 per euro.

"Frankly, I don't think that it was the last time earlier this week that we saw the forint at 300," one dealer said. "Both the forint and the zloty are very vulnerable, they will react to any negative news and their weakening will not be slower than their current firming."

The Romanian leu was flat at 4.25 against the euro, while the Czech crown eased 0.14 percent to 27.985.

The crown gave up Thursday's one percent gains which it posted after the central bank surprised the market with a forecast showing it expected the average crown rate versus the euro at 25.8 this year, much stronger than current levels.

But dealers and analysts expect much weaker levels due to the declining econmy.

"This is an expected pullback for the crown," a Prague dealer said. "There is no reason to see the EURCZK at such low levels."

Czech Deputy Finance Minister Eduard Janota said on Friday that the country would not rush into its planned Eurobond issue because spreads were too high. [ID:NPRA002357]

Czech domestic bond yields ticked up and Hungarian government bonds also extended their losses, taking no encouragement from the forint's rebound which traders said was caused by profit-taking by foreign banks rather than inflows into the debt market.

"It's worrying that the forint recovery had no impact... this is not good news ahead of the planned restart of government bond auctions next week, but it's good to try, if the auctions fail, sentiment cannot become worse than now," one trader said.[ID:nL6582511]

The leu shrugged off central bank comments that Romania needs to keep its monetary policy tight until fiscal and wage restrictiveness is enforced [ID:nL6708438].

"Monetary policy depends on the fiscal policy and the fiscal policy is the biggest uncertainty so far," one dealer said. "Nobody knows how or if the budget deficit target of 2 percent of GDP will be achieved."

Dealers have said they suspected the central bank intervened covertly in the market earlier this week as economic concerns and uncertainty over fiscal plans weighed on the leu.

title: UPDATE: Polish Ctrl Bk Head: No  Intervention  On  Forex  For Now
text:
WARSAW (Dow Jones)--Poland's central bank's president Slawomir Skrzypek reiterated Thursday that there's no need to intervene on the foreign exchange market to stop the zloty's slide.

Speaking in a live interview for Radio Zet, Skrzypek said that any intervention talk or discussion about what zloty level would trigger central bank intervention "would weaken the zloty even further."

However, Skrzypek said the central bank has all the necessary tools to defend the zloty if and when needed, such as foreign currency reserves.

He added that under current conditions, joining the Exchange Rate Mechanism ERM2 "would encourage more speculation on the zloty." He said joining ERM2 "would trigger constant interventions on the forex market."

"I don't think that euro adoption is a cure for everything," Skrzypek said.

The Polish government aims to adopt the euro in 2012. That would mean it has to be euro-ready in 2011 and has to join the EMR2 mechanism by the mid-2009.

Skrzypek also said the weak zloty doesn't mean the central bank's easing policy cycle is over.

"I can't rule out more rate cuts," Skrzypek said.

In January, the central bank's Monetary Policy Council cut key rates by 75 basis points, to 4.25%.

title: WRAPUP 2-East Europe  currencies  slide amid recession fears
text:
(Adds Polish PM on currency interventions, paragraph 12)

WARSAW, Feb 4 (Reuters) - Currencies across Eastern Europe tumbled, Romania cut interest rates and a ratings agency warned of risks facing Hungary on Wednesday as the impact of global recession intensified in the region.

Poland, the European Union's largest former communist member, ruled out intervening to rescue its plunging currency for fear of squandering precious foreign exchange reserves at a time of economic crisis.

Protests flared again in the region as Bulgarian farmers blocked a Danube River border crossing with Romania, demanding subsidies and protection from cheap farm imports in a rally that mimicked protests in Greece.

Foreign investors fleeing a region now perceived as too risky drove Poland's zloty <EURPLN=> down to 4.67 per euro, its lowest level since June 2004, just after the country joined the EU. Hungary's forint hit a record low of 304 per euro.

Investors fear that declining manufacturing output across the region, which is heavily dependent on exports to a euro zone now deep in recession, will hammer tax revenues and force spending cuts that will further squeeze demand in a vicious downward spiral.

Ratings agency Moody's said the gloomy outlook posed a risk to Hungary, which late last year clinched emergency loans from the International Monetary Fund and EU aid to avoid an economic meltdown.

"The negative outlook on Hungary and every other country indicates that the likely direction in the medium term is towards lower rating," Dietmar Hornung, senior analyst at Moody's Investors Service in Frankfurt, told Reuters.

Moody's is content for now with Budapest's rating, he added.

The heavily indebted economy of Hungary is expected to shrink by up to 3 percent in 2009.

Plunging currencies compound the woes of Polish, Hungarian, Czech and other consumers saddled with loans denominated in euros, which in turn raises the risks to the region's mostly foreign-owned banks.

NO INTERVENTIONS

In Poland, still among the region's stronger economies, central bank head Slawomir Skrzypek, the economy minister and head of government all said they saw no reason for market interventions to underpin the zloty.

"Interventions today could have the opposite effect ... it would be using public money without a guarantee that it would work. Today, most experts advise not to do it," Prime Minister Donald Tusk said in an interview on TVN 24.

Poland's centre-right government unveiled plans on Tuesday to find savings worth 19.7 billion zlotys ($5.4 billion) in the state budget.

Defence Minister Bogdan Klich said on Wednesday Poland would withdraw its troops from peacekeeping missions in Chad and the Middle East in a decision expected to save 2 billion zlotys.

Polish economic growth is expected to slow this year to below 2 percent from 4.8 percent in 2008.

Slovakia's growth will drop sharply to 2.4 percent this year, below a previous forecast of 4.6 percent, cutting state revenues and boosting the fiscal deficit, Finance Minister Jan Pociatek said.

In Romania, the central bank cut interest rates by a quarter point to 10 percent, easing the cost of money for the first time in 19 months as cash shortages squeeze its economy.

Economists say Romania, which joined the EU along with southern neighbor Bulgaria in 2007, faces possible recession or even a financing crisis if the new government fails to convince investors it is serious about shoring up the state budget.

The Czech Republic, facing the possibility of zero growth this year, is also expected to cut rates on Thursday, following the example of Poland and Hungary last month. But cutting borrowing costs also piles further pressure on currencies.

The worsening economic situation has recently stirred protests in Greece, Bulgaria, Latvia, Lithuania, Iceland and Russia. On Wednesday, Bulgarian farmers shut down the Danube bridge link with Romania to protest against falling farm prices.

Russia has been especially hard hit by the flight of foreign capital from global emerging markets. On Wednesday, the Fitch ratings agency downgraded Russia's sovereign debt. (Reporting by regional bureaux, writing by Gareth Jones, editing by Tom Hals)

title: UPDATE 1-Polish c.bank says no to  intervention  as zloty dives
text:
(combines urgents, adds more cbanker quotes, other detail)

WARSAW, Feb 4 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank governor on Wednesday said there was no need for intervention to support the zloty, after the currency dived to levels last seen in mid-2004, deepening worries over the EU's largest ex-communist economy. The zloty has slid another 5 percent against the euro in the last day, hit by a broad flight of investors out of eastern Europe that brought the currency's losses to 46 percent since it hit an all-time high last July.

Worries the economy could contract for the first time since the 1990s, and over how its foreign-owned banks will perform and lend in months ahead, have added to investors' aversion to risk in the global financial crisis.

But the zloty was weaker than the current levels before it joined the European Union in 2004 and Poland's central bank and government have stuck to the policy of letting it float freely.

"It doesn't seem to be necessary to undertake interventions on the forex market right now," Governor Slawomir Skrzypek told TVP Info in an interview on Wednesday.

At 1005 GMT the zloty traded at 4.68 against the euro or 1.7 percent down from its Tuesday close.

Earlier on Wednesday, Deputy Prime Minister and Economy Minister Waldemar Pawlak also said there was no need for intervention.

"There is a question whether those interventions would be successful... Moreover, we need the FX reserves we have, more than 55 billion euros, as collateral in case there is a necessity of entering ERM-2," Skrzypek said.

It could be "incredibly costly and incredibly risky" to enter the pre-euro Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM-2) right now, he added, citing some analysts who say Poland's FX reserves would not suffice to keep the zloty within the grid.

Referring to a government plan for almost 20 billion zlotys in budget savings announced on Tuesday, Skrzypek said it was important to maintain tight budget discipline at a time of slowdown.

"The government's push to do so (keep budget discipline) is correct," he said.

The centre-right government announced a savings plan amounting to 19.7 billion zlotys in 2009 budget spending.

It also vowed to keep the budget gap at the previously planned 18.2 billion zlotys even if 2009 growth slows to 1.7 percent, which Prime Minister Donald Tusk has said is its worst case scenario, from an expected 4.8 percent in 2008.

The budget had a surplus in January of 2.8-3.0 billion zlotys, Deputy Finance Minister Elzbieta Suchocka-Roguska told Reuters on Wednesday, adding she expected a deficit in the full January-February period. (Writing by Gabriela Baczynska and Kuba Jaworowski; editing by Patrick Graham)

title: *DJ Poland Ctrl Bk Gov: Growth Could Slow To 1% - 1.5% In 2009
text:
31 Jan 2009 07:45 EDT *DJ  Poland Ctrl Bk: Ready To Intervene On FX But Don't See Need

31 Jan 2009 07:45 EDT *DJ  Poland Ctrl Bk Gov: Could Reduce Obligatory Reserves Ratio

31 Jan 2009 07:45 EDT *DJ  Poland Ctrl Bk Gov: New Financial Instruments Not Needed Now

31 Jan 2009 07:45 EDT =DJ  DAVOS INTERVIEW:Poland Ctrl Bk:Rate Gap With ECB Significant

By Natasha Brereton

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

DAVOS, Switzerland (Dow Jones)--Polish central bank President Slawomir Skrzypek says that risks to inflation are to the downside and called the difference in level between Polish and euro-zone interest rates remains significant.

In an interview with Dow Jones Newswires at the World Economic Forum Friday, Skrzypek also said he doesn't expect Poland's economy to contract at all during the downturn and that there is "no chance" of a recession.

The central bank cut its key interest rate 75 basis points at its meeting earlier this week to 4.25%. The move followed a 75 basis point reduction in December. But that compares with interest rates of only 2% in the euro zone.

"We are in a bias of easing the monetary policy. If you observe interest rates in Poland and in the euro zone, there is still a significant disparity," Skrzypek said, adding: "The decline in interest rates is likely to occur."

That reflects the central bank's expectation that there will be a "significant slowdown" in growth in 2009, to 1% to 1.5%, from around 5% last year and about 7% in 2007.

Despite that, Skrzypek is confident that gross domestic product growth would stay above zero, thanks to the well-diversified nature of Poland's economy.

"In Poland, I think there's no chance of recession," Skrzypek said. "There's no fear of recession."

Inflation could fall below the bank's target of 2.5% "in the next quarters," he said, but he declined to discuss the bank's new forecasts it will publish in February.

While the central bank says it has done everything it needs to do to join the euro, financial turmoil could make concluding the process more tricky.

Earlier this month, Poland's finance minister was reported saying that plans to enter the European Union's ERM2 exchange rate mechanism in mid-2009 and adopt the euro on Jan. 1, 2012 could be delayed if instability persists in global markets.

The E.U.'s Maastricht Treaty requires euro-zone candidate countries to fix their currencies to the euro within ERM2's plus/minus 15% trading band for a minimum of two years before receiving clearance to adopt the currency.

"In normal times, volatility of our currency was about 5%-to-6%. Now its average is 20% but there was a time when it was even 35%," Skrzypek said. "It's not a favorable time to join the exchange rate mechanism."

He noted that it was very hard to predict financial market conditions even a month ahead at the moment.

Skrzypek said he believed the zloty's current value was "below fundamentals," reflecting the flight-to-safe-haven trend and nervousness surrounding the region. Poland's economy has been relatively resilient during the downturn, but the plight of some of its emerging European neighbors has fueled concerns about the area as a whole.

"I'm not worried about the current exchange rate now. Maybe the market judged us unfairly but it also creates a favorable situation for our exports," Skrzypek said.

While there has been increasing discussion of the potential for governments to intervene to adjust their currencies' values to more rational levels, the governor was confident that the zloty would return to fundamentals.

Nevertheless, he indicated the government was ready to take action if it believed that to be necessary.

"We are ready to intervene, but I think such intervention is not needed," Skrzypek said.

"I think the flexibility of the economy and all the positive factors will in a natural way help our currency to come back to fundamentals."

Turning to the financial markets, Skrzypek said that although Poland's market was actually overliquid from a macro perspective, tensions could emerge on a micro basis between financial institutions.

Skrzypek said the bank is exploring introducing new instruments based on the experiences of the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank. "At the moment, it's not required but we are prepared," he said.

The governor said another option is to increase the frequency of central bank operations providing funding in zlotys and euros.

It's also considering whether to lower its mandatory reserve rate, which stands at 3.5%, above the ECB's 2%.

"We are carefully monitoring the market and we are ready to introduce the next measures when they are needed. Reaching this level (2%) in a few steps could be the best strategy," Skrzypek said.

title: UPDATE 2- Poland  should avoid euro vote,  intervention -cbankers
text:
(Adds Deputy PM Pawlak, paragraphs 8-9)

WARSAW, Jan 6 (Reuters) - Poland should avoid a referendum on adopting the euro, a central banker said on Tuesday, as the zloty gained back ground against the single currency and another official played down the chances of market intervention.

The zloty has lost about 30 percent against the euro since last summer amid a general global investor flight from risk, supporting a push by Prime Minister Donald Tusk's cabinet for a swift change to the euro, in early 2012.

But many economists remain sceptical that it can meet this target and central bank policymaker Andrzej Wojtyna said on Tuesday global financial gloom and currency volatility may erode faith in the common currency.

In the first public comment by a central banker on the referendum issue, Wojtyna, a moderate on the bank's 10-strong rate-setting Monetary Policy Council (MPC), said the zloty's volatility could sway Polish voters' views.

"Since the discussions before a referendum would take place in a time of crisis, we can expect high volatility in the zloty, which could in turn trigger significant changes in support for the euro," Wojtyna wrote in an article in Rzeczpospolita daily.

Last week, Tusk himself ruled out a referendum, though the eurosceptical main opposition party Law and Justice (PiS) has made such a vote the price of its support for necessary constitutional changes.

Wojtyna said it might be better to postpone resolving the euro issue until after the next parliamentary elections, due in the autumn of 2011, if the government and opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party fail to reach agreement on a euro timetable.

Later on Tuesday, Deputy Prime Minister Waldemar Pawlak reaffirmed the government's determination to adopt the euro.

"The time (of entry) is of smaller significance, it's the exchange-rate (that matters) and there is no doubt the current currency level is much more beneficial," he told a news conference after a weekly cabinet meeting.

The zloty <EURPLN=>, which has shed some 30 percent since July on the back of the global turmoil, gained 1.7 percent against the euro on the day as global investors' appetite for risk improved at the start of the new year.

NO INTERVENTION

Central Bank Governor Slawomir Skrzypek in December said there might also be a need for the bank to intervene in the currency market to stem the zloty's sharp depreciation, but his deputy Witold Kozinski played down such suggestions on Tuesday.

Kozinski said Poland does not need foreign exchange interventions now, though the MPC would consider such a move "if the zloty weakens significantly like 10-15 percent over a week".

Poland has had a free-floating currency regime since April 2000. The law says the government sets exchange rate policy with the cooperation of the central bank. But the bank can intervene if the currency threatens its inflation target.

The central bank has been broadly supportive of government plans to adopt the euro in 2012, though Governor Skrzypek -- an ally of Law and Justice -- has criticised the strategy.

President Lech Kaczynski, twin brother of PiS leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski, reaffirmed on Tuesday his support for a referendum on the euro and said adopting the common currency in 2012 was "undoable".

Before entering the eurozone a country must keep its currency inside the exchange rate mechanism or ERM-2 for at least two years.

The central bank's deputy governor criticised as premature Tusk's plan to put the zloty into ERM-2 in the coming months.

"When it comes to ERM-2, I think 2009 is not yet good enough," Kozinski told TVN CNBC, without elaborating.

He added that the advantages of euro adoption outweighed the disadvantages for Poland. (Additional reporting by Kuba Jaworowski) (Writing by Gareth Jones; editing by Patrick Graham)

text:
WARSAW, Dec 18 (Reuters) - Emerging Europe's currencies weakened further on Thursday, with the Polish zloty at a 2-1/2 year-low and the Czech crown near its lowest level this year as risks to economic growth build.

Data in the region has drawn a darker picture of its economies and the countries' central banks have moved to cut rates, while appetite for emerging assets has waned.

The Czech crown <EURCZK=> opened lower Thursday, a day after the central bank cut the main repo rate to 2.25 percent, its lowest level since July and hinted at more cuts as the economic crisis gathers pace. [ID:nLH141377]

"Fundamentally the story is the same; the global slowdown is here and there is nothing to hedge (against)," a local Prague-based dealer said.

Data on Thursday showed Czech retail sales unexpectedly dipped in October, prompting some analysts to warn the slowdown in production was starting to hit consumer behaviour harder. [ID:nLI114058]

In Poland, the zloty <EURPLN=> fell slightly to a 2 1/2 year low in early trade, and dealers said prospects for the currency are negative.

"I expect the zloty will reach the level of 4.20 to the euro quickly as risk aversion in the region grows and domestically we have this ongoing options problem," said Jan Koprowski, dealer at BNP Paribas in Warsaw.

The Polish currency has lost more than 24 percent since the summer when it was at its all-time high to the common currency, and the reversal has hit some companies that bet wrongly on further appreciation in the zloty. [ID:nLH476303]

Also on Thursday, Poland's stats office releases industrial output and producer prices data for November and analysts expect output to have fallen as much as 5.1 percent year-on-year.

Romania's leu <EURRON=> was down 0.2 percent in quiet trade, but the regional economic gloom and political uncertainty are seen weakening the currency further.

"Foreign players are buying euros, betting on a recoupling of the leu with the region and especially with the zloty," one dealer said. "It has every reason to do this as Romania has weaker fundamentals than Poland."

"But they still fear central bank intervention, so the recoupling takes some time. Apparently, the central bank does not want the leu to depreciate sharply, but gradually."

The Democrat-Liberals and Social Democrats, who have forged a governing coalition, are expected to announce the names of the future ministers. [ID:nLH159546]

The parliament is expected to endorse the cabinet on Monday.

title: WRAPUP 2-Czech crown, Polish zloty hit records, forint strong
text:
(Adds updated records, Polish central banker comment)

 PRAGUE, July 14 (Reuters) - The Czech crown and Polish zloty inched up to new highs on Monday, extending record gains over  the past month that have spread to other regional currencies helped by interest rate hike expectations.

 The crown <EURCXZK=> hit a record 23.280 against the euro, up from 23.425 at Friday's close. 

 The zloty <EURPLN=> firmed to a new high of 3.2540 to the euro in the afternoon before pulling back to 3.2565 after the central bank said it would not intervene to slow the currency's appreciation. The zloty closed at 3.258 per euro on Friday.

 "It's a continuation of the trend from the past few weeks where we've seen strong outperformance from regional currencies," said Martin Blum, head of emerging macroeconomic research at Unicredit in Vienna.

 The region's currencies have firmed in the past month to record highs as risk averse investors sought alternatives to usual high-return investments and the market bet central banks would further combat inflation with interest rate hikes.

 Blum said the region has been boosted by investors shifting positions from what are perceived as more risky Asian assets.

 "It's an ongoing reallocation," he said.

 STAYING CLEAR

 Central bankers have become increasingly concerned with the impact of currency strength on economies that are already slowing due to lower demand from western trade partners.

 However, that strength has also helped combat price growth, bringing about prospects for a pause in rate tightening, and policymakers have stopped short of intervening in markets.

Poland's central bank Governor Slawomir Skrzypek said on Monday his bank did "not expect to intervene on the foreign exchange market".

 The Czech currency has added 3.5 percent against the euro in the past four weeks and 11.4 percent since Jan. 1. The zloty has firmed 3.8 percent and 9.8 percent in the same periods.

 The Slovak crown, which will be switched for euros on January 1, 2009, has also gained 9.9 percent since the start of the year, and traders say its steep appreciation has brought regional neighbours' prospects for euro zone entry more to the forefront, boosting investor interest.

 "It is sort of a knee-jerk reaction," one trader with a London bank said.

 Hungary's forint <EURHUF=> has done better that the Czech and Polish currencies, strengthening 6.3 percent in the past month and 9.2 percent for the year. It traded near an all-time high of 229.55 to the euro on Monday.

 The Romanian leu <EURRON=> is up 2.4 percent in the past month. It was at 3.57 per euro on Monday, near its 2008 high.

 Analysts say there are still a chance for further interest rate rises in the region due to demand-led inflationary pressures. Data in the past week from the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary and Romania showed inflation in June was nearing predicted peak levels but likely to remain elevated.

 "The strength of the currencies, if it persists, will have an impact," Societe Generale wrote in its weekly Emerging Weekly on Friday. "Does it mean that the rate hike cycle has come to an end in eastern Europe? We do not think so."

(Reporting by Jason Hovet and Dagmara Leszkowicz; Editing by Ian Jones)

title: UPDATE 1-Speculators to drive zloty up before euro-minister
text:
(Updates with details, background)

BRUSSELS, July 8 (Reuters) - Poland's zloty currency <EURPLN=> is likely to face strong appreciation pressure in the pre-euro ERM-2 exchange rate system, as was the case with the Slovak crown, the Polish finance minister said on Tuesday.

Jacek Rostowski told a news conference such pressure might require costly forex market interventions by the central bank, so the government would analyse preventative options.

"Slovakia ... is joining the euro zone after a significant currency appreciation so we can suspect that a well-prepared country like Poland may be subject to strong speculation towards appreciation on the currency market," he said.

"This may create problems, so we will analyse this case (Slovakia), ponder what is the best way to prevent this."

Rostowski was speaking after Slovakia cleared the final hurdle towards joining the euro zone on Jan. 1, 2009. EU finance ministers set the rate at which the single currency will replace its crown <EURSKK=> -- at 30.1260 crowns to the euro.

Many analysts believe Poland could join the ERM-2, the currency stability test for joining the euro, in 2009 at the earliest and adopt the currency in 2012.

The Slovak crown has gained some 22 percent against the euro since July 2006, when the current left-wing government took over. Slovakia has twice revalued the central parity rate in the ERM-2, around which the currency of a euro candidate is allowed to fluctuate within a narrow band.

Poland's zloty is expected to face similar pressure in the ERM-2, so the Polish central bank and the European Central Bank may need to conduct costly intervention on the currency market to keep the zloty within the required band, Rostowski said.

"What happened in Slovakia may encourage players in the currency market to expect appreciation (in Poland), which may mean a need for sizeable intervention to avoid this."

Under Poland's current free-float system, the zloty has gained 8.5 percent against the euro since the start of the year and more than 31 percent since Poland joined the EU in 2004.

The Polish currency hit a record high of 3.2990 against the euro on Tuesday after breaking through the key psychological level of 3.3 zlotys.

Rostowski also said the EU's go-ahead for Slovakia to join the euro zone despite ECB doubts over the country's inflation was a good signal for Poland's euro bid.

"There were certain temptations to sharpen (euro entry) criteria for Slovakia ..., attempts to look for excuses not to accept Slovakia," he said.

"The fact those temptations were rejected is a positive result from the point of view of Poland's future membership of the euro," he added.

The ECB had doubts over whether Slovakia met the euro entry inflation criterion in a sustainable way, but the European Commission, the EU's executive arm, finally decided to recommend that the country be allowed to enter the euro zone. (Editing by Dale Hudson)

title: UPDATE 2-Poland has room for one more hike-MPC's Wojtyna
text:
(Adds MPC member Wasilewska-Trenkner on fx interventions)

 WARSAW, May 19 (Reuters) - Poland has room for more monetary policy tightening soon but it should be limited to one interest rate hike, Monetary Policy Council (MPC) member Andrzej Wojtyna was quoted as saying on Monday. 

 "There is still room for some monetary policy tightening soon," Wojtyna told Rzeczpospolita daily in an interview. "But, like some of my colleagues at the (Monetary Policy) Council, I think it is rather one hike, than two."

 Wojtyna added that April would have been a good time for a rate increase and that it would make little difference now if the next hike came in May or June.

 The MPC has raised its main interest rate seven times since April 2007 to the current level of 5.75 percent to fight accelerating inflation, but left them on hold last month.

 The 10-member council is due to meet again on rates next week and is expected to keep them unchanged again.

 Though inflation slightly eased in April to 4.0 percent from 4.1 percent for March, it is expected to pick up again later in the year.

 Another MPC member, Halina Wasilewska-Trenkner, told Radio PiN the strong zloty, flirting with an all-time high and some 30 percent up against the euro since Poland joined the EU in 2004, also helped to curb the need for monetary tightening.

 For example, the zloty has capped price growth of imported fuel, she said. Asked about the possibility of currencyinterventions to weaken the zloty and help relieve pressure on Polish exporters, she said this would be a bad idea.

 "Interventions in Polish conditions, given today's situation on the global financial markets, are dangerous and would bring no result," Wasilewska-Trenkner said.

 EURO DATE

 Wojtyna also reiterated his view that setting a date to join the euro zone would create incentives for economic reform. 

 "The date factor plays a significant role," Wojtyna said. "We have quite a strange situation now. The declarations of the finance ministry and the government are not clear, especially when it comes to the date."

 "It is said that problems, if they occur, will occur on the central bank and inflationary criteria side and also it may be difficult meeting the budget criteria if a more serious economic slowdown happens." 

 Government officials say Poland, the European Union's biggest ex-communist economy, could join the pre-euro mechanism ERM2 in 2009. This could indicate joining the euro zone in 2011 or 2012, but no official dates have been fixed. 

 The MPC has said in the past it supported euro adoption as soon as possible.   (Writing by Gabriela Baczynska, editing by Gareth Jones and Gerrard Raven)

title: UPDATE 2-INTERVIEW-Polish PM says euro in 2012 probable
text:
(Releads, adds quotes, more detail)   

WARSAW, March 6 (Reuters) - Poland will probably adopt the euro in 2012 if the government can ensure the move will benefit as many Poles as possible, including those who are not well-off, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Thursday.   

Hopes of quicker euro adoption were one of the main reasons behind markets' warm welcome of the election victory of Tusk's centre-right Civic Platform last year, which ran a campaign promising the euro, lower taxes and less red tape.   

Tusk's government, in office for just over 100 days, has so far refused to set a formal entry date, however.   

He said this was because of uncertainties related to the global economic outlook and insisted the government was working to make euro entry possible.   

"2012 is quite probable. We will do it quickly and efficiently, but we are not going to set a specific target date. I prefer to make promises that I can keep," Tusk told Reuters in an interview.   

Tusk said, however, that adopting the single currency may harm the financial standing of Poles, still way behind in the race to catch up with their richer Western counterparts nearly 20 years after the fall of communism in 1989.   

"Poland in no way can be compared to any country that is already in the euro zone ... I am talking about millions of Poles that live on the verge of the social minimum ... The number of people who are not well-to-do is incomparably bigger," Tusk said.   

"We cannot ignore the social problem. We want to enter the euro as quickly as possible but not for the price that large group of Poles would have to pay," Tusk added, pointing to the possible growth of inflation following euro entry as his main concern.   

Tusk played down concerns, however, that the government became cool on the euro after the election victory.   

"Nobody needs to convince me, finance minister (Jacek) Rostowski, other ministers, to undertake action that requires courage, that requires a risk, also in the face of public opinion," he said.   

"(We will enter) when we reach the status of a country that meets all the requirements."   

C.BANK CONTROVERSY   

Tusk said he would not approve one of two candidates for central bank deputy governor, Witold Kozinski, due to his controversial views on currency interventions.   

Kozinski, an ex-central banker, was nominated to join the central bank board by the bank's governor Slawomir Skrzypek earlier this year. He spooked markets by suggesting currency interventions might be used to tame the vibrant zloty.   

Poland has had a free float for almost a decade.   

"I cannot take responsibility regarding Mr. Kozinski," Tusk said.   

He said he would approve the other candidate to the board, commercial banker Piotr Wiesiolek.   

Tusk's comments spurred an immediate reaction from the central bank which said it would not withdraw Kozinski's nomination, signalling a deepening of the row between the government and the central bank.   

The row at the central bank erupted when two of Skrzypek's deputies resigned at the start of the year. One accused the governor of mismanaging the bank and pressing the bank's economists to massage down inflation forecasts.   

When Skrzypek, a political appointee of the previous conservative administration, took the job in January 2007, analysts said he lacked credentials for the job.   

Tusk said the central bank appeared to be in a crisis.   

"I am a fanatic supporter of central bank independence but I am aware that (before Skrzypek) we have never had a political leadership at the central bank," he said. (Writing by Karolina Slowikowska)

title: INTERVIEW-Poland needs caution on euro -econ minister
text:
WARSAW, Jan 10 (Reuters) - Current volatility in global currency markets is complicating Poland's preparations to join the euro zone, Economy Minister Waldemar Pawlak said on Thursday.   

Pawlak said Poland needed time to determine the right exchange rate at which to propose pegging the zloty to the euro to be able to keep it stable for two years inside a special fluctuation band for euro candidate nations, the ERM-2.   

"At the moment, I think we need to think this over again," Pawlak said in an interview.   

He said the risk of getting the peg wrong and the level of global uncertainty was such that discussions about the euro exchange rate or the timing of ERM entry were theoretical at this stage.   

"In my opinion...the two-year period of staying in the corridor, with the current dynamic of currency markets, looks like a theoretical not a practical solution," he said.   

"The time spent in the corridor sometimes costs serious interventions and creates a huge temptation for serious market speculation."   

Poland's centre-right government, which took power in November last year, says it wants to adopt the euro in principle but only when the move will not disturb the economy and when it puts public finances in good order.   

It said entry before the current parliament's term expires in 2011 is unlikely.   

Any euro zone candidate needs to stay in the ERM 2 for two years, meaning Poland should consider pegging the zloty next year or in 2010 to replace zlotys with euros in 2012.   

The largest ex-communist economy in the EU hopes to cut the budget gap to below 3 percent of GDP this year and convince the European Commission to remove it from the blacklist of budgetary offenders, the biggest obstacle to euro entry.   

But rising inflation and the strengthening zloty, which rose 6 percent versus the euro and 14 percent against the dollar last year, have created a new headache for both government and central bank policymakers.   

Pawlak said the zloty's strength is approaching the limits of what is justified by economic fundamentals.   

He acknowledged that entering the ERM-2 sooner rather than later could help provide an anchor to the currency and provide relief to exporters but said he was concerned whether Poland would be able to defend the level from any speculative attack.   

"I think the exchange rate at which to enter is the key issue," he said, adding that inter-government discussions on the euro peg would be strictly confidential.   

Pawlak acknowledged the government and the central bank had little means to keep the currency from rising further on the back of the strong economy.   

"This is largely in the hands of the market and global experience teaches us that direct interventions are very costly and one should keep at arm's length from them," he said.   

He said, however, that the central bank, which is expected to hike interest rates in response to rising inflation, should consider the impact of monetary tightening on the zloty.   

"High interest rates tend to help a currency appreciate by making investments (into money instruments and bonds) more profitable," he said. (Writing by Adam Jasser; editing by Tony Austin)

"I am staunch opponent of intervention, even though it's a policy instrument like any other," Skrzypek told a business gathering in Warsaw. [ 24-09-07 1340GMT ]   

Poland's central bank president explained that central bank currency interventions "make sense when they are to counteract changes in the exchange rate that are not due to economic fundamentals, but to other factors."   

Skrzypek cited the actions of Chile's central bank during Argentina's currency crisis of 2001-2002. He said it was an example of justifiable intervention aimed at preventing the spill-over of a regional crisis from damaging Chile's sound economic fundamentals.   

Monday's statement marks the fullest elaboration of Skrzypek's personal views on currency intervention since he took the reins at the National Bank of Poland in January.   

Skrzypek's economic views weren't well known prior to his appointment because he had made his career in public administration and business, and thus had no monetary policy track record.   

-By David McQuaid, Dow Jones Newswires; +4822 622-2766; david.mcquaid@dowjones.com [ 24-09-07 1414GMT ]

title: INTERVIEW-Polish c.bank won't  intervene  to steady zloty-banker
text:
WARSAW, Jan 11 (Reuters) - Poland's government should stop buying zlotys on the market if it wants a weaker zloty, and cannot count on central bank interventions or deep rate cuts to weaken the currency, a central banker said on Wednesday.  

"If the ministry returned to its previous debt managagement strategy it would help stabilise the exchange rate," Dariusz Filar, a member of the bank's 10-strong monetary policy council, told Reuters.  

"Central bank interventions in the Polish currency market are not likely," he added.  

The central bank has repeatedly criticised the finance ministry's strategy of increasing foreign borrowing and swapping part of the proceeds for zlotys on the interbank market. Filar said in a brief telephone interview that deep interest rate cuts, advocated by some as a way to ease buying pressure on the zloty, should also be ruled out, because such a radical loosening of the monetary reins could threaten price stability.  

"A radical interest rate cut is viewed by some as a method to weaken the currency. But I want to point out that the central bank has an inflation target and a radical cut would threaten this target, so this is out of the question."  

Financial markets expect a modest cut in the bank's 4.50 percent benchmark rate later this month, convinced that the strong zloty will keep inflation well under control.  

But Prime Minister Kazimierz Marcinkiewicz and some members of his Law and Justice party have argued Polish rates should be closer to the euro zone's 2.25 percent, given that inflation in the EU newcomer stands at half of the euro area average.  

Filar, seen as a supporter of restrictive policy conditions on the bank's 10-member policy council and an advocate of fiscal discipline, said Poland's economic growth could suffer if the zloty held near its recent highs.  

"The recent (zloty) strengthening may pose problems for some exporters and could lead to weaker economic growth."  

The zloty, which hit a fresh multi-year high against the euro on Monday, has risen two percent so far this year and is up seven percent since early November.

title: UPDATE 2-Polish c.bank criticises Finmin's zloty, debt plans
text:
(Adds Finance Minister Miroslaw Gronicki's comments)  

WARSAW, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Poland's deputy central bank governor on Wednesday criticised the finance ministry's plan to boost foreign borrowing and then to convert some of the money via the currency market rather than through the central bank.  

In an interview, Jerzy Pruski said the growing reliance on foreign debt issues, set out in the finance ministry's medium-term debt strategy, could make Poland's path towards euro zone membership vulnerable to exchange-rate swings.  

But Finance Minister Miroslaw Gronicki stood firmly by the ministry's plans, saying the foreign exchange transactions were aimed at curbing debt servicing costs and not at a particular zloty impact.  

The zloty <EURPLN=> hit 40 month highs against the euro this week on expectations that the ministry will exchange part of the funds from Wednesday's $1.1 billion U.S. bond issue on the forex market, not through the central bank as it usually does.  

"In bilateral talks we have repeatedly warned the finance ministry of the negative economic aspects of this policy...of selling foreign currency on the market and announcing further such operations," Pruski said told Reuters.  

"We have a floating exchange rate, where market forces shape the zloty rate, and here we have a non-market player interfering by its actions and announcements of future action which influence market expectations of future exchange rates."  

Pruski also said such interference was not needed because the zloty rate was currently strong. The currency has firmed 10 percent against the euro since 2005 lows hit in April.  

"One thing is certain -- the zloty is surely not too weak, regardless of how we assess its strength," he said. "Looking at the prospects for economic growth in Poland, appreciation brought about by such action is not needed."  

Gronicki defied the central bank's criticism and said the ministry might even sell all $1.1 billion from the U.S. issues to curb debt servicing costs if the zloty weakened sharply.  

"It will be aimed at minimising debt servicing costs and not at stabilising the zloty, because the latter is not the finance ministry's goal," Gronicki said.  

"Currently, our foreign debt is lower than in 2003, so the criticism from the central bank is not appropriate and partly emotional," he said.  

EURO RISK?  

The finance ministry's medium-term debt management strategy, published last week, envisages net foreign borrowing at 20 billion zlotys ($6.2 billion) next year with roughly 7 billion due to be exchanged into zloty on the forex market.  

If the free-floating zloty weakens, the value of foreign debt in zloty terms would balloon, potentially boosting the value of total debt beyond limits needed for euro adoption.  

"In the context of meeting (euro zone entry) Maastricht criteria, a situation where our foreign debt is growing in relation to public debt is worrisome in itself, and surely exposes this ratio to exchange rate risk," Pruski said.  

Poland, which has said it wanted to join the euro area by 2010, expects its public debt to reach more than 52 percent of gross domestic product next year, and the weakening of the zloty could push it dangerously close to the EU's 60 percent cap.  

Financial market analysts also said the finance ministry's zloty-buying plans appeared odd given the unit's strength.  

"(Pruski's) statement points to increased tension between the central bank and the finance ministry over the ministry's forex 'interventions'," Poland's Bank BPH said in a report, calling the ministry's currency moves "astonishing".  

Poland's economic growth has failed to pick up much speed after a sharp slowdown early this year, with exporters -- the main engine of growth -- complaining that zloty appreciation is pricing them out of markets. -- additional reporting by Pawel Sobczak

title: FACTBOX-Candidates for Polish economic ministries
text:
Sept 12 (Reuters) - Following are profiles of potential candidates for key economic portfolios under Poland's expected new coalition of the economically liberal Civic Platform (PO) party and conservatives Law and Justice (PiS).  

For a FACTBOX on the two parties economic policy programmes, click on: [ID:nL02669490].  

FINANCE MINISTER  

Barring a strong victory for Law and Justice, politicians and analysts widely expect the ministry to go to the Civic Platform and its agenda of fiscal cuts, fast euro entry and lower corporate and income tax rates.  

But the new minister is likely to face Law and Justice resistance to cuts in welfare benefits and a swift push into the single currency, and will need to manage a compromise over the two parties' differing tax proposals.  

Political sources say the Civic Platform is as yet undecided whether to make a political appointment to the ministry or pick one of the economic experts who work on its policy programme.  

STEFAN KAWALEC (CIVIC PLATFORM)  

A respected economist and finance ministry veteran from the early 1990s, Kawalec, 52, keeps a low public profile and has avoided the political limelight.  

He began his post-communist career during much-praised "shock therapy" market reforms in 1989-1991, when he was chief adviser to then finance minister, and now central bank governor, Leszek Balcerowicz.  

Later a deputy finance minister, he stayed on under the leftist government only to be sacked in 1994 in a controversy surrounding a major banking privatisation, which may make him less palatable for Law and Justice.  

Kawalec has worked in business since and is now director of strategy with Poland's biggest insurer PZU SA. He has led the Platform's economic policy working group for the last two years.  

HANNA GRONKIEWICZ-WALTZ (CIVIC PLATFORM)  

As central bank governor in 1992-2000, Gronkiewicz-Waltz, 53, oversaw reforms which nursed Poland's banking sector out of crisis, re-establishing lender faith and eventually helping make it the most streamlined and competitive in central Europe.  

A law lecturer, she was deputy head of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development after leaving the central bank and remains untested on fiscal policy. She speaks English, Russian and French.  

"It is a very tough job and I think that the minister must be someone who is expert in budget affairs and close to the vision of (Platform prime ministerial candidate) Jan Rokita, who wants to drive economic matters," she told Reuters recently about the finance minister post.  

Well-connected politically, she leads the Platform's Warsaw electoral list, and is also cited as a potential candidate for mayor of the Polish capital.  

ZBIGNIEW CHLEBOWSKI (CIVIC PLATFORM)  

Chlebowski, 41, has been the Platform's main economic spokesman, although he has little practical experience with implementing economic policy at a national level.  

For 11 years the mayor of his home town in lower Silesia, he entered parliament at the last election and cut his policy teeth chairing a committee dealing with fiscal reform plans. If the party opts for a political appointee, sources say Chlebowski could lead the race along Gronkiewicz-Waltz.  

He has a degree from Wroclaw's Academy of Agriculture. He speaks fluent German and some English.  

RAFAL ANTCZAK (CIVIC PLATFORM)  

A die-hard liberal economist, Antczak, 35, works at the CASE research institute, seen as close to the views of central bank chief Leszek Balcerowicz, and is generally seen as the brains behind the Platform's economic policy programme.  

Sharp and uncompromising in arguing his views, he designed the party's flat 15 percent rate corporate, VAT and income tax policy and supports sharp cuts in welfare and administrative spending.  

Since 1994 he has worked as a policy adviser to governments and central banks in Ukraine, Kirgistan, Kazakhstan, Belarus and Moldova. He speaks fluent English, good Russian and some Ukrainian and Belarussian.  

ECONOMY/STATE TREASURY MINISTRY

Political sources and analysts say a strong result for Law and Justice would lead it to fight hard for control of a new economy super-ministry which both parties want to replace the current economy and treasury ministries.  

The new ministry will be charged with speeding up privatisation as well as supporting growth and job creation.  

ADAM SZEJNFELD (CIVIC PLATFORM)  

The head of the lower house of parliament's Economy Committee and a lawyer by training, Szejnfeld. 46, has close ties with business and supports a wide-ranging rationalisation of state administration and taxation.  

In the last parliament he authored numerous bills aimed at encouraging entrepreneurship, investment and job creation, particularly among small and medium-sized businesses but has no experience of running economic policy in government.  

PIOTR KAMINSKI  

Currently a board member at Poland's state-controlled largest bank PKO BP, Kaminski, 36, is a market insider with experience as the deputy head of the Warsaw Stock Exchange and eight years at Poland's Securities Commission.  

He has a business degree from Warsaw University and is known to have good contacts in the Platform.  

CEZARY MECH (LAW AND JUSTICE)  

The author of Law and Justice's economic programme, Mech is an economist by training and the former head of Poland's pension fund watchdog. He favours an interventionist economic policy, but also supports the fiscal reforms needed to stabilise public finances and ensure Poland meets euro entry conditions.  

In July's policy programme Mech proposed freezing the budget deficit at 30 billion zlotys in 2006-9, along with a series of tax rebates for business to spur job creation.  

But he also warned against rushing too fast into the euro, saying it would only benefit foreign speculators, and called for the central bank to significantly lower Polish interest rates to weaken the zloty and boost credit growth.

title: Polish zloty hits new high, bonds rebound.
text:
WARSAW, March 1 (Reuters) - Poland's zloty hit a fresh
32-month high to the euro on Tuesday as foreign investors poured
more capital into central Europe, betting strong growth and a
raised investment profile will back more gains this year.
    Bonds retreated as investors took some profit-taking on an
almost 30 basis point fall in yields since the central bank's
surprise jump to an easing policy bias last Friday.
    Analysts say the zloty has gained in recent days chiefly on
bond market flows, but dealers put Tuesday's gains against both
the euro and dollar down to a combination of speculative and
fund capital, possibly also meant for corporate purchases.
    Current account data on Monday showed foreign funds poured
558 million euros into Warsaw stocks in December while the
treasury on Tuesday invited offers for a power plant worth an
estimated $230 million, one of a series of big privatisations
planned for 2005.
  


    "This is a trend that no-one is willing to oppose and
everyone wants to take advantage of," said a dealer with one
large Warsaw bank. "Gains should continue across the region and
the nearest target is 3.85 to the euro."
    The zloty has gained 23 percent against the euro since
European Union entry last May, including 15 percent in the last
six months, with prospects of interest rate cuts and political
instability ahead of this year's election yet to weaken the
currency.
    On Tuesday it rose 0.7 percent against both the euro and
dollar, also helped by predictions from shadow prime minister
Jan Rokita of further gains when the next government moves
forward on fiscal reform.
    But analysts added Rokita's suggestion Poland could adopt
the euro before joining the European Monetary Union to protect
its economy from further zloty gains, showed the strong
