title: UPDATE 2-Polish cbank's Belka: new govt must tackle deficit-report
text:
* Belka expects public finance reforms from new govt

* Will support govt with moderate monetary policy

* Worried about global impact on Polish banking sector

(Adds Belka comments on banks)

By Gabriela Baczynska

WARSAW, Oct 17 (Reuters) - Poland's newly re-elected government should act decisively to rein in the budget deficit in order to ensure financial stability , central bank Governor Marek Belka said, adding the bank would support Warsaw by pursuing a moderate monetary policy.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk's centre-right Civic Platform (PO) party won a second four-year term in elections this month and Belka said it needed to show determination in reforming public finances.

"I expect another meaningful step in public finance consolidation," Belka wrote in an article for the Bloomberg Businessweek magazine. "A difficult 2012 is coming, when we have to show to the markets, that the deficit is being curbed, borrowing needs are under control."

He said Poland should reform its separate pension system for members of the police, army and other services -- which Tusk's government has been working on for some time -- as well as its costly social security system for farmers.

"The central bank can support government actions by conducting stable monetary policy. In a world engulfed with crisis, its long-term target should be to add to increasing stability. We should fight inflation, but not too hard -- not tighten too much only to be easing excessively in a while," Belka wrote.

"We should avoid being extreme, but, at the same time, persistently aim at bringing inflation to the bank's mid-term target of 2.5 percent plus/minus one percentage point band."

Annual inflation stood at 3.9 percent in September.

Rating agencies have threatened to cut Poland's rating if Warsaw fails to act swiftly on lowering its deficit and public debt, which Warsaw forecasts at 5.6 percent of GDP and 53.8 percent of GDP respectively this year.

But Tusk, who in his first term disappointed liberal market economists by not pursuing radical pro-market reforms, has already said he would not change his gradual approach to reform.

Poland was the only European Union member to avoid recession during the 2008-09 global financial crisis, partly because it is less export-reliant than some of its neighbours and was also helped by a sharp weakening of the zloty, which shed more than a third of its value against the euro.

The Polish currency has also taken a beating this year, weakening 8 percent against the euro, as investors fled riskier emerging markets fearing a renewed global slowdown.

Poland's central bank has intervened three times in the spot market since the start of September to support the zloty.

On Monday, Belka reiterated that more such moves were on the cards, but said the bank was not defending any particular zloty level.

The zloty did not react to his comments. It was up 0.6 percent in morning trade at 4.273 to the euro.

FOREIGN BANKS

Belka said the zloty's volatility was partly due to foreign owners of Polish banks promoting foreign currency mortgages, which accounted for more than 60 percent of Poles' mortgages in the first quarter, according to the market regulator's data.

The country's banking sector weathered the global economic crisis well as no bank went bankrupt and banks' still saw some loan growth, but Belka warned that banks' potential need to raise capital posed risks for Poland.

"With stocks falling, parent banks will have trouble raising capital. This could lead to a strong desire to adjust the bank's balance sheets to the size of the bank's capital, that is lowering assets and, resulting from that, credit limiting. I fear this could affect Poland," he said.

Belka said enhanced cooperation between the government, the central bank as well as the financial sector watchdog (KNF) was essential and he criticised foreign parent banks over setting ceilings for investments in Polish debt.

"Banking sector stability is crucial from my point of view. I'm not against re-Polonisation with private capital participation," he said, referring to the idea of private Polish investors taking over the local units of foreign banks.

"There is this idea to invite private equity funds to (participate in) re-Polonisation. If such chances arise, I have nothing against that. I only warn against re-nationalisation."

(Additional reporting by Piotr Bujnicki, writing by Gabriela Baczynska; Editing by Susan Fenton)

title: UPDATE 2-Polish reserves flat in Sept despite  interventions
text:
* Reserves suggest central bank's interventions were small

* Belka says interventions unable to stop a prevailing trend

* Cbank may limit speedy depreciation, curb speculation - Belka

(Updates with cbank governor, updates prices)

WARSAW, Oct 7 (Reuters) - Poland's foreign exchange reserves

were unchanged in September, the central bank said on Friday, suggesting its two interventions in the month were relatively small in size.

The country's foreign exchange reserves stood at 74.1 billion euros at the end of September, roughly the same as at the end of August.

Poland's central bank stepped into the market to defend the zloty in September for the first time in more than a decade, twice selling foreign currencies and buying zlotys, boosting the Polish currency more than 2 percent to the euro.

The bank intervened again in October, but it has not disclosed the amounts of foreign currencies it sold on the market.

Central bank governor Marek Belka reiterated in an article published after the data that the bank would not defend any given level of the zloty and would not be able to reverse its falling trend if capital exits emerging markets.

"If the trend is such that some categories of capital exit emerging markets, including Poland, we will not be able to do much anyway," Belka was quoted as saying by obserwatorfinasowy.pl, the central bank's news website.

"We can only ensure that the process is not rapid, that the temperature of this phenomenon is not increased by speculative actions," he said.

Poland's economy will not avoid a slowdown, but it does not have to be as deep as elsewhere in Europe, Belka added.

Poland was the only country to avoid a slowdown in the European Union in 2009. Analysts polled by Reuters forecast the economy to expand at 3.1 percent in 2012, down from 4.0 percent seen for 2011.

INTERVENTIONS SMALL?

Poland's central bank reports the value of its reserves at the end of each month in zlotys, euros and dollars, but it does not publish the allocation in particular currencies.

This, economists say, makes it difficult to calculate the exact value of the September interventions, which they estimate at anywhere from 350 million to 1.5 billion euros.

"The very fact they are in the market at all is highly significant but versus average daily turnover (about 5 billion euros), that much for two days of intervention is a small fraction," said Peter Attard Montalto, an emerging markets analyst at Nomura.

The zloty traded up 0.3 percent to the euro on Friday as better-than-expected jobs data in the U.S. boosted investors' risk appetite. The Polish currency is presently over 2 percent stronger than at the time of the first intervention two weeks ago.

Montalto added that larger interventions often account for 20-25 percent of daily turnover. At the lower end of estimates, Poland's intervention accounted to about 3.5 percent.

The bank had around 64 billion euros in securities denominated in convertible foreign currencies in August and gold worth around 4 billion euros at the end of September, the bank's data showed. During September U.S. and German treasury bonds gained in price, but gold fell.

title: CEE MARKETS 4-Zloty leads  FX  bounce, more  intervention  eyed
text:
(Updates after Polish cbank comments)

* Poland holds rates, may intervene again to buoy zloty

* Improved global sentiment lifts stocks, buoys FX

* Hungary cbank minutes come out, eyes on weak forint

By Marcin Goettig and Jason Hovet

WARSAW/PRAGUE, Oct 5 (Reuters) - The zloty bounced to a one-week high on Wednesday after the Polish central bank left open the possibility of more intervention, adding to gains as emerging European currencies recovered more from multi-month lows.

Polish central bank Governor Marek Belka said the zloty, which had recently traded at or around its lowest since June 2009, was "detached from fundamentals" and said the bank could step into the market again as it has done three times in two weeks.

The bank's intervention has helped lift the zloty 3.5 percent since it hit a trough at 4.537 per euro on Sept. 22.

The zloty and Hungarian forint have been the hardest hit of the region's currencies as investors have retreated from emerging European assets on concerns over a weakening global economy and the spiralling debt crisis in the euro zone.

The selloff in the region has turned the focus towards policymakers' responses. Romania has also moved to prop up the leu, while Hungary may be forced into emergency rate hikes.

In Poland, polls have shown the possibility of a close result in a weekend election, adding to market nerves. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk's Civic Platform (PO) party looked set to win, according to the latest poll.

Poland's Monetary Policy Council (MPC) left its key rate on hold at 4.50 percent on Wednesday and said it would take a wait-and-see approach with a tendency towards tightening.

"I was slightly surprised by how relatively hawkish Belka was. It seems to me that the (MPC) is trying to send a slightly more hawkish signal than they fundamentally believe in to give some support to the zloty," Danske Bank's Lars Christensen said.

By 1459 GMT, the zloty firmed 0.7 percent to 4.381 to the euro. Hungary's forint , after see-sawing around a 29-month low at the psychological level of 300 to the euro, rose 0.9 percent to 297.16.

The forint has lost 7.9 percent since Sept. 1, while the zloty is down 5.4 percent.

"We think that EUR/PLN will be capped below 4.45 for the time being. The central bank and finance ministry have shown strong commitment to prevent PLN weakness beyond this level and we expect more FX interventions if necessary," Societe Generale said in a client note earlier in the day.

SAME BOAT FOR FORINT?

Similarly in Hungary, the forint's drop has fuelled speculation the central bank may undertake emergency rate hikes as it did in the 2008-09 financial crisis.

Minutes from a September policy meeting showed Hungary's central bank Deputy Governor Julia Kiraly tabled a proposal for a 25 basis point rise, the first proposal for monetary tightening since January.

But dealers said overall the minutes were not overly hawkish. "It's still a question what (market developments) could scare the central bankers enough to trigger a rate hike," a Budapest fixed income trader said.

"The forint/zloty has fallen apart... The Polish central bank has been intervening, and there is a strengthening group of hedge funds who now play against (forint assets)."

Hungary bond yields fell up to 30 basis points in volatile trade, with more swings likely.

Central European stock markets, which have lost 11-16 percent since Sept. 1 and are down up to 30 percent in 2011, rebounded on Wednesday, led by Budapest's 3.8 percent rise.

The region was supported by gains in global stocks following a European pledge to shore up banks against the euro zone debt crisis.

Moody's placed seven Hungarian banks on review for a possible downgrade. It cited a recently approved law allowing foreign currency mortgage holders to repay their debt at a big discount to market exchange rates.

With the Czech central bank the only in the region likely to tolerate a weak currency thanks to low inflation, Societe Generale recommended buying the euro versus the Czech crown on Tuesday.

The crown -- seen as the safest central European investment and the only currency to hold its 2011 gains -- added 0.8 percent to 24.724, while the Romanian leu inched up 0.1 percent to 4.313 to the euro.

The EUR/RON rate is still above the 4.3 level at which dealers are on alert for central bank support for the currency. The Romanian central bank sold euros through third parties last week, helping the leu rebound from a 15-month low of 4.3725.

title: UPDATE 1- Poland  keeps rates steady,  interventions  in focus
text:
* Rates last raised in June

* Analysts expect rate cuts next year

* Market awaiting comments on FX interventions

(Adds economist quote, details)

WARSAW, Oct 5 - Poland's central bank left its key interest rate unchanged at 4.50 percent on Wednesday as widely expected, as it seeks to balance the impact of a weakening zloty on inflation against a looming economic slowdown.

All 23 analysts polled by Reuters had predicted the central bank would leave borrowing costs unchanged after raising rates by a total 100 basis points this year, most recently in June.

The zloty and bonds did not show any reaction.

The central bank will release its post-decision statement at 1400 GMT, when it also holds a monthly news conference.

Investors are hoping the bank will give details of its three interventions in the foreign currency market over the last two weeks, aimed at preventing a further weakening of the zloty that would feed into inflation.

"The elevated inflation, as well as a weak zloty speak against quick rate cuts," said Piotr Bielski, senior economist at Bank Zachodni WBK. "FX interventions to support the zloty and simultaneous rate cuts would be incoherent."

Annual price growth stood at 4.3 percent in August, still considerably above the bank's 2.5 percent target, after it reached a near-decade high of 5.0 percent in May.

After raising the key interest rate four times this year the MPC has adopted a wait-and-see approach since June to assess the impact of the tightening delivered so far on inflation.

Analysts expect the MPC to start cutting interest rates next year given the expected economic slowdown, with the timing of the first move depending, among other factors, on the zloty exchange rate.

(Reporting by Marcin Goettig, writing by Chris Borowski; Editing by Catherine Evans)

title: UPDATE 2-Poland keeps rates flat, warily eyes weaker zloty
text:
* C.bank holds fire on rates, sees CPI high for now

* Frets over weaker zloty, says more interventions possible

* Analysts expect rate cuts next year

(Recasts with news conference, statement, analyst)

By Piotr Bujnicki

WARSAW, Oct 5 - Poland's central bank kept borrowing costs unchanged on Wednesday and signalled there was unlikely to be any early change as it tries to balance the inflationary risks of a weakening zloty with a looming economic slowdown.

Governor Marek Belka also reiterated the bank's readiness to intervene again on the foreign exchange market in support of the zloty as its level did not reflect Poland's healthy economic fundamentals.

The bank left the main rate at 4.50 percent, as forecast by all 23 analysts polled earlier by Reuters. Polish headline inflation was 4.3 percent in August, well above the bank's 2.5 percent target but off a May peak of 5.0 percent.

"In the coming months, annual CPI inflation will continue to run at an elevated level, primarily due to the previously observed sharp rise in global commodity prices," the bank's Monetary Policy Council (MPC) said in a statement.

"In the medium term, inflation will be curbed by the anticipated decline in domestic economic growth amidst fiscal tightening," it said, adding that CPI should then return to target.

But the MPC, which has been worried by an 11 percentage point fall in the zloty against the euro in the third quarter, also said it did not rule out further hikes.

The Polish authorities have intervened three times since Sept. 23 to buy zlotys for foreign currencies amid a flight of investors from emerging markets due to the deepening euro zone crisis and fears of a second global recession.

"Further such actions (interventions) are possible ... The zloty is detached from (Poland's economic) fundamentals," Belka told a news conference after the rate decision.

Poland's Finance Minister Jacek Rostowski said in comments elsewhere that he supported the central bank's interventions, adding that the ministry will exchange its EU funds on the market from "time to time" at prices it deems "favourable".

ZLOTY

The zloty gained 0.2 percent after these comments but surrendered the gains after Belka added: "Everything is dependent on the global situation. We do not intend to fight with the (prevailing) tendencies."

"We do not have a programme of interventions. Those that took place (...) were aimed at calming the markets. The anti-inflation character of interventions is clear," he added.

The zloty traded at 4.3825 by 1500 GMT, 0.7 percent up on the day thanks to improved sentiment on global markets.

"Overall, the central bank's bias looks to have been maintained with confirmation... that rates are more likely to be raised than cut in the next move," said Peter Attard Montalto of Nomura International.

"But it is rather hard to see the triggers for the next hike till there is actual evidence of (zloty weakening) passing through to CPI, which may not come until the first quarter (of 2012) when there would be falling inflation anyway."

Analysts expect the MPC to start cutting interest rates next year given the expected economic slowdown, with the timing of the first move depending, among other factors, on the zloty exchange rate.

(Additional reporting by Marcin Goettig; Writing by Gareth Jones; Editing by Hugh Lawson)

title: Eastern Europe Steps Up  Currency Interventions
text:
-- Poland sending strong message to the market as it intervenes for third consecutive trading day

-- Russia's central bank also intervenes

-- Romania's central bank also suspected of intervening to prop up the Leu

LONDON -- Authorities in Eastern Europe cranked up their efforts to prop up their currencies Monday, as Poland intervened for the third consecutive trading day and Russia also piled in to support the ruble.

Poland's central bank bought its domestic currency against the euro, while the Bank of Russia is suspected of selling at least $400 million, as well as shifting its trading band--which it uses to contain currency volatility--five kopeks weaker, after news that Greece would miss its deficit targets this year triggered another sell-off in emerging market currencies.

Romania's central bank is also suspected of intervening Monday, according to one dealer as central banks in emerging markets step in to stem currency weakness, which can pose inflationary problems, by lifting the cost of imported goods.

Moreover, for those countries burdened with large amounts of foreign currency-denominated debt, currency weakness is particularly harmful as these debts become much more expensive to pay back.

That is especially the case for Poland, whose central bank kept up its fight Monday to defend the zloty, something for which it has more than enough reserves to do, market participants say.

"The National Bank of Poland has enough ammunition with its $100 billion of foreign-exchange reserves to stay in the game for some time and [it] could be successful," said Murat Toprak, a foreign exchange strategist at HSBC in London.

That being said, the job won't be easy.

"It will be very difficult for the Polish authorities to reverse the trend because foreign investors will use the intervention to scale down long positions in Polish bonds," said Bartosz Pawlowski, head of foreign exchange and interest rate strategy for the Central and Eastern Europe, Middle East and Africa region for BNP Paribas in London.

Currencies in Asia, Latin America, Eastern Europe and Africa have been under heavy selling pressure in recent weeks as a toxic combination of global economy fears and escalating euro-zone debt worries led investors to fold their bets in emerging markets on a colossal scale.

Greece concerns ramped up that pressure Monday forcing central banks in the region into action again. The trading band of the ruble against the central bank's dollar-euro basket now spans 32.55 to 37.55, said Mikhail Anisimov, head of forex at VTB Capital in Moscow. That comes after the Russian central bank spent $2.36 billion defending the ruble, believed to be the biggest one-day dollar sale by the regulator since the financial crisis and oil-price decline that started in 2008.

At 1558 GMT the euro was trading at RON4.315 against the Romanian leu, down around 1% on the day. Against the Polish zloty, the single currency was trading at PLN4.3868, down from session highs hit earlier of PLN4.4401.

-By Clare Connaghan, Dow Jones Newswires; 44 20 7842 94966; clare.connaghan@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE 2-Polish c.bank  intervenes  again, to little effect
text:
* Polish c.bank intervenes again on mkt, fails to boost PLN

 * Market players say amount was small

 * Intervention could boost ECB fixing crucial for farm subsidies 

(Adds more comments, background)

 By Dagmara Leszkowicz

 WARSAW, Sept 30 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank stepped into the foreign exchange market again on Friday a week after an unprecedented intervention to stop the weakening zloty, hinting at a broader determination to halt the currency's fall.

 The zloty has been on the front line of investors' retreat from emerging European assets as the global economy faces a potential new downturn and confidence fades over euro zone policymakers' ability to reverse a debt crisis.

 While Polish authorities' move to firm the zloty last week sent the currency up 3 percent against the euro, dealers said Friday's action was more muted and after an initial boost the impact on the zloty was minimal.

 By 1440 GMT, the zloty was down 0.2 percent on the day to trade at 4.4241 to the euro. It a session high of 4.40 when the central bank initially asked for prices from dealers.

 Markets are testing the thresholds at which eastern European authorities will step in to bolster their currencies and the Polish bank's governor, Marek Belka, has warned of more intervention to battle volatility.  

 Analysts and dealers said the action on Friday was a further warning, but could also be more destabilising.

 "It appears we've been underestimating the scope of the change in the NBP's foreign exchange policy. The central bank is starting to look like a more permanent feature in the (currency) market," Mateusz Szczurek, chief economist for CEE at ING Bank, said in a client note.

 REGULAR DEAL

 Romania's central bank also was seen in the market by dealers in Bucharest on Friday, while emerging market policymakers globally have actively tried to defend currencies from the flight away from risk. 

 A weaker zloty puts pressures on households that have taken out popular foreign currency loans, while the weak exchange rate can also push government debt to near levels that might exceed a legally binding public debt ceiling and trigger spending cuts.

 Even before the interventions this month, Poland has regularly converted EU funds on the market through state-owned bank BGK. The Finance Ministry said on Friday these operations would depend on liquidity.

  Dealers have said this week that markets were testing the added threat of the central bank, and some dealers said the central bank moves would rather contribute to volatility. 

 The zloty touched as low as 4.4650 this week, putting it down 7 percent for September but still well shy of the 27-month low of 4.5370 it hit before the interventions. It has lost a cumulative 10.9 percent since July 1.

 "Given the fact that the move failed to boost the zloty, it appears that if the bank wants to step in again, it needs to sell at least twice as much to succeed," said one Warsaw-based dealer.   

 This week's intervention may have been aimed at strengthing the zloty ahead of Friday's European Central Bank fixing at 1215 GMT, crucial for calculation of European Union subsidies for farmers, some analysts said.

 Poland should get some 3.4 billion euros in direct payments for farmers in 2011-2012, but the payout will be spread between December 2011 and June 2012, according to the Finance Ministry. 

(Addidional reporting by Filip Kochan; Editing by Jason Hovet)

25 Sep 2011 23:59 EDT DJ  INTERVIEW:NBP's Belka: Not Targeting, Defending Any Level For Zloty

--NBP's Belka: Doesn't Rule Out Down Speculation Vs Zloty

--NBP's Belka: EU Needs IMF's Strong Conditionality Approach

--NBP's Belka: EU Needs More Self Confidence, Must Win Back Mkt Trust 


 
   By Gabriele Parussini 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)-Poland's central bank can intervene in the foreign exchange markets whenever it sees excessive volatility, but won't defend a set exchange rate for the zloty, Marek Belka, its governor, said Sunday.

"What has been bothering us is what we call the destabilization of the foreign exchange markets, and we saw some signs of it. We can intervene when we wish to and we can stop intervention when we wish to," he told Dow Jones on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund/World Bank semi-annual meeting. "We didn't intervene to defend any levels; we intervened because it was going in a disorderly way, too far too fast, and - to a certain extent - without a reason."

The central bank, Belka warned, may repeat its surprise action.

"If we think that the situation becomes worrying or something strange is happening on the market then we may intervene."

Belka's comments came two days after the Polish government and central bank propped up the zloty, which had been weakening since July, as investors exited emerging markets over euro-zone sovereign debt concerns and worries about the global economy.

The Polish currency rose nearly 3% against the euro in less than 30 minutes Friday afternoon, back to Wednesday levels, which were still about 6% below the exchange rate of September 1.

Friday's move served to punish speculators who had been betting against the zloty, Belka said, but investors shouldn't read too much into it.

"I can't rule out that some people were speculating against the zloty. We would like to highlight to the people that it's a two-way street. You can burn your fingers, you have to take into account an additional risk factor in your trades: central bank intervention," he said. "It was a random intervention. Don't read any trend in this."

The foreign exchange market has wide-ranging implications for Poland. A weak zloty inflates the country's debts denominated in foreign currencies. Before the zloty began weakening, Poland's public debt was around 53% of gross domestic product, well below the European Union average, but as its currency falls, the country's debt swells. And if the debt-to-GDP ratio crosses the crucial 55% threshold at the end of the year, Polish law requires the government to balance the budget or have a surplus.

And estimations on what's the currency level that will push the country's debt over the threshold vary--around PLN4.66, according to BRE Bank, PLN4.7, according to Citigroup.

But Belka denied he's paying much attention to that.

"All this talk about thresholds on public debt to GDP is just nonsense. This is nothing that really is of major concern to the ministry of finance or to us," he said. "We don't even know what this crucial exchange rate is. It changes every day."

Belka, who faces a tough rate-setting balancing act, juggling slowing economic growth and inflation--at 4.3% in August, well above the NBP's 2.5% target--ruled out swift interest rate moves, and said the 4.5% key rate, which has been hiked 100 basis points in the first half of this year, is unlikely to move any time soon.

"In such an unstable world it's probably quite reasonable to stay put and not to exclude any option either up or down with interest rates," he said. "There is always this call to be ahead of the curve. But in the case of a country like Poland the problem is that the curve is so curvy, so to say, that it is probably better to at least project some stability and continuity on the economy than to try and change gears hectically every now and then as the markets prompt us to."

"We should not follow the markets because they change opinion so fast," Belka said. "I think a good point is to be "behind the curve". Let the markets look at us and follow us. Our planning horizon is much longer than theirs."

Looking outside of the country's borders, the governor expressed preoccupation for the euro zone, arguing that a crisis of the euro as a currency would put in doubt the whole European project, and backed the idea of boosting the resources of the European Financial Stability Facility, or EFSF, to increase its firepower in the event of a crisis, an idea that was one of the main talking points behind the scenes at the IMF meeting.

He also said that talks surfaced of a wider involvement of the IMF in the solution of the European sovereign debt crisis, but then ultimately the only thing that could take markets back to normal would be a confidence boost.

"What Europe needs is the confidence of the markets, as well as the confidence in its own capabilities to solve this crisis," he said, although the issuance of euro zone bonds, which some see as the most radical remedy to solve the crisis, would be an ineffective shortcut before a deeper integration were realized within the euro zone. "It's more or less a political crisis these days."

But high market volatility and investors' hysteria remain the governor's top concerns.

"We're not talking about rational investors anymore," he said. "This is a nuthouse."

-By Gabriele Parussini, Dow Jones Newswires; gabriele.parussini@dowjones.com

title: Poland To Deter Some Investors From Betting Against Zloty
text:
WARSAW (Dow Jones)--Poland's intervention in the currency market last week will deter some investors from betting that the zloty will weaken, while stabilizing the currency in the short term, economists said.

The market may test the resolve of Polish authorities to defend the zloty if turmoil increases, they added.

The Polish government and central bank propped up the zloty Friday. The currency had been weakening since July as investors exited emerging markets due to concerns over the euro zone's sovereign debt and worries about the global economy.

The Polish currency rose nearly 3% against the euro in less than 30 minutes Friday afternoon. At 1451 GMT Monday, it remained close to these levels. It traded at PLN4.4181 to the euro, nearly 1% weaker on the day and nearly 7% lower than on Sept. 1.

The central bank doesn't have a particular target exchange rate, and the purpose of Friday's intervention was to increase risk for those investors who bet the zloty will weaken further, said Marek Belka, governor of the National Bank of Poland, in an interview with Dow Jones Newswires over the weekend.

Belka said last week the zloty was undervalued.

The Bank's intervention was successful, knocking the euro rate down from PLN4.52 to PLN4.36, BRE Bank said. It allowed the central bank and the government to distort the speculative game on the zloty at a relatively low cost, possibly EUR1 billion-EUR2 billion, it added.

The central bank may intervene again, but it will likely do so at a different rate than EUR/PLN4.50, BPH said.

Friday's intervention moved the zloty away from a level that would inflate Poland's external debt, and thus its overall public debt above 55% of economic output.

According to economists, the level that would push debt above this level--triggering austerity measures, according to Polish law--is between EUR/PLN4.60 and EUR/PLN4.80. The debt measurements are taken at the end of the year.

The risk of a fresh intervention by the central bank is now low, said Invest-Bank. The zloty will likely stabilize and investors will be made less eager to bet that the currency will weaken, it added.

If Greece defaults on its debt and markets turn even more averse to holding emerging market assets, investors will be eager to test the resolve of the Polish authorities, which may find it difficult to reverse the negative trend on the zloty, Citi economist Cezary Chrapek said.

-By Marcin Sobczyk, Dow Jones Newswires; +48 22 447 2432; marcin.sobczyk@dowjones.com [ 26-09-11 1443GMT ]

title: Poland c.bank head: ready to aid banks with liquidity
text:
WASHINGTON, Sept 25 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank is ready to supply the country's banking system with liquidity if a need arises and its intervention in the foreign exchange market will be random, Governor Marek Belka said late on Saturday.

The current storms in the European economy carry a risk of shortages of available cash, Belka told journalists at the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund/World Bank autumn meeting in Washington.

"The central bank is ready to, if it becomes necessary, to supply liquidity to Polish banks," he said.

"They should feel secure. Even if the international banking system dries up they can count on us."

Belka also said that should the current destabilisation in the country's forex market continue, the central bank will carry out intermittent intervention aimed at keeping the rouble from sliding and spooking speculative investors.

On Friday, Polish authorities launched an unprecedented coordinated intervention on the forex and debt markets to rescue the zloty and bonds, which have been pummelled this week by the global flight from risk.

The move drove up the zloty more than two percent against the euro.

"We will be intervening - randomly, when we will decide that the market is destabilizing, but not defending any rate," Belka said.

Friday's move was the bank's first forex intervention since April 9, 2010, and only the second since Poland adopted its free-float system for the currency.

The zloty had tested 27-month lows against the euro in recent days amid fears of a second global recession and the debt crisis in the euro zone.

The governor also said that the government has been doing a good job on lowering budget deficit and will have no problem of reaching this year's target of 5.6 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).

"In general I think we will be nicely surprised with our fiscal results this year," Belka said. "Maybe the same will happen next year. Here, we are not that confident."

(Reporting by Lidia Kelly; Editing by Ed Lane)

title: DJ Polish PM: Constant  Forex Intervention  Out Of The Question
text:
WARSAW (Dow Jones)--Constant intervention on foreign currency markets is "out of the question," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk was quoted as saying by PAP state news agency Friday, after the country's currency weakened more than 5% over the past seven days.

"For us, it's key that this storm not destabilize our financial situation," Tusk said. "I say we are well-prepared, constant intervention on financial markets is out of the question."

The zloty is now trading around 4.51 against the euro, compared with 4.29 last Friday. It has weakened about 11% over the past two months as investors have become more risk-averse and are fleeing emerging markets in response to euro-zone sovereign debt concerns.

"Poland, as a country, should not take up the speculation game on a large scale," Tusk said. "We will use our existing tools, meaning common sense and moderate [tools], and will gather supplies in case something really tips over."

Economists increasingly expect Poland's Finance Ministry and central bank to take action to defend the zloty, rather than relying on the verbal intervention the two institutions have engaged in since early September.

Poland has a self-imposed 55% threshold of debt-to-gross domestic product, the crossing of which would trigger an automatic tightening of fiscal policy. A weaker zloty on the last day of the year could increase the country's foreign currency debt, potentially causing a breach of this threshold.

Hence, a continued "disorderly" weakening of the currency from now until the end of the year is the last thing the Polish government wants, economists said, especially as the country is due for a parliamentary election Oct. 9. The ruling Civic Platform party is hoping to become the first party to be re-elected for a second term since 1989.

Polish Central Bank Governor Marek Belka said Thursday the weakened zloty was making it more difficult for the bank to keep inflation in check, while the volatility of the currency and the uncertainty this creates could curb investment in the Polish economy.

"We're observing the scale of events, [and] what is most worrying is that the source of the turmoil is outside Poland," Tusk said. "Speculation on the Polish currency has been an undisputed fact for the last few days."

Late Thursday, Polish Finance Minister Jacek Rostowski said Poland's public debt remains safely below 55% of economic output, the level that would trigger austerity measures, despite the recent weakening of the zloty.

"We're quite far from the exchange rate that would push debt above 55% of gross domestic product at the end of the year," he said on television channel TVN CNBC.

title: DJ Polish Government,  Central Bank Intervene  To Boost Zloty
text:
-- Polish authorities jointly intervened after growing tired of weak zloty

-- Intervention boosts zloty by nearly 3% in less than 30 minutes

-- Zloty dragged away from levels that could trigger austerity measures

-- Prime minister says Poland won't "constantly intervene" 


 
   By Marcin Sobczyk 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

WARSAW (Dow Jones)--The Polish government and central bank intervened in the currency market Friday to boost the zloty, pushing it away from a level that would trigger austerity measures.

Before Friday's intervention, the zloty had been weakening since July as investors exited emerging markets over euro-zone sovereign debt concerns and worries about the global economy. A weak zloty inflates the country's debts denominated in foreign currencies.

The central bank sold an undisclosed amount of foreign currencies to buy the zloty, it said in a statement. The government appeared to be back in the spot market Friday also selling euros, traders said. Both moves came after a series of unsuccessful government and central-bank verbal interventions in recent days that showed their discomfort with the weak zloty.

The zloty rose nearly 3% against the euro in less than 30 minutes Friday afternoon when Polish state-owned Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego and the central bank intervened. At 1332 GMT, the zloty traded at PLN4.38 from PLN4.52 earlier in the day. That put the Polish currency back at Wednesday's levels, which were still about 6% below the exchange rate of Sept. 1.

Before the zloty began weakening, Poland's public debt was around 53% of gross domestic product, well below the European Union average. But as the zloty weakens, debt swells. And if it crosses the crucial 55% threshold at the end of the year, Polish law requires the government to balance the budget or have a surplus.

That is a situation the government would like to avoid because public discussion of the possibility of automatic austerity measures could undermine its chances of getting reelected for a second term when Poland elects its new parliament on Oct. 9.

Poland's debt is still at a safe distance from the 55% threshold, Finance Minister Jan Vincent-Rostowski said late Thursday, and the country has three months until debt measurements are taken, in line with the domestic methodology that excludes certain categories of debt and produces a result about two percentage points lower than what is reported to the European Commission. He and Marek Belka, governor of the National Bank of Poland, said Thursday the zloty is very much undervalued and its exchange rate no longer reflects the fundamentals of the Polish economy, which they called "healthy." The Polish economy grew 4.3% on the year in the second quarter of 2011.

But economists said a zloty at pre-intervention levels leaves little wiggle room for the finance ministry, which has regularly been selling its euros in the spot market since April. Public debt will be above 55% of GDP if the zloty weakens to around PLN4.66, according to BRE Bank, or PLN4.70, according to Citigroup.

The government is likely to sell more euros in the coming days and weeks to raise zlotys that are paid to farmers, said Rafal Benecki, economist at ING. In his view, public debt will cross the 55% threshold with EUR/PLN at 4.60.

title: Currency  Wars Metamorphose Amid Dollar Scramble
text:
--Emerging markets prop up plummeting currencies, having previously tried to cap strength

--Central banks in Asia, Brazil, Poland and Russia take action


 
   By Clare Connaghan 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

LONDON (Dow Jones)--So much for the global battle to hold currencies down to keep a competitive edge. Now authorities around the world are intervening to prop them up in the wake of a mad scramble for dollars, especially in export-orientated Asia.

On Friday, the National Bank of Poland intervened to prop up the flagging zloty, after the Bank of Korea, Reserve Bank of India and Central Bank of Russia were all suspected of stepping in to support the won, rupee and ruble, respectively. That follows a week in which central banks across the developing world bought their local currencies to protect them from the biggest sell-off in emerging market assets since the demise of Lehman Brothers three years ago.

Even Brazil, which until recently was battling hard to cap an appreciating real, was forced to take action after the Brazilian currency racked up losses in excess of 10% in the space of just four trading days.

As a result, the currency wars of the recent past have metamorphosed, with authorities in emerging markets this time having to embark on currency-strengthening programs.

"This is about trying to contain emerging market currency depreciation pressures," said Benoit Anne, head of emerging market strategy at Societe Generale in London. "What we have seen over the past few days is a number of central banks stepping in, with a view to smoothing foreign-exchange volatility," he added.

With investors scrambling to unwind non-core trading positions and switch into dollars due to a toxic combination of weakening global economic data and escalating euro-zone debt worries, currencies in Asia, Latin America, Eastern Europe and Africa have come under intense selling pressure.

Sudden currency weakness can pose inflationary problems, by lifting the cost of imported goods, and for those countries burdened with large amounts of foreign currency-denominated debt, it's particularly harmful as these debts become much more expensive to pay back.

So central banks in Asia, especially, are suspected of intervening this week to defend their currencies, including those in South Korea, Indonesia, Thailand, India, the Philippines, Singapore and Taiwan.

"Many [Asian] central banks have a policy of maintaining low volatility in foreign exchange markets, which meant over the past year it prevented currency appreciation, but now it's the other way round," said Ilan Solot of Brown Brothers Harriman.

Brazil's central bank also stepped in to sell $2.7 billion in foreign-exchange swap contracts Thursday to rein in the depreciating real, while Russia is thought to have sold about $2 billion Friday to support the ruble.

title: INSTANT VIEW 3-Polish c.bank  intervenes  to boost zloty
text:
WARSAW, Sept 23 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank intervened to boost the zloty by selling "a certain amount" of foreign currencies on the market.

The zloty had tested 27-month lows against the euro in recent days as investors fled riskier assets. The unit was more than 2 percent above Thursday's close after the intervention.

It was the first central bank intervention to support the zloty since April 9, 2010 and only the second since Poland adopted its free-float system.

ANALYSTS COMMENTS:

GRZEGORZ MALISZEWSKI, CHIEF ECONOMIST AT MILLENNIUM BANK IN WARSAW:

"The central bank's intervention was a surprise, it was not present directly on the market for a long time. Yesterday we had a verbal intervention by the central bank's governor Marek Belka and it was backed by actions today. Today was a good moment because it is timed close to the session's end and liquidity is lower so smaller amounts can influence the zloty."

"I don't think this will strengthen the zloty permanently because the global sentiment remains negative. However, investors will now be aware that with significant weakening moves they should expect a market intervention."

"I wouldn't pay attention to the level the central bank and BGK want to defend. Direction and dynamics of the move were important, hence the intervention."

CEZARY CHRAPEK, ANALYST AT CITIBANK HANDLOWY IN WARSAW:

"The recent comments by the finance minister, central bank governor and Prime Minister Tusk confirmed the government's unhappiness with the large fall of the zloty and this raised the risk that the debt-to-GDP ratio would surpass 55 percent."

"After these comments, we could have expected that the finance ministry and the central bank would soon begin to act, but it's surprising that they did it so quickly."

"They decided to show they can intervene at any moment to reduce the zloty volatility and negative risks to inflation, the ratio of debt to GDP and for companies."

"The central bank decided that its better to show early that short-term investors cannot feel safe."

PIOTR BIELSKI, BZ WBK ECONOMIST IN WARSAW:

"The central bank intervention is a surprise, mostly because governor Belka numerously said that if someone counts on interventions he will miscalculate.

"The bank wants to limit the volatility of the Polish currency. High volatility is bad both for the financial system and companies.

"There is no guarantee that the intervention will be succesful because we have a lot of uncertainty about the direction of the global economy. The central bank wanted to show the market that it doesn't pay to overreact to global uncertainty."

WASHINGTON, Sept 23 (Reuters) - The recent weakening of the Polish zloty is of a temporary and panicky nature, Finance Minister Jacek Rostowski told Reuters on Friday, adding that the country's economy remains on track for its targeted 4 percent growth in gross domestic product terms.

"Absolutely, it is temporary," Rostowski said in an interview on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund/World Bank fall meeting in Washington, when asked about the zloty's fall.

"It reminds me of hysteria from the first quarter of 2009 ... The panic then was even stronger but it only affected countries of our region, and now it is striking also the strong industrial nations of Asia."

On Friday, Polish monetary authorities launched an unprecedented intervention on the foreign exchange and debt markets to rescue the zloty, pummelled this week by the global flight from risk [ID:nL5E7KN2TJ].

The zloty <EURPLN=> has tested new 27-months lows this week, but it has gained nearly 3 percent after the interventions by Poland's central bank and the state-owned BGK bank. [ID:nP6E7KC04L]

Rostowski also said the zloty's fall is nothing extraordinary and tracks the decline in value of a horde of other currencies such as the Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> <MYR=MY>, Taiwanese dollar <TWD=>, or South Korea's won <KRW=KFTC>.

The Polish finance minister also said that the country's economy is weathering Europe's crisis well, fighting it off with healthy macroeconomic fundamentals, such as August's sound industrial output, retail sales and unemployment data.

"Without underestimating the turbulences, as it would be absurd to do so because they are gigantic, our economy is entering them very, very strong."

He added that, despite the central bank's recent cautious outlook on growth, Poland should meet its official 4 percent GDP expansion for this year.

title: UPDATE: Polish Central Banker, Finance Minister Face Down Traders
text:
(Rewrites throughout, adding comments by Polish finance minister and analyst.)


 
   By Marynia Kruk 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

WARSAW (Dow Jones)--Poland's central bank governor and finance minister faced down currency traders Friday, saying they refused to be pressured into intervening to support the zloty, even as Warsaw-based dealers said state-owned Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego has sold millions of dollars and bought the Polish currency.

The zloty weakened against the euro, the dollar and the Swiss franc Friday, but began strengthening on reports that BGK, which counts the finance ministry among its clients, was being more active on the market than usual.

Usually, BGK sells euros on a daily basis on behalf of the finance ministry, which receives them from the European Union for structural investments.

Peter Attard Montalto, an emerging market economist at Nomura, said the bank sold dollars to make more of impact and convince traders it was meant as an informal intervention.

Central Bank Governor Marek Belka effectively admitted Poland was playing a game of chicken with currency traders when he said he refused to give speculators the satisfaction by getting drawn into a reaction to the zloty's sharp drop and warmed that "someone" could lose money.

"They're waiting for it [a verbal intervention]," Belka told broadcaster TVN CNBC. "I'm not going to give them this pleasure."

Speaking at a regional economic forum, he said he didn't know what was driving the zloty's weakening, but that it had nothing to do with events in Poland.

"If someone is testing [us], that means they're trying to provoke us into some sort of reaction which will then be exploited in future rounds of speculative tests," Belka said. "No, no, no, we're just observing...someone is going to lose money."

His comments followed a similar statement by Finance Minister Jacek Rostowski.

"We will sell European Union structural funds when it's most inconvenient for markets, who are testing us, not when it's most convenient for them," Rostowski said. "Rather, we'll be testing them."

Analysts said the strenuous denials of intervention, combined with BGK's activity in dollars rather than euros, should be interpreted as a warning that the risks to those who are betting on the zloty's weakening are higher than when BGK first began its practice of converting euros on the market instead of with the central bank.

"I still think we are in the danger zone for more sizeable currency intervention from both the Polish central bank and BGK," Montalto said.

A spokesman for BGK declined to comment.

Poland's finance ministry and central bank are loath to see a disorderly sell-off of the zloty, as it raises the likelihood Poland will breach its self-imposed 55% debt-to-gross domestic product limit this year, triggering automatic fiscal tightening.

title: WSJ/Emerging Europe: Will  Poland Intervene  To Boost Zloty?
text:
(This article has been posted on Emerging Europe, The Wall Street Journal Online's site for news and analysis on Central and Eastern Europe http://blogs.wsj.com/emergingeurope )

Posted by Marcin Sobczyk

The Polish zloty's underperformance during the current wave of the euro-zone jitters is again leading to concern that the country's weakening currency may inflate public debt, forcing austerity measures. Economists wonder if the state will intervene anytime soon to prevent that from happening.

Poland's public debt was around 53% of economic output at the end of last year, according to Poland's methodology. Even though debt reported to the European Union is slightly bigger due to accounting differences, both measures are at a level much below average for the euro zone or the European Union. But Poland has a system of self-imposed thresholds and a debt ceiling at 60% of gross domestic product. If it breaches 55% at the end of this year, the government would need to take radical steps to balance the budget next year, the first after its expected reelection.

The government has expected public debt to remain stable around 53% this year. Deputy Finance Minister Ludwik Kotecki said earlier this week there's no risk debt will exceed 55% of output. But economists say it may happen if the zloty is only slightly weaker than today at the end of December.

Part of Poland's public debt is denominated in foreign currencies. The zloty-value of Poland's debt has gone up sharply in recent weeks as the Polish currency plummeted to a one-year low versus the euro at 4.2026 zlotys on Thursday.

According to Nomura economist Peter Attard Montalto, the moment when Poland's public debt would breach the level of 55% is 4.2363 zlotys to the euro. In his view, the government may want to intervene to strengthen the zloty right at the end of the year, as it did last December when it was already wrestling with the debt threshold.

But will they intervene now?

"One the one hand, they may want to keep powder dry for a year-end action, but--equally--showing strength of backstop now and preventing it from spiking higher can make the job easier at the end of the year," Montalto said, adding the finance ministry is likely to sell even more of its euros on the spot market, in line with its recent strategy, and the central bank may also step in soon.

The current central bank is more open to interventions than the previous one was, said Gillian Edgeworth of Unicredit.

"That said, it's our impression at this stage that we will need to see more extreme zloty losses before this materializes," she said.

The zloty is off Thursday's one-year low, trading at 4.1358 zlotys to the euro at 1337 GMT Friday.

Relief for Polish debtors--private mortgage holders--also came Friday when the Swiss franc dropped dramatically against the euro and, consequently, to the zloty as the market speculates the Swiss central bank may intervene more forcefully to weaken the safe-haven currency. The franc was almost 3% lower to the zloty Friday, at 3.76 zlotys. Less than 48 hours earlier, it was near 4.05 zlotys, a sky-high level for Poland's more than 600,000 borrowers with franc-linked loans.

The franc's strength has led to comments the quality of Polish mortgage portfolios could deteriorate and private consumption weaken as people with franc mortgages become increasingly cash-strapped. For the time being, that risk is no longer on the horizon.

By Sandor Peto and Radu Marinas

BUDAPEST, May 6 (Reuters) - Central European currencies edged up modestly, propped up by hopes that falling oil prices will help curb inflation, with hard currency sales by state-owned Polish Bank BGK boosting the zloty.

A dealer said BGK - mandated to conduct foreign exchange operations under a government plan to regularly convert EU funds in order to firm the zloty, keep price pressures in check and reduce the need for more rate hikes - sold euros first and then dollars.[ID:nWSF010280]

On Thursday, Polish Finance Minister Jacek Rostowski confirmed the ministry had started to regularly exchange euro-denominated EU funds for zlotys. [ID:nWSF010278]

Yields on Central European government bonds and forward rate agreements edged lower after the Czech and euro zone central banks held rates the previous day and as crude prices fell.

The Czech crown <EURCZK=> and Hungarian forint <EURHUF=> both firmed 0.2 percent against the euro, to 24.108 and 265.08 respectively. The leu <EURRON=> shed 0.2 percent.

The Czech central bank (CNB) left rates on hold on Thursday at a record low of 0.75 percent -- 50 basis points below the euro zone's key rate -- and struck a dovish tone, analysts said [ID:nLDE744185]. Market rates, which have been pricing in a rise in rates by the end of the summer, fell as a result.

Yields on the 9x12 forward rate agreement (FRA), reflecting three-month rates in nine months' time, eased 2 basis points, bringing total falls to 12 points since Thursday's opening.

Markets are now pricing in two small CNB hikes by end-2011.

"The crown should underperform in the coming months as dividend payments generally weigh in Q2 and the CNB remains dovish," Societe Generale said in a report.

Commodities spiralled lower again on Friday. [ID:nL3E7G605T]

POSSIBLE INTERVENTION IN POLAND

Poland's central bank will be next in the region to decide on interest rates, on May 11. Lowered expectations of another ECB rate rise in June have decreased the perceived chances of rapid tightening in Poland and supported bond prices.

The ECB left euro zone interest rates at 1.25 percent as expected on Thursday and markets interpreted comments by the bank's President Jean-Claude Trichet as suggesting it would not hike again in June. [ID:nLDE7440GG]

However, ECB policymaker Ewald Nowotny said on Friday that financial markets had "over-interpreted" the ECB's intentions by scaling back rate-hike bets, adding: "There can be no idea about (the ECB) being dovish". [ID:nHEL010146]

title: Poland Warms Up To Stronger Zloty As Euro Rises
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--While most emerging markets are doggedly trying to weaken their currencies, Poland actively intervened to strengthen the zloty Thursday, viewing it as the better of two difficult options for keeping it in sync with the euro.

In announcing a plan to convert euros to zlotys in the open market, Polish authorities expressed hope that a stronger currency might substitute for some of the tightening that would otherwise be expected from monetary policy. With the European Central Bank recently raising rates and the euro rising sharply along with that, the risk of a relatively weak zloty has raised concerns over imported inflation.

"This is a fairly significant development," said Manik Narain, emerging-market FX strategist at UBS. "They want to show the markets that they're happy to let their currency strengthen to allow some burden of monetary tightening to be done through the exchange rate."

The zloty exchange rate to the euro is especially important as it is the conduit through which most of Poland trades and foreign investment flows.

Though less significant than Hungary and the Czech Republic, Poland holds strong bilateral ties with the euro zone. The Polish government has hinted that they believe the zloty is still cheap, suggesting that they don't expect complaints from exporters and that a stronger zloty is needed to fend off imported inflation.

Poland's exports make up about a third of gross domestic product, whereas its Eastern European peers are almost double that. And relative to its western European neighbors, Poland runs a smaller economy that is susceptible to conditions abroad.

Thursday's announcement sent the euro diving against the zloty from PLN3.9835 to around PLN3.95, which UBS's Narain points out is the exact level the pair held at the start of this year. Narain added he sees fair value at PLN3.60 on the euro, and targets another 3% appreciation by the zloty.

Others are less optimistic and believe the markets have mistakenly reacted.

Some analysts say currency intervention is only an artificial form of appreciation, and without higher interest rates, the zloty will actually suffer. According to Bartosz Pawlowski, head of regional FX strategy at BNP Paribas, markets had priced in four 25-basis point rate increases this year, and now he sees only two.

Nevertheless, policymakers in Poland are hoping that a stronger currency will slow the pace of rising rates. With its domestic economy still in a tenuous state, it is feared that higher interest could cripple growth.

March unemployment remained elevated at 13.1% and wage growth has been subdued. The nation's consumer price index, however, rose far above expectations to 4.3% last month.

Furthermore, tightening by the ECB may slow activity in Europe and reduce demand for Eastern European exports.

Poland also faces a heavy load of national debt, which is inching closer to the country's statutory limit of 55% of gross domestic product. As the government cracks down on fiscal spending, monetary authorities may be compelled to keep rates accommodative for the time being, while a strong zloty would attract foreign funding.

"I would suspect that the government is happy to let its currency appreciate to make local debt more attractive," said Ilan Solot of Brown Brothers Harriman. "They have to issue a lot of debt, and good yield there will help funding efforts by the government."

As emerging economies fight off rising currencies in an effort to protect exporters, Poland's move may be the latest sign that developing nations are becoming more willing to use currency strength to combat inflation.

While Poland is undoubtedly unique in its ties to the euro zone, analysts at BBH say that the nation's approach is one the "rest of emerging markets should follow," and that "if continued, the strong appreciation observed in many emerging-market currencies will start to trigger policy reposes."

A number of nations have already given in to higher rates--including Poland's two rate increases this year--but inflation has ticked relentlessly higher, and strong currencies may very well be the next line of fire.

The "spot allowing to move in Brazil and the nature of the latest wave of policy measures suggests that even the Brazilians--the biggest proponents of antiappreciation--are changing," said Koon Chow, emerging market director at Barclay's Capital in London.

title: UPDATE 1-INTERVIEW-Poland to use BGK bank to support debt mkt
text:
* Finance ministry says ready to back fixed income market

* State-owned BGK bank could buy bonds in case of turmoil

By Dagmara Leszkowicz and Pawel Sobczak

WARSAW, April 8 (Reuters) - Poland has mandated state-owned bank BGK to intervene on the bond market to soothe potential tensions, the head of the finance ministry's debt department said in comments authorised for release on Friday.

Polish authorities already used BGK at the end of 2010 to sell euros in order to keep the zloty strong and avoid breaching key debt levels. [ID:nLDE6AN140]

"We see the possibility of using BGK to support the bond market in case of tensions unrelated to fundamentals," Piotr Marczak told Reuters.

"BGK would be able to buy bonds on the secondary market. We (the finance ministry) could guarantee to buy back these papers if need be."

The ministry does not rule out running fully transparent debt buy-back auctions, he said.

"Running a buy-back auction requires some time and making declarations of what and how much you want to buy. If we work through BGK we have flexibility both in terms of time, the type of bonds and the sums involved," Marczak said.

Just as with currency market interventions, the ministry will not inform investors when BGK intends to buy bonds from the market but will say when it buys back bonds from BGK, he said.

Foreign investors currently hold Polish treasuries worth over 140 billion zlotys ($51.04 billion) and both the ministry and the central bank must keep reserves to protect against potential capital flight in the case of a major crisis.

The ministry and the central bank would work hand in hand to calm the market in the event of a "large" crisis, Marczak said.

title: Zloty Hits Highest Level Since April 2010  Intervention
text:
WARSAW (Dow Jones)--The zloty hit a nine-month high against the euro Wednesday and closed in on the level it reached last April when the National Bank of Poland intervened to weaken the currency.

The zloty has been supported by expectations of rate increases. Over the past two weeks, comments by members of Poland's Monetary Policy Council, most recently Jan Winiecki speaking today on TVN CNBC, have convinced investors that the council will begin a sequence of interest rate hikes in January to counter rising inflation.

As recently as December, most economists thought the council would hold fire on Jan. 19 but that is slowly changing. At 1047 GMT, the zloty was at PLN3.8419 to the euro from PLN3.9693 Dec. 23.

"The zloty is supported by council member comments," said Piotr Kalisz, an economist at Citi in Warsaw.

Andrzej Bratkowski, another member of the 10-person council commented in detail on the outlook for the zloty on Tuesday.

"The zloty could gain through 2011 even to 3.5 [versus the euro] at the end of the year," Bratkowski said. "Such a level could actually slow economic growth down slightly, but it would not pose any bigger threat."

He added that 3.70-3.80 would be an "optimal" level for the euro-zloty currency pair.

The fact that Bratkowski emphasized 3.50 as a goal for the EUR/PLN was very significant for markets, Kalisz at Citi said.

Winiecki said that although Poland is doing well, inflation is rising and that the rate setting council needs to reflect this in its decisions.

On April 9, a day before Poland's central bank chief as well as the country's president died in a plane crash in Russia that also killed dozens of other officials, Poland's central bank bought an undisclosed amount of euros at PLN3.8450-PLN3.8500, dealers said.

Then, over the following nine months, the zloty's volatility versus the euro moderated. The EUR/PLN broadly fluctuated in a 4.10-3.90 range until the end of 2010.

-By Marynia Kruk, Dow Jones Newswires; +48 22 447-2431; marynia.kruk@dowjones.com [ 12-01-11 1130GMT ]

title: WSJ: Poland's Belka Warns Against  Currency  Devaluation To Promote Economic Growth
text:
WASHINGTON--The head of Poland's central bank warned against using currency devaluations to promote economy growth, saying it is a risky strategy that does nothing to help a country's long-run prospects.

"I am worried because this destabilizes the global economy and it does not lead to rebalancing, something we all long for," Polish Central Bank Gov. Marek Belka said in an interview on the sidelines of annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund.

Exchange rates are a key backdrop to the weekend IMF meetings in Washington. The U.S. and Europe have repeatedly urged China to allow its currency, the yuan, to trade flexibly against other currencies. Japan has intervened in currency markets to keep the yen from strengthening too much. Expectations that the Federal Reserve will take more dramatic steps to strengthen the U.S. economy, including large-scale purchases of Treasury securities known as quantitative easing, has led to a decline in the U.S. dollar, which hit an eight-month low against the euro earlier in the week. The European Central Bank has largely resisted quantitative easing.

"If you want to strengthen your competitiveness by devaluing your currency, this is a sign of despair, this isn't a policy," Belka said.

(This story and related background material will be available on The Wall Street Journal Web site, WSJ.com.)

Belka said the exchange rate of Poland's currency, the zloty, "doesn't make my heart beat faster." But he doesn't rule out intervention if needed to keep the zloty from climbing too high, which would weigh on exports, a key source of Poland's growth. Poland intervened in April to weaken the zloty, the first such move in a decade.

"It's like in a drama, there's a gun hanging on the wall and you know that once in a while it shoots off, but you don't know when," Belka said. "The gun is there, but we have no precommitment to use it."

Belka, a former prime minister and top IMF official, joined the central bank in June following the death of former central bank governor Slawomir Skrzypek, in a plane crash.

Belka said he worries about the global trend toward renewed use of quantitative easing to stimulate growth. The Bank of Japan on Tuesday announced a new asset purchase program. Officials at the Federal Reserve and the Bank of England have signaled they may resume asset purchases amid concerns over growth and employment.

"The American model is entrepreneurial. They have to do everything to avoid long-term structural unemployment," Belka said. "Europeans are sort of accustomed to it. Americans are not."

"This explains this drive to either fiscal stimulus or this quantitative easing too. If the exit is well built into the economy you shouldn't be so concerned; if the mop up of excess liquidity when the time comes is relatively straightforward maybe quantitative easing is not so dangerous," Belka said.

Still, the "ocean of liquidity" in the global financial system could affect Belka's efforts to keep Poland on a steady growth, low inflation path. "We have to be worried about the interest-rate disparity between Polish rates and global rates, especially European rates," Belka said. "Five years ago probably I would have thought of monetary tightening coming in earlier than in a situation like today."

Poland's economy weathered the global recession, and has recovered more quickly than much of the rest of Europe. Poland's GDP was up 3.8% in the second quarter from the previous year, almost double the rate of the European Union as a whole. Poland is in the EU but not the euro zone. The zloty depreciated during the global financial crisis, providing a "shield" for Polish exporters, Belka said.

Though euro membership remains Poland's goal, "I don't think we should drag ourselves into the euro zone now when there are still unresolved issues with countries with strained fiscal positions," he said.

-By Brian Blackstone, The Wall Street Journal; brian.blackstone@wsj.com

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

At 0638 GMT, the zloty was at 3.9302 to the euro, up from 3.9311 late Monday.

Belka also said he is "not sure" Poland needs major fiscal overhaul, as all possible austerity measures would generate savings for the budget only in the long run.

He added that the growth of Poland's debt isn't currently a problem. When asked about Poland's debt--seen growing by about $100 billion over the next four years in comparison with $50 billion of debt taken in the 1970s that eventually led to Poland defaulting in 1989--Belka said $50 billion was Poland's total annual gross domestic product in the 1970s, but only 10% of Poland's current GDP.

Belka said the government's plan for an increase in value-added taxes was a pragmatic way to tame the growth of public debt. He also said Poland should strive to lower its budget deficit to some 30 billion zlotys ($9.8 billion), which should be easy to achieve given the likely acceleration of economic recovery and higher budget revenue.

The central bank governor sees Poland's budget deficit at PLN48 billion this year, compared with the official plan of PLN52.2 billion.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Stocks fall 1 pct, zloty hits 3-mth high
text:
* Emerging stocks drop 1 pct, but debt spreads tighten

* Zloty at 3-mth high, Polish c.bank warns against uptrend

* Ukraine 5-yr CDS trade around 500 bps after rate cut

By Carolyn Cohn

LONDON, Aug 10 (Reuters) - Emerging stocks fell 1 percent to an eight-day low on Tuesday, as caution about Federal Reserve policy dented risky assets, but the Polish zloty hit fresh three-month highs, prompting a central bank warning.

Emerging assets have had a good run in the last few weeks, boosted by the easing of the euro zone sovereign debt crisis and a refocus on strong domestic fundamentals. However, speculation has been growing that the U.S. Federal Reserve will at its meeting later on Tuesday signal a need for more stimulus to support U.S. growth or possibly restart asset purchases, known as quantitative easing.

Chinese stocks <.SSEC> also fell 2.9 percent after weak import data spurred concerns domestic demand was cooling faster than previously thought. "Everywhere is down today, reflecting a general pullback in risk appetite which is hitting emerging markets," said Neil Shearing, senior emerging markets economist at Capital Economics.

The MSCI emerging equities index <.MSCIEF> dropped 1 percent to an eight-day low and the Thomson Reuters Emerging Europe index <.TRXFLDEEPU> fell 0.77 percent.

Emerging sovereign debt spreads tightened by 2 basis points to 261 bps over U.S. Treasuries <11EMJ>, however, and are trading around their narrowest in three months in the absence of new supply over the quiet August period.

The South African rand eased from 2-1/2 year highs against the dollar <ZAR=> set on Monday, as public sector unions threatened a prolonged strike. [ID:nWEB4785] As the zloty hit a fresh three-month high against the euro close to 3.95 <EURPLN=>, Polish central bank governor Marek Belka said he hoped the currency's appreciation trend would not be too strong. [ID:nLDE67905R]

Poland's currency has been volatile in recent months and the central bank has intervened both to buy and sell zloty.

"Poland is likely to hike interest rates as soon as Q4 this year," said analysts at ING in a client note.

"Should this expectation build, euro/zloty may well re-test its April (3.80) mark."

Debt insurance costs climbed slightly in emerging Europe. Ukraine's five-year CDS rose to 505.4 bps, according to CMA DataVision, after dipping to a four-month low below 500 bps on Monday, when the central bank cut its key discount rate by 75 basis points to 7.75 percent, the third cut this year.

Analysts see inflationary pressures in Ukraine.

"Inflation will go up," said Shearing. "We will see the effect from the gas price rise and there is the food angle too."

Ukraine raised domestic gas prices this month and traders say the drought-hit country is holding up wheat exports. [ID:nLDE6781NO]

Russian 5-year CDS also ticked up as oil prices weakened and investors focused on the smog in Moscow and the drought, which prompted Russia last week to ban grain exports.

"The drought will have an impact on the Russian economy and inflation and food prices in particular, and I wouldn't want to underplay that. But comparisons with the food price shocks of 2007-2008 are misplaced," said Shearing.

"Part of the problem back then was that the Russian economy was operating above potential but now it is operating below potential and it's difficult to see the food price inflation leading to wage inflation and feeding through massively into core inflation." title: UPDATE 1-Polish zloty current level satisfactory-c.bank
text:
* Current zloty level satisfactory-c.bank head Belka

* Sharp zloty appreciation could pose threat

* Belka would like to see smaller deficit in 2011 (Adds quotes, detail)

WARSAW, Aug 10 (Reuters) - The level of the Polish zloty is satisfactory and if anything threatens the Polish unit, it is sharp appreciation rather than depreciation, the central bank's governor Marek Belka said on Tuesday.

Belka added that he would have hoped to see a smaller budget deficit next year, but underlined that Poland did not need very deep fiscal cuts.

"If something threatens the zloty, it is its sharp appreciation rather than depreciation," Belka told daily Puls Biznesu in an interview.

"I hope (the zloty) appreciation trend won't be too strong. The current zloty level is satisfactory."

The governor also repeated Poland's central bank may intervene in the foreign currency market if such a need emerges.

The zloty <EURPLN=> has swung back and forth in recent months. The central bank interevened to counter its rising strength in April, while there were reports in May that the finance ministry had sold euros on the market to stop its sharp fall.

It hovered around its 3-month highs early on Tuesday, and was traded at 3.98, a touch below a key level of 4.0 against the euro.

BUDGET

The governor also said he expected the government to curb next year's budget deficit more ambitiously.

"Today it is only a fall to 45 billion zlotys from 52 billion zlotys (envisaged this year)," Belka said. "I expected next year's deficit to be smaller."

Under the government's new financial plan, budget deficit is set to be trimmed gradually to 45 billion zlotys next year and to 40 billion zlotys in 2012. The key goal of the plan is to cut the general budget deficit, that includes shortfalls generated by local government's and agencies, to the EU ceiling of 3 percent in 2013.

The plan envisages a temporary increase in value-added tax (VAT) by 1 percentage points from 2011 and the governor said last week such a move is tolerable.

However, he said now he expected the government to cut spending as other countries consolidate their public finances nowadays.

"However, it doesn't have to be sharp or sudden cuts," Belka said. (Reporting by Dagmara Leszkowicz; Editing by Kim Coghill)

title: UPDATE 1- Poland  does not need  FX interventions  -c.banker
text:
(Adds details, background)

WARSAW, June 16 (Reuters) - Poland does not need interventions on the forex market to defend the zloty but the exchange rate is key for monetary policy, a member of the central bank's Monetary Policy Council (MPC) said on Wednesday.

"I don't see any signals coming from inflation, from wage pressures to change monetary policy," Jerzy Hausner told a seminar.

"The zloty exchange rate is key and any signal to change monetary policy would come frome here."

The Polish currency has see-sawed with choppy global financial markets in recent months, and markets have been watching official comments on the currency closely after the central bank in April intervened to counter zloty strength.

There were also reports in May that the finance ministry had sold euros on the market, something it can do periodically with EU and other inflows to influence the zloty.

Several central bank officials, including new governor Marek Belka, have said they expect the zloty to gain steadily over the longer term against the euro. Belka said last week that the central bank should not target any particular zloty level.

Hausner said that while a steady strengthening of the zloty would not be a cause for concern, a rapid appreciation would be.

"Hausner's comments fit the view of the newly appointed bank's governor Marek Belka," said Jakub Wiraszka, a dealer at BRE bank in Warsaw.

The zloty <EURPLN=> was almost unchanged at 4.0660 to the euro in morning trade. Hausner also expressed concern about Poland's high general government budget deficit, saying that if it remained near 7 percent in 2011, that would be a reason to raise interest rates.

The budget deficit is expected to reach 6.9 percent of gross domestic output this year due to the economic slowdown, which has battered tax revenues.

The centre-right government sees the deficit easing to 5.9 percent of GDP next year and to 2.9 percent in 2012, below the EU's 3 percent ceiling, though some analysts are sceptical that it can fall that fast.

The central bank's main interest rate is currently at a historic low of 3.5 percent. Analysts expect the bank to start hiking rates later this year as the recovery gathers pace. (Reporting by Pawel Sobczak, Writing by Dagmara Leszkowicz and Chris Borowski; editing by Patrick Graham)

WARSAW, June 9 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank may intervene on the foreign currency market to dampen high volalitity but should not seek to target any particular exchange rate, its nominee governor said on Wednesday.

"Currency interventions? Yes, as long as their goal is to limit overly large currency fluctations," Marek Belka said in reply to a question from a lawmaker in parliament's public finance committee during his confirmation hearing.

* Polish Dep PM says rate hikes should be avoided
