WARSAW, May 20 (Reuters) - Poland's zloty currency, which has weakened due to central bank intervention, is now at a competitive rate for the country's economy, Deputy Prime Minister and Economy Minister Waldemar Pawlak said on Thursday. "The zloty exchange rate at a touch above 4 (versus the euro) is a very good exchange rate that improves our competitiveness, " Pawlak, who is the presidential candidate for the junior governing coalition Peasant Party, told reporters.

Poland's central bank intervened in April to help weaken the zloty <EURPLN=D3> when it traded at about 3.84 against the euro. It now trades at about 4.12.

"The market indicates the zloty at 4 zlotys versus euro is the equilibrium rate," Pawlak said.

The intervention in April, supported by the finance ministry, was the first such move since Poland introduced a fully free-floating currency in 2000.

Pawlak also said that the central bank should try to avoid interest rate increases.

"We have interest rates at 3.5 percent and much above the levels in Europe and the United States and slightly above inflation and we should not turn the screw further as it would hurt economic growth," Pawlak said.

Analysts expect the central bank to hike rates by 25 basis points towards the end of the year because inflation is expected to start accelerating some time in autumn.

Poland's economy is also seen growing by about 3 percent this year, up from 1.8 percent in 2009, when Poland was the only European Union economy to have avoided recession thanks to its large internal market and zloty weakening last year. title: INSTANT VIEW-Polish c.bank keeps key rate flat, as expected
text:
WARSAW, April 28 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank kept its main interest rate <PLINTR=ECI> unchanged on Wednesday, in line with market expectations that it would hold fire as inflation is easing and uncertainty over the pace of recovery remains high.

The main rate remains at a record low of 3.5 percent.

The bank will hold a news conference and release a statement explaining its decision at 1300 GMT.

*************************************************************

FORECAST

* All 26 analysts polled by Reuters earlier in April expected the Monetary Policy Council's (MPC) 10 members to keep the main interest rate at its all-time low of 3.5 percent.

MARKET REACTION

* The Polish zloty <EURPLN=D3> <PLN=> and bonds were unchanged immediately after the decision.

ANALYSTS' COMMENTS:

MARCIN MROWIEC, CHIEF ECONOMIST AT PEKAO BANK:

"This isn't a surprise. At the earliest, rates may be increased in the second half of the year, and most probably in the fourth quarter. At the same time we'd like to point out that they don't need to be raised at all.

"Looking at the FX interventions and the fact that inflation will be low, while economic growth below its potential, the situation (of no hikes) is becoming more and more probable."

"What is more, the MPC discussed the possibility of rate cuts. So the probability of no rate hikes is rising and today's decision fits this scenario."

"We expect the next two or three rate sittings to be the same."

RAFAL BENECKI, SENIOR ECONOMIST AT ING BANK:

"We expect rather marginal changes in the statement due to the fact that some of the improvement on the labour market, construction and retail sales is a seasonal phenomenon (the recovery of economic activity after a tough winter). A hawkish statement would also be inconsistent with the MPC's attempts to slow the appreciation, though the importance of this factor recently diminished as lower risk appetite externally diminished the appreciation pressure.

"Economic growth still strongly depends on exports, while domestic demand will remain in the back seat this year. CPI is still decreasing, PPI is in deflation territory, while our forecast of weak consumption for this year and the impact of a stronger zloty in year-on-year terms imply a rather slow recovery of inflation in the second half of 2010. This allows the MPC to stick to its wait-and-see approach."

title: CEE MARKETS 4-Greek aid news boosts region, zloty rangebound
text:
* News on Greek aid activation lifts currencies

* Region's bond markets show no major reaction

* Zloty down, risk of intervention remains

(Updates throughout)

By Krisztina Than and Dagmara Leszkowicz

BUDAPEST/WARSAW, April 23 (Reuters) - Emerging Europe's currencies were mostly higher on Friday, rallying after debt-choked Greece requested the activation of a multi-billion euro EU/IMF-led aid package.

The country appealed to the EU and the International Monetary Fund for emergency loans aimed at pulling it out of a debt crisis and easing fears of a default.

"This is good information and if market players can be confident about this (agreement), it should definitely provide support for our region," said one Warsaw-based dealer.

Central and eastern European assets have not been significantly impacted by Greece's debt woes so far, thanks to the region's relatively buoyant growth outlook and low debt and budget deficit levels.

However, worries about the heavily-indebted euro zone periphery have dampened investor appetite towards the region in recent days.

By 1355 GMT, the Romanian leu <EURRON=> had strengthened 0.3 percent against the euro and Hungary's forint <EURHUF=> edged up 0.2 percent. The Czech crown <EURCZK=> was flat.

ZLOTY UNDERPERFORMS

The zloty <EURPLN=> fell 0.3 percent. Dealers said Polish March retail sales data, though much better than expected, did not have a significant impact on the currency.[ID:nLDE63M0MR]

"Everyone sees Poland's economy is doing well and all the positive news has been already priced in," said another dealer from Warsaw bank.

Some market players said the zloty's recent rangebound performance, despite having room to appreciate further -- reflected concerns over possible intervention on the forex market.

Poland's central bank surprised markets earlier this month with its first intervention since introducing a free float in 2000 to temper the surging currency's impact on exports and the economy overall.

A Reuters polls of analysts showed the zloty could gain some 3 percent in the next 12 months. [ID:nLDE6380S7]

The region's stocks extended recent gains, with most indices rising around 1 percent.

Bond markets hardly reacted to the Greek news, with only Hungarian paper gaining slightly.

Hungarian dealers said the market was still optimistic about the outlook for the forint, which could get a boost from Sunday's run-off parliamentary elections if the centre-right Fidesz party -- which won the first round -- extends its gains to the two-thirds majority that would give it a mandate to implement major reforms.

Hungary's central bank is expected to cut rates by another 25 basis points on Monday to a new all-time low of 5.25 percent. [ID:nLDE63K1XG] [ID:nLDE63K2J8]

title: INSTANT VIEW 3-Polish March wages up 4.8 y/y, above forecast
text:
WARSAW, April 19 (Reuters) - Polish corporate sector wages grew faster than expected in March while the pace of decline in corporate employment slowed, data showed on Monday, cementing expectations for a steady economic recovery.

 Polish corporate sector wages <PLWAGE=ECI> rose 4.8 percent year-on-year in March to 3,493 zlotys per month, up from a 2.9 percent rise in February, the statistics office data showed.

 In monthly terms, wages rose by 6.2 percent.

 Data also showed corporate employment <PLEMPY=ECI> fell 0.6 percent year-on-year in March and was unchanged in monthly terms.

 Analysts said both the wage and employment data boded well for the labour market, consumption and economic growth but said they did not expect any impact on this month's meeting of the central bank's Monetary Policy Council (MPC).

 The MPC is expected to keep the main interest rate flat at 3.5 percent, though some analysts said Monday's better-than- expected data bolstered expectations for monetary tightening in the second half of 2010 to offset increased demand.

 Consumer price inflation in March stood at 2.6 percent and is expected to decline further in coming months before going into reverse as the recovery accelerates.  ***********************************************************

 * Analysts in a Reuters poll <ECONPL> had forecast wages to

 MARKET REACTION:  


 The Polish zloty <EURPLN=D3> <PLN=> and bonds were little
changed immediately after the data. 

 ANALYSTS' COMMENTS

 ARKADIUSZ KRZESNIAK, CHIEF ECONOMIST AT DEUTSCHE BANK IN
WARSAW

 "In terms of wages, the data is better than expected.
Employment data too. The data suggests the situation in the
corporate sector is improving.

 "The acceleration is significant, but we had quite a lot of
volatility in recent months. I think the real growth of wages
will persist in coming months.

 "The data itself will have no impact on the Monetary Policy
Council."

 ELISABETH ANDREEW, FX STRATEGIST AT NORDEA:

 "The data is better than expected and supports our view that
there are some early signs that the weakest point in terms of
the unemployment rate is approaching.

 "Business surveys, for example, show a significant
improvement in the balance between businesses expecting to
increase employment and businesses expecting to reduce
employment, though the gap remains slightly in negative
territory.

 "All in all, the PLN is likely to be unaffected as the
central bank seems committed to taking the FX rate into
consideration in its policy, i.e. risk of postponed rate hikes
and/or intervention.

 "The PLN is also hit by the generally weaker risk sentiment
today and uncertainty about the presidential elections."

 PETER ATTARD MONTALTO, ECONOMIST AT NOMURA IN LONDON:

 "Poland wages surprised strongly to the upside as the
economy bounced back from its soft spot and the labour market
shows signs of turning too.

 "The print is particularly important in our view for the
risk to CPI and supports our view of inflation turning around
and moving back up during the second half of this year,
prompting rate hikes at that time (we pencil in 3x25bp) with
demand pressures starting to become evident. It should also be
remembered that the MPC does have a soft spot for labour data."

 GRZEGORZ MALISZEWSKI, CHIEF ECONOMIST AT MILLENNIUM BANK:

 "Maybe the payout of bonuses was moved to March (and that is
why the data was better than expected). We have to wait for more
detailed data which will show whether this was not a one-off,
which is also possible.

 "It seems, however, that the employment data was more
important because they show that the situation on the labour
market is stabilising. And this is positive."

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Hit by profit-taking; EM debt in demand
text:
* Emerging stocks down almost 1 pct on risk aversion

* Polish zloty slips 0.5 pct as investors book profits

* Argentina unveils debt swap; more emerging issuance seen

By Sujata Rao

LONDON, April 16 (Reuters) - Emerging stocks posted their biggest one-day fall in a month on Friday after weak U.S jobs data raised questions over the pace of economic recovery, but emerging bond issuance continued unabated.

Emerging assets have been fairly resilient to worries about Greek debt amid good growth data in China and the developing world, a raft of strong corporate results, and the likelihood of low interest rates in the core markets for some time to come.

Analysts said markets were taking a breather before the weekend after a strong run of recent gains that saw investors push emerging equities up over 3 percent since the start of April and absorb huge amounts of new bond issuance including from higher-risk names Ukraine and Dubai.

MSCI emerging equities fell 0.9 percent, edging away from the previous session's 19-1/2 month highs <.MSCIEF> while most emerging currencies pulled back against the dollar and the euro.

"There's clearly some profit-taking but markets have done pretty well in recent days. Google's results, which came after hours, beat expectations but investors may be reacting to the performance of the shares before the results," said John Lomax, head of emerging equity strategy at HSBC in London.

"The outlook is positive," he added.

On currencies, the Polish zloty fell half a percent against the euro, <EURPLN=> underperforming its regional peers as investors stayed wary of more central bank intervention following its action in the currency markets last week.

The country's finance minister said on Thursday that Poland may need to continue intervening. [ID: nLDE63D17C]

Data showing consumer inflation slowing in March was also zloty-negative, but the currency remains one of the best performing emerging currencies this year, with gains of almost 6 percent. "Everywhere people are selling risk and that is affecting emerging markets," one currency trader said. "The zloty is seen as more vulnerable after the intervention and now, the verbal intervention .... people are rushing to protect profits."

A stronger dollar forced the Turkish lira off its highest levels in almost three months <TRY=>. Investors have been piling into the lira following a moderation in the central bank's ultra-dovish stance, with some expecting a rate rise by June. The lira is up almost 3 percent since the start of April.

BONDS ON A ROLL

On bond markets, Argentina announced a long-awaited debt swap, offering new bonds and cash to holders of $20 billion in defaulted debt, but investors saw the deal as less generous than expected. [ID:nN15183384].

The deal is expected to have a high take-up rate however and could pave the way for the country to return to global capital markets. Argentina credit default swaps failed to react, quoted at 12.6 percent on an upfront basis.

Emerging sovereign bond spreads over U.S. Treasuries rose 2 bps as Treasury yields fell but Argentine spreads fell 7 bps.

Emerging debt markets are seeing a heavy issuance surge, with sovereigns as well as corporates trying to get funding done while core yields remain low and risk appetite high.

Russia wraps up its roadshow next week and fund managers said it may issue $7-$10 billion in two or three tranches in what will be its first bond in a decade.

But less desirable credits are also in demand. State-run entities from Dubai and Ukraine, where quasi-sovereigns recently restructured debt, successfully tapped markets this week. Kazakstan's Kazmunaigaz picked banks for a dollar bond.

Both Ukreximbank and Dubai's DEWA paid significant 120-180 bps premiums over the sovereign, the likely reason why DEWA's $1 billion bond got $11 billion in orders. Ukreximbank's $500 million issue was eight times subscribed, sources said.

"The market is looking for yield but yields are low in general and we have to invest somewhere," one fund manager said.

That view was backed up by data from EPFR Global which showed inflows into emerging bond funds at a weekly record of $1.8 billion. Click on [ID: nLDE63F0GE].

But others expressed concern.

"I am getting really concerned at the feeding frenzy rebuilding again... as investors dash to get a slice of new issues, and especially as these seem to be moving back down the credit curve in the hunt again for yield," Tim Ash, RBS head of emerging European research, said in a note.

title: WSJ/New Europe:  Poland  Ready for More  Currency Intervention  Despite Crash
text:
(This article has been posted on New Europe, The Wall Street Journal Online's site for news and analysis on Central and Eastern Europe http://blogs.wsj.com/new-europe)


 
   Posted by Marcin Sobczyk 

The National Bank of Poland, just days after the crash of the presidential airplane, which killed the central bank governor and the country's president, is back on its feet and ready for more currency intervention to weaken the zloty.

On the last day in the life of central bank governor Slawomir Skrzypek, the NBP bought an undisclosed amount of euros on the market, showing it's ready to act to weaken what it believed was a currency strengthening too quickly.

A Monetary Policy Council member said Thursday the central bank may intervene again to reduce volatility caused by speculative investors. Citigroup, an investment bank, now says the central bank may intervene on a much bigger scale than on Apr. 9 if the zloty continues to rise against core currencies.

This didn't seem immediately obvious when Skrzypek died Saturday with 95 others in the presidential airplane crash. Questions over succession at the central bank, and over its power to act, started soon after.

After the death of Slawomir Skrzypek, first deputy Piotr Wiesiolek took over as the head of the bank's management, in line with the law. But the governor of the central bank has a dual role in the bank and also acts as a member and chairperson of the Monetary Policy Council. The central bank law makes no mention on who assumes this role in case of the governor's death.

On Monday, the policy council met and decided that it would give the acting governor full voting power and the authority to schedule meetings for the council--matters the central bank legislation doesn't discuss. It didn't adopt a document to this effect--it just discussed various interpretations of the law and unanimously agreed, without voting or signing anything, that one of those interpretations would now be considered correct.

Amid the chaos, some argued the council doesn't even have that power and that no-one now has the right to schedule policy meetings. But the law says three or more members of the council can also decide to formally schedule the council's monthly meeting, which put those concerns to rest.

So, zloty speculators should better brace for more intervention, as the central bank is ready to move, should it deem such a step necessary.

title: FOCUS: Europe's Emerging Markets Embrace  Currency Intervention
text:
LONDON (Dow Jones)--Emerging markets could be set to indulge in a new era of currency interventions after Poland last week zapped the markets with a zloty-weakening sting.

Poland's apparent intervention on April 9 to pull back the zloty--its first in 10 years--shows a strong distaste for export-hampering currency strength as the global economic recovery begins to take hold, and it hints that Europe could start to mimic currency-management techniques that are common in Asia.

Russia already takes frequent action to manage the level of the ruble, but the region's freely floating currencies have generally been left to do just that: float.

Following last week's move on the zloty, however, analysts warn that further action from Poland could be on the way. It isn't alone: small-scale intervention is already suspected in South Africa, whose currency--the rand--is generally treated as though it is from one of Europe's emerging economies. The risk of a substantial hit there is growing.

"The rand is expensive. There's no question about that," said Nigel Rendell, an emerging-markets currencies analyst at The Royal Bank of Canada Capital Markets in London.

Rendell said he suspects that the South African authorities have been selling the rand frequently of late as it has nudged up to its strongest levels against the dollar since August 2008.

However, the interventions have so far been on a small scale. Now, particularly if the rand makes a fresh move higher, "I would not rule out a big sting," he said.

Analysts at Societe Generale agreed, noting that while the South African Reserve Bank has shied away from intervening in recent years, fresh comments from officials this month signal a shift in tactics.

Any move in the dollar below current levels of around ZAR7.30 to ZAR7.20 could easily attract new rand-buyers, pumping the currency swiftly higher. That, Societe Generale said, would very probably draw the central bank into the market to limit the climb.

Feeble interest rates in major economies such as the U.S., the U.K. and the euro zone have pushed investors to search for higher returns elsewhere in the past year or so, boosting the currency in South Africa, for example, with its still-high rate of 6.5%. As the global economy has recovered, investors have also moved back into risky assets, bolstering the rise in these currencies.

For Poland, that pressure became too much last week, after months in which its currency had become one of the most widely favored bets in the world for currencies investors.

The euro had plunged to a 17-month low against the zloty just over PLN3.82 before the central bank acted to slow the descent. Analysts see little chance that this intervention, or any later such moves, will do any more than slow the zloty's climb. The country's robust economy, with little if any prospect of falling interest rates, still makes the currency an attractive bet.

Still, the decision to intervene gives a sharp signal that buying the zloty is no risk-free bet, deflecting some short-term inflows.

Attention is now turning to which other countries are in line to take action on currency strength. Hungary is an unlikely candidate, because it is still in interest-rate-cutting mode, which itself limits currency gains. The Czech koruna, however, "is a possibility," said Rendell at RBC.

Intervention mightn't be the right answer to boosting exports, though. In research issued last week, Stuart Bennett, a senior strategist at French bank Credit Agricole Corporate & Investment Bank, found that euro-zone growth rather than foreign-exchange rates is the key determinant of economic strength in the region's neighboring emerging markets.

The zloty, Hungarian forint and Czech koruna are all overvalued, Bennett said, and that isn't helpful to exports. But "further appreciation should not derail these economies" as long as the euro-zone recovery remains intact.

-By Katie Martin, Dow Jones Newswires; +44 (0) 207 842 9346; katie.martin@dowjones.com [ 04-15-10 0711ET ]

title: RPT-PREVIEW-Polish CPI seen easing to 30-month low in March
text:
* WHAT: March inflation

* WHEN: Thursday, April 15, at 1200 GMT

REUTERS FORECAST: March inflation +2.6 pct y/y, +0.4 pct m/m. For full Polish April macropoll, click on [ID:nLDE6381L5].

FACTORS TO WATCH:

Inflation is expected to ease to just above the central bank's 2.5 percent target and reach its lowest level since September 2007 mostly thanks to statistical base effects and a stronger zloty.

The rise of regulated prices was far less this year than in 2009 and the zloty strength in 2010 makes imports less expensive, which will be now reflected in lower year-on-year inflation indicators.

Price growth is expected to abate in the coming months and inflation should reach its lowest level in the summer at about 2 percent, analysts say.

Inflation has been easing since the beginning of the year with the February reading of 2.9 percent coming well below 3.5 percent recorded for January.

Despite the expected easing in price growth dynamics, analysts polled by Reuters still expect the Monetary Policy Council to raise interest rates by a total of 50 basis points before the end of 2010.

The central bank Governor Slawomir Skrzypek, who was also an MPC member, perished in a plane crash on Saturday, but most analysts said this would not change the short-term interest rate outlook.

The main interest rate currently stands at an all-time low of 3.5 percent.

MARKET REACTION: A lower reading could help improve bond market sentiment, particularly on shorter-dated two-year bonds, which are the most sensitive to indications of future monetary policy. The zloty <EURPLN=>, <PLN=> is often supported by bond market gains.

BACKGROUND:

Poland's inflation is highly sensitive to the exchange-rate. Depreciation can quickly increase price growth, while appreciation does the opposite.

Poland's zloty has been rallying in recent weeks, reaching a 16-month high against the euro and raising concern among central bankers that zloty gains could harm the recovery.

Friday, for the first time since Poland adopted the free-float in 2000, the central bank intervened on the FX market to weaken the zloty.

The currency lost about 1 percent against the euro but analysts remained sceptical about the longevity of the fall. Poland's strong economic fundamentals have pushed the zloty up about 6 percent against the euro since the start of 2010.

The zloty's gains could help cap inflationary pressures and possibly cool monetary policy tightening expectations.

Poland was the only economy in the European Union to avoid recession last year, thanks to a large domestic consumer base and the boost Polish exporters got from a weaker zloty.

Growth is now seen at 2.9 percent in 2010, up from 1.7 percent in 2009. For comparison, the economy grew by 5 percent in 2008. (Writing by Kuba Jaworowski; Editing by Neil Stempleman)

title: INSTANT VIEW 3-Polish CPI slows in March to 2.6 pct as fcast
text:
WARSAW, April 15 (Reuters) - Polish consumer prices inflation <PLCPIY=ECI> slowed in March from the previous month, statistics office data showed on Thursday, confirming expectations that the central bank will keep interest rates unchanged this month.

The data showed consumer prices rose 2.6 percent year-on-year in March, in line with analysts' forecasts and down from 2.9 percent in February.

On a monthly basis <PLCPIM=ECI>, CPI stood at 0.3 percent, against 0.2 percent for February.

Analysts said they expected further declines in CPI in coming months due partly to an annual base effect before strengthening domestic demand starts to exert upward pressure on prices again.

The central bank's Monetary Policy Council (MPC) is not expected to raise rates until the latter part of the year.

*************************************************************

FORECAST:

Analysts polled by Reuters expected:

* March inflation at 2.6 percent year-on-year and 0.4 percent in month-on-month terms.

MARKET REACTION:

The Polish zloty <EURPLN=D3> <PLN=> and bonds were unchanged immediately after the data.

ANALYSTS COMMENTS:

MACIEJ RELUGA, CHIEF ECONOMIST AT BZ WBK IN WARSAW

"I think the inflation data will not affect the market or the thinking of the Monetary Policy Council about interest rates. The trend of easing inflation clearly started last month and March is the second consecutive month for inflation to fall.

"I think the next months will bring a continuation of the trend and that inflation will slow to below 2 percent by mid-2010.

"I think year-end inflation will be close to March levels."

MATEUSZ SZCZUREK, CHIEF ECONOMIST AT ING BANK:

"Core inflation at 2.0-2.1 percent remains almost unchanged. There are no big surprises in any of the sub-categories. We are still in a phase of waiting for the inflation falls to stop. This phase will last about 4-5 months. Only after that the discussion on possible rate hikes will begin."

PETER ATTARD MONTALTO, ECONOMIST AT NOMURA IN LONDON

"CPI should continue to ease to a base of around 2.3 percent in May before remaining broadly flat and then starting to rise back up to the top end of its target band in Q3 as domestic demand pressures start to become more evident and recent commodity price increases feed through."

"Long-run inflation is still seen remaining broadly around target with risks to the upside in our forcast, given demand side pressures and credit expansion through the recovery."

GRZEGORZ MALISZEWSKI, CHIEF ECONOMIST AT MILLENNIUM BANK

"The data is in line with market expectations and is the effect of a high statistical base from last year. We had a hike of regulated prices and a weakening of the zloty last year that boosted prices.

"The data is neutral for the market. It just confirms that the consumer price index is continuing to ease and this should continue further."

title: Poland  may continue  FX interventions -finmin
text:
WARSAW, April 14 (Reuters) - Poland may continue intervening on the foreign exchange market, deputy finance minister said on Wednesday, adding the government could accompany the central bank in carrying out the task.

"We will be actively cooperating with the central bank on the interventions...We do not rule out that the finance ministry may also be buying foreign currencies on the market," Dominik Radziwill told Reuters.

"They (investors) have to take into account the possibility of interventions." (Reporting by Pawel Sobczak, writing by Kuba Jaworowski)

title: UPDATE 2- Poland  may still need  FX intervention  -finmin
text:
(Recasts with deputy finmin, trader comment)

WARSAW, April 14 (Reuters) - Poland may continue intervening on the foreign exchange market, a deputy finance minister said on Wednesday, contradicting earlier comments from an economic aide to Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

Deputy Finance Minister Dominik Radziwill's remarks helped trim some of the zloty's previous gains sparked by aide Michal Boni's suggestion that intervention, used recently to weaken the Polish unit, may not be needed.

"We will be actively cooperating with the central bank on the interventions... We do not rule out that the finance ministry may also be buying foreign currencies on the market," Dominik Radziwill told Reuters.

"They (investors) have to take into account the possibility of interventions."

Radziwill's views seem closer to those of central bank officials, who have indicated that the death of bank governor Slawomir Skrzypek, along with President Lech Kaczynski and dozens of other top officials in a plane crash last weekend, would not impact currency policy.

Last Friday, Poland's central bank intervened on the foreign exchange market for the first time since the country adopted a free float currency regime in 2000.

The bank started buying euros, weakening the Polish unit by 1 percent against the common currency in a move welcomed by the finance ministry, which has often complained about the negative impact of a strong zloty on a still fragile economic recovery.

At 1528 GMT the euro traded at 3.8605 zlotys, 0.3 percent lower than on Wednesday morning.

"Radziwill's comments slightly weakened the zloty but this situation does not make Boni look good," a currency trader at a Warsaw bank said.

"Suddenly Boni speaks against the Monetary Policy Council, the central bank and the interests of the economy. And no one knows why, especially as there had been signals from the central bank, MPC and finance ministry that they actually may intervene." (Additional reporting by Kuba Jaworowski, writing by Karolina Slowikowska and Kuba Jaworowski)

title: CEE MARKETS 4- FX  gain; zloty  intervention  fears ease
text:
* Crown, forint benefit from long zloty cross unwinds

* Forint extends post-election rally, bonds correct

* Zloty supported by PM aide intervention comments

* Prague stocks jump, near pre-crisis levels

(Adds Polish finmin comments)

By Dagmara Leszkowicz and Marius Zaharia

WARSAW/BUCHAREST, April 14 (Reuters) - The Czech crown hit a seven-month peak and Hungary's forint climbed to one-month highs on Wednesday, tracking global equities, while the zloty rose as intervention fears eased.

Strategists expect a recovery in central European exports will help fuel gains this year in the region's currencies, which have already rallied since the beginning of 2010, while strong corporate results have also boosted sentiment.

But questions have arisen on whether stronger currencies could hurt recovery prospects and the Polish central bank surprised markets last Friday with its first intervention since introducing a free float in 2000.

The prime minister's top economic adviser Michal Boni said on Wednesday that Poland may not need to intervene further in the currency market. [ID:nLDE63D17C] Later, deputy finance minister Dominik Radziwill said investors should still take the possibility of interventions into account. [ID:nWSF008941]

At 1530 GMT, the zloty <EURPLN=> was bid 0.3 percent up on the day at 3.859 per euro and was little changed after Radziwill's comments. Dealers said Boni's comments may suggest the bank has not yet decided to intervene further.

The forint <EURHUF=>, the crown <EURCZK=> and Romania's leu <EURRON=> were all up 0.2-0.5 percent.

While the zloty's appreciation will likely cool in the short term, some analysts say markets will probably push the central bank into another intervention.

"The more currency strength you get in this current economic environment, the more these economies will be at risk of disappointing readings ... and slowdown in growth momentum," said Michal Dybula, economist for central and eastern Europe at BNP Paribas. "They will not hesitate to use (intervention)."

The zloty's reversal, after rallying more than 6 percent gains this year, has boosted peers the crown and forint as investors square long zloty positions against them.

The forint and Hungarian bonds have rallied this week after a sweeping first round election win for the centre-right Fidesz party, which gained a near two-thirds majority needed to push through vital reforms. [ID:nLDE63107B]

Markets still price in a 25 basis point interest rate cut on April 26, one day after the election's second round. The central bank's minutes indicated that the end of the rate-cutting cycle was uncertain. [ID:nLDE63D1ID]

"I think the cuts will continue further, perhaps even below 5 percent," one dealer in Budapest said.

Bond yields ticked up on profit taking after dropping around 50 basis points since Sunday's election.

POLAND RESILIENT

Polish markets have held up following the Saturday crash of a government plane that killed President Lech Kaczynski, central bank Governor Slawomir Skrzypek and other senior officials.

The bank's acting governor Piotr Wiesiolek told daily Gazeta Wyborcza on Wednesday the country should name a new central bank head without unnecessary delays. [ID:nLDE63D04J]

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Stocks rise 1 pct; Dubai's DEWA to sell bond
text:
* Stocks jump 1 pct; just off recent 19-1/2 mth peaks

* Lira rises as central bank unveils exit policies

* Dubai's DEWA sets price guidance for dollar bond

By Sujata Rao

LONDON, April 14 (Reuters) - Emerging stocks rose 1 percent on Wednesday as strong corporate results boosted global equities, while a state-run Dubai entity prepared to sell the first bond from the emirate since last year's shock debt freeze.

Forecast-beating results by chipmaker Intel and investment bank JP Morgan as well as a currency revaluation in Singapore that re-ignited expectations of a move in the yuan were catalysts for emerging market gains.

Benchmark MSCI emerging equity index <.MSCIEF> tracked gains on core markets to rise back close to recent 19-1/2 month highs and exchanges in Istanbul <.XU100>, Johannesburg <.JTOPI> and Moscow <.IRTS> rallied almost one percent.

Emerging currencies were moderately higher as the dollar slipped, with the Turkish lira outperforming <TRY=> amid expectations for a rate increase by the second half of 2010.

Asian currencies had been supported by a revaluation in Singapore dollar <SGD=> which hit a 20-month high, indicating the central bank's shift in focus from growth to inflation. Asia's tech-heavy bourses such as Korea and Taiwan were also lifted by the Intel results.

"Asia was first off the block and that fed through (into emerging Europe)," said Nigel Rendell, emerging markets strategist at RBC Capital Markets.

"We are trading one day to the next and valuations, whether on bonds or stocks, are quite expensive but there are quite a few supportive elements so the rally may continue a bit longer."

He identified market-positive Hungarian election results and the Turkish central bank's move to a slightly less dovish stance as supportive for forint and lira -- both currencies are up 1.5 percent this week.

The forint neared a four-week high to the euro <EURHUF=>. while the lira hit a 2-1/2-month high versus the dollar <TRY=>.

Rendell said the Singapore move highlights the theme of rate normalisation across emerging markets, starting with Asia, even though most central banks have been nervous about increasing interest rates to avoid disrupting economic recovery.

TURKEY

Turkey's central bank for instance announced an end to some stimulus measures introduced during the crisis but stressed the exit would be "cautious and gradual". Despite rising inflation, it signalled this week rates would stay low for a while.

Turkish bonds' response was muted while stocks extended gains but analysts say the liquidity withdrawal would eventually hit bonds which are overwhelmingly held by local banks.

"Exit policies, combined with gradually improving prospects for lending....should over time start to weigh on the local bond market. In contrast, these measures are unlikely to curb the recent trend for lira strengthening," Barclays told clients.

Also in emerging Europe, the Czech crown hit a seven-month high <EURCZK=> while the zloty firmed 0.13 percent <EURPLN=>.

Traders said crown gains were not due to Czech-specific factors. Some cited the closure of long zloty/crown trades after Poland's central bank intervened in currency markets last week.

"Everything is fairly strong as nothing has happened to shake the mood. Obviously in Poland, you have to watch for the central bank if we get up to 3.85 again," one trader said.

"I expect there will be another attempt soon, everything points to a stronger zloty."

Bond markets also were demonstrating the strong appetite for emerging market risk -- Turkey's 1.5 billion-euro 2020 issue launched on Tuesday garnered orders of almost 6 billion euros while a raft of quasi-sovereigns are marketing bonds.

Dubai's state-run utility DEWA is expected on Wednesday to price a dollar bond, with price guidance at 8.75 percent but sources said the issue has already traded almost a point higher in the grey market. This is the first issue since Dubai called a standstill on billions of dollars of debt last November.

The deal was said to have received orders of about $4 billion by the time books closed in London.

"The price talk is 8.75 percent which is extremely generous. That's a spread of 615 basis points over U.S. Treasuries," one London-based banker said.

He added the issue also offered a yield pickup of 125 bps over Dubai though Dewa tends to trade flat to the sovereign.

Another deal expected this week is state-run Ukrainian bank Ukreximbank with a five-year dollar issue. That would be the first from the ex-Soviet country following the restructuring of another Ukrainian quasi-sovereign Naftogaz last year and may pave the way for a sovereign bond later this year.

Russia is marketing its first bond in a decade and Montenegro said on Wednesday it plans an issue in May or June.

Sovereign emerging bond yield spreads over U.S. Treasuries fell 4 bps to 240 bps <11EMJ>.

Year-to-date Finland has sold EUR8 billion of government bonds out of the EUR16 billion to EUR17 billion planned for 2010, he calculates. (emese.bartha@dowjones.com)

Maybe Greece can get through without calling upon the EU/IMF reserve, perhaps they will not." The USD is up at Y93.43 while the EUR is up at $1.3628. Strong U.S. retail sales later in the day could boost sentiment even further. However, data showing slower industrial production growth in the euro zone could stop the EUR from rising much more. The GBP is up at $1.5410. nick.hastings@dowjones.com)

Also, he is hardly likely to shift guidance unilaterally ahead of an FOMC in about two weeks time. Nevertheless, says Tullett Prebon, Bernanke's comments to Congress later in the day could still "create some jitters" as he will be keen to discourage complacency among investors and might prove less dovish than the market expects. (neelabh.chaturvedi@dowjones.com)

title: INSTANT VIEW 2-Polish Feb C/A posts 106 mln euro surplus
text:
WARSAW, April 13 (Reuters) - Poland's current account swung into a surplus of 106 million euros in February from a revised deficit of 754 million euros in January, central bank data showed on Tuesday, largely thanks to an inflow of EU funds.

Analysts polled by Reuters had expected a deficit of 203 million euros.

In other data, Poland's trade deficit stood at 248 million euros in the second month of 2010.

The total current account gap in 2009 stood at 4,968 million euros compared with 18,293 million a year earlier.

Analysts attributed the improvement to transfers of European Union funds to Poland and said they expected the current account balance to deteriorate again as the recovery from a sharp slowdown gathers pace.

In a bid to improve the quality of the data the bank initiated a new way of gathering it as of Jan. 1, 2010, but analysts still have doubts over its reliability.

title: FOCUS: Polish Zloty, Bonds Stable Despite Tragedy
text:
Malgorzata Halaba 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

WARSAW (Dow Jones)--Poland's zloty and Treasury bonds are stable despite Saturday's tragedy when President Lech Kaczynski, the central bank's head Slawomir Skrzypek, and a large part of political elite died in a plane crash.

The zloty is clearly supported by Sunday news on the European Union aid package for Greece and any possible uncertainty is related to fears Poland's central bank may intervene again to weaken the currency, economists said.

Shortly after the opening Monday the zloty weakened against the euro, to above the 3.88 level, but immediately came back to Friday afternoon levels.

At 0836 GMT, EUR/PLN traded at 3.87 from 3.88 Friday afternoon and the average yield on a five-year benchmark treasury bond was at 5.14% from 5.17% Friday afternoon.

"The tragedy had no impact on the market," said Maja Goettig, chief economist at Bank BPH in Warsaw, seeing early Monday's weakening as an aftermath of the central bank's intervention rather than the reaction to the tragedy.

On Friday, the central bank intervened on the market for the first time since the zloty was floated ten years ago.

Following the intervention, the zloty weakened to around 3.90 against the euro, from 3.8450, but was back at around 3.88 Friday afternoon.

"Now the investors might be careful because further intervention cannot be excluded," Goetting said, adding that clearly the investors show strong trust in Poland's legal procedures which will ensure there is no risk for the function of the central bank.

"Despite the tragic events on Saturday, we believe any negative implications for financial markets will be short lived, given continuity in both the government and the National Bank of Poland," Piotr Kalisz, chief economist at Citibank Handlowy in Warsaw, wrote in his research note.

Economists pointed out that the responsibilities of the central bank's governor were taken by Skrzypek's first deputy, Piotr Wiesiolek.

And while it's quite possible Skrzypek's successor may be appointed only after the presidential election, this "should not be a reason for concern for the financial markets," Bank Zachodni WBK said in a research note.

"Over the longer term we remain bullish given that economic policy is unchanged and the fact that intervention alone is rarely, if ever, sufficient to do more than slow the pace of currency movement," Royal Bank of Canada said Sunday. "We still look for a move to 3.75-3.80 (against the euro) in the second half of the year."

title: Q&A-What's next for Polish c.bank after governor's death?
text:
WARSAW, April 11 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank governor Slawomir Skrzypek and President Lech Kaczynski died in a plane crash in Russia on Saturday.

Following is analysis of issues surrounding the appointment of Skrzypek's successor and possible policy changes at the central bank. ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ For more stories on the crash, click [ID:nLDE639096] For analysis of the market impact, click [ID:nLDE63A09N] ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

HOW AND WHEN WILL A SUCCESSOR BE APPOINTED?

The Polish constitution stipulates that the governor is appointed by the president for a six-year term, but his candidacy needs to be approved by parliament. Skrzypek was mid-way through his term.

But Kaczynski's death clouds the process; the law does not clearly indicate whether Parliamentary Speaker Bronislaw Komorowski, who has taken over as acting president, can make the appointment before the presidential election that he must call within 14 days and hold within two months after that.

The central bank law requires that a new governor be appointed within three months of a vacancy, which would leave hardly any time after the election. Some analysts say that in order to signal stability at the central bank, the appointment could be made before the election if parliament reaches a consensus on a candidate.

Skrzypek's top deputy Piotr Wiesiolek has taken over day-to-day management of the central bank, but it is not yet clear whether he will take on other responsibilities, such as voting during meetings of the Monetary Policy Council.

MPC member Elzbieta Chojna-Duch said in a television interview on Sunday that the council would discuss several legal questions surrounding the transition period, including how it would choose its chair for upcoming meetings.

The MPC usually meets twice a month, with its second sitting in the last week of the month deciding on interest rates.

WHO ARE POTENTIAL CANDIDATES TO SUCCEED SKRZYPEK?

Analysts are floating several possible candidates:

-- Boguslaw Grabowski, a former MPC member who was known as a monetary policy hawk; he ended his six-year term in 2004 and now heads one of Poland's largest investment funds, Skarbiec.

-- Dariusz Filar, a former MPC member who ended his term this year; also seen as a hawk.

-- Jerzy Pruski, who was the top deputy governor at the central bank for four years before falling out with Skrzypek in 2008. Since then he has served as chief executive of Poland's largest bank, PKO BP , and now heads the Banking Guarantee Fund.

-- Finance Minister Jacek Rostowski, who has held his post since 2007; he is widely respected for his management of the economy during the global financial crisis, from which Poland escaped relatively lightly.

An even more radical step would be to turn to Leszek Balcerowicz, who was governor of the central bank from 2001 to 2007 and was known as a strong hawk. Balcerowicz was one of the architects of Poland's transition to a market economy two decades ago, and was praised abroad and sometimes criticised at home for his role. He pushed for pension and other reforms during a stint as finance minister in the late 1990s.

Some analysts speculate the choice could come from among the nine current MPC members, who took office this year.

WILL MONETARY POLICY CHANGE?

Skrzypek, who had a tie-breaking vote, was once seen as the staunchest dove on the 10-member interest rate-setting body, and was on the losing end of several decisions.

But in recent months, as a new, more government-friendly MPC was appointed, Skrzypek had begun to speak of bringing the key rate above its all-time low of 3.5 percent. The latest Reuters poll, in March, found economists expecting the rate to rise to 4.0 percent by the end of this year. [ID:nLDE6270J3]

Economists expect Komorowski, a member of the ruling party and an early favourite to win the presidential election, to pick a new governor who might be moderately more hawkish than Skrzypek, but there will probably be little if any effect on the full MPC's rate decisions.

FOREIGN EXCHANGE POLICY

Skrzypek orchestrated the central bank's intervention last Friday to halt the strengthening of the zloty <EURPLN=>, its first such move since the zloty's free-float a decade ago. [ID:nLDE63816K]

There is speculation that Skrzypek's successor may be less inclined to intervene against the zloty, but no clear evidence for this; Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government backed the intervention, believing zloty strength could hurt the economic recovery.

POLAND'S ASPIRATIONS TO ADOPT THE EURO?

The central bank under Skrzypek was seen as one of the few remaining bastions of euroscepticism in Poland; like Kaczynski, who appointed him, Skrzypek had appeared reluctant to commit to a target for joining the single currency.

The centre-right government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk aims to adopt the euro as soon as 2015, after dropping a more ambitious target during the global financial crisis. Komorowski is expected to choose a central bank chief who is more supportive of euro entry.

Ultimately it is the government which decides on euro entry, though it must coordinate its policy with the central bank, which would need to take steps to keep the zloty within a euro-anchored ban for at least two years before adoption.

FISCAL POLICY

A new, more government-friendly central bank governor would likely end the row between the bank's management, led by Skrzypek, and new MPC members close to the ruling coalition over the size of the bank's profit, and therefore how much of the profit will go towards meeting Poland's fiscal gap.

Under Polish law 95 percent of the profit is automatically transferred to the government, but there has been a bitter dispute over the size of required reserves; Skrzypek claimed the profit was only 4.2 billion zlotys, while other MPC members estimated it as roughly twice that amount.

Skrzypek's successor may also drop the central bank's opposition to extending Poland's $20.5 billion flexible credit line from the International Monetary Fund, which was opened last year and expires in May. (Edited by Andrew Torchia)

title: ANALYSIS-Polish markets to stabilise after plane disaster
text:
* After early nervousness, impact likely to be minor

* Fiscal, most economic policy in hands of cabinet

* Interest rate path unlikely to change

* Next c.bank governor may not be so keen on FX intervention

By Marcin Goclowski and Chris Borowski

WARSAW, April 11 (Reuters) - Polish markets are expected to stabilise quickly after early jitters following the deaths of the country's president and central bank governor, with currency and interest rate policy unlikely to show any immediate change.

Poland's economic stewardship is mainly in the hands of Prime Minister Donald Tusk and his cabinet, who have maintained growth during the global credit crisis. President Lech Kaczynski played only a secondary, mainly ceremonial role.

Central bank governor Slawomir Skrzypek, also killed by Saturday's plane crash in Russia, was seen as the driving force behind last Friday's currency market intervention to halt strengthening of the zloty.

His replacement could eventually modify that policy, but the new central bank chief may not be chosen for some weeks, during which time current policy should continue. Interest rate policy, which has been broadly supported by the entire 10-member Monetary Policy Council, looks set to stay unchanged.

So while the zloty may weaken slightly when markets reopen on Monday, perhaps to its lows late last month of around 3.90 against the euro, and government bonds could be sold modestly, the markets are not expected to establish new trends.

"The financial markets look at this from a longer perspective, so even with a short-term discounting of this tragedy, I don't see a long-term impact on the economy," said former central bank official Dariusz Filar.

Marek Juras, head of equity research at UniCredit CAIB in Warsaw, said: "The stock market should be the least affected, while we could see some more activity initially in the zloty and the bond markets."

The Polish stock market has been in a strong uptrend for the past two months, hitting a 21-month high last week, because of expectations for an economic recovery.

CURRENCY POLICY

The central bank's intervention against the zloty on Friday was the first since Poland introduced a free float for the currency in 2000.

Tusk's government backed the intervention, fearing a strong zloty could stall the economic recovery, but it might conceivably end up choosing a new central bank governor who is less willing to intervene.

"Until the new governor is chosen, the intervention policy will be continued by the central bank management," said Jakub Borowski, chief economist at Invest-Bank. "But the new governor may oppose it, so some investors may expect future zloty strengthening."

Also, Skrzypek was reluctant to set a firm target for Poland to adopt the euro; his successor may be more euro-friendly.

But it remains unclear when Poland's Acting President Bronislaw Komorowski, a political ally of Tusk, will appoint Skrzypek's successor, because there is uncertainty over the extent of his authority before elections in June.

Piotr Wiesiolek, Skrzypek's top deputy, will serve as acting central bank governor until the appointment. Analysts are floating several potential candidates: former central bank official Boguslaw Grabowski, former central bank deputy governor Jerzy Pruski, or even Finance Minister Jacek Rostowski.

In any case, there is no reason to expect a change of interest rate policy. Skrzypek was once seen as a leading dove on the central bank's rate-setting body, but in recent months he had moderated his views and had spoken of raising the key rate off its all-time low of 3.5 percent.

"The path for interest rates shouldn't change because recent comments by Skrzypek showed that he stopped being a proponent of loose monetary policy, and it's difficut to imagine that a new head of the central bank would have a more dovish approach," said Borowski.

POLITICAL TENSIONS

In the long term, the replacement of Skrzypek is likely to ease a tense relationship between the central bank and the government, and between the central bank governor and other members of the Monetary Policy Council. This could be moderately positive for all the financial markets.

Most of the council were appointed by Poland's centre-right government earlier this year. Skrzypek by contrast was appointed in 2007 by Kaczynski, a founder of main opposition party Law and Justice.

In particular, Skrzypek's replacement may end a conflict over the government's demand that the central bank hand over as much as 8 billion zlotys ($2.8 billion) in last year's earnings to the state coffers to help cover the budget deficit.

"This completely changes the dynamics between the bank and the government in the dispute over what to do with the central bank's profits," said an emerging markets analyst at a foreign institution, who asked not to be named.

Skrzypek had clashed with the government and members of the council over reclassifying the bank's currency reserves to beef up its earnings. (Editing by Andrew Torchia)

title: EMERGING MARKETS  FX -Zloty surges further ahead.
text:
LONDON, Aug 4 (Reuters) - The zloty forged ahead again on Tuesday with no central bank intervention to stem its relentless rise, and traders saw it edging even higher. 

 Analysts said most emerging Asian currencies firmed slightly as the yen inched back under 145 to the dollar, with the rupiah gaining sharply on support from Indonesia's latest round of international aid. 

 In Warsaw, the Polish currency broke through the barrier of nine percent above parity for the first time, closing at a new record of 9.08/9.03 percent above parity compared with Monday's record high close of 8.89/8.84. 

 "It doesn't look like any respite for the strong zloty," said one trader at a London bank, who asked not to be named. 

 By 1245 GMT the Polish unit was at 3.432 bid against the dollar in London and 1.9246 against the mark, the two main currencies in the five-currency basket which determines the central bank's daily parity rate, compared with 3.436 and 1.9255 respectively in late London trade on Monday. 

 The zloty is allowed to fluctuate in a band of plus or minus 10 percent around the parity rate. Last week the National Bank of Poland intervened in the market to cap the rise, but there was no confirmed central bank action on Tuesday in spite of earlier expectations that it would again buy dollars. 

 "Usually the central bank will defend a level for a couple of days and then allow the market to take it through. They're basically slowing the rise," the trader said, adding that he saw the next resistance level at 9.25 percent or even 9.5 percent above parity. 

 Analysts and traders said demand for zlotys was bolstered by privatisation issues and foreign purchases of Polish bonds. 

 Most East Asian currencies firmed slightly as the yen backtracked to below 145 to the dollar after earlier crashing through 146. 

 "Dollar/yen is providing the general framework for movements in regional currencies," said Andrew Fung, an economist at Standard Chartered in London. 

 "Most of the Asian currencies are higher on the back of the slightly firmer yen, although what we've seen in European time is some of these gains being given up." 

 The rupiah saw the biggest gain, climbing back under the 13,000 barrier to 12,800 to the dollar by 1245 GMT, a rise of around 2.7 percent from late Monday's levels in London. 

 Fung said the biggest impetus came from large inflows of aid aimed at dragging Indonesia out of its financial crisis. He said these far outweighed debt service outflows, especially since much of Indonesia's debt servicing was at a standstill. 

 International donors last week pledged $7.9 billion in aid for the current fiscal year to end-March. The IMF has already said it will top up a $41.2 billion international rescue package already in place with a further $6.2 billion in fresh loans. 

 The official launch on Monday of the Indonesian Debt Restructuring Agency (INDRA) was not having much immediate impact on the market, although INDRA's base exchange rate of 13,233 rupiah to the dollar for debt conversion could lend support in the medium term, Fung added. INDRA was born out of a deal struck in June with foreign creditors to restructure the country's $84 billion in private-sector foreign debt. But no companies have yet signed up for the scheme, and Fung said many debtor firms had already acted to restructure their debt. 

 "I don't think we'll see any big move across the board to transfer to INDRA," he said. "But there's a psychological cap at 13,233, and in that sense the market will probably stay away from that (level) unless there's a really serious deterioration on the political front." 

 Elsewhere in emerging markets, the rouble held rock steady at 6.283 bid, unchanged from late Monday's levels in London. 

 The Czech crown lost a little of its recent strength amid jitters over the health of President Vaclav Havel, who was seriously ill in hospital, but analysts and traders said they expected the currency to remain buoyant. 

 The crown eased to 17.367 bid against the mark, compared with 17.226 late on Monday.

title: Zloty hits new high as c.bank stays its hand.
text:
WARSAW, Aug 3 (Reuters) - The zloty slowly firmed to close at a new record high against its basket on Monday with the central bank refraining from intervention. 

 Dealers said continued foreign interest in Polish treasuries pulled the zloty up to close at 8.89/8.84 percent above the parity rate, from Friday's 8.80/8.76 percent finish. 

 It ended at 3.4390/05 to the dollar, against 3.4335/60 on Friday and at 1.9255/65 to the mark, against 1.9300/30. 

 "The zloty gradually gained ground to close around 8.9 percent. The central bank probably wants to keep the market guessing somewhat and so it did not intervene today," said Mateusz Bieniek, chief forex dealer at Bank Handlowy SA. 

 Over the last few weeks the National Bank of Poland (NBP) intervened against the zloty whenever the currency sustained gains above 8.8 percent. 

 "The NBP intervenes to slow the zloty's appreciation rather than to knock it down. If they wanted to weaken it, they would have to spend much larger sums of money," Bieniek added. 

 Dealers expect central bank interventions on Tuesday if the zloty kept trading at these levels. 

 They said foreign investors did not buy large amounts of T-bills at Monday's 700 million zloty tender, but that some sought the benchmark 52-week bill. 

 The benchmark's average yield fell 16.18 percent at the tender, in line with expectations, from last week's 16.65. 

 Analysts said the economy ministry's forecast of 6.7 percent GDP growth in the first half of 1998 had little impact on the market even though it was better than expected. 

 "This number seems a bit high. It may be better to wait for official second quarter GDP data from the statistical office," said one senior banking analyst in Warsaw. 

 Economists expect Poland's economy, which grew 6.9 percent last year, to slow from the second quarter under the weight of a tight monetary policy. 

 The government expects GDP growth of 5.6 percent this year and the central bank about six percent. ((Wojciech Moskwa, Warsaw Newsroom, tel. +48 22 653 9700, fax +48 22 653 9780, warsaw.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Early zloty stays at all-time high, c.bank quiet.
text:
WARSAW, July 31 (Reuters) - The zloty held at an all-time high early on Friday and dealers said the central bank could step in with dollar-buying interventions at any time. 

 At 0800 GMT the zloty was at 8.89/8.86 percent firmer than the trading band centre against the opening 8.89/8.84 percent. 

 It traded at 3.4310/25 to the dollar against 3.4300/15 at the start and at 1.9281/86 to the mark against 1.9290/00. 

 "The zloty is presently at the central bank's intervention levels and around these levels few players want to buy the unit," said Piotr Konarski, senior dealer at WestLB Polska SA. 

 On Thursday the National Bank of Poland bought an estimated $80 million to cool the foreign-charged zloty, but dealers said the move failed to weaken the market's pro-zloty sentiment. 

 "I don't see any reson why the zloty should weaken now and in fact the central bank's interventions instantly trigger more dollar-selling," WestLB's Konarski added. 

Poland's zloty moves within a range of 10 percent above or below a parity rate set each day by the central bank. 

 Zloty parity is determined by the value of a basket of five Western currencies against which the unit is devalued at a rate of 0.65 percent per month. 

 The local money market calmed down on the first day of the new monthly reserve period and overnight and tomorrow/next rates held flat at 19.0/19.4 percent in early Friday trade. ((Pawel Kozlowski, Warsaw Newsroom, tel. +48 22 653 9700, fax +48 22 653 9780, warsaw.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Polish Zloty Higher On Optimism Toward Emerging Mkts
text:
WARSAW (Dow Jones)--The Polish zloty (PLN) is slightly higher against the currency basket on Monday morning in quiet dealing amid improved optimism toward emerging markets.

title: EMERGING MARKETS  FX  - Rouble slips on rate cut.
text:
LONDON, July 24 (Reuters) - The Russian rouble continued its recent weakening trend, spurred on by a cut in the nation's benchmark interest rate on Friday, analysts said. 

 Negative sentiment, already weighing on the rouble, deepened after Russia's central bank cut the refinancing rate to 60 percent from 80 percent, they said. 

 "The drop (in the rouble) is probably related, but it was falling already so the rating cut doesn't help," said Juliet Sampson, emerging markets economist at Bank of America. 

 The rouble has been pulled down by weak Lower-Developed-Countries (LDC) debt and an overall negative sentiment across markets in general, she said. 

 "It's being pulled down by the yen, by the Dow (Jones industrial average), it's taking any excuse," she said. 

 Sampson said market players remained concerned despite the International Monetary Fund's approval on Monday of an $11.2 billion loan bailout for Russia. 

 "There was a lot of enthusiasm when the deal went through and now people are doing their numbers and saying maybe there are still doubts about whether Russia can make it," she said. 

 U.S. Vice President Al Gore said on Friday he was optimistic Russia will turn the corner soon and economic growth will soon appear. 

 Elsewhere in Eastern Europe, the Polish zloty softened in early Friday trade as players continued to take profits on Polish treasuries after recent foreign capital inflows pushed the currency to all-time highs and yields to lows, dealers said. 

 At 1110 GMT the zloty was 8.25 percent firmer than the trading band centre against the opening 8.35/8.29 percent. 

 It traded at 3.4525/40 to the dollar against 3.4500/20 at the start and at 1.9355/60 to the mark against 1.9320/35. 

 Dealers said the overall positive sentiment toward Poland remained intact, adding that the zloty should continue to find support above 8.0 percent from the trading band centre. 

 "We are still seeing some profit-taking, but there are also investors who are selling larger amounts of currencies when the zloty weakens to around 8.15-8.20 percent from parity," said Piotr Konarski, senior forex dealer at WestLB Polska SA. 

 The National Bank of Poland (NBP) did not intervene against the zloty on Thursday after buying roughly $180 million on the market earlier this week to cool the surging zloty. 

 Poland's zloty moves within a range of 10 percent above or below a parity rate set each day by the central bank. 

 Zloty parity is determined by the value of a basket of five Western currencies against which the unit is devalued at a rate of 0.65 percent per month. 

 The Czech crown also slipped on sagging emerging markets sentiment. 

 Newly elected Czech Prime Minister Milos Zeman said on Friday his government would like to participate in the setting of inflation targets along with the central bank. 

 In the Asian currency markets, the election of Foreign Minister Keizo Obuchi as the new leader of Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party had a muted effect. 

 Obuchi's win had been largely factored into the market and players have begun to focus on the make-up of his new cabinet. 

 Even the Malaysian ringgit shrugged off a ratings downgrade from Moody's Investors Service. The U.S.-based ratings agency said it downgraded Malaysia's long-term foreign currency ceilings for bonds and notes to Baa2 from A2. 

 "The downgradings were not particularly surprising and were expected somewhat," said Mitul Kotecha, emerging markets economist at Standard Chartered Bank in London. 

 The ringgit rose to 4.1250/1450 from 4.1430/630 in late European trading on Thursday. 

 Buying interest in Malaysian assets from foreign companies had underpinned the currency, Kotecha said. 

 "There are reports of investments taking place in Malaysian assets from foreign companies and that is probably helping keep up the ringgit at least for today." 

 Moody's said it cut the country ceiling for bank deposits to Baa3 from Baa1, lowered the short-term foreign currency country ceilings for debt and bank deposits to Prime 3 from Prime 2 and cut foreign currency bonds of the government to Baa2 from A2. 

 Moody's said the ratings action reflected the rapid deterioration in Malaysia's economy this year and the expected effects on the banking system and government finance. 

 The Indonesian rupiah slipped below the 14,000 per dollar level, with the market focused on next week's meeting of Indonesia's donors in Paris. 

 Planning Minister Boediono said the group was likely to pledge a larger amount of loans than last year's $5.3 billion. 

 IMF Asia expert Hubert Neiss said the timing for scrapping food subsidies in Indonesia depended on the economic recovery. 

 Indonesia on Thursday approved an adjusted 1998/99 budget of 236.89 trillion rupiah, from the previous 277.14 trillion to reflect a drop in repayment of foreign debt principal. 

 But the country's economic and social woes looked set to persist with national airline Garuda Indonesia saying it expected a net loss of two trillion rupiah in calendar 1998.

title: Zloty rides to new high despite c. bank action.
text:
WARSAW, July 22 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank intervened against the zloty for the second day to cool positive sentiment for the Polish unit but could not stop it closing at a fresh all-time high on Wednesday. 

 The zloty closed at 8.79/8.76 percent above the trading band centre, a touch higher than Tuesday's record close of 8.77/8.74 percent above parity. 

 The National Bank of Poland (NBP) bought an estimated $60-80 million on Wednesday when the zloty was between 8.80 and 8.75 percent, after buying roughly $100 million in the previous session. 

 "Foreign investors mainly stayed on the sidelines today, waiting for the central bank to intervene before making any deals. Today's interventions were just intended to show the NBP is watching, not to weaken the Polish currency," one forex dealer at a foreign bank in Warsaw said. 

 The zloty closed at 3.4374/84 per dollar, against 3.4340/55 on Tuesday and at 1.9214/20 to the mark, against 1.9210/15. 

 "Most players are long on the zloty, waiting for NBP moves, but others feel that this is the top and the zloty could slowly drift down towards 8.5 percent," said Andrzej Fiderkiewicz, forex dealer at Societe Generale in Warsaw. 

 But dealers said that in the longer-term Poland's still high yields and relatively sound fundementals would attract more foreign portfolio capital and keep the zloty buoyant. 

 The benchmark 52-week T-bill yield fell some 0.3 point during Wednesday's session, ending around 16.00/15.80 percent against Monday's primary auction yield of 16.69 percent. 

 Dealers said markets received a small boost from NBP chief Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz's comment that the level of speculative foreign capital in Poland's treasuries was at a safe level. 

 "We are not under presssure from speculative capital," Gronkiewicz-Watlz told the Wprost weekly in an interview.

title: Polish RPP member says  forex interventions  needed.
text:
WARSAW, July 22 (Reuters) - A member of Poland's Monetary Policy Council (RPP) said forex interventions were needed to cool demand for the surging zloty, but that the situation was under control, the Gazeta Wyborcza daily reported on Wednesday. 

 "So far everything is under control, and what is happening is no surprise to us," Gazeta quoted Grzegorz Wojtowicz as saying. 

 "I am not able to say how long this situation will last. I think that after some time, investor interest in the zloty will decline. But now interventions are necessary to cool investor appetite for the zloty," Wojtowicz said. 

 On Tuesday the zloty, buoyant on foreign buying of Polish treasuries, rose to all time highs of around 8.9 percent above the trading band centre before central bank interventions knocked the currency lower. It closed at 8.77 percent. 

 Poland's zloty moves against a basket of major currencies within a range of 10 percent above or below a parity rate set each day by the central bank. 

 The central bank's 10-member RPP council last week cut interest rates and reduced the zloty's official devaluation rate. 

 "The council made a correct decision about cutting interest rates, further cuts were not possible," Wojtowicz said.

title: Zloty at all-time high, eyes turn to Polish c.bank.
text:
WARSAW, July 13 (Reuters) - The zloty hit a record high on Monday and analysts expected the currency to stay under upward pressure on news that Russia received a large rescue package, which brightened sentiment towards the eastern Europe. 

 The zloty firmed to all-time highs in post-fixing trade on Monday to around 8.47/8.35 percent above parity aaginst 8.32 percent at the fixing and Friday's fix at 8.15 percent. The zloty trades in a band of plus/minus 10 percent from parity. 

 Analysts said the Monetary Policy Council's (RPP) meeting on Thursday, where a reduction in interest rates and possibly the zloty's crawl is expected, would now take centre stage with Russia's financial worries seen at least temporarily solved. 

 Some also said Poland's central bank could intervene to keep the zloty from strengthening past resistance at 8.5 percent above the parity rate. 

 "The zloty is approaching 8.5 percent from parity and this may possibly be the top for now as the central bank may want to step in (with interventions)," said Andrzej Fiderkiewicz, forex dealer at Societe Generale in Warsaw. 

 Earlier on Monday Russia reached an agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on an emergency financing package worth a total of $22.6 billion spread over 1998 and 1999. Of this sum, Moscow would receive $14.8 billion in 1998. 

 "That's good news, which may create a run on Russia's debt and, thus, will probably also give a boost to the zloty and our paper," said Rafal Petsch, dealer at Bank of America Polska SA. 

 "The zloty has a chance to test 8.5 percent from parity on Tuesday, but the closer to the top of its band, the more vulnerable the zloty will become," Petsch added. 

 The zloty traded at 3.4550/00 to the dollar aaginst 3.4670 at the fixing and at 1.9150/70 to the mark versus 1.9135 at the fixing. 

 Monday's fixing at 8.32 pct above the trading band centre was the zloty's strongest fix ever against the currency basket. The previous high of 8.31 percent was hit on May 5. 

 Analysts said the 10-member RPP council could trim interest rates by some 50 to 150 bp and slow the zloty's devaluation pace on Thursday after inflation, credit growth and the current acccount balance appeared to be under control last week. 

 Polish T-bill yields dropped at Monday's 600 million zloty tender, with total investor demand topping 2.4 billion zlotys. The benchmark 52-week bill yield fell to 18.20 percent from an average of 18.89 percent at last week's primary auction.

title: Emerging market  forex -Indian rupee weathers storm.
text:
LONDON, May 12 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee held steady in European trading on Tuesday despite a storm of international protest over India's nuclear tests but London analysts warned of possible weakness ahead. 

 Spot rupee was trading around 39.760/770 in light volume, faring better than in Bombay where the six month forward rate against the dollar jumped to a premium of 8.45 percent versus 6.8 percent at Monday's close. 

 "At the moment the currency (rupee) is not one that you can trade actively and the Reserve Bank of India are pretty effective at smoothing things in terms of crisis, so we are unlikely to see a plunge. It's much more likely to happen gently," said Nick Douch, emerging market currency strategist at BZW. 

 The nuclear tests carried out on Monday by India's new coalition government, headed by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), have sparked widespread international condemnation and raised the spectre of sanctions being imposed. 

 Both the United States and Japan have said they are considering sanctions. Japan, which is India's largest foreign aid donor, warned on Tuesday that it may freeze loans to India. 

 "We will have to see wait and see what the world reaction is. It's a non-currency story in terms of movement but it's obviously a story that is going to hang around in terms of potential movement," BZW's Douch said. 

 Among other Asian currencies, the Indonesian rupiah suffered another bout of weakness amid deepening worries over social unrest and a lack of progress on debt restructuring talks. 

 The Philippine peso was little changed after surging in Asian trading on expectations of a landslide victory for Presidential election candidate Joseph Estrada. 

 The Thai baht turned slightly weaker, bucking the firmer trend in Bangkok where corporate selling of the dollar supported the currency. 

 Among European currencies, the Polish zloty was slightly weaker but the easing was expected to be short-lived as foreign capital inflows show no sign of abating. 

 The zloty's persistent rise sparked a bout of central bank intervention to dampen it down on Monday and traders said further intervention was likely. 

 "In Poland there is a lot of speculation about a possible cut in the crawling peg and there is also speculation about a cut in interest rates," said Jesper Dannesboe, economist at ABN AMRO in London. 

 He said that on the one hand the market knows that the monetary policy committee is focusing on putting downward pressure on inflation to hit its 9-1/2 percent target but on the other hand the central bank is worried about the current account deficit and strong capital inflows. 

 "It's not clear if they (the central bank) will cut interest rates yet and the bottom line is that the zloty will stay strong for now because the market gets very high yields and it's hard to see them cutting extremely aggressively in the near term," Dannesboe said. 

 The Czech crown was also slightly weaker but holding at the key support level of 18.252 after inflation data met market expectations. 

 Dannesboe said fundamentals in the Czech republic were far less strong than in Poland. 

 "Nevertheless the Czech crown is very strong so I would be a bit wary about going long the Czech at these levels. We also have the election at the end of June," he said.
