title: Polish  central bank  caps bullish zloty at parity.
text:
WARSAW, Aug 11 (Reuter) - The zloty jumped to its highest level in a month on Monday and had to be capped by currency-buying intervention after the central bank signalled it may tighten Poland's monetary screws. 

 In a Saturday newspaper a senior NBP official said the bank may again tighten monetary policy because commercial banks were not sufficiently raising credit and deposit rates after last week's official interest rate increase. 

 Dealers said that foreign investors remained on the sidelines on Monday and that the zloty soared against the basket as domestic banks reduced foreign currency positions. 

 "There were no foreigners and domestic speculation and position adjustments gave the zloty a boost," said Wojciech Kowalczyk, senior dealer at Bank Handlowy SA. 

 Some said large foreign capital inflows into the Warsaw bourse, which rose 5.2 percent on Friday and 3.3 percent on Monday, may have also boosted the zloty. 

 The zloty briefly climbed above the parity rate, the first time the local unit crossed the mid-point of its trading band since its mid-July decline amid mounting worries over flood losses, a gaping external deficit and parliamentary elections. 

 It closed at minus 0.26/0.31 percent from the trading band centre, against Friday's close at minus 0.73/0.88 percent after the central bank bought at least $20 million when the zloty was hovering slightly above the parity rate. 

 The zloty was at 3.4685/00 to the dollar, against 3.4850/00 on Friday and at 1.8690/00 to the mark, against 1.8750/80. 

 Dealers said, however, that despite recent gains the zloty would probably remain locked in a range between parity and minus 1.5 percent ahead of parliamentary polls on September 21. 

 "The NBP may have stabilised the market by intervening because now the zloty resistance is at parity and the bank earlier gave the local unit support around minus 1.5 percent," said Witold Wozniak, forex dealer at Deutsche Bank Polska SA. 

 Dealers said the market's pro-zloty sentiment would likely run out of steam because longer-term foreign investors would likely stay clear of Polish treasuries ahead of elections and only speculators would dabble in the zloty in the coming month. 

 "This strengthening could be a short-term shot in the arm but the (up) trend could still be reversed ahead of elections," said Miroslaw Winiarczyk, forex dealer at BDK SA. 

 The NBP said in the Saturday paper its further monetary policy tightening would also depend on how the state-owned PKO BP - the country's biggest savings bank -- would react to the central bank's recent rate rise. 

 "We are still waiting for the reaction of (the state savings bank) PKO BP, but basically we already know that the hitherto (rate) increases in commercial banks are too small," NBP monetary policy head Jerzy Stopyra was quoted as saying. 

 "We may use other (monetary policy) instruments," he said. 

 On August 4 the NBP increased its lombard rate by two points to 27 percent and discount by 2.5 to 24.5 percent. 

 The management board of PKO BP is due to meet on Tuesday to decide the bank's new rate levels after PKO sigalled that it would increase rates last week.

 "It was not foreign investors, it seems, who were fleeing the zloty but domestic traders who went wild and began moving from zlotys to dollars. I watch it with calm...I think it will now reverse," he declared.

title: Zloty hits all-time lows without c.bank support.
text:
WARSAW, July 15 (Reuter) - The zloty suffered its largest ever one-day loss to hit a new record low on Tuesday as speculators trampled over the currency, left without a lifeline from the usually protective central bank. 

 Dealers held mixed views mixed about whether the zloty, already only 1.3 percent from the lowest point of its trading band, would ease further on Wednesday but said intervention by the National Bank of Poland could come even if it did not. 

 "The central bank is likely to start currency-selling tomorrow...because it knows that the inflationary consequences of such a sharp devaluation could be severe," said Leszek Szafranek, dealer at Bank Slaski SA. 

 The zloty was fixed at 5.69 percent below the parity rate, some five percent weaker than Monday's fix at -0.77 percent. 

 On the market it closed slightly stronger at -4.39/-4.74 percent from the trading band centre, signalling more currency buying at the fixing. 

 "If the central bank refrains from interventions on Wednesday the zloty could be in danger of reaching the seven percent (below parity trading parity) limit" said Piort Czyzewski, dealer at ING Bank in Warsaw. 

 The zloty closed at 3.5080/53 per dollar, down from 3.3790/30 on Monday and at 1.9560/660 per mark from 1.8790/25. 

 The independent NBP floats the zloty within a 14-percent trading band around the central parity rate, which is now devalued one percent per month against a currency basket. 

 Last May the NBP had sold currencies when the zloty was falling but on Tuesday deputy president Witold Kozinski told a news conference: "At this moment please do not ask me about the exchange rate or about increasing interest rates because right now I have no comment in this matter." 

 On Tuesday both foreign and domestic players sold zlotys in frenzied trade, as small sums moved the market by several figures, dealers said. They said much of the trade was done through zloty short-selling in swaps and other derivatives. 

 "Foreigners attacked the zloty today...and the market was so shallow that sums as small as $5 million often pushed the zloty down by several figures," one dealer said. 

 The zloty had lost steam for several months before this week's steep decline on worries that authorities would not cool booming domestic demand sufficiently to avoid a Czech-style current account crisis, analysts said. 

 These worries have recently been growing by talk of changing this year's state budget to accommodate larger outflows needed to help flood relief efforts in Southern Poland. 

 Kozinski said the NBP was ready to lend the government up to one billion zlotys for flood relief while collecting deposits to offset the monetary effect of such a loan, but the government wants to borrow 2.5 billion from the central bank. 

 The government, which last week said it would not alter this year's budget on account of devastating floods, has in recent days stepped up relief efforts with just three months to go before nationwide parlimamentary polls.

title: Poland Zloty Decline Prompts Talk Of Devaluation
text:
WARSAW (AP-Dow Jones)--The further rapid decline of the zloty on Tuesday - and the absence of central bank intervention - has prompted speculation that a one-off devaluation of the currency may be in the offing. 

 As the zloty lost about 1.7% of its value against the dollar Monday and a further 4.8% Tuesday, foreign exchange dealers awaited a move by the central bank in support of the currency. None came. 

 In a highly regulated market such as Poland's - where relatively small-scale intervention can have a huge impact - the absence of central bank intervention has come to be seen as a tacit acceptance of a weaker currency. 

 The Polish zloty trades in a 14-percentage point band around the central parity rate. On Tuesday, the zloty was nearing the limit of the weak side of the band against the dollar, sinking to 5.7% below the morning parity rate. 

 With the zloty nearing the edge of the band, analysts and traders said the central bank will be forced to intervene to buy zlotys as early as Wednesday morning - or adjust the parity rate in such a way as to allow the zloty to move down within the existing exchange-rate mechanism. 

 'There is no way of halting the trend,' said Andrzej Fiderkiewicz, a dealer at Societe Generale in Warsaw. 'The zloty is overvalued right now.' 

 In trading Tuesday, the central bank fixed the dollar at 3.5550 zlotys, up from 3.3830 zlotys and the Deutsche mark at 1.9780 zlotys, up from 1.8885 zlotys Monday.

 They said a light currency-selling trend remained on the market, which may later on Tuesday push the zloty into battle against National Bank of Poland (NBP) interventions, if the local unit wondered far above 1.5 percent from parity. 

 "The 1.5 percent level should be guarded by the NBP and the zloty should trade between 1.45 to 1.55 percent, with a slight tendency for zloty gains," said Marcin Trzykowski of Pekao SA. 

 At 0852 the zloty was at 1.52/1.40 percent from parity, against opening's 1.55/1.45 percent and stronger than Monday's close at 1.49/1.38 percent. 

 It was at 3.2210/20 to the dollar, against opening's 3.2210/40 and at 1.8645/50 to the mark, against 1.8635/55. 

 Dealers said the forex market waited for foreign investor orders to set the tone of the market on Tuesday. 

 "The market seems set to return to speculating on dollar/mark moves unless some larger foreign orders materialise," Pekao's Trzykowski said. 

 On the money market overnight rates eased to 22.25 percent at bid from opening's 22.30/22.45 as the market continued to remain liquid despite larger outflows stemming from higher obligatory reserve, which were increased at the start of May. 

 "Banks created reserves for the larger outflows and short-term rates are not likely to be affected unless the central bank heavily drains the market," said Marek Wieczorkiewicz, chief dealer at PKO BP. 

 Tomorrow/next rates were at 22.25/22.45 percent, slighly lower at offer from 22.25/22.55. 

 From the start of May, obligatory reserves on zloty call deposits increased by two points to 11 percent and by one point to five percent for foreign currency deposits. 

 The actual cash outflow from the increased reserves has occured from the start of June, as banks pay obligatory reserves according to the previous month's levels.

title: Poland  Zloty Surge Vs Dollar Halted By  Intervention
text:
WARSAW (AP-Dow Jones)--The central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market on Friday to dampen a sudden surge of the zloty against the dollar. 

 Dealers said the National Bank of Poland bought zlotys for dollars twice, first at the level of 3.1950 zlotys and then at 3.2000 zlotys. The scale of the intervention was described as small. 

 Around 0905 GMT, the dollar was at 3.1983 zlotys, up from 3.1910 zlotys at the opening and from Wednesday's fixing of 3.1980 zlotys. Markets were closed on Thursday. 

 The Deutsche mark was at 1.8820 zlotys, down from Wednesday's fixing of 1.8830 zlotys. 

 The central bank bought zlotys when the Polish currency rose to about 1.5% above the parity rate against the currency basket, dealers said. 

 'The central bank has given a signal' as to the desired level of the zloty, said Tomasz Wlad of Amerbank. Following the intervention, 'The market is very conservative,' he said. 'Banks are inactive.' 

 The zloty's surge started late on Wednesday, when the currency started to recover from several days of sharp declines triggered by the currency crisis in the Czech Republic. Dealers now say that the 'Czech effect' has dissipated. 

 The Polish currency's gains were sparked by foreign investors placing orders for shares in the initial public offering of Amica Wronki SA, a maker of household appliances, sources said. 

 The National Bank of Poland set the parity rate for the dollar at 3.2477 zlotys and for the mark at 1.9064 zlotys. 

 The dollar was trading at 1.52% below its parity rate, and the mark was at 1.28% below its parity rate.

title: FOREIGNERS SEEN FLOCKING BACK TO ZLOTY NEXT WEEK.
text:
WARSAW, May 30 (Reuter) - Foreign investors are expected to flock back to high yielding zloty-denominated papers next week after a brief but heavy-handed withdrawal over the past days pushed the zloty down to its lowest levels ever, analysts said. 

 Foreign investors, either covering losses caused by the Czech crown's sharp fall or cutting Central European currency exposure in general, pulled out some $400 million from Poland over the last week, sinking the zloty more than two percent. 

 But on Thursday and Friday the zloty regained initiative and charged upward, backed by bullish statements from Poland's Finance Minister and renewed foreign interest in Polish papers. 

 "After several weeks of minimal interest, foreign investors are likely to again show up in force at Monday's T-bill tender ...(and) put the zloty under upward pressure next week," said Wlodzimierz Kado, dealer at Bank Handlowy SA. 

 Analysts said, however, that the zloty's upward push would probably meet National Bank of Poland interventions against it, after the central bank bought currencies on Friday when the zloty strengthened above 1.5 percent from parity. 

 "Today's intervention showed the NBP believes 1.5 percent would be a good resistance, but it may well have to repeat its currency-buying in order to enforce this level," said Mateusz Bieniek, foreign exchange dealer at Societe Generale in Warsaw. 

 Some other dealers said the central bank's intervention at 1.5 percent from parity may have been made simply to cool the zloty, which soared more than one percent against the basket in several hours of trading, not to establish new resistance. 

 On Friday, the NBP bought some $20 million between 1.62 and 1.47 percent from the parity rate, capping the zloty's gains. 

 The zloty closed the week at 1.53/1.47 percent from the parity rate, up from last Friday's close at 0.64/0.50 percent. 

 It briefly sank on Tuesday to an all-time low against the basket, level with parity, as the Czech crown tumbled some seven to eight percent amid foreign investor withdrawal. 

 Analysts said that more upbeat Polish fundamentals, such as steady economic growth created by largely restructured industry, and tighter regulations over capital markets, kept the zloty from plunging in line with its Czech neighbour. 

 At Monday's 1.6 billion zloty primary T-bill auction yields are likely to hold unchanged or edge upward, dealers said. 

 "Yields should remain on the same level, or nudge upward on the longest bills, as the treasury increased its offer," said Marta Kepa, dealer at Pekao SA. 

 The maximum yield of the benchmark 52-week T-bill was expected to be around 21.48 percent, against a 21.40 percent average yield at Monday's tender. 

 Yields of 26-week, 13-week and eight-week papers were expected to hold steady around 21.34, 20.87 and 20.77 percent. 

 Dealers said that even though the recent foreign sales had absorbed some demand from domestic corporates, Polish banks were still likely to bid for large amounts of bills on Monday, as a new monthly reserve period pulled down one-day rates. 

 "Costs of financing will probably drop next week as a new monthly reserve period begins, so banks may try to buy bills for their trading portfolios," said Robert Gluch, dealer at ING Bank in Warsaw.

title: Polish zloty rebounds as minister lifts confidence.
text:
WARSAW, May 28 (Reuter) - The Polish zloty started to rebound on Wednesday after falling more than two percent over the last four trading days in sympathy with the plunging Czech crown, dealers said. 

 The currency got a boost from Wednesday comments by Finance Minister Marek Belka said the main wave of foreign investor withdrawal from zloty instruments has ended. 

 "Belka signalled that there was no fundamental reason for keeping the zloty weak and a ( hard currency) selling spree ensued," said Piotr Czyzewski, forex dealer at ING bank in Warsaw. 

 "More gains could be in store for the zloty," he added. 

 At 1200 GMT the zloty rebounded to 1.19/1.04 percent stronger than the parity rate, up from 0.47/0.32 percent at opening and Tuesday's intraday lows dipping to parity. 

 It was at 3.2040/00 to the dollar and at 1.8875/95 to the mark, against opening's 3.2285/50 and 1.8990/20. 

 Last Thursday and Friday the zloty dropped two percent against the basket of currencies as foreign investors sold the Polish unit to cut their central European exposure after the sharp fall of the Czech crown. 

 Belka estimated that a total of $1.2 billion of short-term speculative capital was in Poland, which he said was not enough to significantly weaken the zloty even if all of it pulled out. 

 "I estimate that even if all the short-term, speculative capital left Poland, it would only have a minor effect on the zloty exchange rate," Belka told a news conference. 

 But he said he did not know how much foreign short-term capital flowed out of Poland during the pullout but quoted press reports which said the sales totalled some $400 million. 

 He also said the National Bank of Poland's small currency selling intervention last week to stop the zloty's fall proved very effective and made him confident the central bank was in control of the situation. 

 Last Friday the NBP bought an estimated $15 million which stopped the zloty in its tracks at just above the parity rate. 

 Analysts said that Poland's economy, which was in a much better shape than the Czech Republic's, was an unlikely environment for a zloty plunge similar to that of the crown.

title: Polish zloty,  central bank  to lock horns next week.
text:
WARSAW, April 25 (Reuter) - The zloty is poised to fight a lost battle against the central bank on Monday as foreign entry into T-bills and banks' currency position cutting are likely to again pit it against currency-buying interventions. 

 Dealers said foreign investors, eager to lock into high Polish T-bill yields amid falling inflation, would boost demand at Monday's 1.3 billion zloty tender and depress yields. 

 But dealers were mixed on the size of foreign entry. 

 "I would expect foreign demand to be at similar levels as last Monday, when it amounted to 1.7 billion zlotys, and just as last week, they might buy most of what is on offer," said Bartlomiej Kumela of Societe Generale in Warsaw. 

 But others said that although foreigners were likely to come to the Monday tender, their interest was now more likely to turn to the 800 million zloty fixed bond auction on May 7. 

 "I would expect foreign bids at $100-150 million on Monday as the coming fixed bond tender will offer yet more attractive instruments," said Wojciech Kowalczyk of Bank Handlowy SA. 

 Dealers expected the 52-week yield on Monday to ease to 21.50-60 percent from 21.68 percent at the last tender. 

 They saw the 26-week and 13-week yield down to 21.50 percent from 21.69 and 21.74 percent respectively with the 8-week paper down to 21.30 percent from 21.46 percent. 

 Dealers said foreign bids at the T-bill tender would propel the zloty upward, above levels at which the central bank is certain step in with currency purchases. 

 The National Bank of Poland (NBP) said on Wednesday it wanted the zloty no higher than at 2.5 percent from the daily trading band centre after it pounded it for five days in a row with interventions whenever it peeked above that level. 

 Dealers said that although only part of the foreign bids would come from new forex operations as many investors were long on zlotys from deals done earlier this week and last week, the upward pressure on Polish unit would be strong. 

 "On Monday there will be the T-bill tender with foreign entry, but also banks will be cutting their own currency positions to keep higher yielding zlotys over the long weekend," said Karol Zaluski of ING Bank in Warsaw. 

 Next Thursday and Friday are market holidays in Poland. 

 "These two factors combined are likely to trigger an intervention to stop the zloty's rise," Zaluski said. 

 On Friday the zloty around 2.47 percent from the parity rate, nearly flat from last week's close at 2.5 percent. 

 Dealers also expected large liquidity swings on the money market on Monday and Tuesday -- the last two days of the April required reserve period. 

 Spreads on one-day rates widened to 5.0/21.0 percent on Friday amid excess liquidity, not alleviated by the central bank's 343 million zloty reverse repo and a 750 million zloty NBP-bill sale.

title: Polish NBP weakens zloty to aid exports - c.banker.
text:
WARSAW, April 23 (Reuter) - The National Bank of Poland's deputy president said that the bank's interventions that weakened the zloty by about 0.7 percent since last Thursday aimed to help exporters and keep a cap on the trade deficit. 

 The central bank has bought nearly $500 million of the domestic forex market through interventions since Thursday and knocked down the zloty to 2.5 percent from the parity rate from around three percent. 

 "(These interventions) should support exports and act as a coolant for imports," Witold Kozinski told bankers at an annual banking association meeting. 

 "The central bank's exchange rate as well as interest rate policy is aimed at stabilising the trade deficit," he added. 

 Over the first two months of this year the current account deficit amounted to $1.1 billion, against a $1.4 billion shortfall for all of 1996. 

 Kozinski said there were dangers in interventions, including large inflows of money supply-boosting foreign capital into Polish debt. But he said that such a small move in the zloty exchange rate would not push up consumer prices. 

 "This type of policy has its dangers...but we don't think that this move, which pushed the zloty down about 0.7 percentage points, will cause prices to move," Kozinski said. 

 The central bank has recently increased open market operations to sterilise much of the foreign investor inflows into Polish treasuries set off by the zloty's fall last week. 

 The NBP has been keeping real interest rates rising and market rates high since late 1996, to cool quickly growing domestic demand along with thirst for imported consumer goods.

 Delears estimated foreign bids at the 1.3 billion zloty auction at $350 million, a part of which found its way onto the interbank forex market, propelling the zloty past NBP-accepted levels of around 2.5 pecent from the trading band centre. 

 "The zloty charged on foreign bids at the primary tender, but once the NBP bought all that foreigners wanted to sell, the market calmed down," said Tomasz Nowakowski of Bank Handlowy.

title: Polish NBP weakens zloty to help exports - analysts.
text:
WARSAW, April 18 (Reuter) - The National Bank of Poland (NBP) this week has intervened to weaken the zloty while allowing real interest rates to rise to stimulate faster export growth while keeping a lid on imports, analysts said on Friday. 

 In a series of currency-buying interventions on Thursday and Friday the central bank bought some $290 million and pounded the bullish zloty down to 2.5 percent from the trading band centre from above 3.2 percent. 

 It also kept its 273-day paper's average yield flat at 22.00 percent and its benchmark 14-day reverse repo rate at 22.15 percent on Friday despite a drop in inflation to 16.6 percent in March year-on-year from 17.3 percent in February. 

 The NBP, the finance ministry and independent economists agree Poland has every chance to bring inflation down to the targeted 13-percent year-on-year in December. 

 "The NBP is looking at Poland's trade balance, which is deteriorating, and is intervening to weaken the zloty to stimulate exports growth," said Andrzej Ladko, chief dealer at Bank Handlowy SA. 

 "It also keeps high real interest rates to keep domestic demand down and thus cap imports growth," he said. 

 The bank has frequently expressed concern over the widening current account gap and said it would keep real interest rates rising to cool down domestic demand seen in the fast growth of credit for the economy. 

 Poland's current account deficit in February rose to $1.13 billion from $899 million in January against $1.35 billion in the whole of 1996. 

 The trade gap jumped to $2.18 billion in the first two months of this year from $706 million in January and $8.15 in the whole of 1996 as imports keep rising at about 30 percent in year-on-year terms and exports at about nine percent. 

 Analysts said that to offset the monetary effect of the interventions, the central bank offered on Friday a huge 1.2 billion zloty reverse repo and a 300 million zloty sale of its 273-day bills -- the longest the bank has been selling. 

 "It is a safe moment because inflation is falling, but nevertheless the NBP sterilised the purchases with open market operations on Friday," said Zbigniew Chmielewski chief dealer at ING Bank in Wrasaw. 

 Analysts said for the weaker zloty to have an effect on Poland's foreign trade, the central bank is likely to keep the zloty anchored around the 2.5 percent from parity level for some time. 

 "If they did it to stimulate exports, they will have to keep that level for a while," said Marek Zelinski, analyst at Bank Slaski SA.

title: POLISH  FOREX  MARKET MIXED ON C.BANK  INTERVENTION .
text:
WARSAW, April 8 (Reuter) - Polish forex market dealers are mixed on the prospects of a National Bank of Poland (NBP) currency buying intervention this week, as such a move would spark more foreign interest in Polish treasuries. 

 But dealers said the NBP has often intervened when the local unit was more than three percent from the parity rate. On Tuesday the zloty finished around 3.15 percent from parity. 

 "It is not clear whether the central bank will intervene as such a move would make Polish T-bills even more attractive for foreigners. The odds are now 50-50," said Witold Wozniak, forex dealer at Deutsche Bank Polska SA. 

 The central bank has often said that it planned to keep the zloty, traded within a 14 percent daily band around a central parity rate, volatile in the short-term to discourage speculative foreign capital flows. 

 Other dealers said the central bank would intervene on Wednesday if the zloty tried to strengthen further amid foreign entry into Polish treasuries and investment inflows. 

 "If the zloty gains more ground tomorrow we may very well see an intervention," said Karol Zaluski of ING Bank in Warsaw. 

 Dealers said the zloty would be under additional upward pressure on Wednesday as banks shorten currency exposure to hold higher-yielding zloty positions over the week-end. 

 The zloty closed at 3.17/3.13 percent from the trading band centre, stronger than Monday's close at 3.07/3.03 percent. 

 It closed at 3.1070/80 to the dollar, down from 3.0968/78 on Monday and at 1.8120/30 to the mark, up from 1.8191/01. 

 Dealers said that on Tuesday the zloty remained locked under strong resistance at 3.1 percent from parity until about 1200 GMT, when players decided that the central bank would not intervene with currency purchases for the rest of the day. 

 The zloty's charge on Tuesday was caused by foreign investor entry at Monday's T-bill auction, at which they bought an estimated $100 million as well as their entry into short-term bills in secondary trade on Tuesday. 

 "Foreigners were interested in buying two-month paper on Tuesday, but it's like walking on pins and needles because the forex market is wary of central bank action," said Wojciech Kowalczyk, senior dealer at Bank Handlowy SA. 

 Dealers said foreigners would again bid for large amounts of Polish T-bills on Thursday, when the Treasury will hold an additional 500 million zloty tender of 52-week T-bills. 

 Some players said the months-long rise in Polish T-bill yields had likely ended and that the Treasury opted to hold the extra auction to show that yields had stopped their climb.

 Dealers also said that recent price cuts in Polish treasuries would be continued at next Monday's primary T-bill auction, but they still expected demand to fall well short of the finance ministry's one billion zloty offer.

text:

title: Polish NBP ups reserves, knocks zloty to save C/A.
text:
WARSAW, Jan 28 (Reuter) - The Polish central bank's decision to raise obligatory reserves on deposits and its recent interventions against the zloty are aimed to stabilise Poland's deteriorating current account, the bank's deputy head said on Tuesday. 

 "The unjustified rise of the zloty and problems with money supply growth for 1997, provided grounds for exchange rate and obligatory reserve moves aimed at (stabilising) the current account," Witold Kozinski told a news conference. 

 "Polish current account has long been deteriorating and shouldn't deteriorate any more. It is time to do something to stabilise it," he said. 

 On Monday, the central bank said it would raise obligatory reserves on zloty call deposits by three points to 20 percent and on currency deposits by two points to four percent, effective February 28. 

 Kozinski said the bank had to raise the reserves to keep its 1997 money supply growth target of 28 billion zlotys within reach after the finance ministry unexpectedly borrowed 2.2 billion zlotys from the NBP at the end of last year. 

 He also said the higher reserves would likely cause a rise in commercial banks' credit rates and cool down domestic demand, diminishing imports and improving the current account. 

 Poland's current account fell into a deficit of $984 million through November 1996 from a $4,959-billion surplus in the same period 1995. This year, it is seen rising to about $5.8 billion from an estimated $1.2 billion in 1996. 

 "Internal demand can be cooled in several ways, also by diminishing the liquidity of the banking system...through raising obligatory reserves," he said. 

 The central bank also knocked down the bullish zloty with a series of dollar- and mark-buying interventions last week, bringing it down to about 2.5 percent from the trading band centre from highs of four percent. 

 "Knocking the zloty down towards the central parity rate softens the zloty, works against imports and stimulates exports," Kozinski said. 

 He said the NBP would now wait for the market's reaction to the higher obligatory reserve requirements before deciding whether a rise in official interest rates was still needed to additionally cut credit action. 

 "If one raises mandatory reserves then certainly, there should not be an increase in interest rates shortly after because it may happen...that a reserve rise itself will trigger higher credit rates," Kozinski said. 

 The central bank has long signalled it was concerned with fast credit expansion and that it was considering raising the lombard and discount rates, now at 25 and 22 percent, respectively, or other measures, to control money supply.

text:
WARSAW, Jan 21 (Reuter) - The Polish zloty, quietly firming against the basket of currencies over the last few weeks, was stopped in its tracks by central bank interventions on Monday, but analysts say it would not give up its upward thrust easily. 

 The National Bank of Poland has long tolerated the firming of the zloty without any reaction, but finally decided to cap it on Monday at four percent from the trading band centre. 

 Analysts estimated the National Bank of Poland's dollar- and mark-buying interventions on Monday drained some $80 million from the market pushing the Polish unit one percentage point lower to three percent from the band centre. 

 Analysts said the zloty's recent bull run was fuelled by start-of-year position taking in zloty instruments by foreign investors drawn by Poland's better then expected 1996 inflation and its plans to meet European Monetary Union criteria in 2004. 

 "People have got new amounts of money to invest in emerging markets and...they can't keep it in dollars, so at the beginning of the year you often get a rally," said Andrew Kenningham, economist at Merrill Lynch in London. 

 "I think the zloty is likely to stay bullish," he said. 

 Analysts also noted high real interest rates and the central bank's commitment to keeping them high to curb credit growth as well as the NBP's plans to reduce the zloty's monthly devaluation factor this year. 

 Dealers said the fundamental nature of the zloty's recent gains was likely to keep the Polish unit bullish in the near-term despite the threat of an NBP intervention. 

 "(Polish paper) is attractive because real interest rates are still high, the c.bank seems committed to keep them high, and because the crawling peg will be cut further in 1997," said Krassimir Katev, dealer at Paribas Capital Markets in London. 

 The zloty is now devalued one percent a month against a basket of currencies, in a mechanism known as the crawling peg, but the NBP has announced it planned zloty devaluation in 1997 at nine percent, which would entail a cut from current levels. 

 Analysts also noted the large scale of expected foreign direct and portfolio investment, which some put as high as $5 billion this year, as a factor which could largely offset the widening trade gap, seen around $8 billion in 1996. 

 Dealers said that with yields above 20 percent and inflation this year expected at 15-16 percent Polish 12 month or two-year fixed interest paper was very attractive. 

 "All this seems like a good reason to invest, since you get something like 8.5-9.5 percent rate of return in dollar terms," said a dealer at a London-based bank. 

 Dealers expected the central bank's Monday interventions would not deter foreign buyers as many saw the zloty's fall to three percent from the trading band centre from four percent this morning as an opportunity to buy it before it firms again. 

 "T-bill yields could still rise and attract foreign investors. And the zloty is likely to be under upward pressure as those who missed out when it was at four percent the first time want to be there the next time around," a dealer at a major investment bank in London said.

text:

title: Polish zloty seen staying bullish on fundamentals.
text:
WARSAW, Jan 20 (Reuter) - The Polish zloty, quietly firming against the basket of currencies over the last few weeks, was stopped in its tracks by central bank interventions on Monday, but analysts say it would not give up its upward thrust easily. 

 The National Bank of Poland has long tolerated the firming of the zloty without any reaction, but finally decided to cap it on Monday at four percent from the trading band centre. @ 

 Analysts estimated the National Bank of Poland's dollar- and mark-buying interventions today drained some $80 million from the market pushing the Polish unit one percentage point lower to three percent from the band centre. 

 Analysts said the zloty's recent bull run was fuelled by start-of-year position taking in zloty instruments by foreign investors drawn by Poland's better then expected 1996 inflation and its plans to meet European Monetary Union criteria in 2004. @ 

 "People have got new amounts of money to invest in emerging markets and...they can't keep it in dollars, so at the beginning of the year you often get a rally," said Andrew Kenningham, economist at Merrill Lynch in London. 

 "I think the zloty is likely to stay bullish," he said. 

 Analysts also noted high real interest rates and the central bank's commitment to keeping them high to curb credit growth as well as the NBP's plans to reduce the zloty's monthly devaluation factor this year. 

 Dealers said the fundamental nature of the zloty's recent gains was likely to keep the Polish unit bullish in the near-term despite the threat of an NBP intervention. 

 "(Polish paper) is attractive because real interest rates are still high, the c.bank seems committed to keep them high, and because the crawling peg will be cut further in 1997," said Krassi Katov, dealer at Paribas Capital Markets in London. 

 The zloty is now devalued one percent a month against a basket of currencies, in a mechanism known as the crawling peg, but the NBP has announced it planned zloty devaluation in 1997 at nine percent, which would entail a cut from current levels. 

 Analysts also noted the large scale of expected foreign direct and portfolio investment, which some put as high as $5 billion this year, as a factor which could largely offset the widening trade gap, seen around $8 billion in 1996. 

 Dealers said that with yields above 20 percent and inflation this year expected at 15-16 percent Polish 12 month or two-year fixed interest paper was very attractive. 

 "All this seems like a good reason to invest, since you get something like 8.5-9.5 percent rate of return in dollar terms," said a dealer at a London-based bank. 

 Dealers expected the central bank's Monday interventions would not deter foreign buyers as many saw the zloty's fall to three percent from the trading band centre from four percent this morning as an opportunity to buy it before it firms again. 

 "T-bill yields could still rise and attract foreign investors. And the zloty is likely to be under upward pressure as those who missed out when it was at four percent the first time want to be there the next time around," a dealer at a major investment bank in London said. 

 The Monday NBP interventions were the first since May 1996, when they usually came to stop the Polish unit at about 2.5-3.0 percent from the parity rate.

title: Polish c.banker- intervention  can work if done right.
text:
WARSAW, Feb 5 (Reuters) - Central bank intervention on currency markets can succeed under certain conditions and if the right techniques are used, a member of the Polish central bank's rate-setting council said in a newspaper article on Saturday.   

Poland's central bank has not intervened since the zloty was floated in 2000 and has rarely commented on currency market movements.   

But the government has grown increasingly wary of the impact of the zloty's 20 percent rise against the euro since Poland joined the European Union last May.   

"If a central bank manages to use unexpected intervention to shift the rate beyond the line of resistance the market believes in at a given moment, it can cause a rift in the thinking of technical analysts," Andrzej Slawinski wrote in a heavyweight daily Rzeczpospolita.   

He said intervention can work if the market sees it as a signal of a change in monetary policy and if the central bank keeps the details of its actions secret.   

"The rift will widen on its own if the rate moves beyond the stop-loss rate at which banks automatically sell," he added.   

Slawinski, an economics professor, said the forces that drove the zloty last year had not disappeared, without elaborating further on current market conditions.   

So far financial markets have been sceptical about a possibility of currency market interventions.   

But there are growing expectations that the strong zloty's dampening impact on inflation and growth will spur an interest rate cut later this year.

title: UPDATE 3-Polish c.bank chief cautions on zloty appreciation.
text:
WARSAW, Feb 4 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank chief warned financial markets on Friday against betting on a continued climb in the zloty, saying unfinished budget reforms could bring increased volatility.   

A new wave of largely foreign buying this week pushed up the zloty and other central European currencies, reviving a debate on when its gains will hurt exports, the main driver of Poland's rapid economic recovery since 2002.   

The zloty firmed to under four per euro for the first time in over two years on Thursday, prompting the rare reaction from central bank governor Leszek Balcerowicz. "It would be risky to assume the zloty's appreciation will be a lasting trend," Balcerowicz said in a statement.   

"We know from experience that no trend lasts forever. The zloty rate has shown large volatility in the past, while structural problems of public finances, which were an important source of this volatility, did not vanish," he said.   

His comments had no impact on the zloty, but many local bond investors now believe further zloty gains could force the bank to cut interest rates faster than expected, even as early as March or April.   

Bond yields fell 20 basis points on Friday as investors brought forward bets on when the first cut would come. Previously most analysts backed a mid-year cut after an expected shift to a neutral policy bias from tightening this month.   

Last month the bank left its benchmark rate at 6.50 percent, where it has been since August 2004 after rising 125 basis points in the previous three months.   

"One option is Balcerowicz is making an excuse for not cutting rates - that he thinks the zloty will fall later this year and stop threatening to cause inflation to undershoot," said Robert Beange, economist with Lehman Brothers in London.   

"The other is he's trying to stem new capital inflows which would strengthen the zloty, make inflation undershoot and potentially lead to greater volatility later."   

INTERVENTION UNLIKELY   

Poland's central bank has so far kept a hands-off approach to the free-floating zloty, unlike the central bank in fellow EU newcomer Slovakia, which has used market interventions, interest rate cuts and verbal interventions to curb its currency's rise.   

But over recent months the government has grown increasingly wary of the impact of the zloty's 20 percent rise against the euro since Poland's European Union entry in May.   

Economy Minister Jerzy Hausner on Thursday called on the bank to change its monetary policy line to prevent further gains which he said could hurt exporters' profitability and hence growth.   

Yet a central bank survey on Friday showed many exporters can swallow a zloty rate of less than 4 to the euro. It also showed half are ready to use the purchasing power from the strong zloty to buy imports and spark a long-awaited investment boom this year.   

Clear prospects of lower interest rates could help ease the buying pressure on the zloty by making returns on zloty-denominated assets less attractive to foreign investors.   

Balcerowicz is due to meet government ministers on Monday to discuss Poland's plans for euro adoption, but officials have insisted the meeting is not meant to produce any immediate action to counter the currency's strength.

title: Emerging  FX -C.Europe rangebound, eyes euro/dlr moves.
text:
LONDON, Jan 21 (Reuters) - Central European currencies hugged narrow ranges on Friday, struggling to find upward momentum even though the euro managed to haul itself off two-month lows against the dollar.  

A cautious tone prevailed across currency markets, with the dollar still within a cent of two-month highs against the euro , despite its softer tone.  

The U.S. rate outlook is seen key to near-term moves. Federal Reserve officials continued to hint on Thursday U.S. interest rates would rise only steadily, though the prospect of higher U.S. yields has buoyed the dollar so far this year.  

The region's currencies have been tracking euro/dollar moves closely in recent weeks, but after last year's strong gains analysts said further upside might be hard won.  

"Irrespective of euro/dollar, ultimately these currencies seem less attractive than they were a few months ago so we might actually see some weakness, but it also depends whether we get calls for intervention," said Dwyfor Evans, emerging markets analyst at Bank of America.  

"Euro/dollar still holds the key but it's not looking particularly promising for the high-yield regional currencies, given the rate and potential intervention backdrop," he said.  

This year has seen officials in Poland and Hungary express growing concern that currency strength is hurting the domestic economy, while the Slovak central bank has already stepped in to curb crown strength.  

Evans also said signs of downward inflation pressure in the region could also work as a currency negative, adding to the case for lower interest rates.  

ZLOTY, FORINT RANGEBOUND  

The Polish zloty traded sideways after data on Thursday showed industrial output and producer prices grew more slowly than expected in December, fuelling expectations that the central bank may change its interest rate policy bias soon.  

Industrial output grew at an annual pace of 6.4 percent, well below a consensus forecast of 13 percent, while producer price inflation slowed to 5.6 percent, from 6.7 percent the previous month.  

In a Reuters interview earlier this week, monetary policy council member Halina Wasilewska-Trenkner said falling inflation may allow the central bank to change its policy bias to "neutral" from "restrictive" after the first quarter.  

"The numbers were pretty weak and this increases the speculation that there will be a move to a neutral bias from restrictive bias at the monetary policy council meeting next week," said Lars Christensen, analyst at Danske Bank.  

Christensen said an early dip in the zloty had been on speculation of a more dovish stance from the MPC, though it later recovered the lost ground.   


At 1114 GMT, the zloty traded at 4.0856 against the euro  from late
4.0905 late on Thursday and at 3.1452 to the dollar        from
3.1663.
  

The Hungarian forint also traded calmly, with ongoing investor concerns over the fiscal outlook still being offset by the country's attractive yields.  

Opposition leader Viktor Orban said on Thursday Hungary would have to follow neighbouring countries like Slovakia and Romania in adopting flat taxes, if it wants to attract foreign investment inflows.  

Orban, whose centre-right Fidesz party is just ahead in the polls ahead of a 2006 general election, also said a change of government was vital if the country were to join the euro zone by 2010.  

"Any move towards discussing tax reform in Hungary is a positive because that would be investor-friendly and in the longer-run a positive for the forint as long as the markets believe that it could be done without harming public finances," Christensen said.  

The forint traded flat at 246.71 against the euro .

title: INTERVIEW-Stronger zloty could hit growth-c.bank's Slawinski.
text:
WARSAW, Dec 20 (Reuters) - A strengthening zloty has further improved Poland's inflation outlook, but more fast gains could hurt growth and pose a serious challenge to monetary policy, a member of the central bank's policy council said on Monday.  

Last week the 10-member rate-setting body held its key rate unchanged at 6.50 percent for the fourth month running, citing the strong zloty's dampening impact on inflation. "The balance of inflation risks is improving, mainly because of zloty appreciation. It is hard to see any serious threats on the demand side," Andrzej Slawinski told Reuters in an interview.  

"But the appreciation, if it continues at the same pace, can become a potential threat to growth," he said. "This would be a serious problem for monetary policy, which aims to stabilise inflation in the medium term and minimise short term swings in economic growth."  

The zloty climbed 14 percent against the euro this year, sparking a debate among policymakers as to what, if anything, could be done to prevent a further climb from hurting growth and disrupting Poland's preparations for the euro.  

Slawinski declined to say how the central bank, which for years has maintained a hands-off policy to the free-floating zloty, should act if the currency's climb continued.  

ZLOTY PEG  

Slawinski said it was crucial to avoid pegging the zloty to the euro in the ERM-2 currency grid at an excessively strong rate and that interventions could become more likely in the run-up to the mechanism.  

"It is very important to enter ERM-2 with an exchange rate which is not overvalued," Slawinski said, adding the desired equilibrium exchange rate was set to keep on changing to reflect structural changes in the Polish economy.  

"The approach of Poland's entry to ERM-2 may make central bank interventions in the currency market more likely, even though they don't need to be frequent," he said. He added sound budget policy was the best way to prevent market speculation.  

The finance ministry has said Poland could already join in early 2006 and adopt the euro in 2009, but financial markets are less optimistic and Slawinski said the timing would hinge on progress in cutting future budget deficits.  

Slawinski, considered an expert on currency markets, said fellow EU newcomer Slovakia chose to counter excessive market moves with interventions and interest rate cuts, while accepting fundamental strengthening of its crown.  

"In today's globalised currency markets it is very difficult for central banks to counter exchange rate trends. They can only try to slow the trend ... seeking out moments when interventions can be effective and not too expensive," he said.  

Many economists believe zloty interventions would be doomed to fail and advocate easing of monetary policy instead to make zloty assets less attractive to foreign investors.  

Two fellow council members have said the bank could consider a shift to a neutral bias after the first quarter of 2005 if the zloty stayed strong and wages moderate, but Slawinski declined to discuss the timing of such a move.

title: INTERVIEW-Strong zloty behind Polish debt improvement-Fitch.
text:
By Karolina Slowikowska
    WARSAW, Dec 10 (Reuters) - Poland's improving debt and
deficit figures are due mainly to the zloty's gains and not the
underlying fiscal picture which is key for the country's credit
rating, Fitch Ratings said on Friday.
    Fitch's main Poland analyst Ed Parker added the zloty is not
overvalued at current rates and should not harm the EU
newcomer's economic growth, which he sees at a healthy level of
about 5 percent next year.
    Despite progress on fiscal reforms this year, and a fall in
the public debt burden to below 51 percent of GDP, Parker said
he maintained his view that Poland's euro adoption might be
delayed beyond 2010 without further reform of public finances.
    "There has been little change in recent months and the
improvement of the budget position has been mainly helped by the
strong zloty," Parker told Reuters in an interview.
  


 
    "We have a stable outlook that provides a signal that the
degree of fiscal consolidation is key for the rating."
    All three main ratings agencies have punished Poland for
dragging its feet on reforms of its bloated public sector with
ratings or outlook downgrades over the past 18 months.
    In May Fitch cut Poland's local currency rating to "A" from
"A-plus" and shifted its foreign currency outlook to stable from
positive.
    Since then the government has pushed through more of Economy
  

Minister Jerzy Hausner's reforms and a 2005 budget which lowers  

its general government deficit to 3.9 percent of GDP, still well  

above the euro zone's 3 percent entry requirement.  

Parker said the fall in the 2005 deficit to 35 billion  

zlotys ($11.1 billion) is a step in the right direction, but  

that much more is needed to make good on the current target of  

euro entry in 2009.   


 
    "I don't see enough progress here to join the euro zone this
decade. There are many barriers to overcome," he said.
 
    ZLOTY, GROWTH HEALTHY
    Parker said the zloty was not "overstrong" after it gained
  

15 percent this year and the current levels should not hurt  

Poland's largely export-driven economic recovery, despite a  

slowdown in the third quarter.  

Statistical office data on Thursday showed growth slowed to  

4.8 percent from 6.1 percent in the previous quarter as an  

inflation spike dented consumer spending and a long-awaited  

investment recovery proved slow in coming.  

"Poland's economy will grow at around 5 percent next year,  

which is a healthy and sustainable level. It's not a slowdown  

really, just a cyclical change. Investment should pick-up,"  

Parker said.  

Parker also said it is much too early to start a debate  

about the zloty's entry rate for the pre-euro exchange rate  

mechanism (ERM-2) and that he saw no possibility of currency

intervention.  

Comments by central bank and government officials last week  

suggested they could discuss moves to weaken the zloty, although  

ministers have since hurried to reassure markets no immediate  

intervention is in prospect.  

"The central bank's governor Leszek Balcerowicz is firmly  

against interventions and he is a powerful player. I see no  

interventions for now," said Parker.  

"Poland has a floating rate and so the zloty can take care  

of itself," he added.

title: UPDATE 1-Polish zloty to gain below 4.0 vs euro-Orlowski.
text:
WARSAW, Dec 9 (Reuters) - The zloty could strengthen past 4.0 to the euro within half a year, the President's chief economic aide said on Thursday, adding that forex interventions against the Polish unit would make no sense now.   

The zloty has enjoyed a steady climb against a globally strong euro in the past nine months but a 20-month high against the single currency hit last week revived talk of intervention. "The zloty will be strong ... it will break the psychological level of 4.0 versus the euro and some 3.0 zlotys to the dollar within half a year," Witold Orlowski told private radio PIN."But I can also imagine a scenario of the zloty's stabilisation at the level of 4.1-4.2 versus the euro."   

The currency has risen 14 percent against the euro and 26 percent against a falling dollar since Poland's entry to the European Union in May. Thursday mid-morning, it was trading at 4.17 against the single currency and 3.13 versus the dollar.   

Last week both the central bank deputy governor Krzysztof Rybinski and Prime Minister Marek Belka sounded concern over what Belka called the zloty's "worrying, very fast appreciation" which could hurt Poland's export-driven economy.   

Rybinski reminded the market that intervention is one tool which the bank can use to curb the currency. But Orlowski added his voice to signals made by the bank's governor Leszek Balcerowicz that there was no need for intervention now. "Foreign exchange interventions make sense when the market has an idea of what will happen to the currency and when it is not based on solid fundamentals. Then it is enough to spook the market a little," Orlowski said.   

"Now ... the market strongly believes that the zloty is strong and will remain strong and has reasons for this. In such a situation one should ask whether intervention is not like trying to hold back the waves."

title: Polish MinFin sees no need for  fx intervention .
text:
WARSAW, Dec 2 (Reuters) - Poland's Finance Ministry sees no need to intervene on foreign exchange markets in the wake of recent zlotys strengthening, a finance minister's adviser said on Thursday.   

"The finance ministry sees no need to interfere in the free-floating zloty exchange rate," Przemyslaw Kwiecien told Reuters.   

"The central bank's survey showed companies pointed to 4.1 zlotys to the euro as a minimum level of profitability, so... excessive zloty strengthening could have a negative impact on corporate earnings and economic growth," he said.   

"But the free-floating rate exchange regime works well."   

Earlier on Thursday, Prime Minister Marek Belka said he wanted to meet with the central bank to discuss exchange rate policy in light of the zloty's recent appreciation.

title: UPDATE 4-Polish PM wants c.bank meeting over zloty climb.
text:
WARSAW, Dec 2 (Reuters) - Poland's government on Thursday called for prompt talks with the central bank about the zloty's surge, concerned a further climb could complicate the EU newcomer's planned euro adoption later this decade.   

But the finance ministry and the central bank governor said they saw no need for currency market intervention now, as the zloty hovered near 20-month highs against the globally strong euro.   

Prime Minister Marek Belka's call for a meeting follows a series of conflicting signals from policymakers about the economic impact of the strong zloty, which has gained 19 percent against the euro since hitting 2004 lows nine months ago.   

"We don't have time to wait because what is happening on the currency market is potentially quite worrisome," Belka told reporters in Katowice, adding that a meeting with top central bankers should take place within two weeks.   

European Minister Jaroslaw Pietras said the initiative came after a recent cabinet discussion about Poland's European strategy raised concerns the zloty uptrend could have a major impact on growth and euro adoption plans.   

If Poland is to join the pre-euro ERM-2 currency grid in early 2006, as the government wants, Warsaw and EU partners will soon have to begin discussions over exchange rate at which the zloty will lock into the euro.   

"We need to start thinking right now about the exchange rate at which we will join the euro zone," Pietras told Reuters.   

Anchoring the zloty to the euro at too strong a rate could hurt Poland's competitiveness for decades, say analysts.   

NO INTERVENTIONS FOR NOW   

The zloty eased nearly half a percent to 4.166 against the euro.   

A day after his deputy reminded financial markets that interventions were in a central bank's toolbox, Governor Leszek Balcerowicz played down the chances of any near-term action, adding that the economy was coping well with zloty strength.   

"We are among the countries that conduct a direct inflation target policy, with a floating zloty exchange rate set by markets. This strategy has been and is serving Poland well," Balcerowicz told public radio.   

Analysts said the government-central bank meeting would likely concentrate on what, if anything, Poland could do to limit zloty appreciation in the future, not on potential interventions or a change of currency regime now.   

"The central bank will most likely not intervene over the next several months, when the exchange rate is still acceptable," said Stanislaw Gomulka, chief economist at Polish insurer PZU and a former Balcerowicz adviser.   

"But the question is what will happen when we will go below 4 zlotys to the euro and I think Belka wants to open a debate on what to do then," he added.   

The finance ministry said excessive zloty gains would hurt corporate earnings and growth, pointing to a rate of 4.1 zlotys per euro as a pain threshold firms could still live with.   

The central bank declined to comment on the meeting proposal but Jan Czekaj, a member of the bank's rate setting council, said "if the prime minister invites us, we will surely meet".   

Analysts said what they heard from policymakers amounted to a cacophony of voices that could not even be treated as a "verbal intervention".   

"Verbal intervention usually precedes the actual one ... What is happening now is rather seen as talk that will not translate into actions," said Bank BPH analyst Marcin Mrowiec.

title: UPDATE 1-Poland competitive even with strong zloty-c.banker.
text:
WARSAW, Dec 2 (Reuters) - Poland's economy is competitive even with the zloty currency's recent strengthening, central bank governor Leszek Balcerowicz said on Thursday.   

The zloty hit a 20-month high versus the euro on Wednesday, having gained 14 percent against the single currency since European Union accession in May. It has also firmed 28 percent against the globally weaker dollar.   

"If we look at the economy as a whole, we are competitive even with a stronger zloty. And this is reflected in impressive export performance, " Balcerowicz told public radio.   

Polish exports rose 16 percent year-on-year to an all-time high of 6.08 billion euros ($8.08 billion) in September.   

"The current zloty exchange rate is close to levels seen in the first quarter of 2003, but productivity has been rising faster since then," he said in an interview.   

The zloty's 4.163 high against the euro on Wednesday took it just off the 4.15 level cited by companies as a threshold beyond which exports would become unprofitable.   

In a similar survey conducted by the central bank early in 2004, 4.2 zlotys was seen as the pain threshold, showing the Polish economy's growing ability to cope with appreciation.   

Balcerowicz also reiterated the bank's policy of not intervening in the foreign exchange markets. "We are among the countries that conduct a direct inflation target policy, with a floating zloty exchange rate set by markets."   

"This strategy has been and is serving Poland well."   

This week deputy central bank chief Krzysztof Rybinski said that forex interventions - not used in Poland since the zloty's free float in 2000 - were part of a central bank's toolkit.

title: UPDATE 1-Polish c.bank chief dampens  fx intervention  talk.
text:
KATOWICE, Poland, Dec 1 (Reuters) - Polish central bank chief Leszek Balcerowicz sought to dampen talk the bank might begin to intervene to curb the buoyant zloty, saying the current hands-off policy was right.   

"The bank's strategy of not intervening in the forex market has worked well and is working well," Balcerowicz told reporters in the southern Polish city of Katowice.   

Balcerowicz was speaking a day after his deputy Krzysztof Rybinski unexpectedly reminded markets that foreign exchange interventions - not used in Poland since the zloty's free float in 2000 - were part of a central bank's toolkit.   

The topic has surfaced as the Polish currency touched peaks in recent weeks, triggering concern it could hurt exporters and halt economic growth.   

Balcerowicz said the zloty's strengthening against the euro in past months took it back to levels from 2003, adding that Polish firms were better equipped for competition now than then.   

"A return to this zloty level versus the euro is happening when our exporters' competitiveness is higher than it was (in 2003)," he said.   

His remarks appeared to contradict those of Rybinski, who said the zloty was fundamentally overvalued.   

Rybinski, not long ago a market economist, said forex interventions could take place before and during Poland's stay in the pre-euro ERM-2 currency regime to avoid unwanted currency swings which could hurt the EU newcomers competitiveness.   

The zloty has gained 13 percent against the euro since Poland joined the European Union in May. On Wednesday the zloty is a fraction off 20-month highs at 4.18 versus the euro.   

Analysts say the central bank's surprise return to intervention rhetoric reflects its concern about further strengthening ahead of pegging the zloty to the euro, expected in the coming years.   

"The chance of FX intervention used to be zero, but now ... it seems more probable, particularly in the run-up to ERM-2 entry," said Jacek Wisniewski, analyst at Bank Pekao SA.   

"Balerowicz appeared to distance himself from Rybiski's comments, but he did not say that intervention was impossible."   

Poland hopes to adopt the euro in 2009, which would mean locking the zloty into the managed float of the ERM-2 as soon as 2006. The central bank has said the threat of speculative attacks on the zloty was higher during its 2 year ERM-2 stay.

title: Polish cbank - no  fx intervention  "working well".
text:
KATOWICE, Poland, Dec 1 (Reuters) - Polish Central Bank Chief Leszek Balcerowicz said on Wednesday he was happy with the bank's policy of not intervening in the foreign exchange market.   

"The bank's strategy of not intervening in the forex market has worked well and is working well," Balcerowicz told reporters.   

Balcerowicz was speaking a day after his deputy signalled the end of the bank's hands-off approach to the zloty may be drawing to an end, saying it must prepare for forex interventions during its stay in the ERM-2 regime.   

The zloty has gained about 13 percent against the euro since Poland joined the European Union in May.

title: Polish c.banker - must be ready for  fx intervention .
text:
WARSAW, Nov 30 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank must prepare for forex interventions during its stay in the ERM-2 regime and in the run-up to membership in the single currency grid, deputy governor Krzysztof Rybinski said on Tuesday.   

Speaking to private Radio PIN, Rybinski repeated the bank had both its interest rates and market interventions in its arsenal if it wanted to steer the exchange rate.   

Asked whether the bank would dare resorting to market interventions, Rybinski said: "We need to think about ERM-2 very seriously. If Poland were to adopt the euro in 2009, we'd have to enter ERM-2 in the first half of 2006.   

"The central bank has to be prepared to intervene in the market. Possibly it may have to cope with such a problem, what if there will be too much appreciation of the exchange rate before ERM-2 entry and the country will adopt as its central parity a ... rate that will hurt its competitiveness."

title: Polish Econmin says  fx interventions  not expected.
text:
KRAKOW, Poland, Nov 30 (Reuters) - Poland's Economy Minister Jerzy Hausner said on Tuesday he does not expect the central bank to abandon its hands-off policy stance and intervene in the foreign exchange market.   

"I do not expect interventions to weaken the zloty from the National Bank of Poland," Hausner told Reuters.   

The central bank on Tuesday floated the possibility of currency market interventions in the run-up to Poland's euro zone entry.

title: Poland  revives  fx intervention  talk as euro nears.
text:
WARSAW, Nov 30 (Reuters) - "Forex market intervention" reappeared in the Polish central bank's vocabulary on Tuesday, revealing growing concern about the strengthening zloty as the day it is pegged to the euro draws closer, analysts said.  

After years of hands-off policy and rhetoric towards the free-floating zloty, the central bank said it can always use forex interventions to try to counter unwanted currency swings, stunning analysts but leaving the buoyant zloty unfazed.  

In unusually candid comments, deputy central bank chief Krzysztof Rybinski also told a news conference that the zloty's recent strength did not fully reflect economic reality and that speculative flows which boosted it to recent highs may reverse.  

Since Poland joined the European Union in May, the zloty has gained nearly 14 percent versus the globally strong euro on the back of solid economic growth, progress on fiscal reforms and a respite in political uncertainty.  

In a closed-door meeting with commercial bank economists later on Tuesday, Rybinski spelled out the reasons behind his comments, according to analysts who attended the meeting.  

"The central bank is worried about further zloty appreciation. Rybinski said the change in its rhetoric may be linked to Poland's nearing ERM-2 entry," said one analyst, speaking of the mandatory pre-euro Exchange Rate Mechanism currency regime.  

The government has said that Poland could join ERM-2, a managed floating band around a set parity level versus the euro, as early as in the first half of 2006. If the zloty locks into the euro at too strong a level, Poland's exports would suffer.  

An overvalued zloty could also spell trouble if market concerns emerged about the credibility of Warsaw's economic policies, forcing repeated central bank intervention.  

Setting the parity rate involves negotiations between Poland, the EU executive Commission and the European Central Bank, as well as a market reference period.  

The European Central Bank has said there was no single path to the euro, which all new EU members want to adopt by 2010.  

Poland's hands-off approach contrasts with that in Hungary or Slovakia where central bankers have repeatedly dipped in foreign exchange markets or used interest rates to steer exchange rates.  

CLOSER SCRUTINY  

Another analyst who met with Rybinski said the central bank would not say what it believes should be the zloty's parity, but said the subject must be more closely scrutinised by markets.  

"If the results of this analysis are different than the situation on the market, then perhaps actions can be taken," said the analyst, referring to Rybinski's statement.  

Rybinski's comments were made during the presentation of the bank's quarterly inflation projection, which envisages a loweer zloty than levels hit in October.  

The bank said the zloty, trading around 4.21 to the euro on Tuesday, was close to the 4.15 level cited by firms in its regular business survey as a key threshold beyond which a further gains would make exports unprofitable.  

Although Poland's central bank has only one target - an inflation goal - analysts say 4.15 zlotys per euro can be judged as a good indication of what it believes to be the Polish currency's fair value against the euro.  

"In our view fair value is around 4.25, so today's levels are slightly overvalued, but we are close to equilibrium," said Arkadiusz Krzesniak, economist at Deutsche Bank in Warsaw.

title: UPDATE 4-Polish c.bank signals  fx intervention  back in play.
text:
WARSAW, Nov 30 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank signalled on Tuesday that the era of its hands-off approach to the zloty may be drawing to an end as the day it pegs its currency to the euro nears.  

The bank, which for years has left it to the market to set the value of the free-floating currency, warned that zloty strength no longer reflected the economy's health and revived the mantra that currency interventions were part of a central bank's toolkit.  

Poland hopes to adopt the euro in 2009 and this means it would need to fix the zloty to the euro in the ERM-2 managed floating band around a set parity as soon as early in 2006.  

Deputy central bank governor Krzysztof Rybinski said the ERM-2 was close enough for the bank to start thinking about intervening both inside the currency grid and in the run-up to its membership.  

"The central bank has to be prepared to intervene in the market," he told private Radio PIN. "What if there will be too much appreciation of the exchange rate before ERM-2 entry and the country will adopt as its central parity a ... rate that will hurt its competitiveness."  

Analysts said the prospect of the central bank selling the zloty in the market still looked distant, but the comments amounted to a first serious verbal intervention and revealed growing unease with the zloty's relentless climb.  

Speaking about the bank's quarterly inflation projection, Rybinski said it assumed a slightly weaker zloty would better reflect economic reality and warned speculative flows driving the currency to record highs could be reversed.  

"The present zloty exchange rate is overvalued based on what our models say about fundamental factors," Rybinski told a news conference.  

"This is in part a result of speculation, we are witnessing inflows of hot capital and there is a growing likelihood this trend can be reversed," he said.  

Since Poland joined the European Union in May, the zloty has gained nearly 14 percent versus the globally strong euro, buoyed by solid economic growth, progress on fiscal reforms and a respite in political uncertainty.  

TRADING PLACES  

So far government officials have occasionally expressed their concern the zloty's climb could hurt Poland's vital exports, while central bankers used to play down its negative effects and welcome its help in dampening inflation.  

Now, they swapped roles.  

The bank said the zloty was close to a 4.15 per euro level cited in its business survey as a key pain threshold for exporters, while government officials played down the strong zloty as simply a sign of the economy's success.  

"The current zloty rate is not hurting the economy. The zloty is strong because of its fundamentals," Finance Minister Miroslaw Gronicki said after the currency tested 18-month highs at 4.18 to the euro, unfazed by intervention talk.  

Economy Minister Jerzy Hausner on Tuesday reiterated he did not expect the central bank to intervene against its currency, a sentiment shared by analysts.  

"I think we are still quite a way from levels where we could see any action from the central bank," said Oliver Weeks, an economist at Morgan Stanley in London.  

Analysts said Tuesday's comments were, however, a sign that the bank was concerned market players saw the zloty as a one-way bet, lifting the risk of a sharp correction.  

"It's a warning that the zloty appreciation is causing a bubble that might burst because 'hot capital' could leave any time," said Katarzyna Zajdel-Kurowska, economist with Citibank Handlowy in Warsaw.

title: FOCUS: Poland Rate Decision To Set Tone For Markets
text:
WARSAW (Dow Jones)--Whether or not Poland's central bank raises rates Wednesday, its monetary policy decision will serve as a bellwether for markets in the months to come.   

Economists surveyed this week were split on whether we'll see a decision to stand pat or to lift the country's key interest rate this week. Poland's key rate is called the intervention rate. After a 50-basis-point hike last month, it's at 5.75%.   

"It will be a very close shave this time, given the declarations to control inflation," and the expectations for July CPI, SG Bank Economist Marcin Mroz said.   

Economists are, though, unified in saying that if the central bank has any hope of hitting its year-end inflation target, its monetary policy council will have to raise key interest rates by 50-100 basis points this year.   

"Whatever the decision, it doesn't change where we'll be in six months. The question is whether they will go there gradually or more aggressively," Danske Bank senior analyst Lars Christensen said   

If the central bank doesn't hike rates Wednesday, some economists said they'd expect to see it happen in either August or September.   

The policy-making body saw a large amount of turnover from the latter part of 2003 until February of this year. To many in the markets, it's still not clear how hawkish or dovish the country's rate-setting body is.   

"This is one of our key issues for the moment. The jury is still out," ABN AMRO chief economist in London Zsolt Papp said. "How in the medium term can we determine if this group is as hawkish as the last one?"   

July's meeting follows one in June that resulted in a higher-than-expected rate hike. That 50-basis-point rise in June - markets were looking for a 25-basis-point rise - came after months of comments from central bank officials about subtle changes in "degrees of caution," but no rate moves.   

If last month's surprise rate hike was any indication, the zloty stands to gain most from another rate hike Wednesday. Treasury bond yields would also follow the currency higher.   

Since the last RPP meeting the zloty has climbed to PLZ3.6450 from PLZ3.7470 to the dollar on June 30 and to PLZ4.4360 versus the euro from PLZ4.5422 on June 30.   

Two year T-bond yields are trading at about 7.93% versus 7.53% on June 30, and five-year T-bond yields are at 7.98% versus 7.44% on June 30.   

If there is no rate hike, the zloty should stay stable until August's meeting, when a rate hike would be very likely.   

The central bank's policy-making body said it needed to make its 50-point move on June 30 because of unexpectedly high inflation in May. That was a result of food price increases after Poland's May 1 entry into the European Union.   

And inflationary pressure continues. Economists expect July consumer price inflation between 4.7% and 5.0%. The policy-making body's end-2004 inflation target is 1.5% to 3.5%. June CPI was up 4.3% year-on-year, versus 3.4% in May, 2.2% in April and 1.7% in March.   

After making such a big move in June, some economists who spoke with Dow Jones this week said the central bank will likely wait for July CPI results before raising rates again.   

Food and beverage prices in the first half of July were unchanged from the first half of June, meaning the central bank probably needs more evidence of inflation before it acts again, said one economist.   

"Now there is less than a 50% chance so soon after the first increase," BRE Bank Economist Janusz Jankowiak said. "They'll raise by 50 points in August, but will wait for clear picture about July first."   

Those who forecast a rate rise on Wednesday say they expect the young policy-making body to want to be seen by markets as acting decisively on inflation.   

"They'll raise rates now by 50 points to send a strong message to the markets that they have inflation under control, even ahead of what is likely to be lower inflation in August," Bank BZ WBK Economist Piotr Bujak said.   

The policy meeting starts today and resumes on Wednesday, with a rate decision due around 1100 GMT Wednesday.   


-By Andrew Hope; Dow Jones Newswires, +4822 622-2767; andrew.hope@dowjones.com
