title: World Bank chides Polish finmin for  forex  actions.
text:
WARSAW, April 8 (Reuters) - The World Bank on Thursday chided Poland's finance ministry for recent de facto intervention to support the zloty and said exchanges of foreign bond issue proceeds should be conducted by the central bank.  

Poland's finance ministry said in March it had begun exchanging the equivalent of $930 million from Swiss franc and euro bond issues into zlotys, giving the zloty extensive support during recent political instability.  

"Recent government indications that it would sell proceeds from external borrowing in the market appears to be at odds with the (free float) policy and good practice," said the World Bank's chief economist for central Europe, Thomas Laursen.  

"This is normally done through the central bank within the free float exchange regime. If this is now a change in policy it has not been communicated well," he said.  

Poland floated the zloty in April 2000, since when the central bank has made no direct interventions in currency market.

title: Poland finmin - many factors at play in ERM parity.
text:
WARSAW, Dec 18 (Reuters) - Poland's Finance Minister Andrzej Raczko said on Thursday joining the pre-euro ERM-2 system with an exchange rate near the market rate was a less risky option, but factors other than stability should be considered. The European Central Bank said in its preliminary guidlines for euro accession candidates such as Poland that it favoured anchoring domestic currencies to the euro at a level near the market rate upon entering the Exchange Rate Mechanism regime.  

"The closer this (ERM-2 parity) rate is to the market rate, the better from the point of view of possible interventions," Raczko told Reuters.  

"But one always has to keep in mind that there are other factors to consider (when setting the partiy rate)," he added, though he did not name any other factors.  

Analysts believe Poland may want to join the two-year managed float regime of ERM-2 with a weaker exchange rate to boost its competitiveness.  

But the Polish zloty's time in the confines of a plus/minus 15 percent trading band could be risky if speculators seek to knock it out of the range or test the resolve of the ECB to intervene to keep Poland on track for the euro.

title: UPDATE 1-Budget reform key for long-term Polish growth-c.bank.
text:
LODZ, Poland, Dec 9 (Reuters) - Polish central bank governor Leszek Balcerowicz warned on Tuesday that only fiscal tightening will ensure long-term economic growth, saying the government's 2004 forecast of five percent was optimistic, but possible.  

Balcerowicz, an outspoken critic of fiscal loosening, said the government was running out of time to adopt much needed reforms aimed at averting the risk of a public debt blowout at the approach of European Union entry next May.  

He also sounded a calming note to markets by saying finance ministry plans to convert 250 million euros of a loan from the European Investment Bank into zlotys on the interbank market was not perceived by the central bank as any type of intervention.  

"Time is working against us. The faster the cabinet reforms public finances, the more sustainable growth will be," Balcerowicz told a news conference in Lodz.  

"Five percent economic growth next year is within expectations, but this is an optimistic forecast."  

Earlier this month the central bank estimated in its quarterly report that gross domestic product rose 3.7 percent year-on-year in the third quarter and looked poised to accelerate next year and maintain momentum in 2005.  

Commenting on last week's announcement by the finance ministry that it would go to the markets rather than the central bank to exchange half its 500 million euro EIB loan, Balcerowicz said: "I believe in the rationale given by the ministry."  

The ministry said the transaction, stemming from the need to exchange part of the euro loan into zlotys before the end of the year, was a client-driven market transaction and was not meant in any way as a market intervention.  

Poland's zloty has been in free-float since early 2000 and the central bank has kept a firm hands-off approach towards the currency. Finance Minister Andrzej Raczko has also often spoken in favour of free-floating currency regime for the zloty.

title: UPDATE 2-Polish FinMin-planned  fx  buying no  intervention .
text:
WARSAW, Dec 5 (Reuters) - Poland's Finance Ministry announced plans on Friday to exchange 250 million euros into zlotys on the forex market this month but vowed its venture into currency trading was not an intervention.   

The ministry said the transaction reflected the need to exchange into zlotys about half of a 500 million euro ($603 million) loan Poland gained from the European Investment Bank.   

The ministry moved to assure markets that it fully backed Poland's free-floating currency. The announcement of the deal was made to forestall suspicions the ministry was covertly playing the market to bolster the recently weak zloty, it said.   

There are several benefits for Poland if the zloty appreciates this year, such as boosting the budget's cash reserves and helping to keep key debt ratios in check.   

The rise in the zloty means Poland's public debt to gross domestic product ratio will fall because part of the debt is denominated in foreign currency.   

"This transaction should not be treated as a market intervention, it is just another way of gaining zlotys without having to go through the central bank," Jacek Tomorowicz, the head of the finance ministry's foreign department, told Reuters.   

"We did not want to surprise the market so we revealed our intentions," said Tomorowicz, adding that markets should not view the announcement as a shift on currency regime thinking.   

Analysts said the transaction could well strengthen the zloty, but was not to be seen as a parallel to the Hungary where authorities have shown in past weeks they were ready to intervene and hike up interest rates to defend the weak forint.   

"As long as the ministry makes sure to be perceived as a client and not a market player, markets should treat such transactions as fairly natural and its credibility should not suffer," said Jacek Wisniewski, analyst at Bank Pekao.   

The zloty inched up in the wake of the announcement but then backtracked gains to finish the day below morning highs. At 1535 GMT the zloty traded at 4.646 to the euro versus last week's all-time lows against the single currency around 4.71.   

CONTAGION CONTAINED   

The transaction could also stabilise the market as volumes thin out towards the end of the year, helping to contain any potential spillover from still turbulent Hungarian markets. "Right now, particularly towards the end of the year, the market needs a trend setter and awareness that these flows will be going through the market will definitely prop up the zloty," said Marcin Mroz, chief economist at SG Bank in Warsaw.   

Early this year the ministry said it was ironing out ways it can buy or sell zlotys on the interbank market, if it felt such a transaction would benefit the budget or the market.   

Since January, the zloty has weakened by 14 percent versus the euro, while holding steady versus the U.S. dollar. This has helped exporters, but raised worries over the increasing costs of servicing foreign debt and key public debt to GDP ratios.   

If public debt - previously seen at around 53 percent of gross domestic product in 2003 - tops 55 percent, Poland will be forced to take punitive spending cuts which could destabilise public finances and economic growth.

title: IMF: No Room For Polish Rate Cuts In Coming Months
text:
Warsaw (Dow Jones)--Poland's central bank has no room to cut interest rates in coming months, the International Monetary Fund said Thursday, despite market expectations of a cut when the current rate-setting Monetary Policy Council, or RPP, is replaced in January.   

Instead, the IMF urged Poland's central bank to focus on preventing an inflation rebound as the economy continues to recover. It should also retain its cornerstone policy of a free-floating zloty, the IMF said, in a statement summarizing its preliminary conclusions from a mission to Poland.   

"Preserving low inflation and non-intervention in the foreign-exchange market should be the highest priority for the new RPP," the statement said.   

In recent days, Polish government officials have hinted at a possible return to a managed currency regime based on a euro parity rate and a fluctuation band similar to the +/- 15% corridor set out of in European Union's ERMII exchange rate mechanism.   

However, any such intention was vigorously denied by Finance Minister Andrzej Raczko earlier this week.   

The IMF said Poland's parliament needs to quickly approve the government's plan to rein in its ballooning fiscal deficit in 2004-2007 through cuts in defense, administrative, and welfare spending.   

The plan, devised by Deputy Prime Minister Jerzy Hausner, has been heavily criticized by the parliamentary opposition and many members of the ruling Left Democratic Alliance.   

"Time is of the essence, however...We urge speedy consideration of all parts of the (Hausner) program," the IMF statement said.   

It called for a speeding-up of Poland's privatization effort, in part to help reduce the need for borrowing to finance fiscal deficits in coming years.   

The IMF forecast Poland's economy would register full-year GDP growth of 3.25% this year, rising to 4.25% in 2004. The latter projection is slightly below the government's projection of 5% annual growth.   

"In the current setting, where a recovery is in progress, a large fiscal stimulus is looming, and the yield curve is steepening, the scope in coming months for any further easing of monetary policy has largely disappeared," the IMF said.

The IMF said Poland was at an important juncture; recovery led by strong exports and domestic consumption couldn't be sustained under the continued burden of the bloated public sector.   

"Large and poorly addressed social transfers, inefficient public enterprises, and high and rising public debt are challenges Poland must rise to," the statement read.   

Spending cuts and consolidation of public finances proposed in Hausner's plan are aimed to bring the fiscal deficit to 2.1% of gross domestic product by 2007 from the 5.0% planned for 2004.   

IMF said that the government's privatization effort was unimpressive, leaving almost untapped a major source of non-debt budget financing.   

"In our conversations with the Treasury Minister we strongly emphasized the necessity to speed up privatization," head of IMF mission Susan Schadler said.   

Schadler said Poland would sustain low inflation rate by the end of this year and envisaged a moderate pickup in the inflation rate in 2004.   

"Year-end inflation in 2003 will come at 1.5%. A weaker zloty and picking up recovery will drive inflation up to just below 3.0% at the end of 2004," Schadler said.   

In October, annual inflation rose to 1.2% from 0.9% in September.   

Commenting on the IMF assessment Finance Minister Andrzej Raczko said the government was fully committed to a timely implementation of fiscal reform.   

Raczko stressed the main focus of the plan was to bring Poland's rising fiscal deficit and public debt in line with levels required for the adoption of the euro.   

He said the government didn't intend to tap into the central bank's foreign currency provisions to trim the budget deficit.   

"We can't count on miraculous solutions such as untying the central bank's reserves. We have to think in terms of sustainable trimming of the deficit," Raczko said.   

Poland's former Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko wanted to release some 9 billion zlotys ($1=PLN3.8835) of the central bank foreign currency provisions to improve the budget balance.   

-By Marek Strzelecki; Dow Jones Newswires, +4822 622 2767; marek.strzelecki@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE 1-SNB's Roth - ready to  intervene  to stop franc gains.
text:
WARSAW, June 18 (Reuters) - Further appreciation by the Swiss franc could have dire consequences for Switzerland's economy and force the central bank to intervene to weaken the currency, Swiss National Bank Chairman Jean-Pierre Roth said. 

 "If again, as a result of global political uncertainty, the franc becomes a safe haven for investors, we will have no other choice but to intervene to weaken the currency," Roth told Poland's Rzeczpospolita daily in an interview on Wednesday. 

 Roth was in Warsaw on Monday. The interview was published in Polish and translated into English by Reuters. 

 "Things have gone far enough and further appreciation in the current situation could have very negative consequences for the economy," the daily quoted Roth as saying. 

 Roth said the SNB last intervened on the forex market in 1995 in a co-ordinated effort with other central banks to boost the value of the dollar. The SNB's last unilateral market intervention took place in the early 1980s. 

 The SNB, which keeps interest rates 150-200 basis points below those in the euro zone, last week vowed to push beyond the limits of traditional monetary policy to foster growth for the recession-hit, export-dependent Swiss economy. 

 Asked about the risk of deflation, Roth said: "With inflation at 0.4 percent there is a danger that some negative event would bring about a fall in consumer prices. But the real danger for us would be franc appreciation, which could be regarded as deflation of imported goods."

title: Polish Ctrl Bk -3: Euro Adoption Hinges On Fiscal Stance
text:
As part of its strategic shift from inflation reduction to price stability, the RPP said it was abandoning its practice of setting year-end and medium-term inflation targets. 

 Instead, the bank said, it will adopt a continuous CPI target similar to that used by the European Central Bank, which is applied month by month and indefinitely. 

 The RPP said this extended time horizon will give policymakers credibility and allow a more flexible response to short-term external shocks. 

 The RPP reaffirmed its commitment to bring Poland into the euro zone in 2007. 

 It said Poland already met four of the five conditions set in the Maastricht Treaty for candidates to adopt the euro - inflation, currency stability, long-term interest rates and public debt. 

 But the RPP said the public sector deficit remained above 5.0% of gross domestic product in 2002, well above the Maastricht ceiling of 3.0%. 

 According to the revised RPP strategy, cuts in public spending and faster privatization of state-owned enterprises will largely determine the scope for monetary easing in coming years. 

 "The moment of entry into the euro zone - and appropriate adjustments of monetary policy - will depend on the fulfillment of (Maastricht) fiscal criteria," the RPP said. 

 It said retention of lax fiscal policies once the zloty enters the +/-15% trading band set by the ERM II exchange rate mechanism will increase the risk of a currency crisis. 

 As a result, the panel recommended retaining the zloty's current free float until the moment of entry into ERM II and the adoption of the widest possible trading band after entry. 

 Any change in Poland's currency regime, including ERM II entry, requires joint approval by the central bank and the government. A mixed team of finance ministry and central bank officials is currently negotiating details of a currency strategy beyond 2004 when Poland is to join the European Union. 

 Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko and senior ministry officials have repeatedly stressed the need to weaken the zloty in order to boost exports and economic growth. 

 They argue this could be accomplished in the short term via direct central bank intervention on the currency markets. In addition, Kolodko has suggested Poland might introduce a trading band before entering ERM II or devalue the currency by adopting a below-market central parity rate upon entry. 

 In Wednesday's strategy document, the RPP said such a devaluation would contradict the Maastricht requirement to maintain currency stability for at least two years without "excessive market volatility." 

 Despite its five-year time horizon, the strategy document's validity expires with the current RPP's term in January 2004. 

 Of the panel's 10 members, analysts expect only central bank President Leszek Balcerowicz - who holds his seat ex officio - to remain on a reconstituted RPP. 

 Poland's left-dominated parliament, which will nominate six of nine new RPP members, is expected to pack the panel with proponents of more dovish policies.

title: Poland to buy  foreign exchange  to service debt-MinFin.
text:
LONDON, Jan 24 (Reuters) - Poland will buy hard currency on the market later in this quarter of 2003 to service foreign debt, but has not done so yet despite talk that it stood behind a recent drop in the zloty, a senior official said on Friday. 

 Deputy finance minister Ryszard Michalski moved to cool speculation that the ministry sold the zloty currency  earlier this week, when the unit unexpectedly plunged more than two percent in a day. 

 Government officials have long suggested the finance ministry would buy currencies to cover foreign debt servicing costs on the open market in a bid to curb the zloty's strength which they believe is damaging economic competitiveness. 

 Michalski also reiterated the finance ministry's long-standing support for some intervention in the foreign exchange market despite Poland's full-float currency regime, which the central bank says rules out intervening. 

 "We will be buying hard currencies for servicing debt interest costs on market in the first quarter," Michalski told Reuters on the sidelines of a roadshow held by Poland in London to promote its upcoming euro-denominated bond issue. 

 "But we have not done this yet, because we are not ready. We are still preparing the infrastructure and we will be ready soon, sooner than people expect," he said. 

 Poland will have to repay roughly $1 billion worth of foreign debt interest this year. 

 The zloty  has retraced some of the lost ground by Friday, but was still trading just above its lowest level on the euro since June 2000. At 1510 GMT it traded at 4.1851 versus the euro, up from the lows at 4.2482 hit on Thursday. 

 FINANCE MINISTRY 

 But the currency remains extremely volatile because dealers are anxious about any signs of finance ministry involvement, especially after Poland's regional peer Hungary moved to curb its flyaway currency recently. 

 The Hungarian forint's appreciation limit came under fierce attack last week, forcing the central bank to intervene against it on the market, cut interest rates aggressively and place restrictions on short-term deposits. 

 Michalski said Hungary's recent experience only underlined the need to contain currency strength which is plaguing eastern European countries on the verge of accession to the European Union and their subsequent adoption of the euro. 

 The prospects of euro zone entry are luring investors who hope to capitalise on gains in the bond market after eastern European yields converge with the lower euro levels. 

 Despite government pressure, the National Bank of Poland, which under Polish law has to agree to intervene, has so far strongly rejected selling zlotys. 

 "We fully agree that the market should decide, but we are thinking about a civilised market," Michalski told investors during the roadshow. "It seems that the process of appreciation goes too far," he said. 

 "A sort of a regulated market could be a much nicer solution than the volatile, impulsive market we have...Last week's experience was very destructive and shows the market should be regulated and under control," he said.

title: Polish zloty opens firmer, seen inching up.
text:
WARSAW, Jan 24 (Reuters) - The Polish zloty opened higher on Friday, recovering from a 31-month low versus the euro hit on the previous session, and dealers said the unit could post more gains thanks to improved sentiment in the region. 

 The debt market, hit by weak demand on a primary bond tender earlier this week and turmoil on the Hungarian market, has also strengthened, with investors returning to buy Poland's treasuries. 

 "We had some panic and speculative games, but it should fade away. The market might still be a bit nervous, but the zloty might firm in line with the Hungarian forint and the Czech crown," said Wojciech Trzepizur, dealer at BRE Bank in Warsaw. 

 The zloty lost nearly six percent since last week's hefty rate cuts by the Hungarian central bank as investors who suffered losses in the central European country moved to cut their exposure in Poland. 

 Hard-hitting verbal intervention by Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko, who said he expected EU candidate Poland to join the euro zone at a zloty/euro rate of 4.35 also helped spook the market. 

 "The bond market is bottoming out. Investors treated the recent fall as an opportunity to buy treasuries, which offer the highest real interest rates in the region," said Krzysztof Izdebski, dealer at Deutsche Bank. 

 Polish five-year treasuries yielded 5.59 percent, compared to Hungary's 6.81 percent at Thursday's fixing. Polish inflation is just 0.8 percent while Hungary's is 4.8 percent. 

 Dealers also said expectations of a rate cut next week could also slightly support the unit, but stressed a 25-basis-point reduction was fully priced in.

title: Polish Ctrl Bk: Doesn't Rule Out Zloty Trading Band
text:
WARSAW -(Dow Jones)- Poland's central bank said Thursday that it isn't ruling out the possibility of reintroducing a trading band for the free-floating zloty, but a senior bank official said later the reference was to the long-planned adoption of the European Union's ERM II currency mechanism after 2004. 

 In a statement, the bank said its inflation-targeting strategy ruled out adopting a specific exchange-rate goal, but added "it wouldn't exclude the possibility that this strategy is compatible with introducing a wide currency fluctuation band around a market-derived central parity rate." 

 The statement appeared to be in response to a suggestion from Deputy Finance Minister Ryszard Michalski earlier Thursday that Poland might return the zloty to a managed, euro-linked float even before it enters the ERM II - a step expected soon after Poland joins the E.U. in mid-2004. 

 But senior central banker Grzegorz Wojtowicz, a member of the policy-setting Monetary Policy Council, denied there were any plans to drop the zloty free float before joining ERM II. 

 "All we're saying is that a direct inflation target can be reconciled with the process of adopting the euro," Wojtowicz told Dow Jones Newswires in a telephone interview. 

 "Introducing a trading band before joining ERM II would be irresponsible, because the zloty could break through the band at any moment. But once we're in ERM II and have a euro-zloty parity rate agreed with the (European Central Bank), then both sides would have to intervene to protect the band," he said. 

 Since June, Poland's central bank and the finance ministry have been trying to hammer out a currency strategy for the potentially volatile period preceding a direct linkup with the euro under ERM II. The ERM II mechanism would set a central parity rate for the zloty against the euro, bounded by a +/- 15% trading band. 

 The central bank has repeatedly stressed that it sees no  reason to abandon the present currency regime - based since  April 2000 on a free-floating zloty - until Poland enters ERM II. 

 But finance ministry officials have urged an earlier return to a zloty trading band, perhaps accompanied by a devaluation of the currency's central parity rate. They say both moves would help reverse the zloty's current appreciation trend, boosting the competitiveness of Polish exports and reviving economic growth. 

 "We think the objective should be an exchange rate more  favorable to exporters," Deputy Finance Minister Michalski, co-chairman of the government-central bank working group on currency strategy, told the Polish Press Agency in an interview Thursday. 

 But Michalski's main negotiating partner, central bank Deputy President Andrzej Bratkowski, repeated Thursday that weakening the zloty is an unacceptable argument for any change in the currency regime. 

 "We're ready to listen to the finance ministry's arguments and we don't exclude - at least theoretically - the early introduction of a trading band," Bratkowski told Dow Jones Newswires. "But if the goal is simply to weaken the zloty against its underlying trend, this is something we'd definitely oppose." 

 Bratkowski said the central bank might accept the zloty's return to a managed float if the finance ministry demonstrates the move is needed to reduce volatility in the run-up to ERM II entry. 

 "One could imagine early introduction of a trading band  for psychological purposes, to stabilize the market," he said. "But in the present low-inflation environment, we're not expecting big exchange-rate fluctuations." 

 However, Michalski's remarks Thursday indicated the finance ministry is looking beyond the term of the current Monetary Policy Council, which expires in January 2004. 

 "The more rigorously the current Council sticks to conservative monetary policies, the more likely we'll see more innovative approach in the new Council...A lot can happen over the next (18) months," Michalski told PAP. 

 -By David McQuaid and Malgorzata Halaba; Dow Jones Newswires, +4822 622 2766; david.mcquaid@dowjones.com

title: INTERVIEW-Polish c.bank targets euro compliance 2005.
text:
WARSAW, Dec 3 (Reuters) - Poland is on course to meet entry targets for joining the euro zone by 2005, the year after it expects to join the European Union, a top central banker said on Tuesday. 

 Deputy central bank governor Andrzej Bratkowski told Reuters the chances that Poland would meet tough euro-zone qualification targets were actually improving amid a faster-than-expected recovery. 

 The comments by Bratkowski, whose views reflect the thinking of central bank chief Leszek Balcerowicz, came after Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko sought to cool expectations of an early currency switch. 

 "I think we will be ready in 2005, and if I had to weigh our chances I would put them at around 90 percent now," Bratkowski said in an interview. 

 Poland is the largest of 10 candidates hoping to close EU entry talks soon and adopt the euro after spending two years or more in the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM-2), a currency stabilisation regime. 

 Bratkowski said monetary policy must remain cautious and fiscal policy tight to ensure that Poland, having won the battle against inflation, keeps prices under control as it sets its sights on euroland. 

 "Next year and the year after we will have higher economic growth coupled with extra budget expenditures related to EU entry, which will create inflationary pressure," he said. 

 "That, plus uncertainty on whether planned fiscal reforms will be sound, will definitely keep monetary policy on the cautious side." 

 Bratkowski, who is not a member of the rate-setting Monetary Policy Council, said it was difficult to gauge whether interest rates were already where they should be given Poland's long-term growth prospects, but said some more easing was still possible. 

 The central bank has slashed more than twelve percentage points off its main market rate since early 2001. It eased last month by a cautious 25 basis points to 6.75 percent, leaving the main rate still far above inflation of just over one percent. 

 NO INTERVENTION

 Like other central European countries, Poland is battling to curb the strength of its currency as "convergence" investors bet that bond yields will fall towards euro-zone levels and the zloty will rise as Poland's economy catches up with richer western Europe. 

 But Bratkowski said there was no need for Poland to abandon its hands-off policy on the zloty , adding it was "difficult to imagine" circumstances which would force intervention against the free-floating unit. 

 "A country which does not move in to protect the exchange rate is the least likely to be forced to do so," he said. 

 He said further strengthening of the zloty was inevitable, but the trick was to set a credible central parity for the zloty's entry into the ERM-2 which would anchor the currency in a 30 percent fluctuation band. 

 "The key will be to negotiate with the European Central Bank (ECB) a parity rate which would be believable for the markets and which will allow the economy to grow," he added. 

 Bratkowski countered calls by ECB and EU officials for candidates not to rush into the euro zone by saying the so-called Maastricht criteria - which include low inflation and low state borrowing - did not rule out strong growth. 

 "I simply do not believe that those two targets of entering the euro-zone quickly and maintaining high economic growth are contradictory," Bratkowski said. 

 "But I do think that we should try to stay in the ERM-2 for as little time as possible, maybe less than two years, if the ECB agrees. 

 "The final euro-zone accession date is a technical issue, but we do want to be compliant with Maastricht criteria in 2005," Bratkowski said. 

 ECB governing council member Jean-Claude Trichet on Monday warned against admitting countries into the euro zone which were not ready for membership, while Economic Affairs Commissioner Pedro Solbes predicted that at most only one or two applicant countries would be zone members by 2007.

title: UPDATE 1-Rosati says zloty too strong, but may remain firm.
text:
Adds more comments from Rosati, background 

 WARSAW, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Poland's zloty - which has rallied over the past month along with other central European currencies - is too strong given macroeconomic fundamentals, a member of the central bank's interest rate-setting panel said on Monday. 

 "The main reason behind the recent rally in the zloty is the fading uncertainty over Poland's future European Union membership," Dariusz Rosati, one of 10 members of the Monetary Policy Council (MPC) told public radio. 

 "But generally speaking, the zloty is slightly too strong given the macroeconomic fundamentals," he added. 

 But Rosati brushed off expectations of a significant weakening of the zloty in months ahead as Poland appears firmly en route to join the European Union in 2004 and the eurozone later this decade. 

 "I think the strengthening of the zloty might continue. In a perspective of two-three-years, the zloty will remain a strong currency," Rosati - a dove on the 10-member MPC panel said. 

 "It is an illusion, on the part of the government or some businesses that it is possible to weaken the currency in a sustainable way," he added. 

 The zloty has gained six percent against the dollar and three versus the firmer euro over the last month, as fears surrounding Poland's EU accession have eased and foreign portfolio investors are increasingly betting on Polish asset prices quickly converging with those in the euro zone. 

 Such upward pressure has forced Hungary and Slovakia to cut interest rates in past weeks despite a far more uncertain inflation environment than Poland's. Slovakia and the Czech Republic have also intervened in the market to try cap their currencies' uptrend. 

 In an interview last week's with Reuters, Rosati said the zloty's strength was nevertheless not worrying enough to warrant forex interventions or changes to Poland's free-floating currency regime. 

 The Polish government - which together with the central bank decides on the foreign exchange regime - has repeatedly said the zloty was overvalued and hurting struggling exporters. 

 Rosati would not comment on this week's policy meeting, due to make a rate decision on Wednesday, which most analysts expect to order a reduction in the main market rate of seven percent.

title: WRAPUP 1-Polish c.bankers say mkts won't drive rate policy.
text:
WARSAW, Nov 22 (Reuters) - Polish central bankers signalled on Friday they are not likely to follow their regional peers in axing interest rates to curb strong currencies, and suggested markets had gone too far in pricing in EU and euro-zone entry. Policymakers across eastern Europe are scrambling to ward off a flood of foreign money into local currencies as prospects brighten for eight of the region's states to join the wealthy European Union in 2004. 

 But Poland has so far stood by its hands-off foreign exchange policy as other regional central banks slash rates or intervene to curb currency strength. 

 Setting Poland further apart from its peers, Monetary Policy Council (MPC) member Cezary Jozefiak warned that rate cuts may fail to dampen foreign appetitate for local assets, which yield much more than their euro zone equivalents. 

 "I have doubts whether changing the interest rate disparity (between eastern Europe and the euro zone) will help," Jozefiak told Reuters in an interview. 

 Jozefiak also reiterated his long-standing views, shared by many of the MPC's 10 members, that market intervention against the zloty was not a good policy solution in a free-floating currency regime. 

 The zloty firmed on his comments, seen in the market as an assurance that no administrative steps would be taken to stem foreign inflows. Bonds markets were unruffled, continuing to price in a modest rate cut next week. 

 Twelve out of 20 analysts polled by Reuters on Friday said the modest pace of recovery and near-record low inflation still left room for a cut of up to 50 basis points in Poland's main seven percent rate. 

 Comments supportive of easing on Thursday by MPC dove Dariusz Rosati led several analysts to change their minds and predict a modest easing next week rather than later. 

 The Hungarian central bank is meanwhile expected to cut by 50-100 basis points on Monday after last week's half-point cut, while the Czech and Slovak banks have both slashed rates lately. 

 BUDGET CONCERNS 

 Another hawkish MPC member joined forces with Warsaw's chief EU entry negotiator to warn that the government budget was at risk in the future, possibly increasing the risk premiums demanded by foreign investors on zloty assets. 

 Boguslaw Grabowski said Poland risked missing its timetable to meet the Maastricht treaty criteria on economic and monetary convergence with the euro zone by 2005 - the target date agreed by the central bank and the government. 

 "I do see a high risk of a delay to the 2005 timetable for meeting the Maastricht criteria in particular the three percent budget deficit to GDP target," he told reporters in London. 

 Poland has to cut its budget gap to three percent of gross domestic product to meet the euro entry criteria. Based on EU rules, the finance ministry forecasts a deficit of 3.9 percent next year. 

 A smaller deficit will require fast revenue-boosting growth and deep spending cuts, which will be hard to sell to voters before a referendum on joining the EU next year. 

 EU negotiator Jan Truszczynski fanned new worries over fiscal policy, saying Poland faced a budget crunch after EU entry if its financial entry terms are not improved. 

 "A big budget risk will materialise if no changes to our entry conditions are introduced. That is the risk of losing liquidity," Truszczynski told reporters. 

 Truszczynski said it was unfair for Poland to pay full membership dues without receiving full benefits of EU entry, especially in farming subsidies which are to start at 25 percent of what EU members receive and reach full aid in 10 years. 

 But he added the European Commission may sweeten entry proposal for farmers over the next few days.

title: UPDATE 1-Polish c.banker - fundamentals back strong zloty.
text:
ZALESIE, Poland, Nov 21 (Reuters) - Poland's deputy central bank governor Jerzy Stopyra said on Thursday the zloty's recent rally was "justified by fundamentals" and not driven only by speculative inflows. 

 His comments contradict recent statements from central bank and government officials who call the rally, which has swept other central European markets, speculative. 

 "We do not see any speculation," Stopyra, who rarely speaks publicly about his views on the economy and deals mainly with the central bank's operations, told reporters on the sidelines of a banking supervision seminar. 

 Foreign players are piling into the region as prospects brighten for many of the region's states to join the European Union in 2004 and later adopt the lower-yielding euro currency. 

 Such upward pressure on currencies has forced Hungary and Slovakia to cut rates in past weeks despite a far-more uncertain inflation environment than Poland's. Slovakia and the Czech Republic have also intervened to cap their currencies. 

 The zloty has risen three percent to the euro and six percent to the dollar over the last month. 

 Earlier on Thursday, member of the Polish central bank's Monetary Policy Council Dariusz Rosati said the zloty's rally was a "clear speculative inflow based on interest rate cut expectations." 

 But Polish central bankers still steer clear of any hints of possible intervention even though they admit that they are begining to pay attention to the exchange rate as a factor affecting its policy since inflation stabilised at low levels. 

 Government officials have long demanded orchestrated central bank action to curb the zloty and protect Polish exporters. 

 The comments from Stopyra, who advises the central bank governor on all policy issues but has no direct say over exchange rate decisions, shows there is still a strong belief within the Polish national bank that the zloty should be allowed to run its course. 

 "If the market saw as positive the recent data about the Polish economy, including good growth in the third quarter, a very good situation on the current account, a moderate level of state deficit and low inflation, then it priced it in," he said. 

 Asked if he was concerned that the strong zloty could hurt the current account, Stopyra said: 

 "The market regulates itself. So even if the strong zloty worsens the trade situation, then the exchange rate will immediately fall." 

 Poland's economy is now slowly emerging from its deepest growth slowdown in more than a decade, which was driven by the central bank's hawkish anti-inflation policy, high government deficit and poor global performance.

title: INTERVIEW-Zloty appreciation not needed to cap CPI - Rosati.
text:
WARSAW, Nov 21 (Reuters) - Polish rate-setter Dariusz Rosati told Reuters on Thursday that further zloty appreciation would be harmful for the economy and was no longer necessary to reduce inflation. 

 But Rosati, one of 10 Monetary Policy Council (MPC) members, said the zloty's strength was not worrying enough to warrant forexinterventions, as was the case in other east European states, or changes to Poland's free-floating currency regime. 

 His comments signal that the central bank, which has played down the role of zloty movements in its interest rate decisions, may be shifting its policy focus, which would allow for further easing in order to ease upward pressure on the Polish currency. 

 "Over the last several months inflation is at a satisfactory level, where we don't want to lower it but stabilise it," Rosati, a known dove on the Council, said in an interview. 

 "This means that we can change the accents in monetary policy. Strengthening of the zloty exchange rate to lower inflation is no longer needed, and it is harmful." Inflation hit a post-communist low of 1.1 percent year-on-year in October and is expected miss the MPC's end-2002 2-4 percent target on the downside. 

 After the last rate cut in October, the central bank governor said that rates were at or very near their adequate level, limiting scope for more easing after a nearly two-year cycle of cautious, gradual reductions. 

 Rosati said the MPC had been willing to "apply a certain dose of zloty appreciation" to limit inflation - through lowering the price of imports - but that in the present price environment the Council did not have to pay that cost. 

 LOWER RATES A POSSIBILITY 

 The zloty has gained six percent against the dollar and three versus the revved up euro over the last month, as fears surrounding Poland's 2004 accession to the European Union eased and foreign portfolio investors increasingly bet on Polish asset prices quickly converging with those in the euro zone. 

 Such upward pressure on currencies has forced Hungary and Slovakia to cut rates in past weeks despite a far-more uncertain inflation environment than Poland's. Slovakia and the Czech Republic have also intervened to cap their currencies. 

 "There are several possibilities. Lowering interest rates will weaken demand for zlotys stemming from rate cut expectations. We still have this possibility," Rosati said. 

 "Another option is intervention, which is theoretically possible but we have long indicated that such a solution would be costly and ineffective." 

 He said the central bank would consider intervention or a change in the currency regime only if "we are certain that capital inflows are so large, that the zloty would appreciate to such a level that it would have to come crashing down." 

 "But we are still not in such a situation." 

 The government believes the zloty is too strong for exporters and could make Poland's economy uncompetitive if the country joins the euro-zone, expected in 2007 or 2008, before previously weakening the currency. 

 Economy Minister Jacek Piechota earlier called for a rate cut when the MPC meets on November 26-27. 

 "The overly strong zloty is reducing the profitability of our exporters and we are counting on cooperation from the central bank in that respect," he told reporters.

title: Polish c.bank - pre-ERM-2 anti-zloty move unlikely.
text:
WARSAW, Oct 8 (Reuters) - Poland's deputy central bank chief said on Tuesday that forex intervention to weaken the zloty before entry into the pre-euro currency mechanism ERM-2 was unlikely, but could not be ruled out. 

 "If the central bank decides the zloty is overvalued before ERM-2, then we cannot rule out intervention. But there is no reason to believe such circumstances will arise," Andrzej Bratkowski told reporters. 

 The central bank - which can intervene on the forex market - has long been an opponent of intervention against the free-floating zloty. 

 Bratkowski also said that Poland would seek to stay in the ERM-2 system - a currency stabilising mechanism ahead of euro-zone entry - for as short a time as possible. On Tuesday a central bank and finance ministry committee said Poland would seek to meet the euro-zone entry rules by 2005 and to anchor the zloty versus the euro at a level based on market valuation during an unspecified reference period.

title: Polish Ctrl Bk, Govt Set Up Task Force On  Forex  Strategy
text:
WARSAW -(Dow Jones)- The Polish central bank and the finance ministry said Wednesday they have set up a task force to work out strategy for Poland's economic convergence with the euro zone, providing further evidence that an ugly policy feud between the two sides may be subsiding after mediation by President Aleksander Kwasniewski. 

 Deputy Central Bank President Andrzej Bratkowski and Deputy Finance Minister Andrzej Raczko will co-chair the group, which was established by Finance Minister Marek Belka and Central Bbank President Leszek Balcerowicz. 

 The move comes less than a day after a two-hour meeting between Kwasniewski and the central bank's rate-setting Monetary Policy Council, or RPP, which has been resisting government pressure to relax interest-rate and currency policies in order to boost sagging economic growth. 

 After that meeting, Balcerowicz said the RPP was ready to open talks with the government on ways to curb the appreciating Polish zloty and manage currency policy during the run-up to Poland's entry to the European Union and the euro zone, expected in 2004 and 2007, respectively. 

 However, Balcerowicz said the bank did not believe it made sense to drop Poland's present currency regime, which since April 2000 has been based on a free-floating zloty. 

 Belka has been pressing the central bank to consider adjusting exchange-rate policy since mid-May, when the government submitted confidential proposals to the central bank. No details have been released, but Belka has publicly advocated reintroducing a trading band - perhaps similar to the ERM2 exchange rate mechanism Poland must adopt two years before entering the European Economic and Monetary Union. 

 Poland's parliament is now considering several bills sponsored by ruling coalition parties that would water down the central bank's autonomy and pack the policy-making RPP with new members. Belka and, to a lesser extent, the government, have distanced themselves from the legislation, but say it will probably pass unless the RPP eases its tough anti-inflation stance.

title: UPDATE 1-Polish c.bank defends independence before debate.
text:
WARSAW, May 23 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank defended its independence on Thursday ahead of a crunch parliamentary debate where deputies were expected to back proposals to force it to cut interest rates to revive a weak economy. 

 After a months-long war of words between the government and the central bank, the largest party in the left-wing coalition was expected to set the legislative ball rolling by backing two amendments to the National Bank charter. 

 That should ensure a big majority for the proposals, which would require the central bank to consider jobs and growth - and not just prices - in setting policy. 

 They would also increase the size of the rate-setting Monetary Policy Council (MPC), enabling the panel to be packed with doves and creating a stable majority for easy money. 

 Opposing the changes, central bank Governor Leszek Balcerowicz said a central bank free of political interference was a vital part of any properly run country. 

 "In all well-constructed states of the world, the central bank is independent so that it can protect citizens against inflation," Balcerowicz told reporters before the late-night debate, which was due to begin at 8 p.m. (1800 GMT). 

 "Removing the independence of the central bank would have an inflated price. And inflation does not lead to prosperity." 

 EU CONCERNS 

 Poland, the largest of 10 candidates in talks to join the European Union by 2004, needs to kick-start an economy languishing in its worst economic slowdown in a decade to ensure it can compete in the bloc's single marketplace. 

 But leaders worry that tampering with central bank independence will annoy Brussels and make it harder for Poland to realise its longer-term goal of adopting the euro, managed by the independent European Central Bank. 

 "Maybe by introducing these changes the Monetary Policy Council will realise it must increase its cooperation with the government," said Robert Smolen, spokesman of Prime Minister Leszek Miller's Democratic Left Alliance (SLD). 

 "The government must have a bigger say in the decisions made by the MPC. I do not think these bills go against EU norms and introduces changes which threaten the bank's independence." 

 LATE DEBATE 

 The Sejm lower house of parliament was expected to refer the proposals to committee for further work, meaning the threatened loss of independence will be hanging over the MPC when it holds its policy meeting next week. 

 The MPC, which has already halved rates since early 2001 to 9.5 percent, has said further cuts could jeopardise low inflation and risk inflating Poland's current account deficit. 

 It has also resisted government pressure to force down the zloty's exchange rate, with MPC member Boguslaw Grabowski saying Poland should stick to its free-floating regime in the run-up to joining the EU. 

 Grabowski also said any attempt to strip the central bank of its joint role in setting foreign exchange policy would violate Poland's constitution. 

 The heated rates-and-currency debate in Poland reflects a dilemma faced by other EU candidates in eastern Europe, such as Hungary and the Czech Republic, where currency appreciation is putting economies under enormous pressure. 

 The appreciation is driven by investor bets that prices in candidate countries will align themselves with higher levels in the EU over time, threatening a fatal loss of competitiveness in communist-era industries such as steel and shipbuilding. 

 Poland's government has decided to regain control over debt-hit shipyard Stocznia Szczecin, in the first such renationalisation since the fall of communism in 1989. It says the strong zloty is a factor behind the yard's troubles. 

 PRESIDENT OPPOSES 

 President Aleksander Kwasniewski, a former SLD leader, has said he opposes any attack on the central bank's independence. 

 But he is unlikely to risk his veto being overturned by a three-fifths majority. He could instead refer any legislation to the Constitutional Tribunal for a possibly lengthy review. 

 The International Monetary Fund threw its weight behind the central bank in the feud, saying currency intervention was not the right answer to Poland's poor policy balance, characterised by tight money and a loose fiscal stance.

title: UPDATE 2-Polish govt to talk to c.bank on strong zloty.
text:
WARSAW, May 14 (Reuters) - Poland's left-wing government said on Tuesday it wanted to regulate the free floating zloty and would hold talks with the central bank aimed at containing the strength of the currency. 

 Speaking after a cabinet meeting, Finance Minister Marek Belka said the buoyant zloty was hurting exporters and risked causing an extended period of economic stagnation. 

 He said the government had asked his ministry to propose changes to Poland's two-year-old free currency float aimed at preventing excessive appreciation. 

 But the central bank, which under Polish law must approve changes in foreign exchange policy, poured cold water on any expectations that Poland's free float would be changed soon or that it might intervene against the buoyant zloty. 

 Analysts said the government was pnrobably hoping to create an explicit - or secret - trading band around the zloty that would require bankers to intervene if the unit gets too strong. 

 Belka declined to map out his proposal, saying it would not be appropriate to speculate in public about intervention. 

 "Exchange rate policy does not have to be publicly announced, to keep the (financial) market guessing," he said. 

 He did say he opposed fixing the zloty to a hard currency or reintroducing a crawling peg for the unit. 

 The zloty, which had fallen up to 1.5 percent earlier to a seven-month low versus the euro on pre-cabinet jitters, pared losses on hopes the government would refrain from legislative pressure in the talks with the bank. 

CENTRAL BANK DIGS IN HEELS 

 The central bank's top foreign exchange policy official, deputy governor Andrzej Bratkowski, said no changes were needed in the short term, although Poland did need to prepare to adopt the euro currency after joining the European Union. 

 Poland will have to corral the unit into a 30-percentage point band for at least two years after joining the EU, expected in 2004, before it can adopt the euro later in the decade. 

 Hungary, which along with Poland and the Czech Republic is a top candidate for EU entry, created a trading band in line with EU's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM-2) while the Czech central bank has intervened against the fully floated crown. 

 "There is no need for quick action," Bratkowski told Reuters. "If the main point (of talks government-central bank talks) would be to start intervening then an agreement is not likely." 

 Ministers blame the central bank's caution in easing its high interest rates for Poland's worst economic slowdown in a decade and drawing in speculative capital, forcing up the zloty and pricing exporters out of key foreign markets. 

 Their criticism was backed by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) which said monetary policy had been "restrictive" and the central bank had cut interest rates too slowly in response to a weak economy. 

 But, while still seeing scope to ease rates, the EBRD said in a report that political pressure on the National Bank of Poland might actually delay further rate cuts. 

 "The conduct of monetary policy has been complicated by statements of government members that could threaten the operational independence of the Central Bank," the EBRD said. 

 STRONG ZLOTY HELPS SOME 

 Results from eastern Europe's largest mobile phone company and oil refining business, meanwhile, showed that a strong zloty can actually help Polish firms which have borrowed heavily in foreign currencies. 

 Both Polska Telefonia Cyfrowa, operator of the leading Era GSM brand, and oil group PKN Orlen blamed weaker-than-expected first quarter net profits on temporary weakness in the zloty, which forced up the cost of servicing their hard currency debts. 

 Central bankers argue the zloty's strength is unavoidable because the government's hefty treasury issuance, and falling investment risk linked to prospects for Poland's EU entry, will attract capital regardless of intervention.

title: Polish cabinet meets to tackle zloty strength.
text:
WARSAW, May 14 (Reuters) - Poland's leftist government was expected to issue a strongly-worded statement expressing its concern over the strong zloty on Tuesday and may even propose replacing its free float with a trading band, analysts said. 

 A bout of selling ahead of the government decision has pulled the rug from underneath the buoyant zloty - which hit four month highs versus the dollar last week - and the currency continued to lose ground in early trading. 

 The government's meeting started at 1000 GMT, but no time has been set for a news briefing. 

 Senior cabinet ministers have launched a chorus of demands on the central bank to depress the zloty, worried that the currency's strength is pricing Poland's already falling exports out of key western European markets. 

 But some analysts believe the government may go a step further, proposing to enclose the zloty in a trading band that would require the central bank to intervene if it gets too strong. 

 Under Polish law such policy changes would require the approval of the central bank, which has rejected government pleas for zloty-weakening interventions. 

 But analysts now warn the government could even seek legislative amendments to the National Bank of Poland (NBP) charter in order to ensure its plans succeed. 

 "The government's goal has always been to depress the zloty. So now they will propose some kind of a trading band," said Krzysztof Rybinski, chief economist at bank BZ WBK in Warsaw. 

 "But when the NBP refuses to back this, the government will seek legislative amendments to the central bank charter." 

 Other analysts said, however, they did not expect Premier Leszek Miller's cabinet to make any concrete policy proposals. Ministers blame the central bank's caution in gradually easing its official rates for drawing capital to Poland, which hurts exporters with high hard currency prices for their goods. 

 Poland fully floated the zloty two years ago but will have to corral the unit into a 30-percentage point band when it joins the European Union's exchange rate mechanism (ERM II) after becoming the bloc's member. 

 Hungary, which along with Poland and the Czech Republic is a top candidate for EU entry in 2004, established an ERM-style trading band last year, while the Czech central bank occasionally intervenes against the fully floated Czech crown. 

 FUELING UNCERTAINTY 

 Some analysts say the government may be only bluffing to sow uncertainty in the foreign exchange market to weaken the zloty, pointing out that intervention against the currency in the late 1990s proved ineffectual and costly. 

 The recent flurry of verbal intervention by senior government officials, who said the zloty should be between six and 15 percent weaker, as well as rising concern over possible legislative action have already shaken the unit. 

 The zloty lost 1.5 percent to the dollar and the euro in Tuesday morning trade, before rising slightly. At 0912 GMT it was still four percent down to the dollar from four-month highs it hit last week. The zloty also traded at 3.7189 to the euro. 

 "The market has lost its balance. Investors have become scared," said Maciej Krzak, economist at Citibank's Bank Handlowy. "The government will try to verbally intervene again but market intervention needs to be done quietly." 

 Central bankers argue the zloty's strength is unavoidable because the government's hefty treasury issuance and falling investment risk linked to prospects for Poland's EU entry, will attract capital regardless of intervention. 

 In the neighbouring Czech Republic, a concerted government and central bank effort to depress the buoyant crown failed to make significant impact earlier this year.

title: UPDATE 3-Polish leftists to seek  forex  policy changes.
text:
(Recasts with finance minister Belka comment, previous KATOWICE) 

 WARSAW, May 13 (Reuters) - Poland's leftist government will debate ways to depress the buoyant zloty at its Tuesday cabinet meeting with ministers hoping to convince the independent central bank to intervene against the currency. 

 Senior cabinet ministers have already raised a chorus of demands on the central bank to depress the zloty in recent weeks, worried that the currency's strength is making Poland's already falling exports too pricey for European buyers. 

 But Finance Minister Marek Belka signalled in a late-Monday television interview that the cabinet may go a step further, proposing changes to Poland's foreign exchange currency regime which would necessitate intervention against the zloty. 

 Such plans, however, may fall on deaf ears at the central bank, which favours the present, fully-floated zloty regime. Under Polish law, the government sets foreign exchange policy in agreement with the central bank. 

 "The initiative belongs to the government. We will not discuss a "specific" exchange rate to the dollar or the euro," Belka told private TVN television. "But we will discuss the direction in which (exchange rate) policy should be changed. 

 "This direction may be towards some form of intervention...A trading range could be set, a soft or a hard one, disclosed or secret," he said. 

 Poland fully floated the zloty two years ago but it will have to close the unit in a 30-percentage point band when it joins the European Union's exchange rate mechanism (ERM II) after becoming the bloc's member. 

 Hungary, which along with Poland and the Czech Republic is a top candidate for EU entry in 2004, established an ERM-style trading band last year, while the Czech central bank occasionally intervenes against the fully floated Czech crown. 

 BLAMING ZLOTY 

 Earlier on Monday Polish Premier Leszek Miller renewed calls for a weaker zloty, which he says is needed to lift Poland from a deep growth slowdown, saying the unit's strength would be debated at Tuesday's cabinet meeting. 

 Ministers blame the central bank's caution in gradually easing its official rates for drawing capital to Poland, which hurts exporters with high hard currency prices for their goods. 

 "I agree with Finance Minister Marek Belka the zloty should be at 4.25-4.30 (to the dollar). It is too strong and monetary policy is not good for the economy," Miller told a news conference in the southern city of Katowice. 

 The zloty, which was at four-month highs of 3.95 to the dollar last week, fell in response to ministers' verbal pressure, shedding one percent to the greenback on Monday. It was at 4.0550 to the dollar and at 3.6946 to the euro late on Monday. 

 Late last week, Belka said he was seeking help from the central bank to bring the buoyant zloty down around 6 percent to 4.25 versus the dollar. Presidential aide Witold Orlowski went even further, calling for a 10-15 percent weakening. 

 After April's 50 basis point rate cut, Poland's main rate stands at 9.5 percent, 6 percentage points above CPI. 

 UNBENDING CENTRAL BANK

 But a senior central bank official quickly dashed cabinet hopes for imminent intervention, saying such a move against the zloty was "not acceptable now." Other top central bankers have said intervention was too costly and likely inefficient. 

 Bankers argue the zloty's strength is unavoidable because the government's hefty treasury issuance and falling investment risk linked to prospects for Poland's EU entry, will attract capital in spite of intervention. 

 In neighbouring Czech Republic, a concerted government and central bank effort to depress the buoyant crown failed to make significant impact earlier this year. 

 "At this point, intervention is not acceptable," Monetary Policy Council member Boguslaw Grabowski told Reuters in a brief interview. "You do not stand in front of a charging train." 

 He also repeated his support for Poland's present currency regime, which bankers argue gives them best means to fight inflation. "I am absolutely in favour of the present regime. If we had any doubts, we would have already proposed changes."

title: UPDATE 1-Polish FinMin seeks talks with c.bank over zloty.
text:
GDANSK, Poland, May 10 (Reuters) - Polish Finance Minister Marek Belka said on Friday that he was seeking talks with the central bank aimed at weakening the buoyant zloty by around six percent. 

 Belka is at loggerheads with the central bank over what he considers an over tight monetary policy and an overvalued zloty. He said a decline in the zloty to roughly to 4.25 to the dollar would be "safe" and would aid exporters. 

 The zloty has hit four-month highs against the dollar this week at 3.95 and late on Friday it traded at 4.013. Versus the euro it was at 3.663, showing little impact to Belka's comments. 

 The Finance Minister signalled that he was interested in discussions with the central bank over limiting the zloty's strength within the present currency regime - a fully free float since April 2000 - as well as possible alternative forex regimes. 

 "Monetary policy is a very strong factor which impacts the zloty, because it determines short-term cash flows," Belka told reporters on the sidelines of a conference between Baltic and Nordic finance ministers in the port of Gdansk. 

 "If on this issue (interest rates), the MPC does not see any room for manoeuvre, there exists a possibillity of a return to the broader question of currency regimes, or (conducting) exchange rate policy within the framework of the current regime." 

 Earlier this week, top government officials have called on the central bank to intervene to weaken the Polish currency, but bankers have said that intervention would be fruitless. 

 According to Poland's constitution, the government sets the country's exchange rate regime in agreement with the central bank. The central bank, on the other hand, conducts day-to-day activities, such as forex market intervention. 

 Belka conceded that without central bank support the government could not move to change the exchange rate regime. "Without such talks with the central bank, this is not a possibility." 

 This week Belka signalled that he was leaning towards a managed float currency system, saying that he was not against the reversal of a full flotation but against a fixed rate. 

 Poland, in line to join the European Union in 2004, will have to change its exchange rate regime before it enters the euro-zone's waiting room - the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM-2). 

 Belka has said that before the ERM-2 system pegs the zloty to the euro in a 30 percent-wide trading range he would favour devaluing the Polish currency to increase competitiveness. 

 But Poland's "hands-off" central bank has repeatedly said that only market forces can set the zloty's value.

title: UPDATE 4-Polish gov't,  central bank  joust over strong zloty.
text:
WARSAW, May 8 (Reuters) - Senior Polish ministers, opening a new front in their battle with interest rate hawks at the independent National Bank, on Wednesday called for action to push down the buoyant zloty. 

 But a top central banker insisted that intervening on currency markets would not work. 

 Finance Minister Marek Belka called the strong zloty a "curse" on the economy and was backed by Prime Minister Leszek Miller, who demanded a big interest rate cut and called for a "more realistic level" for the zloty to help exporters. 

 President Aleksander Kwasniewski also threw his weight behind the government's bid to weaken the zloty by blaming the central bank's hawkish policy for Poland's export problems in a late television interview by private TVN station. 

 The left-wing government has long complained that interest rates are too high and have caused the worst economic slowdown in a decade and a record 18 percent jobless rate. "The zloty has to be weaker," Belka told the Polish-American Chamber of Commerce in a speech. "I am in favour of opening discussion with the central bank on possible alternatives." 

 Later, Miller said: "The government expects more decisive easing of interest rates and bringing the zloty to a more realistic level, and a more active central bank role." 

 "The overvalued zloty hurts Polish exporters. There should be close cooperation between the central bank and the government on this issue," he said in a speech on Poland's bid to join the European Union. 

 CENBANK: NO INTERVENTION

 The comments, effectively coded calls for foreign exchangeintervention, were rebuffed by the central bank which defended its hands-off approach to Poland's two-year-old free float. 

 "I believe that forex intervention would not be effective in the current situation," Andrzej Bratkowski, deputy governor of the central bank, told reporters. 

 He added that intervention would undermine monetary policy and could even hit budget revenues. Analysts say zloty sales would increase the money supply and potentially endanger efforts to fight inflation. 

 Belka, who has in the past surprised markets by calling for currency devaluation before Poland adopts the euro later this decade, skirted questions over the precise methods he wants to use to weaken the zloty . 

 "I have already once hinted at possible devaluation. So far, there was no regular discussion on this with the Monetary Policy Council (MPC)," he said. "We should put more emphasis on foreign exchange targeting." 

 FOUR-MONTH HIGH 

 The zloty, which reached four-month highs against the dollar on Tuesday and is up 6.6 percent against the U.S. currency and 1.8 percent versus the euro since early February, rose slightly on the central bank comments in seesaw trade. 

 Bratkowski said the zloty's gains against the dollar reflected the greenback's weakness against the euro - the currency in Poland's largest export markets. 

 In the neighbouring Czech Republic, like Poland an EU candidate, the government and the national bank joined forces recently to weaken the skyrocketing crown through market intervention, but their move had limited impact. 

 Belka warned the zloty would be under appreciation pressure in coming years if Poland joins the EU in 2004 as planned, which will open the way for adoption of the euro and hence attract foreign capital betting on asset price convergence. 

 He added he was "not against the reversal of the free-float regime," implemented two years ago, which he blamed for artificially bloating the currency. 

 "The free float is the best protection against currency crisis but it also produces an environment in which excessive appreciation is possible," he said, adding however that he was against a fixed exchange rate regime. 

 MONETARY POLICY ROW 

 Belka, normally the "good cop" in a government which has been overwhelmingly critical of the MPC's interest rate policy, also cranked up his rhetoric over the panel's reluctance to cut interest rates faster and to act against the zloty. 

 "I am deeply critical of the the wrong, misdirected policies of the National Bank," he said. 

 Belka said the central bank hampered Poland's drive to catch up with the richer EU by aggressively targetting only one area of economic convergence, namely inflation. 

 Even though the MPC has halved official interest rates since early 2001 to 9.5 percent, they remain six percentage points above inflation, now at a post-communist low of 3.3 percent.

title: CORRECTED - ANALYSIS-Forint ruled by EU convergence, not politics.
text:
(In the Budapest item "ANALYSIS-Forint ruled by EU 

  convergence, not politics", please read in the 12th paragraph 

  "...attracted subscriptions worth 107 billion forints ($393.7 

  million)...correcting the dollar figure from $442 million.) 

 A corrected repetition follows. 

 By Sandor Peto 

 BUDAPEST, April 18 (Reuters) - Hungary's centre-left will struggle to keep a lid on forint gains if it wins a national election run-off on Sunday as euro convergence is giving the currency a strong boost, analysts said on Thursday. 

 The Socialists, who narrowly beat Prime Minister Viktor Orban's conservative alliance in a first round vote on April 7, have said they would try to take some of the steam out of the forint's recent strength to protect exporters. 

 "The forint's firming trend continues, and it will be even stronger as exports pick up after the recent slowdown," said Istvan Racz, analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston. 

 "The signs of economic pick-up are already here." 

 Analysts said a surge in bond demand and recent forint levels of 242 to the euro indicate optimism over EU convergence is overriding short-term concerns over the election result, inflation and the state budget. 

 "It's clear the markets expect (EU) convergence trends, whoever's in power," said Barbara Nesztor, regional analyst at Commerzbank in Prague. 

 Peter Medgyessy, Socialist candidate for prime minister, told business leaders earlier that a strong forint was diverting firms' resources away from investment in jobs and development. 

 The Socialists are tipped to form a coalition with the liberal Free Democrats and this centre-left grouping favours economic growth at the expense of rushing to cut inflation. 

 The forint has gained 10 percent in nominal terms in the past year and analysts said there would be more speculation on it strengthening further due to convergence with the wealthy euro zone, regardless of which party won. 

 Hungary hopes to join the European Union in 2004 and the single currency zone a couple of years later. 

 BOND AUCTION OVER-SUBSCRIBED 

 Huge demand at state bond auctions earlier confounded predictions that a more relaxed centre-left inflation policy would be less favourable for the currency and bond markets than a second term for Orban's conservatives, analysts said. 

 An auction of the five-year 2007/D bond - seen as Hungary's convergence benchmark - attracted subscriptions worth 107 billion Hungarian forints ($393.7 million), prompting the government to raise the issue to 40 billion forints from 30 billion. 

 Inflation has dropped to under six percent from nearly 11 percent a year ago, and could dip below five percent by June, although higher world crude oil prices will act against this. 

 Both rival political blocs have pledged voters they will raise wages which, in real net terms, jumped 11.5 percent year-on-year in the first two months of this year. 

 Further wage increases will counter inflation cuts by swelling the budget deficit at a time when purchasing power is surging, analysts said. 

 "It seems the central bank underestimated the potential for wage growth this year, prompting them to postpone rate cuts in the near future," Lehman Brothers said in a market update. 

 "If the Socialists win, we assume the budget deficit will be revised higher," said Lehman analyst Robert Beange. 

 With little relief from fiscal pressure, Hungary may only be able to keep trimming inflation via exchange rate appreciation, Commerzbank's Nesztor said. 

 "The Socialists would only be able to curb the forint by verbal intervention," she said, noting recent intervention in Poland and the Czech Republic had had only a limited impact. 

 CSFB's Racz said the forint would continue to rise this year, fuelled by growth that is likely to be higher than the recent three percent and continued gains in Hungarian productivity.

title: Hungary forint, zloty seen diverging on way to ERM.
text:
BUDAPEST, Feb 7 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint is likely to strengthen before it enters the European Exchange Rate Mechanism in 2004, despite a suggestion by Poland's finance minister that the zloty should be devalued before EU entry, analysts said. 

 Marek Belka, stressing he was speaking only for himself, said late on Wednesday that the zloty could suffer speculative attack after Poland wraps up European Union (EU) accession talks, and advocated an "up-front" devaluation of the currency. 

 "The zloty is regarded fundamentally overvalued now," said Gyorgy Kovacs of DZ Bank. "Everybody expects the forint to strengthen, while the best case for the zloty is stability." 

 A weaker unit ahead of Poland's entry into the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM-2) - which is designed to ensure currency stability prior to entering the euro zone - would help bolster the economy. 

 Analysts said Belka was trying to tackle a specific Polish problem of the worst economic slowdown in the largest future EU member, while other candidates in the region performed well. 

 "Belka is trying to ride a weak (bond and zloty) market sentiment and talk the zloty down to even lower levels," said Istvan Racz, regional analyst at CSFB in Budapest. "The economy is weak, unemployment high - the currency is an issue there." Currencies in the largest candidate countries in Central Europe, which are set to close accession talks this year, surged in the past year, weighing on export performances amid a global slowdown. Hungary weathered it well, while Poland was worst hit. 

 European Central Bank officials warned last year that the candidates must meet the EU's strict inflation criteria but also need a pick-up in growth and wages - requirements which would may bring about exchange rate adjustment in the region. 

 DIFFERENT TRACKS, SAME DESTINATION 

 Analysts said Belka's words reflected the rhetoric of other ministers, who advocate a lower exchange rate to boost exports and move the economy out from stagnation. 

 The Czechs are making efforts to curb the surging crown and Hungary can also expect the forint to rise, but both economies are growing robustly at 3-4 percent rates. 

 Poland needs a weak currency to kick-start its economy and currently only verbal intervention is possible as Poland must set up a parity rate for the zloty, which floats freely, if it wants it to devalue, analysts said. A Polish adjustment should be cautious as the applicants must enter the ERM with relatively stable exchange rates, while closing entry talks, a likely global recovery and new productivity gains could put upwards pressure on central European currencies by next year, analysts said. 

 "If you fix the currency at a weaker than justified level (in the ERM), its firming is blocked and this creates inflationary pressure," said Kovacs. 

 Hungary is one step ahead of Poland after adopting an ERM-type 30-percent forint flotation band last year. 

 The band will survive EU entry, but convergence-triggered capital inflows could lead the government to move the parity rate higher by some 10 percent next year so as to prevent the currency banging at the top of the band, analysts said. 

 "The forint is not overvalued, its purchasing power parity is well behind the euro, while its productivity disadvantage narrows," Racz said. "A forint at the top of the band is unpleasant for investors - there is no upside, only downside." The forint and Hungarian bonds weakened this week. The forint traded at 11 percent above parity on Wednesday, dragged down by Polish falls after rises on the wings of rallies in Poland early this year.

title: UPDATE 1-Polish budget gap to stay high through 2004-Belka.
text:
WARSAW, Jan 28 (Reuters) - Polish Finance Minister Marek Belka called his 2002 budget plan 'crisis-proof' on Monday, ruling out a revision to increase the deficit later this year, but said the financing gap would not fall in coming years. The three-month-old leftist administration has had to slash spending and shore up revenues to prevent a financial crisis, capping the 2002 budget deficit at 40 billion zlotys ($9.7 billion) or 5.2 percent of gross domestic product. 

 Without austerity measures the deficit was set to balloon to 90 billion zlotys or an unfinanceable 11 percent of GDP. 

 "I am not considering the possibility of budget revision this year. This budget is crisis-proof," Belka told Reuters in an interview. 

 Poland's brush with financial collapse stemmed from lavish spending plans of the previous right-wing cabinet, an inefficient public sector and a deep economic slowdown which cut into tax revenues. 

 Economic growth is expected to remain around one percent this year, little changed from last year's growth - the worst in a decade and a major handicap in preparing to join the European Union as soon as 2004. 

 "In March I will know more about what the effect of economic stagnation on revenues. And I will be sure that we assumed really conservative tax inflows," Belka said. 

 But Belka said that reducing the deficit - a key precondition set by the central bank for deep interest rate cuts - was not on the card for the next two years. 

 "I am taking it into account that in the next year or two the deficit could oscillate around this year's level or maybe rise slightly to 42 or 43 billion zlotys," he said. 

 ZLOTY INTERVENTION

 Belka also said Poland's free floating currency regime did not rule out foreign exchange intervention against the buoyant zloty, which he has tried to talk down for months. 

 "The free float currency regime we have does not rule out jaw-boning. I tried that and I tried to charm the zloty to fall to 4.25 to the dollar and it just did not work. The free float does not rule out intervention," he said. 

 Earlier this month, Belka said a 4.25 exchange rate of the zloty to the dollar would be favourable for Polish exporters, but his and other cabinet members' verbal attacks on the zloty attracted little more than shrugs from currency market. 

 The Polish unit rose sharply early this year, reaching 2-1/2-year highs to the dollar as money poured in to take advantage of attractive yields in Polish debt instruments. 

 The National Bank of Poland, which shares responsibility for the country's forex regime, says a free floating currency should not be the subject of intervention. The neighbouring Czech Republic has, however, intervened to cool the crown's strength. 

 Earlier this month, markets speculated that the government may have won central bank backing for intervention against the zloty during a rare face-to-face meeting between ministers and bankers. This sent the zloty tumbling by eight percent. 

 Monetary Policy Council members moved to quell such talk. 

 Asked if he wanted the central bank to intervene against the zloty, Belka said: "I think we should aim for some depreciation. There are many ways. We can talk, intervene or cut rates."

title: Polish budget gap may increase in 2003, 2004 - Belka.
