title: Balcerowicz - unclear if Czech  intervention  works.
text:
KRAKOW, Poland, Jan 22 (Reuters) - Poland's national bank Governor Leszek Balcerowicz said on Tuesday it was not clear whether Czech intervention against the buoyant crown would succeed. 

 The Czech central bank (CNB) stepped into the market on Monday to weaken the crown after it rallied sharply, but the unit's subsequent decline was not sustained as buyers returned. 

 "Central bank interventions are not always successful and we will see effects of the Czech intervention after some time passes," Balcerowicz told reporters after receiving an award in the southern city of Krakow. 

 He quickly reiterated the Polish national's bank position against intervention in the currency markets, saying: 

 "In the Czech (market) there were huge inflows from privatisation, causing large influx of foreign currencies. In Poland, the scale of sell-offs is smaller...and the government has a foreign currency account for privatisation inflows." 

 Analysts say the CNB's move did little to address the fundamental reasons behind crown strength and, while it may dent the crown's rise in the short term, it might also store up problems for later. 

 Earlier this year the zloty reached a 2-1/2 year high against the dollar on the back of portolio inflows seeking to lock in high yields before Poland cuts interest rates. 

 It has fallen slightly in recent days on worries that the Monetary Policy Council may not cut rates at its nearest meeting on January 29-30. 

 Some analysts said that rumours, denied by the central bank, of a coordinated effort by the central bank and the government to weaken the zloty have also played a role in the zloty's recent slide.

title: ANALYSIS-Czechs' crown problem mirrored across region.
text:
LONDON, Jan 22 (Reuters) - Czech authorities have adopted a high risk strategy in trying to curb the crown's rise, highlighting a problem facing other emerging European currencies as EU accession triggers strong foreign investment flows. 

 The Czech National Bank (CNB) intervened on Monday and cut interest rates by 25 basis points in an effort to curb the crown's sharp appreciation, but buyers soon returned to the market after an initial spike lower. 

 Analysts said the CNB's move did little to address the fundamental reasons behind crown strength and, while it may hold up the crown's rise in the short term, it might also store up problems for a later date. 

 "If you ask whether this intervention is in line with Czech fundamentals, the answer is no," said Callum Henderson, emerging markets currency analyst at Citibank. 

 Poland and Hungary, which like the Czech Republic are seen likely to join the European Union (EU) in 2004, are also facing problems posed by strong currencies. 

 However, analysts see currency intervention as a high-risk strategy, from which Poland and Hungary have shied away. 

 While authorities in some emerging markets would welcome hefty inflows of foreign investment, for the Czechs they are mainly causing headaches. 

 A deal between the government and the central bank last week arranged to lock away 25 billion Czech crowns ($683 million) in privatisation proceeds in the bank's foreign reserves until 2007. 

 "Even if all privatisation revenues are kept off the market this year, which will be difficult, the Czechs are still going to see strong portfolio inflows," Henderson said. 

 Yet with privatisation revenues of around 144 billion crowns due, and more expected to follow, few believe that the deal will be enough to stem the crown's steep ascent. 

 The Czech bond market also is expected to continue to attract capital inflows as its economy converges ahead of EU accession and interest rates fall towards euro zone levels. 

INTERVENTION AS SMOOTHING MECHANISM 

 While many market players agree the authorities will not be able to stop the crown strengthening over the long term, some accept the central bank has at least managed to slow it down. 

 "One can assume that if the central bank wasn't there the (euro/crown) market would be trading much lower," said a senior dealer at a bank in London. 

 The amount of Monday's intervention was estimated by traders at between 200-400 million euros, and with average daily turnover in the region of 450 million euros it's clear that those amounts can have a significant impact. 

 However, the dealer said the central bank might be storing up trouble for the future if it continues to intervene. 

 The central bank's short crown position is likely to lose money if, as even the authorities expect, the unit strengthens over the long term. This loss will have to be accounted for in the government budget, which is already deep in deficit. 

 Persistent intervention and rate cuts to combat crown strength could also lead to inflationary pressure. 

 DIFFERENT APPROACH IN POLAND, HUNGARY 

 In some ways strong local currencies are more of a headache for Hungary and particularly Poland, because their economies aren't performing as well as in the Czech Republic. 

 But so far the authorities have limited their actions to verbal intervention and monetary easing. 

 "In Poland, the central bank has strongly committed to non intervention since moving to a free-float exchange rate," said Marco Annunziata, chief economist for emerging Europe at Deutsche Bank. 

 Cezary Jozefiak, a member of the Polish Monetary Policy Council, earlier this month reiterated the bank's long-standing view that intervention was not an option. 

 Polish officials believe the market should be left to find its own level and recognise there is little they can do to reverse the trend in the zloty, Annunziata added. 

 In Hungary, the central bank has embarked on an aggressive series of rate cuts which has seen the key two-week deposit rate reduced by 2.5 percent since last May. 

 The cuts are not undertaken to weaken the forint, but justified on the view that currency strength has helped bring inflation down, offering more scope for monetary easing. 

 "Hungarian policy has been far more accommodative of a strong currency than the Czechs'," said Juliet Sampson, emerging markets analyst at Bank of America. 

 "They're unlikely to intervene because they're content with the level of the forint, at least for now, and everything they have said confirms that," she added. 

 Sampson said Czech sensitivity stems from a trade and current account balance hit by currency strength in the past. 

 But she added that there was, as yet, little evidence that strong currencies in emerging Europe were having a major negative impact on exporters. 

 "We're yet to see deficits ballooning, with productivity gains so far helping to offset currency strength."

title: Emerging  FX -Zloty edgy pre rate decision, calm elsewhere.
text:
LONDON, July 20 (Reuters) - The Polish zloty traded a touch softer on Friday as players nervously awaited the Monetary Policy Council (MPC) rate decision. 

 Elsewhere, most emerging market currencies held to established ranges in the absence of any further ructions in Argentina or Turkey. 

 The zloty handed back some of Thursday's gains, with a few players still jittery about a possible rate cut from the MPC. Most analysts still expect rates to be kept on hold, but weak economic data earlier in the week has cast doubt on the outcome. 

 "The latest data was shocking and clearly shows that something needs to be done," said Marco Annunziata, emerging markets analyst at Deutsche Bank. 

 "However, I think the MPC will want to see more evidence that the external environment has settled down before they shift policy," he added. 

 The zloty fell over seven percent against the euro early last week as contagion from Argentina prompted speculators to close out their long positions. 

Poland's main rate, the minimum 28-day intervention rate, currently stands at 15.50 percent. 

 At 0900 GMT the zloty traded at 3.6930 to the euro from 3.6726 late on Thursday, and at 4.2250 to the dollar from 4.2195. 

 EXPORTERS BUOY RAND OFF LOWS 

 Dealers reported rand buying from local exporters and from a fund account around the 8.28 level helped the South African unit rally back from early weakness. 

 Ongoing concerns over Argentina continue to make for nervous trade but, with no major developments overnight, players are expecting a quieter session on Friday. 

 "Barring fresh shocks from Argentina I think the market could settle down from here heading into the weekend," said one London-based trader. 

 The rand traded at 8.2598 to the dollar from 8.2900 late on Thursday. 

 LIRA HOLDS FIRM 

 The Turkish lira was in consolidative mood after strong gains in the past two sessions. 

 Sentiment was bolstered by news HSBC had won the tender to buy the troubled Demirbank. Foreign involvement is seen as key to putting the ailing banking sector back on its feet. 

 The lira was quoted at 1,325,000 to the dollar on the central-bank brokered spot market from 1,340,000 at Thursday's close.

title: Polish govt think-tank sees rates 600bp too high.
text:
WARSAW, May 25 (Reuters) - A Polish government think-tank said on Friday the central bank's current interest rate levels were cramping economic growth and needed to be reduced by 600 basis points. 

 "I repeat, the central bank's interest rates are now 600 basis points too high," RCSS head Jerzy Kropiwnicki told a news conference. 

 "In my view, the MPC should have cut rates by six percentage points in three steps at the start of this year." 

Poland's main interest rate, the minimum 28-day intervention rate, is now at 17 percent, following two 100-basis points cuts over the first quarter of this year. 

 Kropiwnicki, who has repeatedly criticised the central bank's restrictive approach to monetary policy, also said Polish exports would begin to feel the impact of the zloty currency's rally from June.

title: Emerging  FX -zloty buoyant, Czech crown and rand soft.
text:
LONDON, March 7 (Reuters) - The Polish zloty remained buoyant on Wednesday, rising to 19-month highs against the dollar and record peaks against the euro, underpinned by an improving economic outlook and new bond issuance. 

 But the currency edged off those highs after Polish Finance Minister Jaroslaw Bauc moved to weaken the rally and said the unit could fall in coming months. 

 The Czech crown fell to six-week lows against the euro for the second consecutive day and trimmed gains from earlier five-day highs against the dollar. There were lingering fears that crown strength might prompt action by the central bank. 

 Meanwhile, the South African rand continued to struggle, falling to three-week lows against the dollar for the second straight day and nearing four-week lows against the euro. 

 "The zloty is the choice of the day. The zloty opened higher on expectations of strong foreign interest for the 2.5 billion zloty bond tender but has pulled back slightly and we are not yet sure how strong the interest has been," said a trader at a U.S. bank. 

 "We like the zloty because it's a high carry trade opportunity and fundamentals look okay and inflation is dropping. Polish officials are trying to talk it down but we don't expect intervention." 

 POLISH TENDER EYED 

 The results of Poland's 2.5 billion zloty worth of T-bonds were scheduled for later in the day. 

 By 1115 GMT, the zloty rose as far as 3.9470 to the dollar , according to Reuters data. It hit peaks around 3.6835 against the euro . 

 Polish data late Tuesday showed that food prices fell 0.2 percent in the second half of February over the same period in January. The fall in prices fuelled hopes for a sharp decline in February inflation and future rate cuts. 

 A Finance Ministry official said after the data release that CPI probably fell to a year-on-year 6.9-7.0 percent in February from January's 7.4 percent. 

 The Czech crown hit a five-day high of 37.138 per dollar before paring gains. It hit lows around 34.970 per euro . 

 Traders said speculation about central bank intervention was sparked by the minutes of the central bank's February meeting, released this week. The minutes showed the governing board agreed that intervention was an option the bank "is prepared to use if the need should arise". 

 The Czech central bank's foreign exchange reserves edged up marginally to $13.12 billion at the end of February from $13.07 billion in January. 

 RAND SOFT 

 The South African rand fell as far as 7.8913 against the dollar , according to Reuters data, and hit lows around 7.3430 against the euro . 

 Bond exchange data showed that foreigners were net sellers of 66.16 million rand's worth of South African bonds on Tuesday after buying 530.51 million rand on Monday. 

 The central bank governor Tito Mboweni reiterated on Tuesday that the central bank was targeting inflation and the exchange rate. The market has been wary of the government's decision to introduce an inflation target of between three and six percent, which some feel could further curb current sluggish growth. 

 However, traders expected some supoort from potential capital inflows from an upcoming eurobond issue and Anglo American and De Beers deal. 

 "The bond issuance should be good for the rand, but the forex risk is making foreign investors wary," saidStefan Kolek, emerging market strategist at HypoVereinsbank in Munich. 

 "There are still risks that socially and politically things could deteriorate. There are still question marks over whether the government will be able to meet its privatisation target. Mboweni's comments also concerned the market."

title: Polish MPC starts meeting, rates seen flat.
text:
WARSAW, Jan 22 (Reuters) - Poland's Monetary Policy Council (MPC) on Monday was holding its first monthly meeting chaired by ex-finance minister Leszek Balercerowicz on Monday, with analysts expecting no interest rate changes to be made. 

 Balcerowicz, who was responsible for Poland's deep economic reforms of the early 1990s, took over the central bank and the chairmanship of the rate-setting Council this month. 

 Most analysts expect the MPC to refrain from cutting interest rates until at least February, when it will know the effects of start-of-the-year increases in controlled prices. 

 Balcerowicz and the 10-member MPC will likely also withhold rate cuts to weigh the effect of a recent government decision to increase the 2001 budget deficit, analysts said. 

 Balcerowicz, the leader of a liberal party before his nomination for central banker, will probably also want to establish his image as an independent banker by resisting mounting political pressure for lower rates to rekindle growth. 

 "Judging by MPC members' recent statements, they view January as too early to cut," said Krzysztof Rybinski, chief economist at ING Barings in Warsaw. The MPC's history of missing their end-year inflation targets may also make the hawkish council cautious on cutting the costs of borrowing. The Council aims to lower CPI to 6-8 percent by end-2001 from 8.5 percent in December 2000. 

 A Reuters poll from Friday showed that analysts expected the MPC to start their long-anticipated process of lowering rates next month, with a 150 basis point cut. 

Poland's main interest rate, the 19 percent money market intervention rate, stands 10.5 percent above year-on-year inflation. The Lombard rate, a point of reference for many individual credit plans, is at a chokingly high 23 percent. 

 These high rates slowed economic growth to less than three percent in the fourth quarter of 2000 from six percent in the first quarter of last year and froze consumption levels. 

 The zloty, which has steadied after a rapid strengthening in the last months of 2000, is expected to lose ground if rates are unexpectedly cut. 

 If the Council moves to a loosening policy bias from its present neutral stance, the zloty is expected to remain steady. 

 Local-currency debt is expected to remain the focus of international investors even if rates are cut, as the market anticipates a further reduction in rates over 2001. 

 Poland tightened monetary policy in late 1999 to keep a lid on domestic demand and slow a bulging current account deficit, which peaked at 8.3 percent of GDP in March 2000 before narrowing to an estimated 6.2 percent in December.

title: IMF says zloty  interventions  OK to help reserves.
text:
WARSAW, Dec 13 (Reuters) - The International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Wednesday said Poland's central bank could consider foreign exchange intervention to maintain the ratio of foreign reserves to hard currency liabilities. 

 "Currently, reserves are at a comfortable level relative to imports and short-term debt, but these ratios will fall in the absence of intervention," the IMF said in a statement. 

 "To the extent that markets take comfort from these ratios, the NBP may wish at some stage to prevent a sustained decline by setting a neutral rule to intervene to maintain these ratios," the fund said after ending its semi-annual mission to Poland. 

 The National Bank of Poland (NBP) said after it fully floated the zloty in April this year that it would not intervene on the currency market, although it did reserve the right to do so if needed. 

 Poland's foreign currency reserve assets, those held by the central bank, stood at $26.5 billion in November. 

 Not taking into account global currency fluctuations, the level of reserves can only grow if the central bank buys foreign currencies on the forex market. The reserves shrink whenever the government dips into them to finance foreign debt costs. 

 The IMF also said the government's hard currency account, set up to retain off-shore privatisation inflows, should be transaparent and not used to affect the exchange rate levels.

title: Emerging  FX -ECB euro-buying boosts Europe vs dlr.
text:
LONDON, Nov 3 (Reuters) - Emerging currencies in Europe rallied strongly against the dollar on Friday, fuelled by a fresh round of European Central Bank euro-buying which propelled the single currency higher against the dollar. 

 The zloty and Czech crown both rose more than one percent against the dollar and South Africa's rand also pushed higher after the ECB intervention which sent the euro briefly up more than 1.5 cents to peaks near $0.88. 

 The stronger euro was also marked up against its emerging Europe counterparts but dealers said its gains were relatively small compared with those currencies' reaction to the retreating dollar. 

 "Emerging Europe has been strengthening generally even against the higher euro, but it is premature to start talking about a big macroeconomic impact on the basis of these fairly small moves in the euro," said one emerging market analyst. 

 A stronger euro is seen benefiting the trade competitiveness of emerging Europe as the bulk of their exports go to euro-zone countries. At the same time, a weaker dollar makes their dollar-denominated imports, particularly oil, cheaper. 

 The zloty firmed to 4.4750 to the dollar, its strongest levels since September 18. It stood at 3.9152 to the euro from early levels around 3.9250. 

 The Czech crown firmed to 39.68/71 per dollar, just short of a two-month peak it hit earlier. It stood at 34.69/72 to the euro from 34.63/38. 

 Analysts added that investor sentiment towards emerging markets was improving, giving currencies in Europe some independent strength against sharp moves in the euro. 

 "We're seeing better performance in emerging markets in general. JP Morgan's EMBI+ bond index spread over Treasuries has narrowed, stock markets are performing a bit better, conditions are becoming more supportive for emerging markets," said Jake Moore, currency strategist at Barclays Capital. 

 "But it's too early to say if this is just a temporary lull in the pressures on emerging markets." 

 ZLOTY BUOYED BY CURRENT ACCOUNT DATA 

 The zloty was already marked higher before Friday's intervention, buoyed by Poland's better-than-expected current account data for September released late on Thursday. 

 The gap came in at a tame $594 million in September as a slowing economy curbed imports and the country delayed the bulk of its foreign debt servicing costs to October, analysts said. 

 The deficit was lower than analysts' forecasts as well as the $961 million gap in August. 

 "Poland is definitely becoming more attractive but the upside may be limited because of political problems that could erupt at any point. And though the current account deficit is falling, it is still massive," said Barclay Capital's Moore. 

 The slowing economy could also see Polish interest rates - currently 19-23 percent - cut early next year which could erode support for the zloty, analysts said. 

 Data released on Friday showed Hungary's current account posted a 340 million euro deficit in September after a surplus of 176 million euros in August. 

 "The contrast is interesting between Poland and Hungary because now they look to be at opposite ends of the economic cycle," said David Lubin, emerging markets strategist at HSBC. 

 "Poland is slowing down while Hungary is showing increasing signs of overheating...In terms of relative value, it would make sense to get out of the Hungarian bond market and get into the Polish one." 

 Hungary's forint weakened to 1.98 percent above its parity rate within its 4.5 percent wide trading band after the current account data. On Thursday the forint finished at 2.09 percent above parity.

title: Emerging  FX -Zloty absorbs rate rise, shekel surges.
text:
LONDON, Aug 31 (Reuters) - The Polish zloty traded in tight ranges on Thursday following an expected rate rise in the previous session, while the Israeli shekel hit multi-month highs amid speculation over the alteration of its trading band. 

 The zloty recovered from four-week lows against the dollar set on Wednesday ahead of a 150-basis-point increase in Poland's main reference rate, the minimum 28-day intervention rate, to 19.0 percent. 

 High interest rates were likely to continue to attract investors into Poland, so boosting the zloty, despite ongoing worries about inflation, analysts said. 

 "We have not seen the peak in the interest rate cycle," said Stuart Brown, head of emerging markets research at BNP Paribas in London. "We had a rather hawkish statement from the central bank, and Poland already has some of the best levels of return in emerging markets." 

 Monetary Policy Council (MPC) members said the hike was a preventive measure to offset a possible rise in inflationary expectations. They said it would not have a significant effect on economic growth and the zloty. 

 The zloty was trading at 4.3800/4.3815 at 0945 GMT, from Wednesday's lows of 4.4060. 

 Against the euro , the zloty edged off the previous day's one-week highs as the euro recovered slightly across the board, and was trading at 3.9205/28. 

 SHEKEL BREAKS KEY RESISTANCE 

 The shekel firmed to its highest level since March, strengthening beyond the key level of 4.00 to the dollar, as Israeli economic policymakers weighed changing its trading band mechanism and companies converted the currency to pay September 1 wages. 

 A longstanding debate between the Bank of Israel and the Finance Ministry on the shekel's trading band appeared to soften this week. While the ministry opposes removing the band, sources said it has proposed changing the slope of the band, most probably from a two percent incline to zero. 

 The shekel has inched its way in recent months towards the strongest limit of the band - a mechanism that allows the shekel to fluctuate against a basket of foreign currencies some 19 percent above and below a gradually depreciating midpoint. 

 Traders in Israel said that as of early Thursday, the shekel was 1.4 percentage point away from the strongest point in its band and that talk of changing the mechanism emboldened customers to sell more dollars. At current rates, the shekel would need to advance to 3.9330 to the dollar to reach its strongpoint. 

 The shekel retreated beyond 4.00 to the dollar by 0945 GMT from earlier highs of 3.9980, and was trading at 4.0030/70. 

 The central bank seeks to abolish the band and eliminate the need for market intervention when the shekel hits its upper or lower limits. But faced with strong opposition at the Treasury, the Bank of Israel reportedly suggested changing the slope from a two percent depreciation rate to allow for a shekel appreciation of up to three percent yearly. 

 "The trading band discussion is the result of other things which have helped the shekel - higher inflows, falling inflation," said Paul Kinghorn, emerging markets currency strategist at HSBC in London. "But the central bank would have to accompany any change in the band with a rate cut, so we would recommend being long the basket against the shekel." 

 The Bank of Israel said on Monday it would cut its key lending rate by 0.2 of a percentage point to 8.9 percent for September, the eighth reduction in the last 10 months. 

 The Czech crown recovered from the previous day's three-month lows against the dollar in line with a recovery in the euro. 

 All 21 analysts polled by Reuters said the Czech central bank would not move its two-week repo rate, currently at 5.25 percent, following its board meeting later in the day. 

 The crown was trading at 39.510/535 to the dollar and 35.357/387 to the euro , near earlier one-week lows against the euro of 35.408. 

 Czech end-July money supply, measured by the M2 indicator, grew by 7.3 percent year-on-year after growth of 5.7 percent at the end of June. 

 The Slovak crown largely ignored Wednesday's widely expected cut in key interest rates by the central bank (NBS).The NBS cut its overnight rates for sterilising and refinancing operations by 50 basis points each to 6.5 percent and 9.5 percent respectively. It cut its two-week repo rate to 8.25 percent, from 8.5 percent. 

 The Slovak crown also benefited from a recovery in the euro, pulling back from the previous day's three-month lows against the dollar to trade at 47.649/719 . It was rangebound against the euro at 42.681/761.

title: ANALYSIS- FX  history backs call to end shekel trading bands.
text:
LONDON, Aug 21 (Reuters) - The history of currency trading bands backs up the view of Bank of Israel governor David Klein who is calling for the bands which confine the shekel to be scrapped while times are good. 

 The central banker told Reuters in an interview on Sunday that the currency's current trading limits could endanger Israel's inflation target and called for their elimination while the currency market was calm. 

 Analysts agreed, saying the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM) crisis in 1992 and the Asian crisis which broke out five years later highlighted the difficulties of defending a currency linkage in the face of financial market scepticism. 

 By contrast, the Polish zloty, which went into a free float on April 11, was seen offering encouragement for a transition when market conditions were favourable. 

 The shekel is allowed to trade some 17 percent above and below a gradually depreciating midpoint, with the central bank committed to defending the currency once it reaches the upper or lower limits of the band. 

 The band depreciates two percent annually. But the shekel has strengthened to within three percent of the top of its band on the back of a strong domestic equity market, investment flows into its technology sector and healthy export growth. 

 Once the top of the band is reached, the BOI would have to buy foreign currencies to protect the peg. This would result in shekels pouring into the private sector banking system, a development which would be inflationary, as Klein pointed out. 

 "The crawl in any currency leads to predictability and that leads to the perception of reduced foreign exchange risks, which in turn leads to increased inward investment," said Callum Henderson, currency strategist at SSSB/Citibank in London. 

 "The long-term risk of any crawl is that you attract such large amounts of inward investment because of the predictability that that could lead to a substantially overvalued currency - which eventually is reversed and can, like in the case of Thailand, be reversed quite suddenly with nasty results." 

 POLAND'S MOVE SEEN A SUCCESS 

 Despite worries that a shift to free float could trigger a runaway appreciation in the already buoyant shekel and hurt Israel's trade competitiveness, analysts said the country might be wise to remove the band, which looked certain to be tested. 

 "I think the case for moving to a free float is pretty clear and the Bank of Israel has a strong argument for moving in that direction, for asking the government to go along," said Riccardo Barbieri, head of emerging markets economic research at Morgan Stanley Dean Witter in London. 

 "At the moment, the issue is the stronger side of the band. If the shekel gets there, the central bank will be forced to effectively ease interest rates perhaps beyond what they deem appropriate - they want to gain maximum flexibility." 

 Britain's experience of sterling being forced out of the ERM in 1992, highlighted the economic damage that could result from using monetary policy to defend currency trading bands. 

 The British authorities jacked up interest rates in a bid to fend off speculative attack on the pound, even though tighter monetary policy was not what the economy needed. 

 But this only prompted speculators, who did not think higher rates were sustainable, to step up their attack on sterling. 

 To be sure, there is little evidence Israel's economy is overheating, and there has even been speculation the central bank would cut interest rates in the near future anyway. 

 "At some point they will have to ease interest rates irrespective of the exchange rate target because they're overachieving in terms of inflation. But the central bank wants to have maximum flexibility to hit the inflation target also on a medium-term basis," Barbieri said. 

 Analysts said Poland's recent shift to free float has been a success overall, despite some initial market volatility. 

 "Poland adopted a very prudent policy of eliminating the crawl while the market was quite calm in order to avoid a situation whereby it would be forced to abandon the crawl during more volatile and turbulent times," Henderson said. 

 Were Poland forced to defend its old peg through currency intervention, it would have been in more serious trouble in attempting to contain inflation, they said. 

 Polish inflation data last week showed consumer prices had risen by 11.6 percent in July, well above expectations and spurring talk of a near-term interest rate increase of one percentage point or more. 

 "The inflation picture is a little bit different in Israel, but the long-term risk is the same," said a trader at a U.S. bank in London.

title: IMF wants transparent Polish govt  currency  account.
text:
WARSAW, May 18 (Reuters) - The International Monetary Fund said on Thursday Poland should avoid discretionary intervention on the foreign exchange market and keep the special government currency account fully transparent to markets. 

 "Discretionary intervention should be avoided," the IMF said in its bi-annual review of Poland's economy. 

 "(But) a case can be made to raise gross reserves according to a predetermined and announced schedule so as to maintain currently strong vulnerability indicators on reserves," it said. 

 Poland's reserves are now at $25.6 billion, more than seven months' worth of imports. 

Foreign exchange market interventions are in the realm of Poland's independent central bank, which fully floated the zloty in April to increase its volatility and thereby discourage short-term foreign portfolio investment. 

 The bank vowed it would not intervene on the market, saying it would go against the idea of the flotation, and is thought to have kept its word during the recent large zloty swings. 

 But the IMF comments seemed to be directed mainly at the finance ministry, which created a currency account in the central bank earlier this year. 

 It can effectively intervene on the market by announcing flows in and out of the special foreign currency account set up to hold revenues from privatisation deals, which used to boost the level of the zloty artificially. 

 But the finance ministry has been vague on how much cash it plans to keep in the account, when it would deposit it there or when it would withdraw it to pay off Poland's external debt. 

 News of such flows can strongly move the shallow local foreign exchange market. 

 "The foreign exchage account of the government...should be operated in a manner consistent with the principle of non-discretionary intervention," the IMF wrote. 

 Analysts estimate Poland can expect some $5 billion in foreign inflows in privatisation this year alone. 

 "It will be important therefore that early specific public committments should be made concerning the amount of privatisation receipts that will be deposited into and withdrawn from the government account with the NBP," the IMF said. 

 "Balances in the account should be fully transparent to markets," it added. 

 The IMF also said a government plan to sharply curb the fiscal gap and the central bank's aim of improving its inflation targetting framework would create ideal conditions to abolish the remaining controls on short-term capital moves. 

 Poland now allows full zloty convertibility for current account purpuses but has kept some restrictions on short-term portfolio flows to diminish chances of a speculative attack on the zloty. 

 "Given the sizeable spot and forward on-and off-shore market in the zloty, as well as the uninhibited trade in relatively liquid long-term financial instruments it is unlikely that the abolition of the remaining controls would increase Poland's vulnerability," the IMF report said. ((Jan Strupczewski, Warsaw Newsroom, tel.+48 22 653 9700, fax. +48 22 653 9781, warsaw.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Polish c.bank non-committal on zloty  intervention .
text:
WARSAW, April 11 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank has not promised to intervene if the zloty moves sharply after it floats freely from tomorrow, despite requests for such assurances from some government advisers, a deputy finance minister said on Tuesday. 


The Polish government gave final approval for the full flotation of the zloty	  on Tuesday, allowing the central bank to eliminate the unit's 30-point trading band and the 0.3 percent monthly devaluation rate from Wednesday.


 The National Bank of Poland (NBP) asked for the government's approval in the middle of 1999, prompting some finance ministry advisers to seek assurances that the NBP would curb sudden zloty moves, even after the float, to protect exporters. 

 But Deputy Finance Minister Jaroslaw Bauc said no such agreement had been discussed by the government and the central bank. 

 "There was no talk on this issue," Bauc told reporters following a news conference on the flotation. 

 Finance Ministry advisers had earlier warned that surges in the zloty, which they said were more likely after the float, could damage Poland's already weak export performance and cause further expansion of the large current account deficit. 

 "We would expect the NBP to declare it would use the flotation carefully and would not allow the current account gap to deteriorate when the zloty appreciates, by intervening in the forex market," adviser Witold Orlowski said in January. 

 Poland's current account deficit ran at some eight percent of gross domestic product in February and widened to 7.6 percent of GDP in 1999 from 4.4 percent a year before. 

 A member of the rate-setting Monetary Policy Council, Boguslaw Grabowski, told Tuesday's news conference the central bank did not plan to intervene in the market but reserved the right to do so if need arose. ((Justyna Pawlak, Warsaw Newsroom, tel. +48 22 653 9700, fax +48 22 653 9780, justyna.pawlak@reuters.com)).

title: Polish Council not planning zloty  interventions .
text:
WARSAW, Apr 11 (Reuters) - Poland's Monetary Policy Council is not planning to intervene in the zloty exchange market now the currency has been fully floated, although it retains the right to do so, a leading Council member said on Tuesday. 

 "We are not planning to participate in the market but we have such a right," said Boguslaw Grabowski at a news conference after the government agreed to the central bank's council request that the zloty should be freed. 

 The government announced on Tuesday it had given the central bank the right to intervene in the zloty market even though the currency would henceforth trade without restrictions. 

 Grabowski also said there were no reasons why the float should affect the zloty's value in the short-term. 

 "I see no economic reasons for the zloty float to influence the market in the short-term," he said. "This will not change the trends on the forex market." ((Warsaw newsroom +48 22 653 9700, fax +48 22 653 9781, warsaw.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Zloty  intervention  would breach float plan - Pruski.
text:
WARSAW, March 22 (Reuters) - The National Bank of Poland is unlikely to intervene on the foreign exchange market because such a move would contradict plans of floating the zloty, Monetary Policy Council member Jerzy Pruski said on Wednesday. 

 "In mid-1999 we said we wanted to have a floating exchange rate and there is nothing more to add to this statement," Pruski told Reuters in an interview. 

 "Floating is a long-term solution which should not be counterbalanced with short-term consideration and interventions," he said. 

 The zloty has risen sharply this month, prompting some analysts to consider the possibility of a central bank intervention on the local forex market. 

 Pruski rebutted claims by some analysts which suggested the central bank raised rates in Febraury for reasons other than to curb inflation, such as to stun a fast growing current account defcit, which reached 7.6 percent of GDP in 1999. 

 "I believe the problem of the current account deficit is of a structural basis and tools like monetary policy are not very useful in controlling it. Structural changes and a tightening of fiscal policy is mostly needed, not any rate moves," he said. 

 The Monetary Policy Council said it raised interest rates by 100 basis points last month to between 17.5-21.5 percent to help bring inflation down to their end-year target of 5.4-6.8 percent from 10.1 percent in February. ((Wojciech Moskwa, Warsaw Newsroom, tel. +48 22 653 9700, fax +48 22 653 9781, wojciech.moskwa@reuters.com)).

title: FOCUS - Flotation uncertainty leaves zloty volatile.
text:
WARSAW, Jan 11 (Reuters) - The Polish central bank and finance ministry's decision to withhold details of their talks on the zloty's flotation has left the currency vulnerable to speculation, dealers and analysts said on Tuesday. 

 Traders have been left to read between the lines, with some betting that a full float of the Polish currency could be on the cards shortly, despite the official communique released on Monday which gave no clues as to the timing of any flotation. 

 Finance Minister Leszek Balcerowicz met the central bank's Monetary Policy Council (RPP) for a widely-trailed discussion on the timetable for the full flotation of the currency. 

 Afterwards the central bank said only that coordination between monetary and fiscal policies had been discussed. 

 "It is a negative for the zloty that no statement had been issued. The market is now acting as if it had some information. The morning rally was caused by that," said Juliet Sampson, currency strategist at Bank of America in London. 

 "I think I would expect an announcement not in the immediate future but within three months. However, we may not hear about it until the float actually happens," she added. 


In the wake of the meeting the zloty	  fell to below three percent above parity at Tuesday's open, from a near five-month high of around 3.5 percent touched on Monday.



It rebounded later on Tuesday, reaching 3.5 percent stronger than its trading basket centre on the back of foreign demand.



At 1345 GMT it traded at 3.19 percent above parity. It was at 4.0670 to the dollar and at 4.1775 to the euro.



The zloty's floation, which would include the abolition of its 30-percent trading band, the 0.3 percent per month crawling devaluation and the central parity, now depends on government approval.



The central bank asked the finance ministry for a go ahead last year, but fiscal policy makers have been hesitant for fear that full flotation would make the zloty vulnerable to destabilising speculation or excessive strength.



Last week Finance Ministry advisor Witold Orlowski said the ministry wanted the central bank to pledge it would intervene against the floated zloty to defend Poland's fragile export recovery if the unit rose sharply.



A source close to talks said consensus was reached between the parties but refused to say if the central bank had agreed to try to prevent sharp zloty appreciation.



"The meeting most likely led to a clearer consensus between the central bank and the ministry but I don't think a final decision was reached. When it is made the government will most likely announce it," Orlowski said on Tuesday.



Analysts said the finance ministry might be hesitant to free the zloty in the early days of the year, when it is being driven upwards by heavy portfolio inflows.



"There is a lot of volatility in the zloty now and strong appreciation potential. The currency swaps and FRAs (forward rate agreements) market signal that," said Andrzej Rzysko, treasurer at SG bank in Warsaw.



"So maybe it is too early now," he said. ((Warsaw Newsroom, tel. +48 22 653 9700, fax. +48 22 653 9781, warsaw.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Emerging  FX -Zloty, shekel lead Europe higher.
text:
LONDON, Jan 10 (Reuters) - Hopes that the Polish authorities will agree to a full float of the zloty	  lifted the currency to four-month highs on Monday in a busy European session for emerging market currencies.
Israel's shekel	  rallied as the market welcomed the nomination of a tough central bank chief, while the Czech crown	  gained after robust inflation data reinforced expectations of higher interest rates.



The zloty surged to 3.52 percent bid above the central bank's parity level from 3.0 percent on Friday, buoyed by hopes that the finance minister will agree at a 1500 GMT meeting with the central bank to fully float the currency.


 Analysts say such a move would show the authorities were confident in the zloty and would give a psychological boost to the currency, which is already allowed to fluctuate in a band of 15 percent on either side of the parity rate. 

 The latest firming of the currency came after a ministry adviser said the central bank should pledge to intervene against the zloty to protect Poland's current account if the floated unit rose sharply. 

 "That seemed to trigger quite a bit of zloty buying," said Bank of America currency strategist Juliet Sampson, adding that she was surprised at the market's reaction. "It looks like there's still going to be a lot of volatility, which has to be taken as a negative." 


The zloty	     was trading at 4.1538 to the euro compared with 4.1935 on Friday, around levels not seen since late August.



ISRAEL RISKS POLICY CLASH



Prime Minister Ehud Barak's choice of David Klein to succeed Jacob Frenkel as Bank of Israel governor, announced on Friday, boosted the shekel on expectations Klein will stick to a tough monetary policy.



"Klein is clearly a hawk, perhaps more hawkish that Frenkel, and that should be taken well by the markets," said Sampson. But the likelihood that Klein would clash more with the finance ministry, which wants lower interest rates, could destabilise economic policy, she said.



The shekel strengthened to 4.119 to the dollar from 4.1390 on Friday.



The Czech crown firmed slightly to around three-week highs against the euro after higher-than-expected inflation figures bolstered the view that a long series of interest rate cuts was over.

title: Poland finmin wants cbank to cap zloty after float.
text:
WARSAW, Jan 9 (Reuters) - The Polish finance ministry should seek assurances from the central bank that it would intervene against the zloty if the unit rose steeply, before agreeing to fully float the currency, a ministry advisor said on Sunday. 

 A substantial zloty appreciation would hurt Poland's exports and harm the already-strained current account deficit, Witold Orlowski told Reuters. 

 Finance Minister Leszek Balcerowicz is due to meet members of the central bank's decision-making Monetary Policy Council (RPP) at 1500 GMT on Monday to discuss the zloty's full flotation. 

 "We would expect the National Bank of Poland to declare it would use the flotation carefully and would not allow the current account gap to deteriorate when the zloty appreciates, by intervening on the forex market," Orlowski said. 

 "Poland's current account is still at risk and I can see a scenario when the zloty appreciates greatly this year due to privatisation inflows...That would harm the current account and Poland cannot afford to allow that," he said. 

 Poland's current account deficit is expected to have widened to some seven percent of the GDP in 1999 from 4.3 percent in the previous year following a sharp decrease in exports. It is seen stabilising around seven percent in 2000. 

 The 10-member RPP, which alone sets Poland's monetary policy and co-decides with the government on changes in foreign exchange regime, asked the government to make a decision on freeing the zloty last year. 

 But the government has been delaying the move, fearing that the zloty would become prone to destabilising currency speculation. 

 The zloty jumped last week following reports of the finance ministry and central bank meeting, on expectations that the long-awaited float was nearing, reaching four-month highs around three percent above parity on Friday. 

 But ministry and bank officials have said the Monday meeting would not necessarily be conclusive. 

 The zloty now trades inside a 30 percent daily band, centred on the so-called parity rate set daily by the central bank against a basket of the dollar and the euro. 

 The parity is adjusted by a devaluation factor of 0.3 percent per month to compensate for Poland's inflation. 

 The free flotation of the Polish unit would mean scrapping the daily trading band, the crawling devaluation and the parity rate. The move would give the zloty a boost, analysts say. ((Justyna Pawlak, Warsaw Newsroom, tel. +48 22 653 9700, fax. +48 22 653 9781, warsaw.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: INTERVIEW-Polish c.bank ready to defend the zloty.
text:
HELSINKI, Nov 12 (Reuters) - The National Bank of Poland will spare no expense intervening on the foreign exchange market to defend the zloty if such a need arose, deputy central bank chief Ryszard Kokoszczynski said on Friday. 

 "We are always ready to defend the zloty. We have in the past intervened a number of times for various reasons. We have set procedures and are closely observing the market," Kokoszczynski told Reuters. 

 "To make such a decision is a question of seconds rather than minutes," he said in an interview during a two-day summit of the European Central Bank with eastern European central bankers. 

 Asked how much of its roughly $26 billion in currency reserves the central bank would be willing to spend on forex interventions, Kokoszczysnki said: "As much as it takes." 

 A ago the zloty tumbled to all-time lows on a deteriorating macroeconomic picture and worries that the respected Finance Minister Leszek Balcerowicz would resign, but it rebounded as political tensions eased. The NBP did not intervene.

 Kokoszczynski said he was not worried by a possible withdrawal of foreign portfolio capital from Poland, because foreign holdings are relatively small compared to state reserves and because the forex market is volatile. 

 "If somebody wants to sell zlotys at all costs, even paying a 10 or 15 percent premium for withdrawing, then he must be expecting a catastrophe and there are no fundamental reasons to expect such a black scenario," he said. title: Polish c.bank sees no need to support zloty now.
text:
WARSAW, Nov 4 (Reuters) - The National Bank of Poland does not currently see a need to intervene on the foreign exchange market to support the falling zloty, deputy central bank governor Ryszard Kokoszczynski told Reuters. 

 The zloty tumbled to all-time lows on Thursday after Finance Minister Leszek Balcerowicz threatened he would quit if parliament failed to pass his tax-cutting reform in time for it to be implemented next year. 

 "For the time being the situation on the market would not justify intervention, especially since the developments of the last two days are of a political nature," Kokoszczynski said. 

 He said the bank would consider interventions if the zloty weakening lasted long enough to threaten its medium-term inflation target, which envisages bringing price growth below four percent in 2003 from 8-9 percent in 1999. 

 "If the weakness does not stem from fundamentals and lasts too long from the point of view of our medium-term goals and if we decide that direct interventions are better than using other monetary policy instruments, then we will do it," he said. 

 The central bank wants to bring inflation down to 5.4-6.8 percent in December 2000 and has already raised its main intervention rate by 100 bp in September to defend that goal from a recent inflation surge. 

 Analysts expect the bank to raise its interest rates again on November 17 in response to fast growing production which is not accompanied by exports growth, suggesting high domestic demand and inflationary pressure. 

 Kokoszczynski said foreign exchange market interventions would be all the more questionable because of the volatility of a market that has been thinned by the departure of foreign investors wary of millennium computer bug risks. 

 "The market is extremely thin and fundamentals have little influence on what is happening and it will probably stay that way until the end of the year," he said. 

 The zloty plummeted to 4.86 percent weaker than the parity rate on Thursday morning on the Balcerowicz resignation worries, but rebounded to around 4.2 later in the day on central bank comments there were no fundamental reasons for such weakening. 

 Kokoszczynski also said that the macroeconomic data still to hit the market in the next two months would more likely be positive than negative. 

 "The poor data has already been priced in, so unless there is more bad news from politics, what we can expect is data which would improve the perception of the economy," Kokoszczynski said. 

 He said the market already knew that year-on-year inflation would be somewhere between eight and nine percent in December against 8.6 percent in December 1998. 

 He also said the current account deficit would most probably be smaller than the 7.5 percent of GDP predicted by a government think-tank, giving a the market a positive impulse. ((Jan Strupczewski, Warsaw Newsroom, tel.+48 22 653 9700, fax. +48 22 653 9781, warsaw.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Emerging market  FX -Zloty at fresh lows, rand firms.
text:
LONDON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - The Polish zloty tumbled to fresh record lows on Friday as the finance minister's threat to resign continued to undermine the market, while the South African rand strengthened on strong foreign demand for bonds, emerging market currency specialists said. 

 The zloty opened more than 5.2 percent below the central bank's parity rate, a percentage point lower than Thursday's close, as it continued to reel from poor economic data and Finance Minister Leszek Balcerowicz's ultimatum to resign if parliament did not pass his tax reform plan. 

 But the currency rebounded strongly, moving back above the five percent level, amid speculation that the central bank might intervene. 

 The deputy governor of the National Bank of Poland, Ryszard Kokoszczynski, told Reuters intervention was not justified "for the time being" but that it would consider stepping in if the weakening lasted long enough to threaten its inflation target. 

 "If the price action just became one way they will step in as they stepped in on the other side," when the currency was strong, said Jake Moore, currency analyst at Barclays Capital. 

 He said the zloty might be further hurt by news on Thursday that U.S.-based telecoms firm SBC Communications had withdrawn its bid for 25-35 percent of Polish state-controlled telephone operator TPSA. 

 The move means France Telecom , now the lone bidder, may reduce its offer price and decrease the foreign currency privatisation receipts the government plans to exchange in the market. 

 At 0907 GMT the zloty was trading at 4.5153 bid to the euro, stronger than an early low of 4.5490 but weaker than 4.5050 on Thursday. 

 CZECH CROWN GAINS 

 Elsewhere in Europe, the Czech crown gained against the euro as the euro remained weak against the dollar in the wake of the European Central Bank's rate rise. The crown was trading at 36.606 to the euro versus 36.690 on Thursday. 

 The Hungarian forint held steady at the strong end of its trading band even after the central bank said it would cut its base rate to 15 percent from 15.5. The cut followed a 25 basis point reduction in benchmark rates on Thursday. The forint was at 254.97 against the euro versus 255.05. 

 The rand strengthened for a second day on the back of firmer South African bonds, climbing to 6.109 to the dollar from 6.1270 on Thursday. 

 Benchmark bond yields fell below 14 percent, a level they have not closed below since June 1998, on the eve of last year's currency crisis. 

 Bonds are benefiting from stability in global debt markets and comments from Deputy Reserve Bank Governor Gill Marcus that the bank was using an informal three to five percent inflation target, Moore said. 

 "The market's getting to grips with the Reserve Bank being committed to reducing inflation expectations," he said. 

 In Asia, the Indonesian rupiah dipped to 6,795 to the dollar from 6,740 and the Korean won slipped to 1,186 from 1,184.

title: FOCUS-Zloty falls to fresh lows as confidence fades.
text:
WARSAW, Nov 3 (Reuters) - The Polish zloty	  fell sharply on Wednesday as mounting worries over Poland's macroeconomy and political rifts within the government coalition triggered selling in a thin market.



Market talk that the reform-minded Finance Minister Leszek Balcerowicz had resigned - later denied by government officials - sparked the first wave of sales, which were exacerbated by stop-loss trades, dealers said.


 At 1712 GMT the zloty traded at 3.82 percent weaker than its trading band centre, against intraday lows around four percent and Wednesday's average fixing of 2.62 percent. It last traded at such levels in July 1997. 

 It was at 4.2835 to the dollar and at 4.4970 to the euro. 

 "First, rumours that Balcerowicz had resigned fuelled a mild panic. Even though the talk was refuted, some players had to realise stop-losses and the negative sentiment persisted," said Mateusz Bieniek, chief forex dealer at Bank Handlowy in Warsaw. 

 The rumours of Balcerowicz's departure arose despite the coalition's late Tuesday agreement on a tax reform introduced by the Finance Minister, which ended a heated debate within the government and eased worries of a political crisis. 

 The junior coalition partner Freedom Union (UW), headed by Balcerowicz, said it had accepted a less radical version of its tax reform proposal put forward by the Solidarity Election Action (AWS). 

 MACROECONOMIC WORRIES PREVAIL 

 Dealers said the plunge signalled the high level of foreign investors caution about the Polish currency due to worries over runaway inflation and widening current account deficit. It was part of a now-established downtrend, they said. 

 Member of the rate-setting Monetary Policy Council (RPP) Wieslawa Ziolkowska told Reuters the zloty's plunge was "unjustified" because the Polish economy remained sound. 

 "The Polish economy has sound foundations. Industrial output is rising. Cross-border trade data suggests exports may finally rebound. This is not the right time for such reactions...This unjustified move should be short-lived," she said. 

 Investor caution over Poland's economy started after a steep CPI pickup in recent months, which forced the Finance Ministry to increase its end-year inflation forecasts from around seven percent to some eight percent. 

 In September inflation rose to a year-on-year eight percent, forcing the RPP to give up on its end-year CPI target of 6.6-7.8 percent. 

 Dealers said the National Bank of Poland called them for zloty rates several times during the day, which some said signalled the central bank considered intervening in the market. 

 "The central bank's goal is to limit inflation. Protecting the current account deficit and growth is the responsibility of the government," Ziolkowska said when asked about the possibility of central bank intervention to protect the zloty. 

Poland's current account gap widened to $1.115 billion in September from August's $786 million and the deficit is expected to reach seven percent of gross domestic product by end-year. ((Warsaw Newsroom, tel. +48 22 653 9700, fax. +48 22 653 9781, warsaw.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: INTERVIEW-Polish CPI a dilemma for  central bank .
text:
WARSAW, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Poland's central bank faces a tough choice between raising interest rates in response to rising inflation or trusting price growth will slow in the second half of 2000, senior finance ministry adviser Stanislaw Gomulka said. 

 Gomulka said the year-on-year inflation index would likely inch up well into the first half of next year because the statistical base of the second half of 1998 and early 1999 was the lowest since 1991. 

 "But for the same reason, the year-on-year index will start falling sharply in the second half of next year, because the base of the second half of this year is high," he told Reuters. 

 "However, in the meantime, the Monetary Policy Council (RPP) will be under enormous pressure to raise rates because of growing inflation expectations, which translate into phenomena such as wage growth in the real economy," he said. 

 "This is a genuine economic argument for raising interest rates," he added. 

 The more than six month delay in the transmission of monetary policy changes into the real economy would mean that any rate rise would take effect only when inflation was already falling again, he said. 

 "Interest rates should not be a reaction to what is happening, but an anticipation of what will happen with inflation, and not just for the next few months," Gomulka said. 

 "But the RPP cannot ignore the psychological factor, so if the perception is that there is something wrong with inflation and that the credibility of the council is in danger, then they will be under enormous pressure (to raise rates)." 

 Gomulka said year-on-year inflation could rise to between eight and nine percent in December from eight percent in September and 8.6 percent in December 1998. The central bank wanted to bring inflation down to 6.6-7.8 percent this year. 

 The index dropped to a low of 5.6 percent in February as a result of an economic slow-down in the wake of the Russian financial crisis in the second half of 1998. 

 The RPP raised its main market rate by 100 basis points to 14 percent in September but held off from a further rise this month. 

 CURRENT ACCOUNT GAP MAY RISE 

 Gomulka said Poland's high current account deficit, which may reach seven percent of gross domestic product this year against 4.3 percent in 1998, may be even higher next year, because of a central bank policy of stable currency reserves. 

 "If we have a flexible exchange rate regime with stable reserves, the deficit on the current account has to be equal to the surplus on the capital account, which is currently around seven percent of GDP," he said. 

 The central bank has not been intervening on the Polish foreign exchange market this year and stopped trading currencies with commercial banks at the daily fixing session in June as part of its policy to prepare to freely float the zloty in 2000. 

 "Next year the capital account surplus may rise, maybe a percentage point or so," Gomulka said. 

 "So even if there are better external conditions and exports start growing it will not help the current account because it (the capital account) will also affect the exchange rate and imports - its an economic axiom," he said. 

 Gomulka said that if, for instance, the capital account surplus reached levels of 12-15 percent of GDP, Poland should change its exchange rate regime and intervene on the market to keep the current account gap at relatively safe levels. 

 "This is only contingency thinking, because we do not expect that kind of capital inflows," he said. 

 What will determine a safe deficit level is the quality of the capital account surplus - if it was mainly valuable foreign direct investment (FDI) or volatile portfolio flows. 

 "If we see that we have more FDI, we can allow ourselves a higher current account deficit and keep the flexible exchange rate," he said. 

 The government estimates foreign direct investment this year at $7.0 billion and forecasts next year's FDI at $7.5 billion. ((Warsaw Newsroom, tel.+48 22 653 9700, fax. +48 22 653 9781, warsaw.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: FOCUS-Czech  FX  tussle marks emerging Europe's week.
text:
PRAGUE, Oct 8 (Reuters) - The Czech central bank's (CNB) moves to knock down the buoyant crown currency dominated Prague financial markets, while Warsaw and the Baltics led gainers in emerging Europe equity trading this week. 

 The CNB abruptly ended speculation about how far it would let the crown appreciate on the back of strong foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows by a surprise rate cut on Monday followed by two heavy interventions on the currency market. 

 In Poland, the ruling coalition was locked in debates on reshaping the unpopular cabinet, but the equity market jumped on improved investor sentiment, following no change in interest rates in the eurozone and the United States. 

 CZECH CENTRAL BANK SHOOTS AT CROWN 

 The central bank shocked the market on Monday when its monthly monetary meeting, expected to bring no news, resulted in a 25 basis point cut in the two-week repo rate to 5.75 percent quickly followed by heavy selling of crowns on the open market. 

 The first Czech intervention since July 1998 knocked the crown 2.5 percent lower to 36.85 to the euro. Traders said the central bank bought hundreds of millions of euros. The bank struck again on Thursday, selling crowns at around 36.45. 

 The cabinet and the CNB have said the crown was too strong and may harm exports, the main source of economic recovery. 

 The CNB also said it had agreed in principle with the Finance Ministry to propose unspecified measures to the full cabinet to tame the effects of the FDI inflow, expected to rise with a wave of privatisations planned for the next year. 

 The crown closed the week at around 36.60 to the euro. 

 Meanwhile, better prospects for banking privatisation and a firming of telecom stocks, put Prague stock indices more than two percent higher on the week, as equities largely ignored the turmoil on the currency market. 

 POLAND REBOUNDS DESPITE POLITICAL TROUBLES 

 Polish shares rebounded this week on improved global sentiment after more than a month of steep falls, but analysts said the recovery was half-hearted. 

 The rise came as investor confidence improved, despite continued worries about Poland's internal political situation and a recent run of poor macroeconomic data. 

 Poland's fractious ruling coalition is locked in discussions to reshape the cabinet in a bid to improve its dismal popularity ratings. Talk of dismissing the prime minister or a government collapse have diminished as the week went on. 

 The market began to slide on Friday, after the all-share WIG index peaked at just below the 15,000-point resistance level on Thursday. 

 But analysts said Friday's positive U.S. employment data may persuade some foreign investors back into the market. 

 The zloty lingered just below the centre of its 30-point trading band throughout the week mired by an unclear outlook for Poland's economy after better current account gap figures took the edge off worse-than-feared inflation numbers. 

 HUNGARY HIGHER IN SLOW TRADE 

 Hungarian shares gained over two percent this week but traders said that despite the gains - which followed a run of losses in recent weeks - cash flows by foreign investors, who usually account for the bulk of turnover, remain miniscule. 

 Fears of the impact of the Y2K computer bug on markets and worries of a potential rate hike in the United States ahead of Fed meeting late on Tuesday weighed on sentiment, they said. 

 "There's not a lot of money flowing this way," said Balazs Bence, trader at Cashline Securities. "This uncertainty on the American market is likely to remain...(and) because of this year 2000 problem a lot of people think investors are waiting the market out and that things will only pick up again in January." 

 OTHER MARKETS 

 * Baltic shares were higher across the board, with investors focusing on Lithuanian bank issues after leading bank Vilniaus' takeover of rival Hermis for $58 million got final clearance from the competition authority. 

 * Slovenian SBI share index almost unchanged this week amid poor liquidity and little foreign interest. 

 * Turnover and volumes fell on the Bulgarian Stock Exchange in five trading sessions in the week ending Friday as real-time trade was light and only one block deal was sealed. 

 Total weekly turnover fell to 694,922 levs ($380,400) from 1.87 million levs in five sessions in the previous week as weekly traded volume fell to 172,663 units from 213,769. 

 * Croatian stocks rose almost five percent before giving back some of the gains on Friday as two separate German investments helped improve the country's poor image with the international financial community. 

 * The Bucharest bourse slipped after state-run commercial bank Banca Agricola lost ground in the week to Friday on high liquidity following a share split, traders said.

title: FOCUS-Czech  FX  battle marks emerging Europe's week.
text:
PRAGUE, Oct 8 (Reuters) - The Czech central bank's (CNB) repeated moves to knock down the buoyant crown currency dominated Prague financial markets, while Warsaw led emerging Europe's gains in equity trading this week. 

 The CNB abruptly ended speculation about how far it would let the crown appreciate on the back of strong foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows by a surprise rate cut on Monday followed by two heavy interventions on the currency market. 

 In Poland, the ruling coalition was locked in debates on reshaping the unpopular cabinet, but the equity market jumped on improved investor sentiment, following no change in interest rates in the eurozone and the United States. 

 CZECH CENTRAL BANK SHOOTS AT CROWN 

 The central bank shocked the market on Monday when its monthly monetary meeting, expected to bring no news, resulted in a 25 basis point cut in the two-week repo rate to 5.75 percent quickly followed by heavy selling of crowns on the open market. 

 The first Czech intervention since July 1998 knocked the crown 2.5 percent lower to 36.85 to the euro. Traders said the central bank bought hundreds of millions euro. 

 The cabinet and the CNB have said the crown was too strong and may harm exports, the main source of economic recovery. The crown started recovering prompting the bank to strike again on Thursday, selling crowns at around 36.45 to the euro. 

 The CNB also said it had agreed in principle with the Finance Ministry to propose unspecified measures to the full cabinet to tame the effects of the FDI inflow, expected to rise with a wave of privatisations planned for the next year. 

 Meanwhile, better prospects for banking privatisation and a firming of telecom stocks, put Prague stock indices more than two percent higher on the week, as equities largely ignored the turmoil on the currency market. 

 POLAND REBOUNDS DESPITE POLITICAL TROUBLES 

 The Warsaw bourse rebounded this week after more than a month of steep falls on improved worldwide sentiment and relief that major international interest rates were kept on hold. 

 The four percent increase came as investor confidence improved, despite continued worries about Poland's internal political situation and a recent run of poor macroeconomic data. 

 Poland's fractious ruling coalition is locked in discussions to reshape the cabinet in a bid to improve its dismal popularity ratings. Talk of dismissing the prime minister or a government collapse have diminished as the week went on. 


The zloty	  lingered just below the centre of its 30-point trading band throughout the week mired by an unclear outlook for Poland's economy after better current account gap figures took the edge off worse-than-feared inflation numbers.



HUNGARY EDGES HIGHER IN SLOW TRADE



Hungarian shares gained over one percent this week but traders said that despite the gains - which followed a run of losses in recent weeks - cash flows by foreign investors, who usually account for the bulk of turnover, remain miniscule.



Fears of the impact of the Y2K computer bug on markets and worries of a potential rate hike in the United States ahead of Fed meeting late on Tuesday weighed on sentiment, they said.



"There's not a lot of money flowing this way," said Balazs Bence, trader at Cashline Securities. "This uncertainty on the American market is likely to remain...(and) because of this year 2000 problem a lot of people think investors are waiting the market out and that things will only pick up again in January."

title: Poland c.banker says does not target zloty level.
text:
SALZBURG, Austria July 1 (Reuters) - Poland's Central Bank will not intervene in the market to influence the level of the zloty, governor Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz told Reuters in an interview on Thursday. 

 The central bank governor said Monday's action by the central bank was "more correctly arbitrage than intervention." 

 On Monday and last Friday the central bank undertook its first foreign exchange operations in 10 months, buying and selling euros for zlotys to smooth the market. 

 Gronkiewicz-Waltz told Reuters that the zloty's full float could happen within 12 months after discussions with the government. 

 She added that Poland could not expect any downward move on interest rates in the near future.

title: Poland's monetary council unlikely to cut rates on Wed.
text:
WARSAW, April 13 (Reuters) - Analysts expect Poland's Monetary Policy Council (RPP) to hold interest rates steady at its meeting on Wednesday, because inflation may rise later this year after a sharp fall in recent months. 

 Analysts from Polish and foreign banks said a rate cut was unlikely even after the Hungarian and Czech monetary authorities cut their interest rates following the European Central Bank's (ECB) rate 0.5 point rate lowering last week. 

 "It's a tough call after the ECB decision and if anythinig the move would be small, but I don't think they will cut at all," said Thomas Brown, currency strategist at JP Morgan in London. 

 "The CPI is a key driver. If we have an uptick in inflation for the first time in 12 months, which would be in line with the finance ministry's forecasts, then that would suggest inflationary pressures," he said. The finance ministry estimated prices rose 1.1 percent in March against 0.6 percent in February, bringing the year-on-year index up to 6.2 percent from 5.6 percent in February. Official inflation data for March will be published by the Central Statistical Office on April 15. 

 "They (the RPP) are afraid of the perception that a rate cut would provide an inflationary impulse and that such expectations would actually boost inflation," said Sonja Gibbs, currency strategist at Nomura International in London. 

 The International Monetary Fund recently said that Poland should be cautious about further cuts after January's sweeping 250-300 basis point rate cut and should wait to see its effects on the economy before easing policy again. 

Poland's main market rate, the minimum 28-day intervention rate, is now at 13.0 percent, the discount rate is at 15.5 percent and the lombard rate at 17.0 percent. 

 Analysts said that both external and internal inflationary pressures have increased recently, and the RPP may have to be more cautious with monetary policy after it lowered its 1999 inflation target to 6.6-7.8 percent at the March 24 meeting. "It is possible that inflation will rise from now until the end of the year. After the RPP lowered its inflationary target, they cannot allow themselves to cut rates now," said Mateusz Szczurek, economist at ING Barings in Warsaw. "Strong dollar, weak zloty, the rebound in oil prices and the recently imposed food tariffs are likely to boost inflation," he said. 

 But analysts also expect the RPP may still lower interest rates by some 100-250 basis points by year-end. 

 "If economic growth doesn't show signs of improvement, the zloty stays on the strong side of parity and the April budget comes out well, maybe they will cut rates even in mid-May," Nomura's Gibbs said. 

 Poland's gross domestic product growth slowed to 4.8 percent in 1998 from 6.8 percent in 1997 after the Russian crisis and slower growth in Western Europe depressed exports. In 1999, GDP is expected to grow by some four to 4.5 percent. 

 "They will want to cut before they free-float the zloty, which they indicated they would do, because liberalising the exchange rate policy without cutting rates would be a recipe for appreciation," JP Morgan's Brown said. 

 Analysts do not expect the RPP to change the foreign exchange policy at the Wednesday meeting. ((Warsaw newsroom, tel +48 22 653 9700, fax +48 22 653 9781, warsaw.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Polish Zloty Lower On Continued Selling After Rate Cuts
text:
WARSAW (Dow Jones)--The Polish zloty (PLZ) is lower against the currency basket midmorning Friday, as investors continue to sell the zloty after the central bank's sharp rate cuts Wednesday. 

 Dealers also said falls on global stock markets are causing the zloty to weaken. 

 Dealers said the zloty is 5.2% above the mid-point against its basket, down from around 5.75% at the close of trading Thursday. 

 The Polish zloty is fixed to a dollar/euro basket and is devalued at a rate of 0.5% a month. It is allowed to fluctuate within plus or minus 12.5% of the central parity rate. 

 The National Bank Of Poland Wednesday cut the 28-day money market intervention rate to 13% from 15.5%, the Lombard rate to 17% from 20% and the discount rate to 15.5% from 18.25%. Market participants had expected a rate cut of between 100 and 150 basis points. 

 "It's a consequence of the rate cuts," said Tomasz Wlad, broker at AmerBrokers. Wlad said interest in Polish debt is declining and investors are closing positions because the rate cut has made Polish debt less attractive. 

 Around 0910 GMT, the dollar was at PLZ3.5900, up from PLZ3.5700 at the opening and up from Thursday's fixing of PLZ3.5730. 

 The euro was at PLZ4.1680, up from Thursday's fixing of PLZ4.1330. 

 The National Bank of Poland set the parity rate for the dollar at PLZ3.7868 and for the euro at PLZ4.3946. 

 The dollar is 5.2% below its parity rate, and the euro is 5.2% below parity. 

 Overnight money market rates are between 14.00% and 15.20%.

title: Polish Zloty Closes Down On Heavy Selling Of Polish Debt
text:
WARSAW (Dow Jones)--The Polish zloty (PLZ) closed lower against the currency basket Thursday as investors sold Polish debt following the central bank's sharp cut in interest rates Wednesday. 

 The zloty closed 5.75% above the mid-point against its basket, sharply down from around 6.9% at the close of trading Wednesday. 

 The zloty is fixed to a basket composed of the dollar and euro and is devalued at a rate of 0.5% per month. It is allowed to fluctuate within plus or minus 12.5% of the central parity rate. 

 On Wednesday, the National Bank of Poland cut the 28-day money market intervention rate to 13% from 15%, the Lombard rate to 17% from 20% and the discount rate to 15.5% from 18.25%. Most analysts had expected a rate cut of between 100 and 150 basis points. 

 "After the unexpected big cut in rates, lots of investors closed their debt positions and bought dollars," said Marek Cherubin, dealer at Creditanstalt. 

 The dollar was fixed Thursday at PLZ3.5730, up from the open of about PLZ3.5400 and sharply up Wednesday's fixing of PLZ3.5280.
